entries.en: I believe that in antiquity, honoring the aged meant freedom from office rather than weight of rank; Your Majesty should grant what Shi steadfastly requests."
entries.literal: Your servant believes that in antiquity nurturing the old prized freedom from office rather than exalting official rank; it is fitting to grant what Shi steadfastly holds to."

entries.zh: 三年，詔曰：「昔虞任五臣，致垂拱之化，漢相蕭何，興寧一之譽，故能光隆於當時，垂裕於百代。
entries.en: In the third year an edict declared, "Ancient Shun ruled through five ministers and achieved the government of folded hands; Han's chancellor Xiao He brought an age of unity and calm—thus they shone in their own day and left an example for a hundred generations.
entries.literal: In the third year an edict said, "Formerly Yu employed five ministers, achieving the transformation of folded hands; Han's chancellor Xiao He raised the praise of peaceful unity; therefore they were able to shine in their time and leave abundance for a hundred generations.

entries.zh: 朕紹天明命，臨御萬邦，所以崇顯政道者，亦賴之於元臣庶尹，畢力股肱，以副至望。
entries.en: I have received Heaven's mandate to rule the myriad regions; to exalt the way of government I depend on great ministers and heads of office who give their full strength as my arms and legs, answering my deepest hopes.
entries.literal: I continue Heaven's bright mandate, face and govern the myriad regions; the means by which to exalt and display the way of government, also rely on these chief ministers and many directors, exhausting strength in arms and thighs, to match utmost expectation.

entries.zh: 而君年耆告老，確然難違。
entries.en: Yet you, venerable in years, have asked to retire, and your resolve cannot lightly be set aside.
entries.literal: Yet you, lord, in years old announce old age; firmly it is hard to go against.

entries.zh: 今聽君以侯就第，位居三司之上，秩祿准舊，賜几杖不朝及宅一區。
entries.en: I grant you, lord, to retire to your mansion as a marquis with standing above the Three Dukes, stipend as before, the gift of a folding-stool and staff exempting you from court, and one residence.
entries.literal: Now I listen to you, lord, as marquis to go to mansion; position placed above the Three Dukes; rank and emolument accord with the old; bestow folding-stool and staff, not attending court, and one mansion plot.

entries.zh: 國之大政，將就諮於君，副朕意焉。」
entries.en: On weighty affairs of state I shall still seek your counsel, that you may answer my deepest purpose."
entries.literal: The state's great policies will go to consult with you, lord, matching my intent."

entries.zh: 歲余薨，時年九十一，諡曰元。
entries.en: A little over a year later he died, aged ninety-one, with the posthumous name Yuan, "Primal."
entries.literal: After a little more than a year he died; at the time his years were ninety-one; his posthumous name was Yuan.

entries.zh: 寔少貧窶，杖策徒行，每所憩止，不累主人，薪水之事，皆自營給。
entries.en: In youth Shi was destitute; leaning on a staff he went on foot, and wherever he lodged he imposed no burden on his host, gathering his own firewood and water.
entries.literal: Shi in youth was poor and mean; staff and plan, walking on foot; each place he rested, he did not burden the host; firewood and water matters, all he himself supplied.

entries.zh: 及位望通顯，每崇儉素，不尚華麗。
entries.en: Even when rank and fame were at their height he clung to plain frugality and scorned display.
entries.literal: When position and repute were thorough and eminent, he always honored frugality and plainness, did not esteem splendor and beauty.

entries.zh: 嘗詣石崇家，如廁，見有絳紋帳，裀褥甚麗，兩婢持香囊。
entries.en: Once at Shi Chong's house he stepped into what he thought was a lavatory and found crimson brocade curtains, sumptuous mats, and two maids bearing sachets of incense.
entries.literal: Once he went to Shi Chong's house, entered the privy, and saw there were crimson-patterned curtains, cushions and bedding very beautiful, two maids holding incense pouches.

entries.zh: 寔便退，笑謂崇曰：「誤入卿內。」
entries.en: Shi drew back at once and said with a smile, "I have blundered into your private rooms."
entries.literal: Shi then withdrew, laughed and said to Chong, "I mistakenly entered your inner chambers."

entries.zh: 崇曰：「是廁耳。」
entries.en: Chong replied, "That is the privy."
entries.literal: Chong said, "It is the privy only."

entries.zh: 寔曰：「貧士未嘗得此。」
entries.en: Shi said, "A poor scholar like me has never seen such a privy."
entries.literal: Shi said, "A poor scholar has never obtained this."

entries.zh: 乃更如他廁。
entries.en: He asked directions to an ordinary latrine instead.
entries.literal: Then he again went to another privy.

entries.zh: 雖處榮寵，居無第宅，所得俸祿，贍恤親故。
entries.en: Though he stood high in favor, he owned no grand mansion and spent his salary supporting kinsmen and old friends.
entries.literal: Although dwelling in glory and favor, he had no mansion house; what stipend he obtained, he relieved and aided kin and old friends.

entries.zh: 雖禮教陵遲，而行己以正。
entries.en: Even as public morals slackened, he kept his own conduct upright.
entries.literal: Although ritual teaching declined and lagged, in conducting himself he used the straight.

entries.zh: 喪妻為廬杖之制，終喪不禦內。
entries.en: When his wife died he observed the mourning hut and staff rites and took no concubine until the mourning ended.
entries.literal: On losing his wife he made the hut-and-staff system; to the end of mourning he did not take the inner chambers.

entries.zh: 輕薄者笑之，寔不以介意。
entries.en: Wits mocked him for it, but he paid them no heed.
entries.literal: Frivolous men laughed at him; Shi did not on that account take it to mind.

entries.zh: 自少及老，篤學不倦，雖居職務，卷弗離手。
entries.en: From youth to old age he studied tirelessly; even in office he never laid down his books.
entries.literal: From youth to old age he loved learning without weariness; although occupying official duties, scrolls did not leave his hand.

entries.zh: 尤精《三傳》，辨正《公羊》，以為衛輒不應辭以王父命，祭仲失為臣之節，舉此二端以明臣子之體，遂行於世。
entries.en: He mastered the three commentaries on the Spring and Autumn and corrected the Gongyang tradition, arguing that Prince Kuaire of Wei should not have refused the throne citing his grandfather's order and that Zhai Zhong had failed a minister's duty; by these two cases he defined the proper relation of subject to ruler, and his reading won wide acceptance.
entries.literal: He was especially refined in the Three Traditions, discriminating and correcting the Gongyang, holding that Wei Kuaire ought not to have declined citing grandfather's command, that Zhai Zhong lost a minister's integrity; raising these two ends to clarify minister-and-son's substance, it then was practiced in the age.

entries.zh: 又撰《春秋條例》二十卷。
entries.en: He also compiled twenty fascicles of Spring and Autumn precedents and principles.
entries.literal: Again he composed Spring and Autumn Regulations and Cases in twenty scrolls.

entries.zh: 有二子，躋、夏。
entries.en: He had two sons, Ji and Xia.
entries.literal: He had two sons, Ji and Xia.

entries.zh: 躋字景雲，官至散騎常侍。
entries.en: Ji, courtesy name Jingyun, rose to cavalier attendant-in-ordinary.
entries.literal: Ji, courtesy name Jingyun, office reached Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.

entries.zh: 夏以貪污棄放於世。
entries.en: Xia was cast out of public life for corruption.
entries.literal: Xia because of corruption was cast aside in the world.

entries.zh: 史臣曰：下士競而文，中庸靜而質，不若進不足而退有餘也。
entries.en: The historians write: Petty men strive for outward polish and the middling keep a dull quiet—both fall short of advancing with restraint and withdrawing while still leaving something in hand.
entries.literal: The historian says: Lower gentlemen strive and are ornate; the middle way is quiet and plain; not as good as advancing insufficient yet retreating having surplus.

entries.zh: 魏舒、劉寔發慮精華，結綬登槐，覽止成務。
entries.en: Wei Shu and Liu Shi brought the finest of their judgment to bear, took high office beneath the court locusts, and saw their policies through to completion.
entries.literal: Wei Shu and Liu Shi emitted thought's essence, tied ribbons and ascended the locust, viewed stop and completed tasks.

entries.zh: 季和切問近對，當官正色。
entries.en: Li Xi of courtesy Jihe answered sharp questions with plain good sense and kept a straight face in office.
entries.literal: Jihe cut questions and near answers; holding office with correct color.

entries.zh: 詩云「貪人敗類」，豈劉夏之謂歟！
entries.en: The Classic of Poetry says, "Greedy men destroy their kin"—can that mean anyone but Liu Xia!
entries.literal: The Odes says, 'Greedy men ruin the kind' — how could it mean Liu Xia!

entries.zh: 贊曰：舒言不矜，憙對千乘。
entries.en: Encomium: Shu spoke without swagger; Xi faced princes of a thousand chariots undaunted.
entries.literal: The encomium says: Shu's words were not boastful; Xi faced a thousand chariots.

entries.zh: 子真、宣茂，雅志難陵。
entries.en: Zizhen and Xuanmao—noble purpose none could overthrow.
entries.literal: Zizhen, Xuanmao — lofty aims hard to violate.

entries.zh: 進忠能舉，退讓攸興。
entries.en: They pressed loyalty and lifted the worthy; in yielding office they set a lasting example.
entries.literal: Advancing loyalty, able to raise; withdrawing yielding, thereby rising.

entries.zh: 皎皎瑚器，來光玉繩。
entries.en: Bright as ritual coral, they brought luster to the constellations of state.
entries.literal: Bright bright coral vessel; coming light to jade cord.

entries.zh: 弟智，字子房，貞素有兄風。
entries.en: His younger brother Zhi, courtesy name Zifang, was as upright and spare in habit as his brother.
entries.literal: Younger brother Zhi, courtesy name Zifang, chaste and plain had the elder brother's style.

entries.zh: 少貧窶，每負薪自給，讀誦不輟，竟以儒行稱。
entries.en: He grew up in want, often carried firewood to live, and never stopped his studies; in the end he won fame as a Confucian gentleman.
entries.literal: In youth poor and mean, he often carried firewood to supply himself, reading and chanting without ceasing; in the end by Confucian conduct he was praised.

entries.zh: 曆中書黃門吏部郎，出為潁川太守。
entries.en: He served as gentleman at the palace secretariat, at the yellow gates, and in the personnel ministry, then became governor of Yingchuan.
entries.literal: He successively served as gentleman of the Palace Writers, of the Yellow Gates, and of the Personnel Ministry, then went out as governor of Yingchuan.

entries.zh: 平原管輅嘗謂人曰：「吾與劉潁川兄弟語，使人神思清發，昏不假寐。
entries.en: Guan Lu of Pingyuan once remarked, "Conversation with Governor Liu of Yingchuan and his brothers clears the mind so that even at dusk I need no nap.
entries.literal: Guan Lu of Pingyuan once said to someone, "When I with Liu of Yingchuan and his brothers speak, it causes people's spirit-thought to clear and rise; in dusk I need not borrow sleep.

entries.zh: 自此之外，殆白日欲寢矣。」
entries.en: With anyone else I could fall asleep in broad daylight."
entries.literal: Outside of this, probably in broad daylight I wish to sleep."

entries.zh: 入為秘書監，領南陽王師，加散騎常侍，遷侍中、尚書、太常。
entries.en: He was recalled as director of the palace library and tutor to the prince of Nanyang, with the added title cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, then rose to palace attendant, minister of the secretariat, and minister of ceremonies.
entries.literal: He entered as Director of the Palace Library, concurrently tutor to the Prince of Nanyang, added Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, transferred Palace Attendant, Minister of the Secretariat, Minister of Ceremonies.

entries.zh: 著《喪服釋疑論》，多所辨明。
entries.en: He wrote the Discourse Resolving Doubts on Mourning Garments, which settled many disputed points.
entries.literal: He composed Discourse Explaining Doubts on Mourning Dress, much was discriminated and clarified.

entries.zh: 太康末卒，諡曰成。
entries.en: He died toward the end of the Taikang era with the posthumous name Cheng, "Accomplished."
entries.literal: He died at the end of Taikang; his posthumous name was Cheng.

entries.zh: 高光，字宣茂，陳留圉城人，魏太尉柔之子也。
entries.en: Gao Guang, courtesy name Xuanmao, was a native of Yucheng in Chenliu, the son of Grand Commandant Gao Rou of Wei.
entries.literal: Gao Guang, courtesy name Xuanmao, was a man of Yucheng in Chenliu, son of Wei Grand Commandant Rou.

entries.zh: 光少習家業，明練刑理。
entries.en: From youth he trained in his family's legal tradition and became expert in penal law.
entries.literal: Guang in youth practiced the family occupation, was clear and practiced in punishments and principles.

entries.zh: 初以太子舍人累遷尚書郎，出為幽州刺史、潁州太守。
entries.en: He began as household gentleman to the heir apparent and rose to gentleman of the masters of writing, then became inspector of You province and governor of Yingzhou commandery.
entries.literal: At first as householder to the heir apparent by accumulated transfers became Secretariat gentleman, went out as Inspector of You Province, governor of Yingzhou.

entries.zh: 是時武帝置黃沙獄，以典詔囚。
entries.en: At that time Emperor Wu founded the Yellow Sand prison for prisoners sentenced by imperial edict.
entries.literal: At this time Emperor Wu established Yellow Sand prison, to manage edict prisoners.

entries.zh: 以光曆世明法，用為黃沙御史，秩與中丞同，遷廷尉。
entries.en: Because his family had long mastered the code, Guang was named censor of Yellow Sand with rank equal to the palace assistant secretary, then promoted director of justice.
entries.literal: Because Guang through generations understood law, he was used as Yellow Sand censor; rank was the same as the palace assistant secretary; he was promoted Director of Justice.

entries.zh: 元康中，拜尚書，典三公曹。
entries.en: During Yuankang he was appointed minister of the masters of writing in charge of the Three Dukes section.
entries.literal: In Yuankang he was appointed Minister of the Secretariat, in charge of the Three Dukes bureau.

entries.zh: 時趙王倫篡逆，光於其際，守道全貞。
entries.en: When Sima Lun, prince of Zhao, usurped the throne, Guang held to principle and kept his integrity intact.
entries.literal: When Prince of Zhao Lun usurped and rebelled, Guang at that juncture kept the Way and preserved integrity.

entries.zh: 及倫賜死，齊王冏輔政，復以光為廷尉，遷尚書，加奉車都尉。
entries.en: After Lun was forced to take his life and Prince Jiong of Qi directed the government, Guang was again named director of justice, then minister of the masters of writing with the added title colonel who conducts the carriage.
entries.literal: When Lun was ordered to die, Prince of Qi Jiong assisted governance; again they made Guang Director of Justice, promoted Minister of the Secretariat, added Colonel Who Conducts the Carriage.

entries.zh: 後從駕討成都王穎有勳，封延陵縣公，邑千八百戶。
entries.en: Later he accompanied the imperial train against Prince Ying of Chengdu and earned distinction; he was enfeoffed as duke of Yanling county with one thousand eight hundred households.
entries.literal: Later following the carriage in punishing Prince of Chengdu Ying he had merit; he was enfeoffed duke of Yanling county, fief one thousand eight hundred households.

entries.zh: 于時朝廷咸推光明于用法，故頻典理官。
entries.en: The whole court acknowledged his clarity in applying the law, so he was repeatedly placed over the judiciary.
entries.literal: At that time the court all pushed Guang as clear in applying law; therefore repeatedly he managed judicial offices.

entries.zh: 惠帝為張方所逼，幸長安，朝臣奔散，莫有從者，光獨侍帝而西。
entries.en: When Emperor Hui was driven by Zhang Fang to take refuge in Chang'an and the court fled in panic with none willing to follow, Guang alone accompanied the emperor westward.
entries.literal: Emperor Hui was pressed by Zhang Fang, traveled to Chang'an; court ministers ran and scattered; none had followers; Guang alone attended the emperor going west.

entries.zh: 遷尚書左僕射，加散騎常侍。
entries.en: He was promoted left vice-director of the masters of writing with the added title cavalier attendant-in-ordinary.
entries.literal: He was promoted Left Supervisor of the Masters of Writing, added Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.

entries.zh: 光兄誕為上官巳等所用，曆徐、雍二州刺史。
entries.en: Guang's elder brother Dan was employed by Shangguan Si and his faction and served as inspector of Xu and Yong provinces in turn.
entries.literal: Guang's elder brother Dan was used by Shangguan Si and others, successively was Inspector of Xu and Yong provinces.

entries.zh: 誕性任放無倫次，而決烈過人，與光異操。
entries.en: Dan was wild and unmethodical, yet bolder than most—a temper quite unlike his brother's.
entries.literal: Dan's nature was unbridled and unrestrained without order, yet decisive and fierce surpassing others; with Guang his conduct differed.

entries.zh: 常謂光小節，恆輕侮之，光事誕愈謹。
entries.en: He constantly mocked Guang for fussiness and treated him with contempt, yet Guang served his elder brother with growing deference.
entries.literal: He always called Guang petty scruples, constantly treated him lightly and insulted him; Guang serving Dan became more careful.

entries.zh: 帝既還洛陽，時太弟新立，重選傅訓，以光為少傅，加光祿大夫，常侍如故。
entries.en: After the emperor returned to Luoyang, the imperial younger brother had just been installed as heir and tutors were chosen with care; Guang was named junior tutor with the added title grand master of splendid carriage while keeping his post as attendant-in-ordinary.
entries.literal: When the emperor had returned to Luoyang, at the time the imperial younger brother was newly established; heavily selecting tutors and instruction, they made Guang Junior Tutor, added Grand Master of Splendid Carriage, attendant-in-ordinary as before.

entries.zh: 及懷帝即位，加光祿大夫金章紫綬，與傅祗並見推崇。
entries.en: When Emperor Huai came to the throne, Guang received the grand master of splendid carriage's gold seal and purple ribbon and was honored together with Fu Zhi.
entries.literal: When Emperor Huai ascended, he added Grand Master of Splendid Carriage gold seal purple ribbon, together with Fu Zhi both were seen honored and promoted.

entries.zh: 尋為尚書令，本官如故。
entries.en: Soon he was named director of the masters of writing while retaining his other titles.
entries.literal: Shortly he became Director of the Masters of Writing; original offices as before.

entries.zh: 以疾卒，贈司空、侍中。
entries.en: He died of illness and was posthumously named minister of works and palace attendant.
entries.literal: Because of illness he died; posthumously Minister of Works, Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 屬京洛傾覆，竟未加諡。
entries.en: The fall of Luoyang followed so closely that no posthumous title was ever conferred.
entries.literal: It fell when capital and Luoyang overturned; in the end no posthumous name was added.

entries.zh: 魏舒，字陽元，任城樊人也。
entries.en: Wei Shu, whose courtesy name was Yangyuan, came from Fan in Rencheng commandery.
entries.literal: Wei Shu, courtesy name Yangyuan, was a man of Fan in Rencheng.

entries.zh: 少孤，為外家寧氏所養。
entries.en: He lost his father while still young and was brought up by his mother's people, the Nings.
entries.literal: In youth he was orphaned and was reared by his maternal kin, the Ning clan.

entries.zh: 寧氏起宅，相宅者云：「當出貴甥。」
entries.en: When the Nings raised a new house, a geomancer told them, "This site will produce a distinguished nephew."
entries.literal: The Ning family built a house, and a geomancer of the site said, "A noble nephew will come forth."

entries.zh: 外祖母以魏氏甥小而慧，意謂應之。
entries.en: His maternal grandmother, seeing that the Wei boy was young but bright, assumed the omen pointed to him.
entries.literal: His maternal grandmother, because the Wei nephew was small yet clever, in her mind thought it referred to him.

entries.zh: 舒曰：「當為外氏成此宅相。」
entries.en: Shu said, "It falls to me to fulfill that houselot prophecy for our mother's family."
entries.literal: Shu said, "I shall for the maternal clan complete this houselot omen."

entries.zh: 久乃別居。
entries.en: Only after many years did he move out and keep a separate household.
entries.literal: After a long time then he lived apart.

entries.zh: 身長八尺二寸，姿望秀偉，飲酒石餘，而遲鈍質樸，不為鄉親所重。
entries.en: He stood eight chi and two cun tall, carried himself with striking presence, and could put away more than a shi of wine, yet he seemed slow and unpolished, so neighbors and relatives thought little of him.
entries.literal: His body was eight chi two cun in height, his bearing fine and grand, he drank more than a shi of wine, yet was slow, dull, plain, and was not esteemed by townsmen and kin.

entries.zh: 從叔父吏部郎衡，有名當世，亦不之知，使守水碓，每歎曰：「舒堪數百戶長，我願畢矣！」
entries.en: His paternal uncle Heng, a Personnel Ministry officer celebrated in their day, never recognized his gifts either and set him to mind the water-powered mill, sighing, "If Shu can serve as headman over a few hundred households, I shall ask nothing more!"
entries.literal: His father's cousin Heng, Personnel Ministry gentleman, had fame in the age, also did not know him, made him guard the water trip-hammer, and often sighed, saying, "Shu can suffice as chief of several hundred households — my wishes are fulfilled!"

entries.zh: 舒亦不以介意。
entries.en: Shu did not resent him for it.
entries.literal: Shu also did not on that account take it to mind.

entries.zh: 不修常人之節，不為皎曆之事，每欲容才長物，終不顯人之短。
entries.en: He scorned petty convention and avoided ostentatious moralism, preferring always to nurture others' strengths and never to expose their faults.
entries.literal: He did not cultivate ordinary men's scruples, did not do bright-harsh matters, always wished to accommodate talent and lengthen things, and to the end did not display people's shortcomings.

entries.zh: 性好騎射，著韋衣。
entries.en: He loved riding and archery and habitually dressed in leather hunting clothes.
entries.literal: By nature he loved riding and shooting, and wore leather garments.

entries.zh: 入山澤，以漁獵為事。
entries.en: He roamed hills and wetlands and made fishing and hunting his chief pastime.
entries.literal: He entered mountains and marshes and took fishing and hunting as his occupation.

entries.zh: 唯太原王乂謂舒曰：「卿終當為台輔，然今未能令妻子免饑寒，吾當助卿營之。」
entries.en: Wang Yi of Taiyuan alone told him, "You are destined for the highest councils of state, yet you cannot yet keep your wife and children from want; let me help you set them up."
entries.literal: Only Wang Yi of Taiyuan said to Shu, "You in the end will become a pillar minister, yet now are not able to cause wife and children to escape cold and hunger; I shall help you arrange it."

entries.zh: 常振其匱乏，舒受而不辭。
entries.en: Wang regularly supplied what the household lacked, and Shu accepted without demur.
entries.literal: He regularly relieved their want; Shu accepted and did not decline.

entries.zh: 舒嘗詣野王，主人妻夜產，俄而聞車馬之聲，相問曰：「男也，女也？」
entries.en: On a visit to Yewang, while his host's wife labored in the night, voices like chariots and horses suddenly sounded outside, asking, "Boy or girl?"
entries.literal: Shu once went to Yewang; the host's wife gave birth in the night; presently they heard the sound of horses and chariots, mutually asking, "Male or female?"

entries.zh: 曰：「男，書之，十五以兵死。」
entries.en: The answer came: "A son. Record it—he will die by the sword at fifteen."
entries.literal: It was said, "Male; write it; at fifteen he will die by weapons."

entries.zh: 復問：「寢者為誰？」
entries.en: Then they asked, "Who lies abed here?"
entries.literal: Again they asked, "Who is the one sleeping?"

entries.zh: 曰：「魏公舒。」
entries.en: The reply was, "Lord Wei Shu."
entries.literal: It was said, "Lord Wei Shu."

entries.zh: 後十五載，詣主人，問所生兒何在，曰：「因條桑為斧傷而死。」
entries.en: Fifteen years later he looked up the host and asked after that child; the man said, "He died when an axe slipped as he was pruning mulberry."
entries.literal: After fifteen years he went to the host, asked where the born child was, and it was said, "Because trimming mulberry he was wounded by an axe and died."

entries.zh: 舒自知當為公矣。
entries.en: Shu understood then that he was fated to rise to the rank of duke.
entries.literal: Shu himself knew he would become a duke.

entries.zh: 疏奏，優詔答之。
entries.en: The throne answered with a gracious edict.
entries.literal: When the memorial was submitted, a gracious edict replied.

entries.zh: 後司空衛瓘等亦共表宜省九品，復古鄉議里選。
entries.en: Later Wei Guan and others jointly urged cutting nine ranks and reviving village recommendation.
entries.literal: Later Minister of Works Wei Guan and others jointly memorialized that one ought to reduce the nine ranks and restore ancient village deliberation and hamlet selection.

entries.zh: 帝竟不施行。
entries.en: The emperor never acted on it.
entries.literal: The Emperor in the end did not implement it.

entries.zh: 由是毅遂為州都，銓正人流，清濁區別，其所彈貶，自親貴者始。
entries.en: Yi took the provincial seat, sorted candidates, split worthy from worthless, and struck kin and grandees first.
entries.literal: By this Yi became provincial rectifier—evaluating and rectifying the human stream—clear and muddy distinguished—those he impeached and demoted began from kin and nobility.

entries.zh: 太康六年卒，武帝撫幾驚曰：「失吾名臣，不得生作三公！」
entries.en: He died in Taikang 6; Emperor Wu smacked the rail: "We lost a pillar—he never lived to join the Three Dukes!"
entries.literal: In the sixth year of Taikang he died; Emperor Wu stroked the armrest and said startled: "We have lost Our famed minister—cannot have him live to serve among the Three Dukes!"

entries.zh: 即贈儀同三司，使者監護喪事。
entries.en: They granted him parity with the Three Offices with courtiers overseeing his obsequies.
entries.literal: Immediately posthumously conferred parity with the Three Offices; envoys supervised the funeral.

entries.zh: 羽林左監北海王宮上疏曰：「中詔以毅忠允匪躬，贈班台司，斯誠聖朝考績以毅著勳之美事也。
entries.en: Colonel Wang Gong wrote: "The palace honors Yi's loyalty—posthumous Three Offices rank crowns real service.
entries.literal: Colonel of the Feathered Forest left guard, Wang Gong of Beihai, submitted a memorial: "The inner edict because Yi was loyal and fair without sparing himself grants Three Offices rank—this is truly the sagely court examining merit for Yi's manifest achievement.

entries.zh: 臣謹按，諡者行之跡，而號者功之表。
entries.en: Posthumous names record conduct; noble titles record deeds.
entries.literal: Your servant respectfully examines—posthumous title is the trace of conduct—while honorific title is the showing of merit.

entries.zh: 今毅功德並立，而有號無諡，於義不體。
entries.en: Yi earned both virtue and achievement yet lacks a posthumous name—that breaks precedent.
entries.literal: Now Yi's merit and virtue both stand—yet he has title without posthumous name—in righteousness not a proper body.

entries.zh: 臣竊以《春秋》之事求之，諡法主於行而不系爵。
entries.en: The Spring and Autumn ties posthumous names to deeds, not to pedigree.
entries.literal: Your servant privately seeks it in Spring and Autumn affairs—posthumous law masters conduct and does not tie to noble rank.

entries.zh: 然漢、魏相承，爵非列侯，則皆沒而高行，不加之諡，至使三事之賢臣，不如野戰之將。
entries.en: Han and Wei withheld posthumous praise from anyone below full marquis—so loyal ministers ranked beneath battlefield brutes.
entries.literal: Yet Han and Wei inherit—if rank is not ranked marquis then all die with high conduct—none adds posthumous title—until worthy ministers of the Three Departments prove less honored than wild campaign generals.

entries.zh: 銘跡所殊，臣願聖世舉《春秋》之遠制，改列爵之舊限，使夫功行之實不相掩替，則莫不率賴。
entries.en: Your servant asks this court to revive ancient naming rules so merit matches tribute—none would doubt Your fairness.
entries.literal: What inscription traces distinguish—your servant wishes the sagely age would raise Spring and Autumn's distant system—alter the old limit of ranked nobility—so that merit and conduct's reality do not obscure each other—then none would fail to depend.

entries.zh: 若以革舊毀制，非所倉卒，則毅之忠益，雖不攻城掠地，論德進爵，亦應在例。
entries.en: If reform cannot come overnight, Yi's steadfast counsel—though no conqueror—still merits posthumous grace by precedent.
entries.literal: If because altering old destroys regulation—not something for haste—then Yi's loyal benefit—even though not storming cities or plundering lands—debating virtue advancing rank—also ought to fall within precedent.

entries.zh: 臣敢惟行甫請周之義，謹牒毅功行如石。」
entries.en: Following the precedent of humble memorials to Zhou, Your servant lists Yi's deeds below."
entries.literal: Your servant dares follow Xingfu's meaning in begging Zhou—respectfully presenting Yi's merit and conduct as stone."

entries.zh: 帝出其表使八坐議之，多同宮議。
entries.en: The emperor circulated Wang Gong's text to the Eight Seats—most concurred.
entries.literal: The Emperor produced his memorial and had the Eight Seats debate—most agreed with Gong's memorial.

entries.zh: 奏寢不報。
entries.en: The memorial vanished into silence—no answer came.
entries.literal: Memorial submitted—slept—no reply.

entries.zh: 二子：暾、總。
entries.en: He left two sons: Liu Tun and Liu Zong.
entries.literal: Two sons: Tun and Zong.

entries.zh: 暾遷太原內史，趙王倫篡位，假征虜將軍，不受，與三王共舉義。
entries.en: Made Taiyuan steward, he refused usurper Lun's general's baton and marched with the allied princes.
entries.literal: Tun promoted to interior steward of Taiyuan—Prince Zhao Lun usurped—false general Who Subdues Caitiffs—he did not accept—joined the Three Princes in righteous rising.

entries.zh: 惠帝復阼，暾為左丞，正色立朝，三台清肅。
entries.en: Under restored Emperor Hui he served as left aide—grim propriety quieted the three bureaus.
entries.literal: Emperor Hui restored the throne—Tun became left aide—stern dignity at court—the Three Terraces pure and solemn.

entries.zh: 尋兼御史中丞，奏免尚書僕射、東安公繇及王粹、董艾等十餘人。
entries.en: He soon concurrently served as palace assistant and memorialized the removal of the vice director, the Prince of Dong'an You, along with Wang Cui, Dong Ai, and more than ten others.
entries.literal: Soon concurrently palace secretary—memorialized removal of vice director of the right Prince of Dong'an You—Wang Cui—Dong Ai and over ten others.

entries.zh: 朝廷嘉之，遂即真。
entries.en: The court approved and confirmed his posts.
entries.literal: Court praised him—then confirmed full tenure.

entries.zh: 遷中庶子、左衛將軍、司隸校尉，奏免武陵王澹及何綏、劉坦、溫畿、李晅等。
entries.en: He rose to heir adviser—left guard colonel—metropolitan governor—and cashiered Prince Dan and several ministers.
entries.literal: Promoted heir-adjunct—colonel of the left guard—metropolitan governor—memorialized removal of Prince of Wuling Dan—He Sui—Liu Tan—Wen Ji—Li Xuan and others.

entries.zh: 長沙王乂討齊王冏，暾豫謀，封朱虛縣公，千八百戶。
entries.en: He helped Prince Yi against Prince Jiong and earned a Zhuxu dukedom with eighteen hundred households.
entries.literal: Prince of Changsha Yi attacked Prince of Qi Jiong—Tun planned beforehand—ennobled duke of Zhuxu—one thousand eight hundred households.

entries.zh: 乂死，坐免。
entries.en: When Yi fell Tun lost office too.
entries.literal: Yi died—by association dismissed.

entries.zh: 頃之，復為司隸。
entries.en: Soon he returned as metropolitan governor.
entries.literal: Shortly—again metropolitan governor.

entries.zh: 及惠帝之幸長安也，留暾守洛陽。
entries.en: Emperor Hui fled west—Tun stayed to hold Luoyang.
entries.literal: When Emperor Hui went to Chang'an—left Tun to guard Luoyang.

entries.zh: 河間王顒遣使鴆羊皇后，暾乃與留台僕射荀藩、河南尹周馥等上表，理后無罪。
entries.en: Prince Yong tried to poison Empress Yang—Tun joined Xun Fan and Zhou Fu to plead her cause.
entries.literal: Prince of Hejian Yong sent agents to poison Empress Yang—Tun with caretaker minister Xun Fan—Henan governor Zhou Fu memorialized her innocence.

entries.zh: 語在《后傳》。
entries.en: (See the "Biography of Empress Yang.")
entries.literal: Language is in Empress's biography.

entries.zh: 顒見表，大怒，遣陳顏、呂朗率騎五千收暾，暾東奔高密王略。
entries.en: Yong sent riders to arrest Tun—who fled to Prince Lue.
entries.literal: Yong seeing the memorial raged—sent Chen Yan and Lu Lang with five thousand riders to seize Tun—Tun fled east to Prince of Gaomi Lue.

entries.zh: 會劉根作逆，略以暾為大都督，加鎮軍將軍討根。
entries.en: During Liu Gen's revolt Lue named Tun commander-in-chief to crush him.
entries.literal: When Liu Gen rebelled—Lue made Tun grand commander—added general Who Guards the Army to strike Gen.

entries.zh: 暾戰失利，還洛。
entries.en: He lost and fell back to Luoyang.
entries.literal: Tun fought—lost—returned Luoyang.

entries.zh: 至酸棗，值東海王越奉迎大駕。
entries.en: At Suanzao he met Prince Yue escorting the throne eastward.
entries.literal: Reaching Suanzao—met Prince of East Sea Yue welcoming the imperial carriage.

entries.zh: 及帝還洛，羊后反宮。
entries.en: When the emperor came home Empress Yang reentered the palace.
entries.literal: When Emperor returned Luoyang—Empress Yang returned palace.

entries.zh: 后遣使謝暾曰：「賴劉司隸忠誠之志，得有今日。」
entries.en: The empress sent envoys to thank Tun: "We owe today's restoration to Metropolitan Liu's loyal purpose."
entries.literal: Empress sent envoy thanking Tun: "We rely on Metropolitan Liu's loyal intent—we could reach today."

entries.zh: 以舊勳復封爵，加光祿大夫。
entries.en: Her gratitude restored his fief and added a supernumerary minister title.
entries.literal: By old merit again ennobled—added grand messenger at court.

entries.zh: 和嶠
entries.en: He Jiao
entries.literal: He Jiao

entries.zh: 和嶠，字長輿，汝南西平人也。
entries.en: He Jiao, styled Changyu, hailed from Xiping in Runan.
entries.literal: He Jiao, courtesy name Changyu, was a native of Xiping in Runan.

entries.zh: 祖洽，魏尚書令。
entries.en: His grandfather He Qia was Wei minister over the bureaucracy.
entries.literal: Grandfather Qia—Wei minister of state affairs.

entries.zh: 父逌，魏吏部尚書。
entries.en: His father He You held Wei’s ministry of personnel.
entries.literal: Father You—Wei minister of personnel.

entries.zh: 嶠少有風格，慕舅夏侯玄之為人，厚自崇重。
entries.en: From boyhood he carried himself like his uncle Xiahou Xuan—aloof and exacting.
entries.literal: Jiao from youth had bearing—admired maternal uncle Xiahou Xuan’s person—greatly esteemed himself.

entries.zh: 有盛名于世，朝野許其能風俗，理人倫。
entries.en: Court and countryside praised him for shaping manners and moral order.
entries.literal: He had great fame in the world—court and wild approved his ability to move custom and order human relations.

entries.zh: 襲父爵上蔡伯，起家太子舍人。
entries.en: He succeeded the barony of Shangcai and entered service as heir‑apparent attendant.
entries.literal: Inherited father’s noble rank Baron of Shangcai—first office heir-apparent attendant.

entries.zh: 累遷潁川太守，為政清簡，甚得百姓歡心。
entries.en: As Yingchuan prefect he ruled plainly and won the people.
entries.literal: Promoted repeatedly to prefect of Yingchuan—administration clear and simple—greatly won common people’s hearts.

entries.zh: 太傅從事中郎庾敳見而歎曰：「嶠森森如千丈松，雖磥砢有節目，施之大廈，有棟樑之用。」
entries.en: Yu Ai marveled: "He Jiao is a thousand-foot pine—rough bark and all—yet palace timber."
entries.literal: Adjutant to the grand tutor Yu Ai saw him and sighed: "Jiao stands tall like a thousand-foot pine—though gnarled and knotty—applied to a great hall—has timber-and-beam use."

entries.zh: 賈充亦重之，稱于武帝，入為給事黃門侍郎，遷中書令，帝深器遇之。
entries.en: Jia Chong praised him to the throne; he entered the palace secretariat and became an imperial favorite.
entries.literal: Jia Chong also esteemed him—praised him to Emperor Wu—entered as gentleman attendant at the yellow gate—promoted director of the palace secretariat—Emperor deeply prized him.

entries.zh: 舊監令共車入朝，時荀勖為監，嶠鄙勖為人，以意氣加之，每同乘，高抗專車而坐。
entries.en: Overseer and director once rode together; Jiao scorned Xun Xu and insisted on a separate cart.
entries.literal: By old practice overseer and director shared carriage into court—at time Xun Xu was overseer—Jiao despised Xu’s person—applied spirit of pride—each time riding together—held head high and sat exclusive carriage.

entries.zh: 乃使監令異車，自嶠始也。
entries.en: Separate carts for overseer and director began with He Jiao.
entries.literal: Thereupon made overseer and director different carriages—beginning with Jiao.

entries.zh: =郁字仲輿，才望不及嶠，而以清幹稱，歷尚書左右僕射、中書令、尚書令。
entries.en: He Yu, styled Zhongyu, was leaner in fame than He Jiao but famed for efficiency—he rose to chief minister posts.
entries.literal: =Yu courtesy name Zhongyu—talent and reputation did not match Jiao—but by clarity and efficiency praised—served vice director left and right of the ministry—director of palace secretariat—minister of state affairs.

entries.zh: 洛陽傾沒，奔于苟晞，疾卒。
entries.en: When Luoyang fell he fled to Gou Xi and died sick.
entries.literal: Luoyang collapsed—fled to Gou Xi—died of illness.

entries.zh: 及惠帝即位，拜太子少傅，加散騎常侍、光祿大夫。
entries.en: Under Emperor Hui he tutored the crown prince with added honorifics.
entries.literal: When Emperor Hui mounted throne—appointed junior tutor to heir—added regular attendant at casual riding and grand messenger at court.

entries.zh: 太子朝西宮，嶠從入。
entries.en: He accompanied the heir to the western palace.
entries.literal: Heir apparent attended western palace—Jiao followed within.

entries.zh: 賈后使帝問嶠曰：「卿昔謂我不了家事，今日定云何？」
entries.en: The empress had the emperor ask him: "You once said I could not manage the household—what is your judgment today?"
entries.literal: Empress Jia had Emperor ask Jiao: "You once said I could not manage household affairs—today settled how?"

entries.zh: 嶠曰：「臣昔事先帝，曾有斯言。
entries.en: He Jiao said: "Your servant once served the late emperor and spoke this warning.
entries.literal: Jiao said: "Your servant formerly served late Emperor—once had this saying.

entries.zh: 言之不效，國之福也。
entries.en: That it proved false was the realm’s luck.
entries.literal: Words not fulfilled—state’s fortune.

entries.zh: 臣敢逃其罪乎！」
entries.en: How dare your servant flee the blame!"
entries.literal: Your servant dare flee the blame!"

entries.zh: 元康二年卒，贈金紫光祿大夫，加金章紫綬，本位如前。
entries.en: He died in Yuankang 2 and was posthumously honored as Grandee of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple, with gold seal and purple sash, his original rank unchanged.
entries.literal: He died in Yuankang 2; he was posthumously granted Grandee of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple, with gold seal and purple ribbon added, while his original rank remained as before.

entries.zh: 永平初，策諡曰簡。
entries.en: Early Yongping era he was canonized “Jian.”
entries.literal: Early Yongping—canon posthumous title Jian.

entries.zh: 嶠家產豐富，擬于王者，然性至吝，以是獲譏于世，杜預以為嶠有錢癖。
entries.en: He rivaled princes in wealth yet was famously stingy—Du Yu called it coin‑counting mania.
entries.literal: Jiao household property rich—rivaling kings—yet nature utmost stingy—thereby earned ridicule in the world—Du Yu thought Jiao had money mania.

entries.zh: 以弟郁子濟嗣，位至中書郎。
entries.en: He adopted nephew Ji who rose to the secretariat.
entries.literal: Younger brother Yu’s son Ji succeeded—rank reached gentleman of the palace secretariat.

entries.zh: 吳平，以參謀議功，賜弟郁爵汝南亭侯。
entries.en: After Wu was pacified, for He Jiao’s merit in planning counsel his younger brother Yu was granted the rank of Marquis of Runan Pavilion.
entries.literal: When Wu was pacified—for planning merit—granted younger brother Yu noble rank Marquis of Runan Pavilion.

entries.zh: 嶠轉侍中，愈被親禮，與任愷、張華相善。
entries.en: As palace attendant he grew closer to the throne and befriended Ren Kai and Zhang Hua.
entries.literal: Jiao transferred to palace attendant—more favored—in friendship with Ren Kai and Zhang Hua.

entries.zh: 嶠見太子不令，因侍坐曰：「皇太子有淳古之風，而季世多偽，恐不了陛下家事。」
entries.en: At leisure he said: "The crown prince has an antique plainness, yet a decadent age breeds sham—I fear he cannot manage Your Majesty's household."
entries.literal: Jiao seeing heir apparent was not sound—therefore sitting attendance said: "Crown prince has pure antique manner—but declining age abounds in sham—fears he cannot manage Your Majesty’s household affairs."

entries.zh: 帝默然不答。
entries.en: The emperor stayed silent.
entries.literal: Emperor silent—did not answer.

entries.zh: 後與荀顗、荀勖同侍，帝曰：「太子近入朝，差長進，卿可俱詣之，粗及世事。」
entries.en: Later, with the Xuns attending, the emperor said: "The heir has lately entered court and made some progress—you may all visit him and touch on affairs of state."
entries.literal: Later together attending with Xun Yi and Xun Xu—Emperor said: "Heir apparent lately entered court—somewhat grown—you may all visit him—roughly touch on worldly affairs."

entries.zh: 即奉詔而還。
entries.en: They bowed and withdrew.
entries.literal: Immediately obeyed edict and returned.

entries.zh: 顗、勖並稱太子明識弘雅，誠如明詔。
entries.en: Xun Yi and Xun Xu flattered the prince’s polish.
entries.literal: Yi and Xu together praised heir apparent’s bright understanding—vast and refined—truly as enlightened edict.

entries.zh: 嶠曰：「聖質如初耳！」
entries.en: He Jiao said: "His sagely substance is just as before!"
entries.literal: Jiao said: "Sagely substance like first!"

entries.zh: 帝不悅而起。
entries.en: The emperor rose in anger.
entries.literal: Emperor displeased—rose.

entries.zh: 嶠退居，恆懷慨歎，知不見用，猶不能已。
entries.en: He brooded—knowing his counsel spurned yet unable to stay mute.
entries.literal: Jiao withdrew—always harbored sighing regret—knew not employed—still could not stop.

entries.zh: 在御坐言及社稷，未嘗不以儲君為憂。
entries.en: Whenever talk touched the realm’s fate he fretted over the heir.
entries.literal: On imperial seat speaking of altars of soil and grain—never without taking heir as worry.

entries.zh: 帝知其言忠，每不酬和。
entries.en: The emperor knew him faithful yet refused to engage.
entries.literal: Emperor knew his words loyal—each time did not respond in harmony.

entries.zh: 後與嶠語，不及來事。
entries.en: Later audiences skirted the succession entirely.
entries.literal: Later speaking with Jiao—did not reach future matters.

entries.zh: 或以告賈妃，妃銜之。
entries.en: Word reached Empress Jia—she nursed a grudge.
entries.literal: Someone informed Consort Jia—consort bore grudge.

entries.zh: 太康末，為尚書，以母憂去職。
entries.en: Late in Taikang he headed the ministry until mourning his mother.
entries.literal: Late Taikang—became minister of state affairs—left office for mother’s mourning.

entries.zh: 弟郁
entries.en: His brother He Yu
entries.literal: Younger brother Yu

entries.zh: =茂以德素稱，名亞於陔，為上洛太守、散騎常侍、侍中、尚書。
entries.en: Wu Mao, famed for plain virtue just below Wu Gai, governed Shangluo and reached the ministries.
entries.literal: =Mao by plain virtue praised—name second to Gai—prefect of Shangluo—regular attendant at casual riding—attendant-in-ordinary—minister of state affairs.

entries.zh: 潁川荀愷年少於茂，即武帝姑子，自負貴戚，欲與茂交，距而不答，由是致怨。
entries.en: Xun Kai of Yingchuan, younger than Mao and a son of Emperor Wu’s paternal aunt, prided himself on noble kinship, wished to befriend Mao, was refused, and therefore resented him.
entries.literal: Yingchuan Xun Kai younger than Mao—being Emperor Wu’s cousin by aunt—self-important as noble kin—wished befriend Mao—refused distance—thereby incurred resentment.

entries.zh: 及楊駿誅，愷時為僕射，以茂駿之姨弟，陷為逆黨，遂見害。
entries.en: After Yang Jun fell, Xun Kai framed Wu Mao as Jun’s kin and had him killed.
entries.literal: When Yang Jun executed—Kai then vice director—because Mao Jun’s maternal nephew—trapped as rebel clique—thereupon harmed.

entries.zh: 茂清正方直，聞於朝野，一旦枉酷，天下傷焉。
entries.en: Wu Mao’s wrongful death shocked the realm.
entries.literal: Mao pure upright square straight—heard at court and wild—one morning twisted cruelty—world mourned.

entries.zh: 侍中傅祗上申明之，後追贈光祿勳。
entries.en: Fu Zhi cleared his name and won posthumous honors.
entries.literal: Attendant Fu Zhi upward clarified—later posthumously gifted superintendent of the household.

entries.zh: 充既為帝所遇，欲專名勢，而庾純、張華、溫顒、向秀、和嶠之徒皆與愷善，楊珧、王恂、華廙等充所親敬，於是朋黨紛然。
entries.en: Favored by the emperor, Jia Chong wished to monopolize fame and power, while Yu Chun, Zhang Hua, Wen Yong, Xiang Xiu, He Jiao and their like all befriended Kai, and Yang Yao, Wang Xun, and Hua Yi were those Chong held dear, so factional cliques flared.
entries.literal: Chong having been favored by Emperor wished monopolize fame and power—while Yu Chun, Zhang Hua, Wen Yong, Xiang Xiu, He Jiao and their like all befriended Kai—Yang Yao, Wang Xun, Hua Yi and such Chong held dear—thereby faction cliques flared.

entries.zh: 帝知之，召充、愷宴於式乾殿，而謂充等曰：「朝廷宜一，大臣當和。」
entries.en: The emperor summoned both factions to Shiqian Hall and said: "The court should be one; great ministers should harmonize."
entries.literal: Emperor knowing it—summoned Chong and Kai to feast at Shiqian Hall—and said to Chong and others: "Court ought be one—great ministers ought harmonize."

entries.zh: 充、愷各拜謝而罷。
entries.en: Both sides bowed off and left.
entries.literal: Chong and Kai each bowed thanks and ceased.

entries.zh: 既而充、愷等以帝已知之而不責，結怨愈深，外相崇重，內甚不平。
entries.en: Assured the throne would not punish them, Jia Chong and Ren Kai feigned respect while hating each other more.
entries.literal: Thereafter Chong, Kai and others because Emperor already knew yet did not blame—knot of hatred grew deeper—outwardly mutual esteem—innerly very unbalanced.

entries.zh: 或為充謀曰：「愷總門下樞要，得與上親接，宜啟令典選，便得漸疏，此一都令史事耳。
entries.en: A counselor urged Jia Chong: "Ren Kai controls the privy chancery and has intimate access—memorialize to put him in charge of selection and he will grow distant; that is only a capital clerk's affair.
entries.literal: Someone for Chong schemed: "Kai governs privy-chamber pivot—gains close access to superiors—ought memorialize to make him superintend selection—then can gradually grow distant—this is one capital clerk’s affair.

entries.zh: 且九流難精，間隙易乘。」
entries.en: Moreover the nine grades are hard to master—cracks invite attack."
entries.literal: Moreover nine currents hard to master—cracks easy to exploit."

entries.zh: 充因稱愷才能，宜在官人之職。
entries.en: Jia Chong praised Ren Kai’s fitness for personnel.
entries.literal: Chong therefore praised Kai’s talent—ought hold office of ordering men.

entries.zh: 帝不之疑，謂充舉得其才。
entries.en: Emperor Wu trusted the nomination.
entries.literal: Emperor did not suspect—said Chong’s recommendation obtained right talent.

entries.zh: 即日以愷為吏部尚書，加奉車都尉。
entries.en: Ren Kai became minister of personnel with added military rank.
entries.literal: Same day appointed Kai minister of personnel—added commandant of palace carriage.

entries.zh: 愷有經國之幹，萬機大小多管綜之。
entries.en: He mastered statecraft large and small.
entries.literal: Kai had capacity for ordering the state—myriad threads small and large mostly managed comprehensively.

entries.zh: 性忠正，以社稷為己任，帝器而昵之，政事多諮焉。
entries.en: Loyal and upright, he took the altars of the state as his own charge; the emperor prized and favored him and consulted him on most government affairs.
entries.literal: Nature loyal upright—took altars of soil and grain as self-task—Emperor prized and favored—state affairs mostly consulted.

entries.zh: 泰始初，鄭沖、王祥、何曾、荀顗、裴秀等各以老疾歸第。
entries.en: Early Taishi the elder ministers retired ill.
entries.literal: Taishi beginning—Zheng Chong—Wang Xiang—He Zeng—Xun Yi—Pei Xiu each by old age illness returned mansion.

entries.zh: 帝優寵大臣，不欲勞以筋力，數遣愷諭旨于諸公，諮以當世大政，參議得失。
entries.en: Wu sent Ren Kai to relay policy to the retired elders.
entries.literal: Emperor graciously favored great ministers—did not wish labor them with sinews—often sent Kai conveying intent to each lord—consulting on age’s great policies—debating gain and loss.

entries.zh: 愷惡賈充之為人也，不欲令久執朝政，每裁抑焉。
entries.en: He worked to curb Jia Chong’s power.
entries.literal: Kai hated Jia Chong’s person—did not wish him long hold court governance—each time restrained.

entries.zh: 充病之，不知所為。
entries.en: Jia Chong despaired.
entries.literal: Chong sick at heart—knew not what to do.

entries.zh: 後承間言愷忠貞局正，宜在東宮，使護太子。
entries.en: He urged posting Ren Kai to tutor the heir—ostensibly praise.
entries.literal: Later seizing interval spoke Kai loyal steadfast upright—ought be eastern palace—make protect heir.

entries.zh: 帝從之，以為太子少傅，而侍中如故，充計畫不行。
entries.en: The emperor followed and made him junior tutor to the heir, remaining palace attendant as before; Chong’s plan did not succeed.
entries.literal: Emperor followed—thought junior tutor to heir—palace attendant as before—Chong’s plan did not proceed.

entries.zh: 會秦、雍寇擾，天子以為憂。
entries.en: Qinzhou and Yongzhou revolted—Wu fretted.
entries.literal: When Qin and Yong raided and disturbed—Son of Heaven took as worry.

entries.zh: 愷因曰：「秦、涼覆敗，關右騷動，此誠國家之所深慮。
entries.en: Ren Kai said: "Qin and Liang have collapsed and the west is in turmoil—this truly is the state's deep worry.
entries.literal: Kai therefore said: "Qin and Liang overturned defeated—right of Pass disturbed—this truly state’s deep worry.

entries.zh: 宜速鎮撫，使人心有庇。
entries.en: It needed a credible marshal to reassure the west.
entries.literal: Ought quickly pacify soothe—make people’s hearts have shelter.

entries.zh: 自非威望重臣有計略者，無以康西土也。」
entries.en: Only a veteran minister of prestige and stratagem can pacify the western lands."
entries.literal: Unless prestige-weighted minister with stratagem—none can heal western lands."

entries.zh: 帝曰：「誰可任者？」
entries.en: “Who fits?” asked the emperor.
entries.literal: Emperor said: "Who can be appointed?"

entries.zh: 愷曰：「賈充其人也。」
entries.en: “Jia Chong,” said Ren Kai—setting a trap.
entries.literal: Kai said: "Jia Chong is the man."

entries.zh: 中書令庾純亦言之，於是詔充西鎮長安。
entries.en: Yu Chun echoed the call—so Jia Chong was ordered west.
entries.literal: Director of the palace secretariat Yu Chun also spoke—thereupon edict Chong west guard Chang’an.

entries.zh: 充用荀勖計得留。
entries.en: Jia Chong used Xun Xu’s ruse to remain at court.
entries.literal: Chong using Xun Xu’s plan obtained stay.

entries.zh: 愷素有識鑒，加以在公勤恪，甚得朝野稱譽。
entries.en: Ren Kai’s discernment and diligence won wide praise.
entries.literal: Kai by nature had judgment—added to public diligence scrupulous—greatly won court and wild praise.

entries.zh: 而賈充朋黨又諷有司奏愷與立進令劉友交關。
entries.en: Jia’s clique tied him to Prefect Liu You.
entries.literal: Yet Jia Chong faction again hinted responsible offices memorialize Kai connected with Director of Stand-Fast Advance Liu You.

entries.zh: 事下尚書，愷對不伏。
entries.en: Ren Kai pleaded innocent before the ministry.
entries.literal: Matter sent to ministry—Kai replied not submitting.

entries.zh: 尚書杜友、廷尉劉良並忠公士也，知愷為充所抑，欲申理之，故遲留而未斷，以是愷及友、良皆免官。
entries.en: Du You and Liu Liang stalled to clear him—all three were cashiered.
entries.literal: Minister Du You, commandant Liu Liang both loyal fair gentlemen—knew Kai suppressed by Chong—wished clarify—therefore delayed without deciding—thereby Kai and You and Liang all dismissed office.

entries.zh: 愷既失職，乃縱酒耽樂，極滋味以自奉養。
entries.en: Out of office he drowned in wine and food.
entries.literal: Kai having lost office—thereupon indulged wine and pleasure—extreme flavors to support himself.

entries.zh: 初，何劭以公子奢侈，每食必盡四方珍饌，愷乃逾之，一食萬錢，猶云無可下箸處。
entries.en: He outspent He Shao’s legendary feasts—ten thousand cash per sitting yet claiming nothing worth eating.
entries.literal: Earlier He Shao as noble son extravagant—each meal must exhaust four quarters’ rare delicacies—Kai then surpassed—one meal ten thousand cash—still said nowhere to place chopsticks.

entries.zh: 愷時因朝請，帝或慰諭之，愷初無復言，惟泣而已。
entries.en: At audiences the emperor consoled him—Ren Kai could only weep.
entries.literal: Kai sometimes by court briefing—Emperor occasionally comforted instruct—Kai at first had no further words—only weeping.

entries.zh: 後起為太僕，轉太常。
entries.en: He returned as grand coachman then minister of ceremonies.
entries.literal: Later raised grand coachman—transferred minister of ceremonies.

entries.zh: 何攀，字惠興，蜀郡郫人也。
entries.en: He Pan, styled Huixing, came from Pi in Shu.
entries.literal: He Pan, courtesy name Huixing, native of Pi in Shu commandery.

entries.zh: 仕州為主薄。
entries.en: He began as a provincial chief clerk.
entries.literal: Served province as chief clerk.

entries.zh: 屬刺史皇甫晏為牙門張弘所害，誣以大逆。
entries.en: Inspector Huangfu Yan was murdered by Zhang Hong and smeared as a traitor.
entries.literal: When Inspector Huangfu Yan was harmed by camp gate Zhang Hong—slandered with great treason.

entries.zh: 時攀適丁母喪，遂詣梁州拜表，證晏不反，故晏冤理得申。
entries.en: Though mourning his mother, he rode to Liangzhou and cleared Huangfu Yan’s name.
entries.literal: At time Pan happened mourning mother—thereupon went to Liangzhou submitting memorial—proved Yan did not rebel—therefore Yan’s wrong managed to clear.

entries.zh: 王濬為益州，辟為別駕。
entries.en: Wang Jun made him provincial aide in Yi.
entries.literal: Wang Jun as Yi province—summoned as aide.

entries.zh: 濬謀伐吳，遣攀奉表詣台，口陳事機，詔再引見，乃令張華與攀籌量進時討之宜。
entries.en: He Pan carried Wang Jun’s Wu campaign memorial to Luoyang and planned timing with Zhang Hua.
entries.literal: Jun schemed attacking Wu—sent Pan bearing memorial to court—orally stated opportunity—edict twice summoned audience—ordered Zhang Hua with Pan deliberate advancing timing of attack fitness.

entries.zh: 濬兼遣攀過羊祜，面陳伐吳之策。
entries.en: He also briefed Yang Hu in person on the Wu invasion.
entries.literal: Jun also sent Pan visit Yang Hu—face to face state attacking Wu strategies.

entries.zh: 攀善於將命，帝善之，詔攀參濬軍事。
entries.en: His diplomacy pleased Emperor Wu, who attached him to Wang Jun’s staff.
entries.literal: Pan good at carrying orders—Emperor praised—ordered Pan assist Jun military affairs.

entries.zh: 及孫皓降于濬，而王渾恚於後機，欲攻濬，攀勸濬送皓與渾，由是事解。
entries.en: When Wang Hun nearly attacked Wang Jun over Sun Hao’s surrender, He Pan urged handing the captive to Hun to prevent civil bloodshed.
entries.literal: When Sun Hao surrendered to Jun—yet Wang Hun angry at late timing—wished attack Jun—Pan urged Jun deliver Hao to Hun—thereby matter resolved.

entries.zh: 以攀為濬輔國司馬，封關內侯。
entries.en: Wang Jun named him auxiliary marshal—Marquis Within the Pass.
entries.literal: Made Pan Jun aids-state marshal—enfeoffed marquis within Guan.

entries.zh: 轉滎陽令，上便宜十事，甚得名稱。
entries.en: As Xingyang magistrate he offered ten reform memos and won fame.
entries.literal: Transferred Xingyang magistrate—submitted convenient matters ten items—greatly earned reputation.

entries.zh: 除廷尉平。
entries.en: He became a justice assessor.
entries.literal: Appointed commandant-ping of justice.

entries.zh: 時廷尉卿諸葛沖以攀蜀士，輕之，及共斷疑獄，沖始嘆服。
entries.en: Zhuge Chong sneered at his Shu origins until joint trials proved his genius.
entries.literal: At time commandant of justice Zhuge Chong because Pan Shu gentleman—slighted him—when together judged doubtful lawsuits—Chong then sighed admiration.

entries.zh: 遷宣城太守，不行，轉散騎侍郎。
entries.en: He declined Xuancheng but joined the attendant corps.
entries.literal: Promoted prefect of Xuancheng—did not go—transferred regular attendant at casual riding.

entries.zh: 楊駿執政，多樹親屬，大開封嘗，欲以恩澤自衛。
entries.en: Regent Yang Jun stuffed offices with kin and blanketed them with patents.
entries.literal: Yang Jun holding power—planted many kin—greatly opened investitures rewards—wished by grace shield self.

entries.zh: 攀以為非，乃與石崇共立議奏之。
entries.en: He Pan and Shi Chong jointly condemned the policy.
entries.literal: Pan thought not right—thereupon with Shi Chong jointly stood memorial submitting.

entries.zh: 語在崇傳。
entries.en: (See the biography of Shi Chong.)
entries.literal: Language is in Chong biography.

entries.zh: 帝不納。
entries.en: The emperor ignored them.
entries.literal: Emperor did not accept.

entries.zh: 以豫誅駿功，封西城侯，邑萬戶，賜絹萬匹，弟逢平卿侯，兄子逵關中侯。
entries.en: For merit in executing Yang Jun he was enfeoffed Marquis of Xicheng with ten thousand households and ten thousand bolts of silk; his younger brother Feng became Marquis of Pingqing and his elder brother’s son Kui Marquis Within the Pass.
entries.literal: By merit participating executing Jun—enfeoffed marquis of Xicheng—ten thousand households—gift silk ten thousand bolts—younger brother Feng Pingqing marquis—elder brother’s son Kui marquis within Guan.

entries.zh: 攀固讓所封戶及絹之半，餘所受者分給中外宗親，略不入己。
entries.en: He refused half the silk and fiefs—sharing the rest with kin—keeping nothing.
entries.literal: Pan firmly declined half of granted households and silk—remainder received distributed inside outside kin—almost none entered self.

entries.zh: 遷翊軍校尉，頃之，出為東羌校尉。
entries.en: He became aide colonel then Eastern Qiang colonel.
entries.literal: Promoted colonel Who Aids Army—shortly—went out colonel of Eastern Qiang.

entries.zh: 徵為揚州刺史，在任三年，遷大司農。
entries.en: After three years as Yangzhou inspector he headed the ministry of agriculture.
entries.literal: Summoned inspector of Yang province—in office three years—promoted minister of agriculture.

entries.zh: 轉兗州刺史，加鷹揚將軍，固讓不就。
entries.en: He refused Yanzhou despite general’s banners.
entries.literal: Transferred inspector of Yanzhou—added general Who Raises Hawk—firmly declined did not take.

entries.zh: 太常成粲、左將軍卞粹勸攀蒞職，中詔又加切厲，攀竟稱疾不起。
entries.en: Minister of Ceremonies Cheng Can and General of the Left Bian Cui urged him to take the post; an inner edict grew stern, but Pan claimed illness and would not rise.
entries.literal: Minister of ceremonies Cheng Can—general left Bian Cui urged Pan take office—inner edict again stern—Pan ultimately claimed illness did not rise.

entries.zh: 及趙王倫篡位，遣使召攀，更稱疾篤。
entries.en: Prince Lun’s summons met another refusal—grave illness.
entries.literal: When Prince Zhao Lun usurped—sent envoy summon Pan—again claimed grave illness.

entries.zh: 倫怒，將誅之，攀不得已，扶疾赴召。
entries.en: Lun threatened death—He Pan dragged himself to Luoyang.
entries.literal: Lun angry—would execute—Pan had no choice—supported illness answered summons.

entries.zh: 卒于洛陽，時年五十八。
entries.en: He died there at fifty-eight.
entries.literal: Died in Luoyang—age fifty-eight.

entries.zh: 攀居心平允，蒞官整肅，愛樂人物，敦儒貴才。
entries.en: Fair-minded and orderly in office, he honored scholars and talent.
entries.literal: Pan dwelling mind fair—holding office stern—loved delighted men—esteemed Confucian prized talent.

entries.zh: 為梁、益二州中正，引致遺滯。
entries.en: As Liang-Yi rectifier he recalled unjustly blocked men.
entries.literal: As grand rectifier for Liang and Yi provinces—drew in stranded men.

entries.zh: 巴西陳壽、閻乂、犍為費立皆西州名士，並被鄉閭所謗，清議十餘年。
entries.en: Chen Shou and western scholars suffered decade-long village boycotts.
entries.literal: Baixi Chen Shou—Yan Yi—Fei Li of Qianwei—all western province famed gentlemen—together slandered by villages—pure discussion over ten years.

entries.zh: 攀申明曲直，咸免冤濫。
entries.en: He Pan reversed their verdicts—clearing injustice.
entries.literal: Pan clarified crooked straight—all spared wrongful overflow.

entries.zh: 攀雖居顯職，家甚貧素，無妾媵伎樂，惟以周窮濟乏為事。
entries.en: Despite high rank he stayed poor—no concubines or musicians—only charity.
entries.literal: Pan though occupied eminent office—house very poor plain—no concubines singing girls—only took relieving poverty aiding want as task.

entries.zh: 子璋嗣，亦有父風。
entries.en: Son He Zhang inherited his integrity.
entries.literal: Son Zhang succeeded—also had father manner.

entries.zh: 史臣曰：幽厲不君，上德猶懷進善；
entries.en: Even under tyrants worthies still hoped to counsel virtue;
entries.literal: Historians say: You and Li did not lord—high virtue still cherished advancing goodness;

entries.zh: 共驩在位，大聖之所不堪。
entries.en: Gong and Huan in power were more than even a great sage could endure;
entries.literal: Gong Huan on throne—great sage cannot endure.

entries.zh: 況乎志士仁人，甯求苟合！
entries.en: how much less would principled men trim truth for favor!
entries.literal: How much more intent gentlemen and benevolent men—would they seek careless conformity!

entries.zh: 懷其寵秩，所以系其存亡者也。
entries.en: Rank and stipend bind ministers’ survival—
entries.literal: Cherishing their favor and salary—thereby ties their survival.

entries.zh: 雖復自口銷金，投光撫劍，馳書北闕，敗車猶踐，而諫主不易，譏臣實難。
entries.en: yet even facing ruin remonstrating proves harder than flattering—truth cuts both ways.
entries.literal: Though again mouths melt metal—cast aside brilliance grasp sword—gallop memorial northern gate—broken cart still tread—yet remonstrating lord not easy—mocking ministers truly hard.

entries.zh: 劉毅一遇寬容，任和兩遭膚受，詳觀餘烈，亦各其心焉。
entries.en: Liu Yi won rare patience—Ren Kai and He Jiao suffered credulous courts—each followed conscience nonetheless.
entries.literal: Liu Yi once met tolerance—Ren and He twice suffered shallow belief—closely observing remaining deeds—each also their hearts.

entries.zh: 若夫武陔懷魏臣之志，崔洪愛郤詵之道，長升勸王彌之尊，何攀從趙倫之命，君子之人，觀乎臨事者也。
entries.en: Wu Gai kept Wei-minister resolve; Cui Hong loved Xi Shen's way; Changsheng urged honor for Wang Mi; He Pan obeyed Zhao Lun's order—a gentleman is seen in the crisis.
entries.literal: As for Wu Gai cherishing Wei minister resolve—Cui Hong loving Xi Shen’s way—Changsheng urging Wang Mi’s honor—He Pan obeying Zhao Lun’s order—gentleman quality—observe them at crisis.

entries.zh: 贊曰：仲雄初令，忠謇揚庭。
entries.en: Verse: Liu Yi’s early zeal shook the court—
entries.literal: Praise says: Zhongxiong first command—loyal blunt raised court.

entries.zh: 身方諸葛，帝擬桓、靈。
entries.en: likened to stern ministers—yet matched with doomed Han emperors;
entries.literal: Body compared Zhuge—Emperor likened Huan Ling.

entries.zh: 大業非楊，元褒誚賈。
entries.en: Daye refused Yang Jun’s tide—Ren Kai mocked Jia Chong;
entries.literal: Daye rejected Yang—Yuanbao mocked Jia.

entries.zh: 和氏條暢，堪施大廈。
entries.en: He Jiao stood tall as ridge timber;
entries.literal: He clan lithe—fit to roof great hall.

entries.zh: 崔門不謁，聲飛朝野。
entries.en: Cui Hong barred favor-seekers yet fame soared;
entries.literal: Cui gate unvisited—voice flies court wild.

entries.zh: 侯史、武陔，輔佐之才。
entries.en: Houshi Guang and Wu Gai served as fine assistants;
entries.literal: Houshi and Wu Gai—aiding talents.

entries.zh: 何攀平允，冤濫多回。
entries.en: He Pan’s fairness redeemed many wrongs.
entries.literal: He Pan fair—wrongful overflow much turned.

entries.zh: 劉毅
entries.en: Liu Yi.
entries.literal: Liu Yi.

entries.zh: 惠帝即位，楊駿輔政。
entries.en: When Emperor Hui came to the throne, Yang Jun directed the government as regent.
entries.literal: When Emperor Hui mounted the throne, Yang Jun assisted the government.

entries.zh: 咸言於駿曰：「事與世變，禮隨時宜，諒暗之不行尚矣。
entries.en: Fu Xian said to Yang Jun: “Circumstances change with the times, and ritual must suit the moment; it has been clear for ages that the old palace mourning cannot be kept unchanged.
entries.literal: Xian spoke to Jun, saying: “Affairs change with the age; ritual follows what fits the times; that mourning seclusion is not practiced has long been clear.

entries.zh: 由世道彌薄，權不可假，故雖斬焉在疚，而躬覽萬機也。
entries.en: The moral climate has thinned, and supreme authority cannot be handed off; that is why even a ruler in the deepest mourning still has to take up the myriad affairs of state himself.
entries.literal: Because the Way of the world grows ever thinner, power cannot be lent away; therefore although one is cutting grief in deep mourning, yet one personally inspects the ten thousand threads of business.

entries.zh: 逮至漢文，以天下體大，服重難久，遂制既葬而除。
entries.en: Emperor Wen of Han, seeing the realm too vast for prolonged heavy mourning, decreed that mourning dress end with the burial.
entries.literal: Down to Emperor Wen of Han, because the realm under Heaven was large in scale and heavy mourning could not be prolonged long, thereupon the rule was to remove mourning garments once burial was complete.

entries.zh: 世祖武皇帝雖大孝蒸蒸，亦從時釋服，制心喪三年，至於萬機之事，則有不遑。
entries.en: Emperor Wu, our dynastic founder, was deeply filial, yet he too laid aside formal mourning when the times required it, keeping a three-year grief in his heart while knowing he could not neglect the myriad tasks of rule.
entries.literal: Our founding emperor Emperor Wu, though his filial devotion was abundant, also followed the times in laying aside mourning garments, setting heart-mourning for three years; as for the ten thousand threads of business, then there was no leisure.

entries.zh: 今聖上欲委政於公，諒暗自居，此雖謙讓之心，而天下未以為善。
entries.en: The reigning emperor wishes to leave government in your hands while he withdraws in mourning; that may show modest intent, but the empire does not read it as wise.
entries.literal: Now the sagely sovereign wishes to entrust government to your lordship and dwell in mourning seclusion himself—this, although a mind of yielding, is not what all under Heaven takes for good.

entries.zh: 天下未以為善者，以億兆顒顒，戴仰宸極，聽於冢宰，懼天光有蔽。
entries.en: People look up to the throne alone; if they hear that only the chief minister decides policy, they fear the sovereign’s light will be hidden.
entries.literal: The reason all under Heaven does not take it for good is that the millions lift their heads, looking up to the pole star; hearing that the grand steward alone decides, they fear the heavenly light may be blocked.

entries.zh: 人心既已若此，而明公處之固未為易也。
entries.en: Hearts are already uneasy; for you, sir, the position cannot be an easy one.
entries.literal: Human hearts are already like this, yet your lordship’s handling of it is surely not easy.

entries.zh: 竊謂山陵之事既畢，明公當思隆替之宜。
entries.en: Once the imperial burial is over, you must weigh what will strengthen the state and what will weaken it.
entries.literal: Your subject privately holds that once matters on the hills and tombs are finished, your lordship ought to weigh what suits flourishing or decline.

entries.zh: 周公聖人，猶不免謗。
entries.en: Even the Duke of Zhou, a sage, could not escape slander.
entries.literal: The Duke of Zhou was a sage, yet even he could not escape slander.

entries.zh: 以此推之，周公之任既未易而處，況聖上春秋非成王之年乎！
entries.en: If the Duke of Zhou’s burden was hard to bear, how much harder when our emperor is not a child like King Cheng of old!
entries.literal: From this one infers: the Duke of Zhou’s burden was already not easy to bear—how much more when the sagely sovereign’s years do not match King Cheng’s!

entries.zh: 得意忘言，言未易盡。
entries.en: When the point is taken, words may cease; yet words can never say everything.
entries.literal: When the meaning is grasped, words are forgotten; words are not easy to exhaust.

entries.zh: 苟明公有以察其悾款，言豈在多。」
entries.en: If you can see the earnest loyalty behind my bluntness, I need not say more.”
entries.literal: If your lordship can see the sincerity in my earnest dullness, words need not be many.”

entries.zh: 時司隸荀愷從兄喪，自表赴哀，詔聽之而未下，愷乃造駿。
entries.en: Meanwhile Xun Kai, the colonel director of retainers, had petitioned to mourn a deceased cousin; the throne had granted leave but the edict had not yet been issued when Kai went to Yang Jun’s house.
entries.literal: At that time the colonel director of retainers Xun Kai, on a cousin’s death, personally memorialized to go to mourning; an edict had approved it but not yet been issued, yet Kai went to Jun’s place.

entries.zh: 咸因奏曰：「死喪之戚，兄弟孔懷。
entries.en: Fu Xian seized on this and memorialized: “The grief of death strikes brothers most keenly.
entries.literal: Xian thereupon memorialized: “The grief of death: brothers greatly cherish one another.

entries.zh: 同堂亡隕，方在信宿，聖恩矜憫，聽使臨喪。
entries.en: A cousin has just died; barely two nights have passed. The court in its mercy would let him attend the rites.
entries.literal: A hall-mate has died and fallen; we are still within two nights; the sagely grace pities and allows attendance at mourning.

entries.zh: 詔未下而便以行造，急諂媚之敬，無友于之情。
entries.en: To hurry to a private visit before the edict appears is eager flattery, not the affection due between brothers.
entries.literal: The edict had not been issued yet he used motion to go pay visit—hasty flattery’s reverence, no fraternal feeling toward friends.

entries.zh: 宜加顯貶，以隆風教。」
entries.en: He should be publicly demoted to uphold public morals.”
entries.literal: He ought plainly to be demoted to thicken customs and teaching.”

entries.zh: 帝以駿管朝政，有詔不問，駿甚憚之。
entries.en: The emperor, because Yang Jun ran the government, ordered the charge dropped; Jun nonetheless came to fear Fu Xian deeply.
entries.literal: The emperor, because Jun controlled court government, issued an edict not to pursue the matter; Jun greatly feared him.

entries.zh: 咸復與駿箋諷切之，駿意稍折，漸以不平。
entries.en: Fu Xian wrote again to needle Yang Jun; Jun yielded a little on the surface but grew quietly resentful.
entries.literal: Xian again wrote Jun a letter exhorting him incisively; Jun’s intent bent slightly but gradually turned resentful.

entries.zh: 由是欲出為京兆、弘農太守，駿甥李斌說駿，不宜斥出正人，乃止。
entries.en: Jun then planned to send Fu Xian out as governor of Jingzhao or Hongnong, but Li Bin, Jun’s nephew, argued that an upright man should not be banished from the capital, and Jun dropped the idea.
entries.literal: Thereupon [Jun] wished to send [Xian] out as governor of Jingzhao or Hongnong; Jun’s nephew Li Bin persuaded Jun that one should not expel an upright man, and so it stopped.

entries.zh: 駿弟濟素與咸善，與咸書曰：「江海之流混混，故能成其深廣也。
entries.en: Yang Ji, Jun’s younger brother, who was friendly with Fu Xian, wrote: “Rivers and seas run broad and muddy, and that is how they grow deep and wide.
entries.literal: Jun’s younger brother Ji had always been on good terms with Xian; he wrote to Xian: “River and sea currents are turbid and vast, therefore they can achieve depth and breadth.

entries.zh: 天下大器，非可稍了，而相觀每事欲了。
entries.en: The empire is no trifle to be ticked off in pieces, yet you try to finish every matter at a glance.
entries.literal: The great vessel of all under Heaven cannot be grasped in little bits; yet you inspect everything wishing to get it all done.

entries.zh: 生子癡，了官事，官事未易了也。
entries.en: The proverb runs, “Raise a dull son, leave him office work”—office work is never really finished.
entries.literal: Have a dull son and set him to finishing official business—official business is not easy to finish.

entries.zh: 了事正作癡，復為快耳！
entries.en: To “finish” business is to play the fool, yet people call that clever!
entries.literal: Finishing affairs is precisely making foolishness, yet we call it sharp!

entries.zh: 左丞總司天臺，維正八坐，此未易居。
entries.en: The left assistant steers the high ministries and keeps the eight senior seats in line—that is no easy seat.
entries.literal: The left assistant oversees the celestial terrace and aligns the eight seats—this is not an easy place to stand.

entries.zh: 以君盡性而處未易居之任，益不易也。
entries.en: For a man of your uncompromising nature to hold such a post is harder still.
entries.literal: That you, with full nature, occupy a place not easy to stand—that is even less easy.

entries.zh: 想慮破頭，故具有白。」
entries.en: I worry until my head aches, so I spell it all out here.”
entries.literal: My thoughts worry until they break my head; therefore I write this in full.”

entries.zh: 咸答曰：「衛公云酒色之殺人，此甚於作直。
entries.en: Fu Xian answered: “Lord Wei says wine and lust kill more surely than blunt honesty.
entries.literal: Xian replied: “Lord Wei says wine and sex kill people—this is worse than acting straight.

entries.zh: 坐酒色死，人不為悔。
entries.en: Men die of drink and lust without a twinge of regret.
entries.literal: Dying through wine and sex, people do not regret it.

entries.zh: 逆畏以直致禍，此由心不直正，欲以苟且為明哲耳！
entries.en: To shun disaster by silence shows a heart that is not straight—it is cowardice dressed up as wisdom.
entries.literal: Contrariwise fearing that straightness brings disaster—that is because the heart is not straight and upright, wishing to take evasive compromise as wise clarity!

entries.zh: 自古以直致禍者，當自矯枉過直，或不忠允，欲以亢厲為聲，故致忿耳。
entries.en: Those who court ruin by bluntness usually overcorrect, or lack true loyalty, or play the martyr for fame—and so they earn resentment.
entries.literal: From antiquity those who brought disaster on themselves by straightness were either bending the straight too far, or not being loyal and sincere, wishing to borrow harshness for reputation, therefore incurring resentment.

entries.zh: 安有空空為忠益，而當見疾乎！」
entries.en: Would plain loyalty for the public good alone earn hatred?”
entries.literal: How could blandly being loyal and beneficial then meet with jealousy!”

entries.zh: 居無何，駿誅。
entries.en: Soon afterward Yang Jun was executed.
entries.literal: Before long, Jun was executed.

entries.zh: 咸轉為太子中庶子，遷御史中丞。
entries.en: Fu Xian was moved to palace attendant to the heir apparent, then promoted to metropolitan censor.
entries.literal: Xian was transferred to palace subordinate to the heir apparent, then promoted metropolitan censor.

entries.zh: 時太宰、汝南王亮輔政，咸致書曰：咸以為太甲、成王年在蒙幼，故有伊、周之事。
entries.en: When the grand preceptor, Sima Liang, king of Runan, directed policy, Fu Xian wrote to him: I hold that Tai Jia and King Cheng were still in their minority, and therefore there occurred the regencies of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou.
entries.literal: When the grand preceptor, the king of Runan, Liang, directed the government, Xian sent a letter saying: Xian holds that Tai Jia and King Cheng, in years still tenderly young, therefore had the acts of Yi and Zhou.

entries.zh: 聖人且猶不免疑，況臣既不聖，王非孺子，而可以行伊、周之事乎！
entries.en: Even sages could not escape suspicion in such cases; how much less can I, no sage, claim the regency of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou when the king is no child!
entries.literal: Even sages could not avoid suspicion—how much more when your subject is not a sage and the king is no child, yet one could perform the acts of Yi and Zhou!

entries.zh: 上在諒暗，聽於冢宰，而楊駿無狀，便作伊、周，自為居天下之安，所以至死。
entries.en: The emperor was in mourning seclusion and entrusted affairs to the chief steward, yet Yang Jun, utterly without propriety, cast himself as Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou, imagining he could hold the realm secure—and that is why he met his death.
entries.literal: The sovereign was in mourning seclusion and listened to the chief steward, yet Yang Jun, lacking all propriety, at once played Yi and Zhou, thinking himself secure in possession of all under Heaven—this is why he died.

entries.zh: 其罪既不可勝，亦是殿下所見。
entries.en: His crimes were beyond counting, as Your Highness yourself witnessed.
entries.literal: His crimes were already beyond numbering, as Your Highness also saw.

entries.zh: 駿之見討，發自天聰，孟觀、李肇與知密旨耳。
entries.en: Yang Jun's execution came from the emperor's own decision; only Meng Guan and Li Zhao knew the secret orders.
entries.literal: Jun's being punished issued from Heaven's discernment; Meng Guan and Li Zhao alone shared knowledge of the secret intent.

entries.zh: 至於論功，當歸美於上。
entries.en: When merit is assessed, the credit should go to the throne.
entries.literal: As for discussing merit, credit ought to be returned in praise to the sovereign.

entries.zh: 觀等已數千戶縣侯，聖上以駿死莫不欣悅，故論功寧厚，以敘其歡心。
entries.en: Guan and the others were already county marquises with estates of several thousand households. Since all rejoiced at Yang Jun's death, the emperor was willing to be generous in rewarding merit so as to share in that joy.
entries.literal: Guan and the others were already county marquises of several thousand households; the sage sovereign, since none failed to rejoice at Jun's death, therefore in assessing merit would rather be generous, so as to express their glad hearts.

entries.zh: 此群下所宜以實裁量，而遂扇動，東安封王，孟、李郡公，余侯伯子男，既妄有加，復又三等超遷。
entries.en: Subordinates should have measured rewards by actual merit, yet agitation followed: the Lord of Dong'an was enfeoffed as a prince, Meng and Li as commandery dukes, and the rest as marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons—first granted without warrant, then promoted three ranks beyond measure.
entries.literal: This is what the host of subordinates ought to measure by reality, yet they stirred things up: the Lord of Dong'an was enfeoffed as a king, Meng and Li as commandery dukes, the rest as marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons—first granted rashly, then promoted three ranks beyond measure.

entries.zh: 此之熏赫，震動天地，自古以來，封賞未有若此者也。
entries.en: Such dazzling rewards shook Heaven and Earth; never in history had enfeoffment and reward reached such heights.
entries.literal: Such blazing splendor shook Heaven and Earth; from antiquity to the present, enfeoffments and rewards have never been like this.

entries.zh: 無功而厚賞，莫不樂國有禍，禍起當復有大功也。
entries.en: When men are richly rewarded without merit, all come to hope for national calamity, since calamity would bring fresh chances for great reward.
entries.literal: Rewarding generously without merit—none failed to rejoice that the state would have disaster, for when disaster arose there would again be great merit.

entries.zh: 人而樂禍，其可極乎！
entries.en: When men rejoice in disaster, where will it end!
entries.literal: If men rejoice in disaster, can it have a limit!

entries.zh: 作此者，皆由東安公。
entries.en: All of this was the work of the Lord of Dong'an.
entries.literal: Those who did this all came through the Lord of Dong'an.

entries.zh: 謂殿下至止，當有以正之。
entries.en: When Your Highness takes charge, you should set this right.
entries.literal: I say that when Your Highness arrives and stops, there ought to be means to set it right.

entries.zh: 正之以道，眾亦何所怒乎！
entries.en: Set it right by proper principle, and what cause would the multitude have for anger!
entries.literal: If it is set right by the Way, what would the multitude have to resent!

entries.zh: 眾之所怒，在於不平耳。
entries.en: The multitude's anger rests on unfairness alone.
entries.literal: What the multitude resents lies in unfairness alone.

entries.zh: 而今皆更倍論，莫不失望。
entries.en: Yet now rewards are reckoned at double measure, and all have lost hope.
entries.literal: Yet now all are again counted at double measure, and none failed to lose hope.

entries.zh: 咸之愚冗，不惟失望而已，竊以為憂。
entries.en: In my dull incompetence I am not merely disappointed; I am privately deeply worried.
entries.literal: Xian's stupidity and redundancy is not only disappointment; I privately hold it a matter for worry.

entries.zh: 又討駿之時，殿下在外，實所不綜。
entries.en: Moreover, when Yang Jun was punished, Your Highness was away and in truth had no part in directing it.
entries.literal: Further, at the time of punishing Jun, Your Highness was outside and in truth did not oversee it.

entries.zh: 今欲委重，故令殿下論功。
entries.en: Now that weighty authority is to be entrusted to you, they have made Your Highness assess merit.
entries.literal: Now wishing to entrust weighty matters, they therefore have Your Highness assess merit.

entries.zh: 論功之事，實未易可處，莫若坐觀得失，有居正之事宜也。
entries.en: Assessing merit is truly no easy task. Better to watch how things turn out and intervene only when a matter of right principle requires it.
entries.literal: The matter of assessing merit is in truth not easy to handle; better to sit and observe gains and losses, and when there are matters of upright standing, then act.

entries.zh: 時朝廷寬弛，豪右放恣，交私請托，朝野溷淆。
entries.en: The court had grown lax; great families traded private favors until court and countryside were a blur.
entries.literal: At that time the court was lax and slack; powerful magnates gave free rein, mingling private requests and entrustments; court and countryside were confused.

entries.zh: 咸奏免河南尹澹、左將軍倩、廷尉高光、兼河南尹何攀等，京都肅然，貴戚懾伏。
entries.en: Fu Xian impeached the governor of Henan (surnamed Dan), the general of the left (surnamed Qian), the commandant of justice Gao Guang, and the concurrent governor of Henan He Pan; the capital grew orderly and the great houses trembled.
entries.literal: Xian memorialized to dismiss the governor of Henan, Dan, the general of the left, Qian, the commandant of justice Gao Guang, concurrent governor of Henan He Pan, and others; the capital was austere, and noble in-laws were awed into submission.

entries.zh: 咸以「聖人久于其道，天下化成。
entries.en: Fu Xian quoted: “When the sage long pursues his course, the realm is shaped by it.
entries.literal: Xian cited: “When the sage is long on his way, all under Heaven is transformed and completed.

entries.zh: 是以唐、虞三載考績，九年黜陟。
entries.en: Thus under Tang and Yu officials were graded every three years and promoted or demoted over nine.
entries.literal: Therefore Tang and Yu examined achievements over three years, promoting and demoting over nine years.

entries.zh: 其在《周禮》，三年大比。
entries.en: The Rites of Zhou prescribes a great review every three years.
entries.literal: In the Rites of Zhou, there is the great comparison every three years.

entries.zh: 孔子亦云，『三年有成』。
entries.en: Confucius too said, “Give three years and there will be results.”
entries.literal: Confucius also said, “In three years there is accomplishment.”

entries.zh: 而中間以來，長吏到官，未幾便遷，百姓困于無定，吏卒疲於送迎」。
entries.en: Yet of late magistrates are shuffled after a short stay; the people suffer endless instability, and runners collapse escorting one chief after another.”
entries.literal: Yet in the middle period since then, when senior officers reach their post, before long they are transferred; the hundred surnames are worn out by having no stability, clerks and soldiers exhausted by seeing off and welcoming.”

entries.zh: 時僕射王戎兼吏部，咸奏：「戎備位臺輔，兼掌選舉，不能謐靜風俗，以凝庶績，至令人心傾動，開張浮競。
entries.en: Vice-director Wang Rong then ran the ministry of appointments; Fu Xian charged: “Rong sits among the chief ministers and holds appointments, yet he cannot steady custom or settle administration; hearts waver and empty rivalry spreads.
