entries.literal: At that time the vice-director Wang Rong concurrently held the ministry of appointments; Xian memorialized: “Rong occupies a place among ministerial supports and concurrently controls selection; he cannot calm custom and stillness, to coalesce the duties of the many—to the point of letting human hearts tilt and drift, opening and spreading empty rivalry.

entries.zh: 中郎李重、李義不相匡正。
entries.en: The gentleman-attendants Li Chong and Li Yi never correct him.
entries.literal: The gentleman-attendants Li Chong and Li Yi do not correct him.

entries.zh: 請免戎等官。」
entries.en: I ask that Wang Rong and his like be removed from office.”
entries.literal: I ask that Rong and others be dismissed from office.”

entries.zh: 詔曰：「政道之本，誠宜久於其職，咸奏是也。
entries.en: The edict said: “Long tenure is the root of good government; Fu Xian is right.
entries.literal: The edict said: “The root of governing the way truly lies in long tenure in one’s post; what Xian memorialized is right.

entries.zh: 戎職在論道，吾所崇委，其解禁止。」
entries.en: Wang Rong’s duty is to counsel on the Way, which I value; lift the restrictions on him.”
entries.literal: Rong’s duty lies in discussing the Way—I esteem and entrust him; as for him, dissolve the prohibition.”

entries.zh: 御史中丞解結以咸劾戎為違典制，越局侵官，干非其分，奏免咸官。
entries.en: Metropolitan censor Xie Jie argued that impeaching Wang Rong broke the rules, overstepped Fu Xian’s charge, and meddled beyond his rank; he asked that Fu Xian be dismissed.
entries.literal: Metropolitan Censor Xie Jie held that Xian’s impeachment of Rong violated canonical regulation, overstepped his office and encroached on another’s duty, meddling beyond his portion, and memorialized to dismiss Xian from office.

entries.zh: 詔亦不許。
entries.en: The throne again refused.
entries.literal: An edict again did not permit it.

entries.zh: 咸上事以為「按令，御史中丞督司百僚。
entries.en: Fu Xian argued in a memorial: "By statute the metropolitan censor supervises every official at court.
entries.literal: Xian submitted a memorial holding: "According to the ordinance, the metropolitan censor supervises the hundred officials.

entries.zh: 皇太子以下，其在行馬內，有違法憲者皆彈糾之。
entries.en: Everyone from the crown prince downward who breaks the law inside the imperial patrol corridor falls under his impeachment.
entries.literal: Below the crown prince, those within the mounted patrol corridor who violate statutes are all impeached and investigated.

entries.zh: 雖在行馬外，而監司不糾，亦得奏之。
entries.en: Even outside that corridor, if the regional inspectors fail to act, he may still memorialize against them.
entries.literal: Although outside the mounted corridor, if supervising officials do not impeach, he may still memorialize on them.

entries.zh: 如令之文，行馬之內有違法憲，謂禁防之事耳。
entries.en: The statute’s wording ties the corridor to palace security alone.
entries.literal: As the ordinance's wording stands, violations of statutes within the mounted corridor refer to matters of forbidden-precinct security alone.

entries.zh: 宮內禁防，外司不得而行，故專施中丞。
entries.en: Inner-palace security is closed to outside bureaus, which is why the metropolitan censor alone holds that beat.
entries.literal: Forbidden precincts inside the palace—outside agencies may not act therein—therefore authority is vested solely in the central censor.

entries.zh: 今道路橋梁不修，鬥訟屠沽不絕，如此之比，中丞推責州坐，即今所謂行馬內語施於禁防。
entries.en: Neglected roads, endless lawsuits, unruly markets—the censor blames the province, yet people now stretch the phrase ‘inside the corridor’ to cover such civic ills.
entries.literal: Now roads and bridges are not repaired, brawls and butchers and peddlers do not cease—such cases: the censor presses blame on the province to sit—then what is now called 'within the mounted corridor' language is applied to security matters.

entries.zh: 既雲中丞督司百僚矣，何復說行馬之內乎！
entries.en: If the censor already oversees all officials, why narrow him again to the corridor?
entries.literal: Since it already says the central censor supervises the hundred officials, why again speak of 'within the mounted corridor'!

entries.zh: 既雲百僚，而不得復說行馬之內者，內外眾官謂之百僚，則通內外矣。
entries.en: The ‘hundred officials’ means everyone at court and in the provinces—inside and outside together.
entries.literal: Since it says 'hundred officials,' yet may not again speak of 'within the mounted corridor'—the many officials inside and out are called the hundred officials, then it comprehends inside and outside.

entries.zh: 司隸所以不復說行馬內外者，禁防之事已於中丞說之故也。
entries.en: The colonel director omits the corridor because the censor’s statute already covers palace security.
entries.literal: The reason the colonel director of retainers does not again speak of inside or outside the mounted corridor is that security matters were already stated with regard to the central censor.

entries.zh: 中丞、司隸俱糾皇太子以下，則共對司內外矣，不為中丞專司內百僚，司隸專司外百僚。
entries.en: Censor and colonel both impeach from the crown prince down; they share inner and outer duty—it is not a split between two separate rosters.
entries.literal: Central censor and colonel director of retainers together impeach from the crown prince downward, then they jointly face duties inside and outside—it is not that the central censor solely supervises inner hundred officials and the colonel solely outer hundred officials.

entries.zh: 自有中丞、司隸以來，更互奏內外眾官，惟所糾得無內外之限也。
entries.en: Since both offices were created they have taken turns impeaching officials everywhere, with no hard line between inner and outer.
entries.literal: From the time there have been central censor and colonel director of retainers, they have alternately memorialized on many officials inside and out—only when impeaching there is no inside-outside limit.

entries.zh: 而結一旦橫挫臣，臣前所以不羅縷者，冀因結奏得從私願也。
entries.en: Xie Jie suddenly blocked me; I had not argued every clause because I hoped his memorial would win me the ruling I sought.
entries.literal: Yet Jie in one morning harshly thwarted your subject; the reason your subject earlier did not belabor detail was that I hoped through Jie's memorial my private wish might be granted.

entries.zh: 今既所願不從，而敕雲但為過耳，非所不及也，以此見原。
entries.en: Now my request is denied, yet the edict calls it a mere excess—not something beyond my duty—and forgives me on that ground.
entries.literal: Now since what was wished is not followed, yet the edict says it was only excess, not what one could not reach, and by this pardons me.

entries.zh: 臣忝司直之任，宜當正己率人，若其有過，不敢受原，是以申陳其愚。
entries.en: I hold the post of censor-in-chief: I must set the example. If I was wrong I should not be excused, so I lay out my reasoning bluntly.
entries.literal: Your subject disgraces the duty of director of correctness—ought to rectify self and lead others; if there is fault, I dare not accept pardon—therefore I declare this foolishness.

entries.zh: 司隸與中丞俱共糾皇太子以下，則從皇太子以下無所不糾也。
entries.en: If censor and colonel both impeach from the crown prince downward, nothing below that rank lies outside their reach.
entries.literal: When colonel director of retainers and central censor together impeach from the crown prince down, then from the crown prince down there is nothing they do not impeach.

entries.zh: 得糾皇太子而不得糾尚書，臣之暗塞既所未譬。
entries.en: I may impeach the heir yet not the secretariat director—this blind spot I cannot understand.
entries.literal: To be able to impeach the crown prince yet not be able to impeach the director of the secretariat—your subject's dim obstruction I have never grasped the parallel.

entries.zh: 皇太子為在行馬之內邪，皇太子在行馬之內而得糾之，尚書在行馬之內而不得糾，無有此理。
entries.en: Is the heir inside the corridor or not? If the heir inside may be impeached but the secretariat director inside may not, that rule does not exist.
entries.literal: Is the crown prince inside the mounted corridor or not? If the crown prince inside the mounted corridor may be impeached, yet the director of the secretariat inside the mounted corridor may not be impeached—there is no such principle.

entries.zh: 此理灼然，而結以此挫臣。
entries.en: The logic is obvious, yet Xie Jie used it to block me.
entries.literal: This principle is glaringly clear, yet Jie for this thwarted your subject.

entries.zh: 臣可無恨耳，其於觀聽，無乃有怪邪！
entries.en: I can swallow the insult—but will not the world find it absurd?
entries.literal: Your subject may have no resentment—but for those who look and listen, is it not strange!

entries.zh: 臣識石公前在殿上脫衣，為司隸荀愷所奏，先帝不以為非，于時莫謂侵官；
entries.en: I recall when Lord Shi stripped in the hall and Xun Kai impeached him—the late emperor approved, and no one cried ‘overreach.’
entries.literal: Your subject remembers when Lord Shi bared his torso in the hall, impeached by colonel director Xun Kai—the late emperor did not think it wrong; at the time none said it encroached on office;

entries.zh: 今臣裁糾尚書，而當有罪乎？」
entries.en: Am I now to be punished for impeaching only the secretariat director?"
entries.literal: now when your subject only impeached the director of the secretariat, should there be guilt?"

entries.zh: 咸累自上稱引故事，條理灼然，朝廷無以易之。
entries.en: Fu Xian piled precedent on precedent until the case was airtight and the court could not refute him.
entries.literal: Xian repeatedly cited himself to superior, adducing precedents; the ordering was clear and the court had no way to change it.

entries.zh: 傅祗
entries.en: Fu Zhi
entries.literal: Fu Zhi.

entries.zh: 祗字子莊。
entries.en: Fu Zhi, courtesy name Zizhuang.
entries.literal: Zhi's style name was Zizhuang.

entries.zh: 父嘏，魏太常。
entries.en: His father, Fu Gu, had been grand master of ceremonies under the Wei.
entries.literal: His father was Gu, grand master of ceremonies of Wei.

entries.zh: 祗性至孝，早知名，以才識明練稱。
entries.en: Deeply filial and famous early, he was admired for shrewd, seasoned ability.
entries.literal: Zhi by nature was utmost filial, early known by name, praised for talent, insight, clarity, and experience.

entries.zh: 武帝始建東宮，起家太子舍人，累遷散騎黃門郎，賜爵關內侯，食邑三百戶。
entries.en: When Emperor Wu of Jin founded the heir’s palace, Fu Zhi left mourning to become an heir’s attendant, rose to cavalier attendant and gentleman at the yellow gate, and received a secondary marquisate within the passes with three hundred households.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu of Jin first built the eastern palace, on leaving mourning he became attendant to the heir apparent; by stages he was promoted to cavalier attendant and gentleman at the yellow gate, enfeoffed secondary marquis within the passes with three hundred households' income.

entries.zh: 母憂去職。
entries.en: He resigned to mourn his mother.
entries.literal: On his mother's bereavement he left office.

entries.zh: 及葬母，詔給太常五等吉凶導從。
entries.en: For her burial the court ordered the grand master of ceremonies to supply the full five-grade funeral escort.
entries.literal: When burying his mother, an edict granted the grand master of ceremonies the five-grade auspicious and inauspicious escort squads.

entries.zh: 其後諸卿夫人葬給導從，自此始也。
entries.en: Later, when ministers’ wives were buried, they too received such escorts—the practice began with him.
entries.literal: Afterwards when ministers' wives were buried they were given escort squads—this began here.

entries.zh: 服終，為滎陽太守。
entries.en: When mourning ended he became governor of Xingyang.
entries.literal: When mourning ended he became governor of Xingyang.

entries.zh: 自魏黃初大水之後，河濟泛溢，鄧艾嘗著《濟河論》，開石門而通之，至是復浸壞。
entries.en: After Wei’s Huangchu flood the Yellow and Ji had burst their banks; Deng Ai’s treatise and the stone sluice he opened had long held the waters—by now the works had failed again.
entries.literal: From after the great flood of Wei Huangchu, the Yellow and Ji rivers overflowed; Deng Ai once wrote the "On the Ji and Yellow Rivers," opening the stone gate to connect them—to this point they were again inundated and ruined.

entries.zh: 祗乃造沈萊堰，至今兗、豫無水患，百姓為立碑頌焉。
entries.en: Fu Zhi built the Shen and Lai embankments; Yan and Yu have been free of floods since, and the people raised a stele in his honor.
entries.literal: Zhi thereupon built the Shen-Lai weirs; to this day Yan and Yu have no water harm; the hundred surnames erected a stele in praise.

entries.zh: 尋表兼廷尉，遷常侍、左軍將軍。
entries.en: Soon he added the post of commandant of justice, then became a regular attendant and general of the left army.
entries.literal: Soon he memorialed to concurrently hold commandant of justice, was promoted to regular attendant and general of the left army.

entries.zh: 及帝崩，梓宮在殯，而太傅楊駿輔政，欲悅眾心，議普進封爵。
entries.en: While the emperor’s coffin still lay in mourning, Grand Tutor Yang Jun ran the government and proposed blanket promotions to buy popularity.
entries.literal: When the emperor died, while the catalpa coffin was still in the mourning shed, grand tutor Yang Jun directed the government, wishing to please the multitude's hearts, debated universally advancing noble ranks.

entries.zh: 祗與駿書曰：「未有帝王始崩，臣下論功者也。」
entries.en: Fu Zhi wrote to Yang Jun: "No worthy court has ever handed out rewards for merit the moment an emperor dies."
entries.literal: Zhi wrote to Jun: "Never yet has there been discussion of ministers' merits when an emperor has first died."

entries.zh: 駿不從。
entries.en: Jun ignored him.
entries.literal: Jun did not follow.

entries.zh: 入為侍中。
entries.en: He was summoned to palace attendant.
entries.literal: He entered as palace attendant.

entries.zh: 時將誅駿，而駿不之知。
entries.en: The coup against Jun was already set, yet Jun knew nothing.
entries.literal: At the time they were about to execute Jun, yet Jun did not know it.

entries.zh: 祗侍駿坐，而雲龍門閉，內外不通。
entries.en: Fu Zhi was sitting with Jun when word came that the Dragon Gate was sealed and the palace cut off from the city.
entries.literal: Zhi attended Jun seated, yet it was said the Dragon Gate was closed, inside and outside not communicating.

entries.zh: 祗請與尚書武茂聽國家消息，揖而下階。
entries.en: Fu Zhi asked to go with Wu Mao of the secretariat to learn the court’s fate, bowed, and stepped down from the hall.
entries.literal: Zhi asked to go with Wu Mao of the secretariat to listen for news of the state, bowed and went down the steps.

entries.zh: 茂猶坐，祗顧曰：「君非天子臣邪！
entries.en: Wu Mao remained seated; Fu Zhi turned and cried, ‘Are you not a minister of the throne?’
entries.literal: Mao still sat; Zhi looked back saying: "Are you not the Son of Heaven's minister!

entries.zh: 今內外隔絕，不知國家所在，何得安坐！」
entries.en: ‘Inside and outside are sealed—we do not even know where the sovereign is—how can you sit at ease?’"
entries.literal: Now inside and outside are cut off; we do not know where the court is—how can you sit at ease!"

entries.zh: 茂乃驚起。
entries.en: Wu Mao leapt up in alarm.
entries.literal: Mao then rose in alarm.

entries.zh: 駿既伏誅，裴楷息瓚，駿之婿也，為亂兵所害。
entries.en: When Jun fell, Pei Kai’s son Pei Zan—Jun’s son-in-law—was cut down by mutinous troops.
entries.literal: After Jun was put to death, Pei Kai's son Zan, Jun's son-in-law, was killed by mutinous soldiers.

entries.zh: 尚書左僕射荀愷與楷不平，因奏楷是駿親，收付廷尉。
entries.en: Left vice-director Xun Kai, who hated Pei Kai, memorialized that Kai was Jun’s intimate and had him arrested for the commandant of justice.
entries.literal: Vice-director of the secretariat, left, Xun Kai was not at peace with Kai, therefore memorialized that Kai was Jun's close kin and had him seized and handed to the commandant of justice.

entries.zh: 祗證楷無罪，有詔赦之。
entries.en: Fu Zhi testified that Pei Kai was innocent, and an edict freed him.
entries.literal: Zhi testified that Kai had no crime; an edict pardoned him.

entries.zh: 時又收駿官屬，祗復啟曰：「昔魯芝為曹爽司馬，斬關出赴爽，宣帝義之，尚遷青州刺史。
entries.en: When Jun's staff were also arrested, Fu Zhi submitted another statement: "In the past Lu Zhi served as Sima to Cao Shuang, broke through the gates and rode out to join him, and Emperor Xuan approved his loyalty and still promoted him to inspector of Qingzhou.
entries.literal: At the time they also seized Jun's subordinates; Zhi again stated: "In the past Lu Zhi was Sima to Cao Shuang, broke the gate bars and rode out to join Shuang—Emperor Xuan praised his righteousness and still promoted him to inspector of Qingzhou.

entries.zh: 駿之僚佐不可加罰。」
entries.en: Yang Jun’s aides should not be punished further."
entries.literal: Jun's staff aides must not receive added punishment."

entries.zh: 詔又赦之。
entries.en: Another edict pardoned them.
entries.literal: An edict again pardoned them.

entries.zh: 祗多所維正皆如此。
entries.en: Time and again Fu Zhi steadied justice in this way.
entries.literal: Zhi's many upholdings of rectitude were all like this.

entries.zh: 除河南尹，未拜，遷司隸校尉。
entries.en: He was named governor of Henan but before taking office was made colonel director of retainers.
entries.literal: He was appointed governor of Henan; before investiture he was promoted colonel director of retainers.

entries.zh: 以討楊駿勳，當封郡公八千戶，固讓，減半，降封靈川縣公，千八百戶，餘二千二百戶封少子暢為武鄉亭侯。
entries.en: For crushing Yang Jun he merited a commandery-duke’s fief of eight thousand households; he refused until the court halved it to a district duke of Lingchuan with eighteen hundred households and enfeoffed his youngest son Chang as village marquis of Wuxiang with the remainder.
entries.literal: For merit in striking Yang Jun he ought to have been enfeoffed duke of a commandery with eight thousand households; he firmly declined, halved it, was demoted in enfeoffment to duke of Lingchuan district with one thousand eight hundred households, the remaining two thousand two hundred households enfeoffed his youngest son Chang as village marquis of Wuxiang.

entries.zh: 又以本封賜兄子雋為東明亭侯。
entries.en: From his original grant he also made his nephew Jun village marquis of Dongming.
entries.literal: Further with his original fief he bestowed on elder brother's son Jun village marquis of Dongming.

entries.zh: 楚王瑋之矯詔也，祗以聞奏稽留，免官。
entries.en: When Prince Chu, Sima Wei, forged an edict, Fu Zhi was dismissed for slow reporting.
entries.literal: When Prince Chu, Wei, forged the edict, Zhi because reporting was delayed was dismissed.

entries.zh: 期年，遷光祿勳，復以公事免。
entries.en: A year later he became grand master of splendid horses, then was removed again over a public affair.
entries.literal: After a full year he was promoted grand master of splendid horses; again for public affairs he was dismissed.

entries.zh: 氐人齊萬年舉兵反，以祗為行安西軍司，加常侍，率安西將軍夏侯駿討平之。
entries.en: When the Di leader Qi Wannian rebelled, Fu Zhi served as acting chief of staff for the Army of the West with concurrent regular attendant, accompanying General Who Pacifies the West Xiahou Jun to crush the revolt.
entries.literal: The Di man Qi Wannian raised troops in revolt; Zhi was made acting army director of Pacifying-the-West, with concurrent regular attendant, and led General Who Pacifies the West Xiahou Jun to strike and pacify him.

entries.zh: 遷衛尉，以風疾遜位，就拜常侍，食卿祿秩，賜錢及床帳等。
entries.en: Promoted commandant of the guards, he resigned with a palsy, was kept as regular attendant on ministerial salary, and given cash, bedding, and the like.
entries.literal: He was promoted commandant of the guards, on wind illness yielded place, was then appointed regular attendant, ate ministerial salary ranks, was granted cash, bed-curtains, and so on.

entries.zh: 尋加光祿大夫，門施行馬。
entries.en: Soon he added the title grand counsellor of splendid horses and was allowed the mounted patrol barrier at his gate.
entries.literal: Soon he was added grand counsellor of splendid horses; mounted patrol lanes were set up at his gate.

entries.zh: 及趙王倫輔政，以為中書監，常侍如故，以鎮眾心。
entries.en: When Prince Zhao, Sima Lun, took charge, he made Fu Zhi overseer of the secretariat, still a regular attendant, to calm public opinion.
entries.literal: When Prince Zhao, Lun, directed the government, he made him overseer of the secretariat, regular attendant as before, to steady the host of hearts.

entries.zh: 祗辭之以疾，倫遣御史輿祗就職。
entries.en: Fu Zhi pleaded illness; Lun sent a censor with a litter to force him to his desk.
entries.literal: Zhi declined on grounds of illness; Lun sent a censor to carry Zhi in a litter to take up office.

entries.zh: 王戎、陳准等相與言曰：「傅公在事，吾屬無憂矣。」
entries.en: Wang Rong and Chen Zhun said to each other, ‘With Lord Fu at the helm we need not worry.’
entries.literal: Wang Rong, Chen Zhun, and others spoke together: "With Lord Fu in charge, our sort has no worries."

entries.zh: 其為物所倚信如此。
entries.en: Such was the trust men placed in him.
entries.literal: Thus he was trusted by others to this degree.

entries.zh: 倫篡，又為右光祿、開府，加侍中。
entries.en: When Lun seized the throne, Fu Zhi became right grand master of splendid horses with independent establishment and added palace attendant.
entries.literal: When Lun usurped, he again was right grand master of splendid horses, established office, added palace attendant.

entries.zh: 惠帝還宮，祗以經受偽職請退，不許。
entries.en: After Emperor Hui returned, Fu Zhi asked to resign for having served the usurper; the court refused.
entries.literal: When Emperor Hui returned to the palace, Zhi because he had received illicit office asked to retire—not permitted.

entries.zh: 初，倫之篡也，孫秀與義陽王威等十餘人預撰儀式禪文。
entries.en: When Lun first usurped, Sun Xiu, Prince Yiyang Sima Wei, and a dozen others had drafted the abdication liturgy and text.
entries.literal: At first when Lun usurped, Sun Xiu and Prince of Yiyang, Wei, and more than a dozen others pre-drafted the ceremonies and abdication texts.

entries.zh: 及倫敗，齊王冏收侍中劉逵、常侍騶捷、杜育、黃門郎陸機、右丞周導、王尊等付廷尉。
entries.en: When Lun fell, Prince Qi Sima Jiong arrested Liu Dai, Zou Jie, Du Yu, Lu Ji, Zhou Dao, Wang Zun, and others for the commandant of justice.
entries.literal: When Lun fell, the prince of Qi, Jiong, seized palace attendant Liu Dai, regular attendants Zou Jie, Du Yu, yellow gate gentleman Lu Ji, right aide Zhou Dao, Wang Zun, and others and handed them to the commandant of justice.

entries.zh: 以禪文出中書，復議處祗罪，會赦得原。
entries.en: Because the abdication edict had issued from the secretariat, some wanted Fu Zhi punished, but a general amnesty spared him.
entries.literal: Because the abdication text came from the secretariat, they again debated punishing Zhi's crime, but a general amnesty arrived and he was pardoned.

entries.zh: 後以禪文草本非祗所撰，於是詔復光祿大夫。
entries.en: Later it was shown the draft was not his hand, and an edict restored him as grand counsellor of splendid horses.
entries.literal: Later because the abdication draft in manuscript was not written by Zhi, thereupon an edict restored him as grand counsellor of splendid horses.

entries.zh: 子宣，尚弘農公主。
entries.en: His son Fu Xuan married the princess of Hongnong.
entries.literal: His son Xuan married the Princess of Hongnong.

entries.zh: 尋遷太子少傅，上章遜位還第。
entries.en: Soon he became junior tutor to the heir apparent, then begged leave to retire home.
entries.literal: Soon he was promoted junior tutor to the heir apparent; he submitted a memorial yielding office and returning home.

entries.zh: 及成都王穎為太傅，復以祗為少傅，加侍中。
entries.en: When Prince Chengdu Sima Ying became grand tutor, he again named Fu Zhi junior tutor with added palace attendant.
entries.literal: When Prince Chengdu, Ying, was grand tutor, again he made Zhi junior tutor, added palace attendant.

entries.zh: 懷帝即位，遷光祿大夫、侍中，未拜，加右僕射、中書監。
entries.en: Under Emperor Huai he rose to grand counsellor of splendid horses and palace attendant, then—before the first appointment took effect—added right vice-director and overseer of the secretariat.
entries.literal: When Emperor Huai mounted the throne, he was promoted grand counsellor of splendid horses and palace attendant; before investiture he was added right vice-director and overseer of the secretariat.

entries.zh: 時太傅東海王越輔政，祗既居端右，每宣君臣謙光之道，由此上下雍穆。
entries.en: While Grand Tutor Prince Donghai Sima Yue governed, Fu Zhi as senior minister on the right preached mutual deference between sovereign and ministers, and court relations grew calm.
entries.literal: At that time grand tutor Prince of Donghai Yue directed the government; Zhi already stood at the head of the right—often he proclaimed the way of ruler and ministers yielding glory, and thereby above and below were harmonious and reverent.

entries.zh: 祗明達國體，朝廷制度多所經綜。
entries.en: He grasped how the state should run and had shaped many of its institutions.
entries.literal: Zhi understood the state's body; many court systems he had managed and drawn together.

entries.zh: 曆左光祿、開府，行太子太傅，侍中如故。
entries.en: He passed through left grand master of splendid horses with independent establishment, acting grand tutor to the heir apparent, still a palace attendant.
entries.literal: He served as left grand master of splendid horses, established office, acting grand tutor to the heir apparent, palace attendant as before.

entries.zh: 疾篤遜位，不許。
entries.en: Gravely ill, he asked to retire; the court refused.
entries.literal: On grave illness he yielded office—not permitted.

entries.zh: 遷司徒，以足疾，詔版輿上殿，不拜。
entries.en: Raised to minister of education, he was carried in a litter to court because of his feet and excused from bowing.
entries.literal: He was promoted minister of education; on foot ailment an edict ordered a litter to the hall; he did not bow.

entries.zh: 大將軍苟晞表請遷都，使祗出詣河陰，修理舟楫，為水行之備。
entries.en: General Gou Xi proposed moving the capital and sent Fu Zhi to Heyin to ready boats for a river retreat.
entries.literal: Great general Gou Xi memorialized requesting removal of the capital, sent Zhi out to Heyin to repair boats and oars, preparing for travel by water.

entries.zh: 及洛陽陷沒，遂共建行台，推祗為盟主，以司徒、持節、大都督諸軍事傳檄四方。
entries.en: When Luoyang fell, the exiles set up a mobile command, chose Fu Zhi as their head, and issued calls in his name as minister of education, credential-bearing supreme commander.
entries.literal: When Luoyang fell and was lost, they thereupon jointly set up a mobile headquarters, pushed Zhi to be covenant lord, transmitting proclamations in the four directions as minister of education, bearer of the staff of authority, grand governor of military affairs.

entries.zh: 遣子宣將公主與尚書令和郁赴告方伯征義兵，祗自屯盟津小城，宣弟暢行河陰令，以待宣。
entries.en: He sent Fu Xuan with the princess and He Yu, the director of the secretariat, to rally regional lords while he himself held the small fort at Meng Ford; his younger son Chang served as magistrate of Heyin to cover the crossing.
entries.literal: He sent son Xuan leading the princess and Director of the secretariat He Yu to notify regional governors and summon righteous troops; Zhi himself camped at the small fort of Meng Ford; Xuan's younger brother Chang acted as magistrate of Heyin to await Xuan.

entries.zh: 祗以暴疾薨，時年六十九。
entries.en: Fu Zhi died of a sudden illness at sixty-nine.
entries.literal: Zhi died of sudden illness at age sixty-nine.

entries.zh: 祗自以義誠不終，力疾手筆敕厲其二子宣、暢，辭旨深切，覽者莫不感激慷慨。
entries.en: Believing his duty of loyalty unfinished, he dragged himself from his sickbed to write a fierce testament for Xuan and Chang; every reader was moved to tears.
entries.literal: Zhi himself thought his obligation of loyalty unfinished; with force of sickness he personally wrote in brush stern admonition to his two sons Xuan and Chang; the wording was bitter and deep, none who read it failed to be moved and roused.

entries.zh: 祗著文章駁論十餘萬言。
entries.en: He left more than a hundred thousand characters of essays and polemics.
entries.literal: Zhi authored refutation essays of over a hundred thousand graphs.

entries.zh: 史臣曰：武帝覽觀四方，平章百姓，永言啟沃，任切爭臣。
entries.en: The historians write: Emperor Wu surveyed the realm and weighed the welfare of the people; longing for frank counsel, he charged his remonstrating ministers with a heavy trust.
entries.literal: The history clerk says: Emperor Wu surveyed the four quarters and balanced assessment of the hundred surnames; ever speaking of opening and fertilizing, he entrusted a cutting task to ministers who contend.

entries.zh: 傅玄體強直之姿，懷匪躬之操，抗辭正色，補闕弼違，諤諤當朝，不忝其職者矣。
entries.en: Fu Xuan was rigid and upright, selfless in devotion, spoke his mind with stern dignity, and strove to mend faults at court—he did honor to his office.
entries.literal: Fu Xuan embodied the posture of forceful straightness, cherished the integrity of not being for himself alone, resisted in words with upright countenance, mended omissions and aided against error; forthright in court, he did not disgrace his office.

entries.zh: 及乎位居三獨，彈擊是司，遂能使台閣生風，貴戚斂手。
entries.en: Once he held one of the three independent censorial posts and wielded the power of impeachment, the ministries stiffened with discipline and the great families pulled in their claws.
entries.literal: When he reached office among the three independents and impeachment was his charge, then he could make the bureaus catch a new wind and noble in-laws draw in their hands.

entries.zh: 雖前代鮑、葛，何以加之！
entries.en: Even Han’s Bao Xuan and Ge Ying would not have surpassed him.
entries.literal: Even the Bao and Ge of former dynasties—how could one add beyond them!

entries.zh: 然而惟此褊心，乏弘雅之度，驟聞競爽，為物議所譏，惜哉！
entries.en: Yet his narrow temper lacked easy magnanimity; quick to bristle at rivals, he earned public ridicule—a pity.
entries.literal: Yet only this narrow mind lacked breadth in magnanimous demeanor; abruptly hearing rival brilliance, he was mocked by public opinion—pity!

entries.zh: 古人取戒于韋弦，良有以也。
entries.en: The ancients took both the soft leather and the tight bowstring as their teachers—how true that remains.
entries.literal: The ancients took warning from leather and bowstring—truly there was reason.

entries.zh: 長虞風格凝峻，弗墜家聲。
entries.en: Fu Xian’s manner was grave and austere; he did not shame his father’s name.
entries.literal: Changyu's manner was concentrated and stern; he did not let the family reputation fall.

entries.zh: 及其納諫汝南，獻書臨晉，居諒直之地，有先見之明矣。
entries.en: When he pressed his advice on the king of Runan and sent his memorials from the Linjin command, he stood in the place of blunt loyalty and showed real foresight.
entries.literal: When it came to his offering remonstrance at Runan and presenting writings at Linjin, occupying a place of honesty and straightness, he had foresight indeed.

entries.zh: 傅祗名父之子，早樹風猷，崎嶇危亂之朝，匡救君臣之際，卒能保全祿位，可謂有道存焉。
entries.en: Fu Zhi, son of a famous minister, showed his quality early; through a time of coups and chaos he steadied sovereign and subject and kept his honor and salary—clearly the Way lived in him.
entries.literal: Fu Zhi, son of a renowned father, early set his course; in a court rugged with peril he righted ruler and minister at the crisis, and in the end could preserve rank and stipend—one may say the Way was in him.

entries.zh: 贊曰：鶉觚貞諒，實惟朝望。
entries.en: The encomium reads: The baron of Chungu, steadfast and true, was indeed the court’s moral backbone.
entries.literal: Encomium says: Chungu's steadfast loyalty—truly a pillar of the court.

entries.zh: 志厲強直，性乖夷曠。
entries.en: His will was fierce and upright; his temper turned away from easy-going tolerance.
entries.literal: His will was stern with straightness; his nature ran against easy breadth.

entries.zh: 長虞剛簡，無虧風尚。
entries.en: Fu Xian’s stern simplicity never betrayed the family’s standards.
entries.literal: Changyu was stern and simple, without loss to conduct.

entries.zh: 子莊才識，爰膺袞職。
entries.en: Fu Zhi, styled Zizhuang, matched talent to insight and shouldered the highest offices.
entries.literal: Zizhuang's talent and insight—then bore the robes of office.

entries.zh: 忠績未申，泉途遽逼。=
entries.en: His loyal service was cut short; the road to the grave came all too soon.
entries.literal: Loyal deeds not fully declared, the road to the springs pressed suddenly.

entries.zh: 宣字世弘。
entries.en: Fu Xuan, courtesy name Shihong.
entries.literal: Xuan's style name was Shihong.

entries.zh: 年六歲喪繼母，哭泣如成人，中表異之。
entries.en: At six he lost his stepmother and wept like a grown man; kinsfolk marveled.
entries.literal: At age six he lost his stepmother; he wept like an adult, and cousins marveled.

entries.zh: 及長，好學，趙王倫以為相國掾、尚書郎、太子中舍人，遷司徒西曹掾。
entries.en: As an adult he loved books; Prince Zhao Lun made him aide to the minister of state, secretary, heir’s gentleman, then aide in the minister of education’s western bureau.
entries.literal: When grown he loved learning; Prince Zhao Lun made him aide to the minister of state, gentleman of the secretariat, palace gentleman to the heir apparent; he was promoted aide in the western bureau of the minister of education.

entries.zh: 去職，累遷為秘書丞、驃騎從事中郎。
entries.en: After resigning he rose to secretary’s aide and staff officer to the general who gallops to battle.
entries.literal: Leaving office, by stages he was promoted secretary assistant, aide-de-camp on the staff of the general who gallops to battle.

entries.zh: 惠帝至自長安，以宣為左丞，不就，遷黃門郎。
entries.en: When Emperor Hui returned from Chang’an, Fu Xuan was named left aide but declined, then was made gentleman at the yellow gate.
entries.literal: When Emperor Hui returned from Chang-an, Xuan was made left aide—he did not take office—and was promoted gentleman at the yellow gate.

entries.zh: 懷帝即位，轉吏部郎，又為御史中丞。
entries.en: Under Emperor Huai he became a gentleman in the ministry of personnel, then metropolitan censor again.
entries.literal: When Emperor Huai mounted the throne, he was transferred to gentleman of the ministry of personnel, again became metropolitan censor.

entries.zh: 卒年四十九，無子，以暢子沖為嗣。
entries.en: He died at forty-nine without a son, so his brother Chang’s son Chong inherited the line.
entries.literal: He died at age forty-nine, without sons; Chang's son Chong was made heir.

entries.zh: 傅玄
entries.en: Fu Xuan
entries.literal: Fu Xuan.

entries.zh: 永甯初，出為郟令。
entries.en: In Yongning he became magistrate of Jia.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Yongning—went out as magistrate of Jia.

entries.zh: 于時兵亂之後，境內饑饉，譚傾心撫䘏。
entries.en: After war famine stalked his district—Tan poured himself into relief.
entries.literal: At that time after military chaos—within the borders famine—Tan poured heart into comforting relief.

entries.zh: 司徒王戎聞而善之，出穀三百斛以助之。
entries.en: Wang Rong heard and sent three hundred hu of grain.
entries.literal: Minister Wang Rong hearing praised him—issued grain three hundred hu to assist.

entries.zh: 譚甚有政績，再遷廬江內史，加綏遠將軍。
entries.en: His rule excelled—he rose to interior governor of Lujiang with the Pacify-the-Distant generalship.
entries.literal: Tan had very good administrative merit—promoted again to Interior Governor of Lujiang—added General Who Pacifies the Distance.

entries.zh: 時石冰之党陸圭等屯據諸縣，譚遣司馬褚敦討平之。
entries.en: When Lu Gui's band held counties for Shi Bing, Tan sent Chu Dun to crush them.
entries.literal: At that time Shi Bing's faction Lu Gui and others garrisoned and held various counties—Tan dispatched Marshal Chu Dun to punish and pacify.

entries.zh: 又遣別軍擊冰都督孟徐，獲其驍率。
entries.en: Another column struck Meng Xu—taking his fiercest captain.
entries.literal: He also dispatched separate troops to strike Bing's commander-in-chief Meng Xu—captured his fierce leader.

entries.zh: 以功封都亭侯，食邑千戶，賜絹千匹。
entries.en: For merit he became Village Marquis—thousand-house fief and thousand bolts of silk.
entries.literal: By merit ennobled Village Marquis—food estate thousand households—silk thousand bolts.

entries.zh: 郤詵
entries.en: Xi Shen.
entries.literal: Xi Shen.

entries.zh: 邵續，字嗣祖，魏郡安陽人也。
entries.en: Shao Xu, courtesy Sizu, came from Anyang in Wei Commandery.
entries.literal: Shao Xu, style name Sizu, was a man of Anyang in Wei Commandery.

entries.zh: 父乘，散騎侍郎。
entries.en: His father, Shao Cheng, had risen to gentleman attendant at leisure.
entries.literal: His father Shao Cheng was gentleman attendant at leisure.

entries.zh: 續樸素有志烈，博覽經史，善談理義，妙解天文。
entries.en: Shao Xu lived plainly and held fierce convictions; he read deeply across the classics and histories, argued principle with ease, and read the stars with uncommon skill.
entries.literal: Shao Xu was plain and frugal and possessed of fierce resolve; he read widely in the classics and histories, was skilled at discussing principle and meaning, and had a subtle grasp of astronomy.

entries.zh: 初為成都王穎參軍，穎將討長沙王乂，續諫曰：「續聞兄弟如左右手，今明公當天下之敵，而欲去一手乎？
entries.en: He first joined the staff of Prince Chengdu, Sima Ying. When Ying prepared to strike Prince Changsha, Sima Yi, Shao Xu urged him: "They say brothers are like a man's two hands; you stand against the whole realm—would you willingly cut one off?
entries.literal: At first he served as army adviser to Prince Chengdu Sima Ying; when Ying was about to campaign against Prince Changsha Sima Yi, Shao Xu remonstrated: "I have heard that brothers are like the left and right hand; now the enlightened lord faces the empire's foes—would you wish to remove one hand?

entries.zh: 續竊惑之。」
entries.en: He could not fathom Ying's plan."
entries.literal: Shao Xu privately was perplexed by this."

entries.zh: 穎不納。
entries.en: Ying would not listen.
entries.literal: Ying did not accept it.

entries.zh: 後為苟晞參軍，除沁水令。
entries.en: He later served on Gou Xi's staff and was named magistrate of Qinshui.
entries.literal: Later he served as army adviser to Gou Xi and was appointed magistrate of Qinshui.

entries.zh: 李矩，字世回，平陽人也。
entries.en: Li Ju, courtesy Shihui, came from Pingyang.
entries.literal: Li Ju, style name Shihui, was a man of Pingyang.

entries.zh: 童齔時，與群兒聚戲，便為其率，計畫指授，有成人之量。
entries.en: Even as a boy, when he played with neighborhood children he always commanded them, laying plans like a grown man.
entries.literal: In childhood when he gathered with other children to play, he became their leader, planning and directing as would an adult.

entries.zh: 及長，為吏，送故縣令于長安，征西將軍梁王肜以為牙門。
entries.en: As a young man he served as a clerk; escorting a former magistrate to Chang'an, he was recruited as a gate guard by Sima Rong, Prince of Liang, the general commanding the western expedition.
entries.literal: When grown he became a clerk; seeing off a former magistrate to Chang'an, the western expedition general Sima Rong, Prince of Liang, took him on as yamen guard.

entries.zh: 伐氐齊萬年有殊功，封東明亭侯。
entries.en: He won outstanding distinction against the Di rebel Qi Wannian and was created village marquis of Dongming.
entries.literal: In the campaign against the Di rebel Qi Wannian he had exceptional merit and was enfeoffed as village marquis of Dongming.

entries.zh: 還為本郡督護。
entries.en: Back home he became chief of staff of his commandery.
entries.literal: On his return he was chief of staff for his native commandery.

entries.zh: 太守宋胄欲以所親吳畿代之，矩謝病去。
entries.en: Prefect Song Zhou meant to swap him for a favorite, Wu Ji; Li Ju pleaded illness and stepped down.
entries.literal: The prefect Song Zhou wished to replace him with his intimate Wu Ji; Li Ju pleaded illness and departed.

entries.zh: 畿恐矩復還，陰使人刺矩，會有人救之，故得免。
entries.en: Wu Ji dreaded his return and hired an assassin; a passerby saved him and he lived.
entries.literal: Wu Ji feared Li Ju might return and secretly sent someone to stab Li Ju; someone rescued him, therefore he escaped.

entries.zh: 屬劉元海攻平陽，百姓奔走，矩素為鄉人所愛，乃推為塢主，東屯滎陽，後移新鄭。
entries.en: When Liu Yuan stormed Pingyang and the people scattered, the locals, who loved Li Ju, made him chief of their fort; he moved east to Xingyang and later shifted to Xinzheng.
entries.literal: When Liu Yuan attacked Pingyang and the common people fled in panic, Li Ju was loved by his townspeople and was pushed to be fortress chief; he encamped east at Xingyang and later moved to Xinzheng.

entries.zh: 矩所統將士有陰欲歸勒者，矩知之而不能討，乃率眾南走，將歸朝廷，眾皆道亡，惟郭誦及參軍郭方，功曹張景，主簿苟遠，將軍騫韜、江霸、梁志、司馬尚、季弘、李瑰、段秀等百餘人棄家送矩。
entries.en: Some of Li Ju's men were slipping away to Shi Le; he saw it but dared not purge them, so he struck south for the capital. The army melted away on the march until only Guo Song, Guo Fang, Zhang Jing, Gou Yuan, Qian Tao, Jiang Ba, Liang Zhi, Sima Shang, Ji Hong, Li Gui, Duan Xiu, and a hundred-odd loyalists forsook home to stay with him.
entries.literal: Among the officers and soldiers Li Ju commanded, some secretly wished to join Shi Le; Li Ju knew it but could not punish them; he therefore led the host south, intending to return to the court; all along the road they deserted, and only Guo Song, adjutant Guo Fang, merit clerk Zhang Jing, secretary Gou Yuan, generals Qian Tao, Jiang Ba, Liang Zhi, Sima Shang, Ji Hong, Li Gui, Duan Xiu, and more than a hundred others abandoned their homes to escort Li Ju.

entries.zh: 至於魯陽縣，矩墜馬卒，葬襄陽之峴山。
entries.en: At Luyang he was thrown from his horse and died; they laid him on Xian Hill outside Xiangyang.
entries.literal: When they reached Luyang county, Li Ju fell from a horse and died; he was buried on Xian Mountain at Xiangyang.

entries.zh: =該一名亥，本僑居京兆陰磐。
entries.en: Wei Gai was also called Hai and had lived as a sojourner at Yinpan in Jingzhao.
entries.literal: = Gai's other name was Hai; originally he sojourned at Yinpan in Jingzhao.

entries.zh: 河間王顒之伐趙王倫，以該為將兵都尉。
entries.en: When Prince Hejian marched against Prince Zhao, Sima Lun, he named Wei Gai colonel of troops.
entries.literal: When Prince Hejian Sima Yong campaigned against Prince Zhao Sima Lun, he appointed Gai colonel commanding troops.

entries.zh: 及劉曜攻洛陽，隨浚赴難，先領兵守金墉城，故得無他。
entries.en: During Liu Yao's siege of Luoyang he rode with Wei Jun to the rescue and held the Metal Moat first, so the line held.
entries.literal: When Liu Yao attacked Luoyang, he followed Jun to answer the crisis, first leading troops to defend the Metal Moat fort, therefore there was nothing else amiss.

entries.zh: 曜引去，餘眾依之。
entries.en: When Liu Yao drew off, the survivors rallied to him.
entries.literal: Yao led his forces away; the remaining host relied on him.

entries.zh: 邵續
entries.en: Shao Xu
entries.literal: Shao Xu

entries.zh: 王導，字茂弘，光祿大夫覽之孫也。
entries.en: Wang Dao, whose courtesy name was Maohong, was the grandson of Wang Lan, who had held the office of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
entries.literal: Wang Dao, courtesy name Maohong, was the grandson of the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Wang Lan.

entries.zh: 父裁，鎮軍司馬。
entries.en: His father, Wang Cai, had served as Army Adjutant on the staff of the general titled "He Who Guards the Army."
entries.literal: His father was Wang Cai, Army Adjutant of the General Who Guards the Army.

entries.zh: 導少有風鑒，識量清遠。
entries.en: Even as a young man, Wang Dao showed a gift for reading men; his judgment ran clear and deep.
entries.literal: Dao from youth had insight into character and discernment; his capacity for judgment was limpid and far-reaching.

entries.zh: 年十四，陳留高士張公見而奇之，謂其從兄敦曰：「此兒容貌志氣，將相之器也。」
entries.en: When he was fourteen, a respected gentleman surnamed Zhang in Chenliu took note of him and pronounced him remarkable; Zhang said to Wang Dao's elder cousin Wang Dun, "In face and in spirit, this lad has the makings of a commander or a chief minister."
entries.literal: At age fourteen, the eminent gentleman Zhang of Chenliu saw him and deemed him extraordinary; he said to Dao's elder cousin Dun, "This boy's appearance and resolve have the capacity of a general or minister."

entries.zh: 初襲祖爵即丘子。
entries.en: He first inherited his grandfather's noble title as Baron of Jiqiu.
entries.literal: At first he inherited his grandfather's noble rank as Baron of Jiqiu.

entries.zh: 司空劉實尋引爲東閣祭酒，遷秘書郎、太子舍人、尚書郎，並不行。
entries.en: Minister of Works Liu Shi soon had him appointed Libationer of the Eastern Pavilion, then nominated him for Palace Secretary, Attendant in the Heir Apparent's Household, and Gentleman of the Masters of Writing—but Wang Dao declined every one of those appointments.
entries.literal: The Minister of Works Liu Shi soon sponsored him as Libationer of the Eastern Pavilion; he was transferred to Palace Secretary, Attendant in the Heir Apparent's Household, and Gentleman of the Masters of Writing, but he took none of these posts.

entries.zh: 後參東海王越軍事。
entries.en: He later joined the military secretariat of Sima Yue, the Prince of Donghai.
entries.literal: Afterwards he served on the military staff of Prince Donghai, Sima Yue.

entries.zh: 劭弟 薈
entries.en: Wang Hui, younger brother of Wang Shao
entries.literal: [Typographical section label: Shao's younger brother Hui (Wang Hui)]

entries.zh: 薈字敬文。
entries.en: His courtesy name was Jingwen.
entries.literal: Hui, courtesy name Jingwen.

entries.zh: 恬虛守靖，不競榮利，少曆清官，除吏部郎、侍中、建威將軍、呉國內史。
entries.en: He lived quietly without ambition, served in unsullied posts, and rose to personnel gentleman, palace attendant, general who establishes might, and Wu interior clerk.
entries.literal: He was tranquil-empty guarding quietude, not competing for glory and profit; in youth passed through pure offices; appointed Gentleman of Personnel Ministry, Palace Attendant, General Who Establishes Might, Interior Clerk of Wu.

entries.zh: 時年饑粟貴，人多餓死，薈以私米作饘粥，以飴餓者，所濟活甚眾。
entries.en: When famine struck he brewed gruel from his own grain and saved countless lives.
entries.literal: At that time there was famine and grain was dear; many people starved to death; Hui used private grain to make gruel porridge to feed the starving—those rescued and kept alive were very many.

entries.zh: 征補中領軍，不拜。
entries.en: He declined appointment as central army commander.
entries.literal: He was summoned to supplement Central Army Commander; he did not accept.

entries.zh: 徙尚書，領中護軍，復爲征虜將軍、呉國內史。
entries.en: He moved to the Masters of Writing with protecting army command, then general who subdues brigands and Wu interior clerk.
entries.literal: He was shifted to Masters of Writing, concurrent Protecting Army Commander; again became General Who Subdues Brigands and Interior Clerk of Wu.

entries.zh: 頃之，桓沖表請薈爲江州刺史，固辭不拜。
entries.en: Huan Chong nominated him for Jiangzhou; Wang Hui refused.
entries.literal: Shortly, Huan Chong memorialized requesting Hui as Inspector of Jiang Province; he firmly declined and did not accept.

entries.zh: 轉督浙江東五郡、左將軍、會稽內史，進號鎮軍將軍，加散騎常侍。
entries.en: He supervised five eastern commanderies as general of the left and Kuaiji interior clerk, took the banner general who guards the army, and added cavalier attendant.
entries.literal: He was transferred to supervise east of Zhejiang five commanderies, General of the Left and Interior Clerk of Kuaiji; advanced title General Who Guards the Army, added Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.

entries.zh: 卒于官，贈衞將軍。
entries.en: He died in harness and was honored as general who guards.
entries.literal: He died in office; gifted General Who Guards.

entries.zh: 薈子 廞
entries.en: Wang Xu, son of Wang Hui
entries.literal: Hui's son Xu.

entries.zh: 王導
entries.en: Wang Dao
entries.literal: Wang Dao.

entries.zh: 郗鑒，字道徽，高平金鄉人，漢御史大夫慮之玄孫也。
entries.en: Xi Jian of Jinxiang in Gaoping—courtesy Daohui—descended from the Han imperial counselor Xi Lu.
entries.literal: Xi Jian, courtesy name Daohui, was a man of Jinxiang in Gaoping, great-great-grandson of Imperial Counselor Lu of Han.

entries.zh: 少孤貧，博覽經籍，躬耕隴畝，吟詠不倦。
entries.en: He grew up poor and fatherless but devoured the canon, tilled his own fields, and never tired of poetry and song.
entries.literal: Orphaned young and poor, he broadly read the classics, personally plowed the fields, chanting and reciting tireless.

entries.zh: 以儒雅著名，不應州命。
entries.en: Scholars praised his cultivation; he ignored appointments from the province.
entries.literal: He was famed as a Confucian gentleman and did not answer provincial summons.

entries.zh: 趙王倫辟為掾，知倫有不臣之迹，稱疾去職。
entries.en: Prince Zhao Lun offered him a staff post; seeing Lun's treasonous ambitions, he resigned on grounds of illness.
entries.literal: Prince Zhao Lun summoned him as aide; knowing Lun bore tokens of disloyalty, he pleaded illness and left office.

entries.zh: 及倫篡，其黨皆至大官，而鑒閉門自守，不染逆節。
entries.en: When Sima Lun seized the throne his followers climbed to power; Xi Jian barred his doors and kept clean of the coup.
entries.literal: When Lun usurped, his clique all rose to high office, yet Jian shut his gate and kept himself pure, stained by no rebellion.

entries.zh: 惠帝反正，參司空軍事，累遷太子中舍人、中書侍郎。
entries.en: After Emperor Hui returned, Xi Jian joined the minister of works' staff and rose to secretary and palace attendant to the heir.
entries.literal: When Emperor Hui was restored, Jian joined the Minister of Works' military staff, rising through Palace Junior in the Heir's Household and Secretariat Gentleman.

entries.zh: 東海王越辟為主簿，舉賢良，不行。
entries.en: Sima Yue of Donghai named him chief clerk and nominated him as "worthy and good"; he declined.
entries.literal: Prince Donghai Sima Yue summoned him as chief clerk; recommended as Worthy and Good—he did not take office.

entries.zh: 征東大將軍苟晞檄為從事中郎。
entries.en: Gou Xi, general who conquered the east, summoned him as senior clerk.
entries.literal: General Who Conquers the East Gou Xi summoned him by proclamation as senior clerk.

entries.zh: 晞與越方以力爭，鑒不應其召。
entries.en: Gou Xi and Sima Yue were at war; Xi Jian ignored the call.
entries.literal: Xi and Yue were then locked in struggle for power; Jian did not answer the summons.

entries.zh: 從兄旭，晞之別駕，恐禍及己，勸之赴召，鑒終不廻，晞亦不之逼也。
entries.en: His cousin Xi Xu—Gou Xi's aide—feared for himself and urged compliance; Xi Jian still refused, yet Gou Xi did not press him.
entries.literal: His cousin Xu, Xi's aide, fearing disaster reaching himself, urged him to obey the summons; Jian never turned back; Xi also did not force him.

entries.zh: 及京師不守，寇難鋒起，鑒遂陷於陳午賊中。
entries.en: When Luoyang fell and rebels multiplied, Xi Jian fell captive to Chen Wu's gang.
entries.literal: When the capital did not hold and bandit calamities sprang like spear-points, Jian thereupon fell among Chen Wu's bandit band.

entries.zh: 邑人張實先求交於鑒，鑒不許。
entries.en: A neighbor, Zhang Shi, had courted his friendship before; Xi Jian rejected him.
entries.literal: Townsmen Zhang Shi earlier sought friendship with Jian; Jian refused.

entries.zh: 至是，實於午營來省鑒疾，既而卿鑒。
entries.en: Zhang Shi then visited him sick in Chen Wu's camp and presumed upon familiarity.
entries.literal: Thereupon Zhang from Wu's camp came to inquire after Jian's illness; afterward he addressed Jian with undue familiarity.

entries.zh: 鑒謂實曰：「相與邦壤，義不及通，何可怙亂至此邪！」
entries.en: Xi Jian told him, "We were neighbors yet never exchanged courtesy—how dare you exploit rebellion to force intimacy!"
entries.literal: Jian said to Shi: "We share neighboring soil yet courtesy never brought us together—how dare you rely on chaos to reach this point!

entries.zh: 實大慙而退。
entries.en: Zhang Shi withdrew in shame.
entries.literal: Shi was greatly ashamed and withdrew.

entries.zh: 午以鑒有名於世，將逼為主，鑒逃而獲免。
entries.en: Chen Wu meant to make the celebrated Xi Jian his figurehead; Xi Jian escaped.
entries.literal: Wu because Jian had fame in the world was about to force him to be chief; Jian fled and escaped.

entries.zh: 午尋潰散，鑒得歸鄉里。
entries.en: Chen Wu's band soon dissolved and Xi Jian went home.
entries.literal: Wu soon scattered and collapsed; Jian was able to return to his village.

entries.zh: 于時所在饑荒，州中之士素有感其恩義者，相與資贍。
entries.en: Famine stalked the region, yet local scholars who remembered his decency pooled supplies for him.
entries.literal: At that time famine raged everywhere; gentlemen of the province who long felt his kindness and righteousness together supplied him.

entries.zh: 鑒復分所得，以賉宗族及鄉曲孤老，賴而全濟者甚多，咸相謂曰：「今天子播越，中原無伯，當歸依仁德，可以後亡。」
entries.en: He shared the gifts with kinsmen and destitute neighbors. Many survived thanks to him. They said, "The emperor is a refugee and the heartland lacks a lord—only humane leadership offers shelter."
entries.literal: Jian again divided what he received to relieve his lineage and village orphans and elders; many relied on him and were wholly saved—all said together: "Now the Son of Heaven wanders lost; no protector holds the central plain—we ought to attach to humane virtue and may survive afterward.

entries.zh: 遂共推鑒為主，舉千餘家俱避難於魯之嶧山。
entries.en: They chose Xi Jian as their leader and moved more than a thousand households to Yi Mountain in Lu for safety.
entries.literal: Thereupon together they pushed Jian as chief; over a thousand households jointly fled hardship to Yi Mountain in Lu.

entries.zh: 永昌初，徵拜領軍將軍，既至，轉尚書，以疾不拜。
entries.en: Early in Yongchang he was recalled as colonel of the guards; transferred to secretary but declined on grounds of illness.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Yongchang he was summoned as Colonel of the Garrison Army; having arrived, he was transferred to Secretary—because of illness he did not accept.

entries.zh: 時明帝初即位，王敦專制，內外危逼，謀杖鑒為外援，由是拜安西將軍、兗州刺史、都督揚州江西諸軍、假節，鎮合肥。
entries.en: Emperor Ming faced Wang Dun's dictatorship and stationed Xi Jian west as general who pacifies the west, inspector of Yanzhou, area commander from the Yangzi westward—with credential and headquarters at Hefei.
entries.literal: At the time Emperor Ming had newly ascended; Wang Dun monopolized power; internal and external peril pressed—the plot leaned on Jian as outer support; therefore he was appointed General Who Pacifies the West, Inspector of Yanzhou, Area Commander of Jiangxi military affairs south of Yangzhou, acting credential, garrisoned at Hefei.

entries.zh: 敦忌之，表為尚書令，徵還。
entries.en: Wang Dun envied him and engineered his recall as director of state affairs.
entries.literal: Dun envied him and memorialized him as Director of the Department of State Affairs, summoning him back.

entries.zh: 道經姑孰，與敦相見，敦謂曰：「樂彥輔短才耳。
entries.en: At Gushu Wang Dun sneered, "Yue Guang is second-rate.
entries.literal: Passing through Gushu he met Dun; Dun said to him: "Yue Yanfu is but minor talent.

entries.zh: 後生流宕，言違名檢，考之以實，豈勝滿武秋邪？」
entries.en: Those gifted youngsters break every rule—tell me how Yue Guang outranks Man Yi."
entries.literal: Later youths drift dissolute; speech violates name and scrutiny—examining by facts, how could he surpass Man Wuqiu?

entries.zh: 鑒曰：「擬人必于其倫。
entries.en: Xi Jian replied, "Compare like with like.
entries.literal: Jian said: "When comparing men one must match kind.

entries.zh: 彥輔道韻平淡，體識沖粹，處傾危之朝，不可得而親疏。
entries.en: Yue Guang moves through a dangerous court with serene detachment—neither push nor pull him off balance.
entries.literal: Yanfu's Dao charm is placid and plain; his substance and insight are limpid and pure; in a tottering court one cannot draw him near or push him far.

entries.zh: 及愍懷太子之廢，可謂柔而有正。
entries.en: When they cashiered Crown Prince Minhuai he remained gentle yet principled.
entries.literal: At the deposition of Crown Prince Minhuai he may be called yielding yet upright.

entries.zh: 武秋失節之士，何可同日而言！」
entries.en: Man Yi broke his oath—no comparison."
entries.literal: Wuqiu is a man who lost integrity—how may they be spoken of the same day!

entries.zh: 敦曰：「愍懷廢徙之際，交有危機之急，人何能以死守之乎！
entries.en: Wang Dun shot back, "During that crisis who could die on principle?
entries.literal: Dun said: "At the deposition and exile of Minhuai, mutually there was crisis acute—how could men guard it with death!

entries.zh: 以此相方，其不減明矣。」
entries.en: Then Yue Guang shines brighter."
entries.literal: Using this to compare squarely, his inferiority is clear.

entries.zh: 鑒曰：「丈夫既潔身北面，義同在三，豈可偷生屈節，靦顏天壤邪！
entries.en: Xi Jian said, "A man who serves the throne upholds the three bonds—he does not cling to life and betray honor.
entries.literal: Jian said: "A gentleman having purified himself to serve the north face, duty joins the Three Bonds—how may he steal life and bend his integrity, shame-faced between Heaven and earth!

entries.zh: 苟道數終極，固當存亡以之耳。」
entries.en: When fate ends, you accept survival or ruin with it."
entries.literal: If the Dao's reckoning reaches its end, indeed one should live or die by it.

entries.zh: 敦素懷無君之心，聞鑒言，大忿之，遂不復相見，拘留不遣。
entries.en: Wang Dun—who already disdained emperors—raged at that speech, refused further audiences, and held Xi Jian hostage.
entries.literal: Dun always harbored a heart without a lord; hearing Jian's words he greatly resented him; then would no longer meet him and detained him without sending him away.

entries.zh: 敦之黨與譖毀日至，鑒舉止自若，初無懼心。
entries.en: While Wang Dun's clique daily maligned him, Xi Jian stayed calm and afraid of nothing.
entries.literal: Dun's faction daily spread slander; Jian's bearing remained composed—at first no fear.

entries.zh: 敦謂錢鳳曰：「郗道徽儒雅之士，名位既重，何得害之！」
entries.en: He told Qian Feng, "Xi Jian is a scholar of stature—we cannot murder him."
entries.literal: Dun said to Qian Feng: "Xi Daohui is a Confucian gentleman; name and position are already weighty—how could we harm him!

entries.zh: 乃放還臺。
entries.en: He released Xi Jian to return to the capital.
entries.literal: Thereupon he was released to return to the metropolitan apparatus.

entries.zh: 鑒遂與帝謀滅敦。
entries.en: Xi Jian then joined Emperor Ming to plot Wang Dun's destruction.
entries.literal: Jian thereupon with the emperor plotted to destroy Dun.

entries.zh: 恢以隨郡太守夏侯宗之為河南太守，戍洛陽。
entries.en: Xi Hui put Xiahou Zongzhi in charge of Luoyang.
entries.literal: Hui made Suizhou Administrator Xia Hou Zongzhi Administrator of Henan—garrisoned Luoyang.

entries.zh: 姚萇遣其子略攻湖城及上洛，又使其將楊佛嵩圍洛陽。
entries.en: Yao Chang struck Hucheng and besieged Luoyang.
entries.literal: Yao Chang sent son Lue attack Hucheng and Shangluo—also sent officer Yang Fosong besiege Luoyang.

entries.zh: 恢遣建武將軍辛恭靖救洛陽，梁州刺史王正胤率眾出子午穀，以為聲援。
entries.en: Xi Hui sent Xin Gongjing to Luoyang and Wang Zhengyin through Ziwu as diversion.
entries.literal: Hui sent General Who Establishes Martial Xin Gongjing rescue Luoyang—Liangzhou Inspector Wang Zhengyin led hosts out Ziwu Valley as sounding support.

entries.zh: 略懼而退。
entries.en: Yao Lue retreated.
entries.literal: Lue feared and withdrew.

entries.zh: 恢以功進征虜將軍，又領秦州刺史，加督隴上軍。
entries.en: Xi Hui earned promotion to general who conquers captives and added Qinzhou.
entries.literal: Hui by merit promoted General Who Conquers Captives—also concurrently Inspector of Qinzhou—additionally commanded Longshang armies.

entries.zh: 隆少為趙王倫所善，及倫專擅，召為散騎常侍。
entries.en: Prince Zhao Lun favored him and named him attendant cavalry.
entries.literal: Long in youth favored by Prince Zhao Lun—and when Lun monopolized power—summoned Attendant Cavalry Regular.

entries.zh: 倫之篡也，以為揚州刺史。
entries.en: Sima Lun made him Yangzhou inspector.
entries.literal: At Lun's usurpation—appointed Inspector of Yangzhou.

entries.zh: 僚屬有犯，輒依台閣峻制繩之，遠近咸怨。
entries.en: He policed staff harshly—everyone resented him.
entries.literal: When subordinates offended—always applied terrace severe statutes binding them—far and near alike resented.

entries.zh: 尋加甯東將軍，未拜，而齊王冏檄至，中州人在軍者皆欲赴義，隆以兄子鑒為趙王掾，諸子悉在京洛，故猶豫未決。
entries.en: Sima Jiong summoned loyal troops; Xi Long hesitated because kin served Sima Lun.
entries.literal: Shortly additionally General Who Pacifies the East—not invested—and Prince of Qi Sima Jiong's proclamation arrived—men of Central Plain in army all wished to respond to righteousness—Long because elder brother's son Jian was Zhao prince aide—all sons in capital Luo—therefore hesitated undecided.

entries.zh: 主簿趙誘、前秀才虞潭白隆曰：「當今上計，明使君自將精兵徑赴齊王；
entries.en: Zhao You and Yu Tan offered three plans: "As the best plan, my lord should personally lead elite troops straight to the Prince of Qi;
entries.literal: Chief Clerk Zhao You—former Cultivated Talent Yu Tan informed Long saying: "Upper plan—enlightened envoy lord personally lead crack troops straight proceed Prince of Qi;

entries.zh: 中計，明使君可留督攝，速遣猛將率精兵疾赴；
entries.en: Next—stay behind but rush crack troops.
entries.literal: Middle plan—enlightened envoy lord may remain supervise command—swift dispatch fierce general lead crack troops urgent proceed;

entries.zh: 下計，示遣兵將助，而稱背倫。」
entries.en: As the worst plan, appear to dispatch generals to aid him while claiming betrayal of Lun."
entries.literal: Lower plan—show dispatch troops generals aiding—yet claiming betray Lun.

entries.zh: 隆素敬別駕顧彥，密與謀之。
entries.en: Xi Long respected aide Gu Yan and conspired in secret.
entries.literal: Long since always esteemed aide Gu Yan—secretly plotted with him.

entries.zh: 彥曰：「趙誘下計，乃上策也。」
entries.en: Gu Yan said Zhao You's "worst" option was actually best.
entries.literal: Yan said: "Zhao You's lower plan is indeed the upper strategy.

entries.zh: 西曹留承聞彥言，請見，曰：「不審明使君當今何施？」
entries.en: Liu Cheng asked for an audience and said, "I do not know what course my lord intends now?"
entries.literal: Western Bureau aide Liu Cheng hearing Yan's words requested audience saying: "May not ask enlightened envoy lord nowadays what policy shall apply?

entries.zh: 隆曰：「我俱受二帝恩，無所偏助，惟欲守州而已。」
entries.en: Xi Long said, "I alike received grace from both emperors and favor neither side—I only wish to hold the province."
entries.literal: Long said: "I alike received grace from two emperors—without partial aid—I only wish to guard the province.

entries.zh: 承曰：「天下者，世祖皇帝之天下也。
entries.en: Liu Cheng said, "The realm belongs to Emperor Wu's succession.
entries.literal: Cheng said: "The realm belongs to Emperor Wu's succession.

entries.zh: 太上承代已積十年，今上取四海不平，齊王應天順時，成敗之事可見。
entries.en: Emperor Hui had ruled a decade; turmoil ruled the land; Prince of Qi held Heaven's mandate—the outcome was plain.
entries.literal: Grandfather succeeding substitute already piled ten years—present emperor obtaining realm unpeaceful—Prince of Qi responds Heaven obeying season—success or defeat's matter may be seen.

entries.zh: 使君若顧二帝，自可不行，宜急下檄文，速遣精兵猛將。
entries.en: Honor both Simas if you must—but issue orders now and rush reinforcements.
entries.literal: If envoy lord attends two emperors—of himself may not march—fitting urgently issue proclamation—swiftly dispatch crack troops fierce generals.

entries.zh: 若其疑惑，此州豈可得保也！」
entries.en: If you hesitate, can this province be preserved!"
entries.literal: If you hesitate—can this province be preserved!

entries.zh: 隆無所言，而停檄六日。
entries.en: Xi Long stalled six days without issuing orders.
entries.literal: Long said nothing—and halted proclamation six days.

entries.zh: 時甯遠將軍陳留王邃領東海都尉，鎮石頭，隆軍人西赴邃甚眾。
entries.en: Prince Sima Sui of Chenliu held Stone City; Xi Long's men streamed west to join him.
entries.literal: At the time General Who Pacifies the Distance Prince of Chenliu Sima Sui concurrently held Donghai commandant—garrisoned Stone Fortress—Long's troops westward to join Sui were extremely numerous.

entries.zh: 隆遣從事于牛渚禁之，不得止。
entries.en: Xi Long tried to block Niuzhu—they could not stem the tide.
entries.literal: Long dispatched clerk at Niuzhu to forbid them—they could not stop.

entries.zh: 將士憤怒，夜扶邃為主而攻之，隆父子皆死，顧彥亦被害，誣隆聚合遠近，圖為不軌。
entries.en: Soldiers installed Sima Sui as leader, killed Xi Long and Gu Yan, then framed them as traitors.
entries.literal: Officers and soldiers enraged—night raised Sui as chief and attacked him—Long father and son both died—Gu Yan also suffered harm—slandering Long gathered far and near plotting unorthodox rebellion.

entries.zh: 隆之死也，時議莫不痛惜焉。
entries.en: Every observer mourned Xi Long.
entries.literal: When Long died—court debate none failed to grieve.

entries.zh: 溫嶠
entries.en: Wen Jiao.
entries.literal: Wen Jiao.

entries.zh: 應詹字思遠，汝南南頓人，魏侍中璩之孫也。
entries.en: Ying Zhan, whose courtesy name was Siyuan, came from Nandun in Runan; he was the grandson of Ying Qu, who had served Wei as Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: Ying Zhan, courtesy name Siyuan, was a native of Nandun in Runan, and a grandson of Ying Qu, Palace Attendant of Wei.

entries.zh: 詹幼孤，爲祖母所養。
entries.en: He lost his parents while still a boy and was brought up by his grandmother.
entries.literal: In youth he was orphaned and was raised by his grandmother.

entries.zh: 年十餘歲，祖母又終，居喪毀頓，杖而後起，遂以孝聞。
entries.en: After his grandmother died when he was just past ten, he mourned until his body gave way and he needed a walking stick to stand; word of his filial piety spread.
entries.literal: When he was a little over ten sui, his grandmother also died; in mourning he wasted away so badly that he could rise only with a staff, and he came to be known for his filial devotion.

entries.zh: 家富於財，年又稚弱，乃請族人共居，委以資產，情若至親，世以此異焉。
entries.en: The family was wealthy, but he was still a child; he asked his kinsmen to share one roof with him and handed his assets into their care, treating them as his nearest kin—an act that struck people of the time as extraordinary.
entries.literal: His household was rich in wealth, and he was still very young, so he invited his clansmen to live together with him, entrusting them with his property; their feelings were like those of the closest kin, and the world marveled at this on that account.

entries.zh: 弱冠知名，性質素弘雅，物雖犯而弗之校，以學藝文章稱。
entries.en: After his capping he won a reputation; he was steady, broad-minded, and elegant by temperament, slow to take offense when others crossed him, and admired for his scholarship, arts, and writing.
entries.literal: At the capping age he was already well known; by nature he was plain, magnanimous, and refined, and though things might offend him he did not contend with them; he was esteemed for learning, craft, and literary skill.

entries.zh: 司徒何劭見之曰：「君子哉若人！」
entries.en: When Situ He Shao met him, he exclaimed, “Here is a true gentleman.”
entries.literal: Situ He Shao, seeing him, said, “What a gentleman this man is!”

entries.zh: 初辟公府，爲太子舍人。
entries.en: He first received appointment from the general administration and served as Gentleman Attendant of the heir apparent.
entries.literal: At first he was summoned to office from the princely administration and became Attendant to the Heir Apparent.

entries.zh: 趙王倫以爲征東長史。
entries.en: Sima Lun, Prince of Zhao, named him senior clerk on the staff of the eastward expedition.
entries.literal: The Prince of Zhao, Sima Lun, appointed him Senior Clerk of the East Expedition.

entries.zh: 倫誅，坐免。
entries.en: After Sima Lun was put to death, Ying Zhan was stripped of office by association.
entries.literal: When Lun was executed, he was implicated and dismissed.

entries.zh: 成都王穎辟爲掾。
entries.en: Sima Ying, Prince of Chengdu, recruited him to his secretariat.
entries.literal: The Prince of Chengdu, Sima Ying, summoned him as a retainer.

entries.zh: 時驃騎從事中郎諸葛玫委長沙王乂奔鄴，盛稱乂之非。
entries.en: At the time Zhuge Mei, who served as clerk on the dashing cavalry general’s staff, had left Prince Sima Yi of Changsha for Ye and was loudly blackening Yi’s name.
entries.literal: At that time Zhuge Mei, Attendant Clerk on the staff of the Cavalry-in-Attendant, had abandoned Prince Sima Yi of Changsha and fled to Ye, loudly denouncing Yi’s faults.

entries.zh: 玫浮躁有才辯，臨漳人士無不詣之。
entries.en: Zhuge Mei was volatile yet eloquent, and everyone of standing around Linzhang beat a path to his door.
entries.literal: Mei was restless and sharp-tongued; there was not a person of note in Linzhang who did not go to call on him.

entries.zh: 詹與玫有舊，歎曰：「諸葛仁林何與樂毅之相詭乎！」
entries.en: Zhan had known Zhuge Mei for years and sighed, “How can Zhuge Renlin diverge so wildly from the conduct of Yue Yi!”
entries.literal: Zhan had old ties with Mei and sighed, saying, “How can Renlin of the Zhuge clan be so unlike the way Yue Yi comported himself!”

entries.zh: 卒不見之。
entries.en: He never went to see him.
entries.literal: In the end he did not go to see him.

entries.zh: 玫聞甚愧。
entries.en: When Zhuge Mei heard, he was mortified.
entries.literal: When Mei heard of this he was deeply ashamed.

entries.zh: 鎮南大將軍劉弘，詹之祖舅也，請爲長史，謂之曰：「君器識弘深，後當代老子於荊南矣。」
entries.en: Liu Hong, General Who Guards the South and Zhan’s grandfather on his mother’s side, invited him as senior clerk and told him, “Your talent and judgment run deep; in time you will succeed me in holding the Jing southlands.”
entries.literal: General Who Guards the South, Liu Hong—Zhan’s maternal grandfather—asked him to serve as senior clerk and said to him, “Your capacity and insight are broad and deep; one day you will take this old man’s place south of the Jing region.”

entries.zh: 仍委以軍政。
entries.en: He then placed military affairs in his hands.
entries.literal: Thereupon he entrusted him with military administration.

entries.zh: 弘著績漢南，詹之力也。
entries.en: Liu Hong’s record of achievement in the southern Han basin owed much to Ying Zhan’s exertions.
entries.literal: Hong achieved merit south of the Han, and it was through Zhan’s efforts.

entries.zh: 遷南平太守。
entries.en: He rose to become administrator of Nanping commandery.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Administrator of Nanping.

entries.zh: 卞壼字望之，濟陰冤句人也。
entries.en: Bian Kun, style Wangzhi, was a man of Yuanju in Jiyin.
entries.literal: Bian Kun, courtesy name Wangzhi, was a native of Yuanju in Jiyin.

entries.zh: 祖統，琅邪內史。
entries.en: His grandfather Bian Tong had been interior minister of Langya.
entries.literal: His grandfather Tong was interior minister of Langya.

entries.zh: 父粹，以清辯鑒察稱。
entries.en: His father Bian Cui was celebrated for lucid argument and sharp discernment.
entries.literal: His father Cui was famed for clear disputation and keen judgment.

entries.zh: 兄弟六人並登宰府，世稱「卞氏六龍，玄仁無雙」。
entries.en: Six brothers reached high ministry together; contemporaries called them “the six dragons of the Bian house, with none the equal of Xuaren.”
entries.literal: Six brothers together ascended to ministerial offices; the age called them “the six dragons of the Bian clan—none matched Xuaren.”

entries.zh: 玄仁，粹字也。
entries.en: “Xuaren” was Bian Cui’s courtesy name.
entries.literal: Xuaren was Cui’s courtesy name.

entries.zh: 弟裒，嘗忤其郡將。
entries.en: His brother Bian Pou once crossed the regional commander.
entries.literal: His younger brother Pou once offended his commandery general.

entries.zh: 郡將怒訐其門內之私，粹遂以不訓見譏議，陵遲積年。
entries.en: The commander retaliated with gossip about the Bian household, so Cui was faulted for lax family discipline and languished for years.
entries.literal: The commandery general angrily denounced private matters within Pou’s household, and Cui therefore came under censure as failing to instruct his family; for years he was held back.

entries.zh: 惠帝初，爲尚書郎。
entries.en: When Emperor Hui took the throne he entered the palace secretariat as a gentleman.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Emperor Hui’s reign he became a gentleman of the Palace Secretariat.

entries.zh: 楊駿執政，人多附會，而粹正直不阿。
entries.en: While Yang Jun dominated the court, flatterers swarmed him; Bian Cui stayed straight and aloof.
entries.literal: When Yang Jun held power, many men attached themselves to him, but Cui was upright and did not curry favor.

entries.zh: 及駿誅，超拜右丞，封成陽子，稍遷至右軍將軍。
entries.en: After Yang Jun fell, Cui vaulted to right secretariat aide, village marquis of Chengyang, and eventually General of the Right Army.
entries.literal: When Jun was executed, Cui was abruptly promoted to right aide and enfeoffed as village marquis of Chengyang, and by stages rose to General of the Right Army.

entries.zh: 張華之誅，粹以華婿免官。
entries.en: When Zhang Hua died, Cui lost his post as Zhang’s son-in-law.
entries.literal: At Zhang Hua’s execution, Cui was dismissed from office as Zhang Hua’s son-in-law.

entries.zh: 齊王冏輔政，爲侍中、中書令，進爵爲公。
entries.en: Under Prince Sima Jiong of Qi he served as palace attendant and palace secretary and was raised to a ducal fief.
entries.literal: When Prince Sima Jiong of Qi assisted the government, Cui became palace attendant and palace secretary and was advanced in fief to duke.

entries.zh: 及長沙王乂專權，粹立朝正色，乂忌而害之。
entries.en: When Prince Sima Yi of Changsha seized power, Cui faced court with icy dignity; Yi envied him and had him killed.
entries.literal: When Prince Sima Yi of Changsha monopolized power, Cui stood in court with stern dignity; Yi resented him and killed him.

entries.zh: 初，粹如廁，見物若兩眼，俄而難作。
entries.en: Once, relieving himself, Cui saw what looked like two eyes in the dark; soon after came his death.
entries.literal: Earlier, when Cui went to the privy, he saw something like two eyes; shortly afterward the disaster occurred.

entries.zh: 敦弱冠仕州郡，辟司空府，稍遷太子舍人、尚書郎，朝士多稱之。
entries.en: After his capping he served locally, entered the works directorate, rose to heir’s attendant and palace gentleman, and won wide praise at court.
entries.literal: At the capping age Dun served in province and commandery, was summoned to the directorate of works, and by stages rose to Gentleman Attendant of the heir apparent and gentleman of the Palace Secretariat; court gentlemen much praised him.

entries.zh: 東海王越聞，召以爲主簿。
entries.en: Sima Yue of the East Sea made him chief clerk.
entries.literal: Prince Sima Yue of the East Sea heard of him and summoned him as chief clerk.

entries.zh: 王彌逼洛，敦及胡毋輔之勸越擊王彌，而王衍、潘滔共執不聽，敦庭爭苦至，眾咸壯之。
entries.en: As Wang Mi threatened Luoyang, Dun and Hu Wuzhi begged Sima Yue to attack; Wang Yan and Pan Tao blocked the plan while Dun shouted himself hoarse in open court—the crowd admired his nerve.
entries.literal: When Wang Mi pressed Luoyang, Dun together with Hu Wuzhi urged Yue to strike Wang Mi, but Wang Yan and Pan Tao together seized control and would not listen; Dun argued bitterly in court to the utmost, and the crowd all thought him heroic.

entries.zh: 出補汝南內史。
entries.en: He went out as interior minister of Runan.
entries.literal: He went out to fill the vacancy as interior minister of Runan.

entries.zh: 元帝之爲鎮東，請爲軍諮祭酒，不就。
entries.en: Emperor Yuan as east-general wanted him as army libationer; he declined.
entries.literal: When Emperor Yuan was east-general, he asked Dun to be libationer-adviser of the army, but Dun did not accept.

entries.zh: 征南將軍山簡以爲司馬。
entries.en: Shan Jian named him marshal.
entries.literal: General Who Conquers the South, Shan Jian, made him marshal.

entries.zh: 尋而王如、杜曾相繼爲亂，簡乃使敦監沔北七郡軍事、振威將軍、領江夏相，戍夏口。
entries.en: When Wang Ru and Du Zeng revolted, Shan Jian put him over seven northern Han commanderies as General Who Rouses Might and Jiangxia administrator, based at Xiakou.
entries.literal: Soon Wang Ru and Du Zeng rose in succession; Jian then had Dun supervise military affairs in seven commanderies north of the Mian, as General Who Rouses Might, concurrently grand administrator of Jiangxia, garrisoned at Xiakou.

entries.zh: 敦攻討沔中皆平。
entries.en: He cleared the Han basin by force.
entries.literal: Dun attacked and campaigned until all the middle Han was pacified.

entries.zh: 既而杜弢寇湘中，加敦征討大都督。
entries.en: When Du Tao struck Xiang, he became grand commander of suppression.
entries.literal: Afterward Du Tao raided Xiang commanderies, and Dun was additionally named supreme area commander for conquest.

entries.zh: 伐弢有功，賜爵安陵亭侯。
entries.en: Crushing Du Tao won him the village marquisate of Anling.
entries.literal: For merit in campaigning against Tao he was enfeoffed as village marquis of Anling.

entries.zh: 鎮東大將軍王敦請爲軍司。
entries.en: Wang Dun, east-guarding general, recruited him as army director.
entries.literal: General Who Guards the East, Wang Dun, asked him to be army director.

entries.zh: 孫惠，字德施，吳國富陽人，吳豫章太守賁曾孫也。
entries.en: Sun Hui, whose courtesy name was Deshi, came from Fuyang in the old state of Wu and was a great-grandson of Ben, the Yuzhang grand administrator who had served Wu.
entries.literal: Sun Hui, courtesy name Deshi, was a native of Fuyang in the state of Wu; he was a great-grandson of Ben, who had been Grand Administrator of Yuzhang under Wu.

entries.zh: 父祖並仕吳。
entries.en: Both his father and his grandfather had served the Wu regime.
entries.literal: His father and grandfather both held office in Wu.

entries.zh: 惠口訥，好學有才識，州辟不就，寓居蕭沛之間。
entries.en: He was awkward in speech but a devoted student, with real ability and insight. Though the provincial authorities tried to appoint him, he stayed out of office and lived for a time between Xiao and Pei.
entries.literal: Hui was slow of tongue, loved learning, and had talent and judgment; the province summoned him but he did not take office, and he lodged between Xiao and Pei.

entries.zh: 永甯初，赴齊王冏義，討趙王倫，以功封晉興縣侯，辟大司馬戶曹掾，轉東曹屬。
entries.en: When Yongning began, he joined Sima Jiong, the Prince of Qi, in the loyalist campaign against Sima Lun, the Prince of Zhao. His service earned him the county marquisate of Jinxing, a post as clerk in the minister of war's revenue office, and then a place on the eastern staff.
entries.literal: At the beginning of the Yongning era, he answered Prince of Qi Jiong's call to righteous arms and campaigned against Prince of Zhao Lun; for merit he was enfeoffed marquis of Jinxing County, appointed clerk in the Revenue Bureau of the Minister of War, then transferred to a subordinate post in the eastern bureau.

entries.zh: 冏驕矜僭侈，天下失望。
entries.en: Jiong grew haughty and overbearing, overstepping his rank and spending on a princely scale until the empire had lost faith in him.
entries.literal: Jiong was arrogant, boastful, presumptuous, and extravagant; all under Heaven were disappointed in him.

entries.zh: 惠獻言於冏，諷以五難、四不可，勸令歸籓，辭甚切至。
entries.en: Sun Hui laid before him a carefully framed remonstrance—the 'five difficulties' and 'four impossibilities'—urging him to withdraw to his princely domain. The tone was urgent and uncompromising.
entries.literal: Hui submitted advice to Jiong, using 'five difficulties' and 'four impossibilities' as indirect admonition, urging him to return to his fief; the wording was extremely blunt and thorough.

entries.zh: 冏不納。
entries.en: Jiong refused to listen.
entries.literal: Jiong did not accept it.

entries.zh: 惠懼罪，辭疾去。
entries.en: Fearing reprisals, Sun Hui pleaded illness and slipped away.
entries.literal: Hui feared punishment, pleaded illness, and departed.

entries.zh: 頃之，冏果敗。
entries.en: Soon afterward Jiong fell, exactly as he had warned.
entries.literal: Before long, Jiong indeed was defeated.

entries.zh: 成都王穎薦惠為大將軍參軍、領奮威將軍、白沙督。
entries.en: Sima Ying, the Prince of Chengdu, then recommended him as an adviser on the grand general's staff, with the concurrent titles of General Who Rouses Might and commander of the Baisha garrison.
entries.literal: Prince of Chengdu Ying recommended Hui as staff adviser to the grand general, concurrently General Who Rouses Might, and commander at Baisha.

entries.zh: 是時，穎將征長沙王乂，以陸機為前鋒都督。
entries.en: Ying was preparing to move against Sima Yi, the Prince of Changsha, and named Lu Ji to lead the van.
entries.literal: At this time Ying was about to campaign against Prince of Changsha Yi and appointed Lu Ji as commander of the vanguard.

entries.zh: 惠與機同鄉里，憂其致禍，勸機讓都督于王粹。
entries.en: As a townsman of Lu Ji, Sun Hui worried the appointment would destroy him and urged him to step aside in favor of Wang Cui.
entries.literal: Hui was from the same home region as Ji; fearing that Ji would bring disaster on himself, he urged Ji to yield the commander's post to Wang Cui.

entries.zh: 及機兄弟被戮，惠甚傷恨之。
entries.en: When Lu Ji and his brothers were put to death, Sun Hui mourned them bitterly.
entries.literal: When Ji and his brothers were executed, Hui deeply grieved and resented it.

entries.zh: 時惠又擅殺穎牙門將梁俊，懼罪，因改姓名以遁。
entries.en: He had already killed Liang Jun, one of Ying's gate generals, without orders. Dreading the consequences, he took a new identity and went into hiding.
entries.literal: At that time Hui had also on his own authority killed Liang Jun, a gate-guard general under Ying; fearing punishment, he changed his name and fled into hiding.

entries.zh: 鑒弟濤及弟子戭，並有才筆。
entries.en: His brother Wang Tao and his nephew Wang Yan were both fine writers.
entries.literal: Jian's younger brother Tao and his nephew Yan both had talent with the brush.

entries.zh: 濤字茂略，曆著作郎、無錫令。
entries.en: Wang Tao, courtesy Maolue, rose through editorial director to magistrate of Wuxi.
entries.literal: Tao, courtesy name Maolue, successively served as editorial director and magistrate of Wuxi.

entries.zh: 戭字庭堅，亦為著作。
entries.en: Wang Yan, courtesy Tingjian, also held a compiler's post.
entries.literal: Yan, courtesy name Tingjian, also served as editorial director.

entries.zh: 並早卒。
entries.en: Both died young.
entries.literal: Both died early.

entries.zh: 劾案沛王韜獄，未竟，會解結代楊准為刺史，韜因河間王顒屬結。
entries.en: He was investigating Prince Pei's man Tao when Xie Jie replaced Yang Zhun as regional inspector; Tao then leaned on Sima Yong, the Prince of Hejian, to bring pressure on Xie Jie.
