entries.literal: He impeached and investigated the case of Prince of Pei's Tao; it was not finished when Xie Jie replaced Yang Zhun as inspector, and Tao through Prince of Hejian Yong importuned Jie.

entries.zh: 結至大會，問主簿史鳳曰：「沛王貴籓，州據何法而擅拘邪？」
entries.en: When Xie Jie took up his post he called a full meeting and asked his chief clerk Shi Feng, 'The Prince of Pei is a royal fief—what statute let your office seize him on its own?'
entries.literal: When Jie arrived he held a great assembly and asked chief clerk Shi Feng, "The Prince of Pei is a noble princedom—on what law of the province did you dare detain him without authority?"

entries.zh: 時頵在坐，對曰：「甲午詔書，刺史銜命，國之外台，其非所部而在境者，刺史並糾。
entries.en: Chen Yun, who was in the hall, answered: 'The jiawu edict made the inspector Heaven's agent beyond the capital: anyone inside his circuit, whether or not under his nominal department, falls under his remit.
entries.literal: At the time Yun was present and replied, "The jiawu-year edict: the inspector bears charge; beyond the capital he is the state's outer terrace; those who are not of his department but are within his borders—the inspector investigates them all.

entries.zh: 事征文墨，前後列上，七被詔書。
entries.en: The paperwork went up again and seven imperial replies confirmed the procedure.
entries.literal: The affair is verified in documents; forward and backward it was listed and submitted, seven times receiving edict responses.

entries.zh: 如州所劾，無有違謬。」
entries.en: If the province's impeachment follows that paper trail, it is legally sound.'
entries.literal: If it is as the province impeached, there is no violation or error."

entries.zh: 結曰：「眾人之言不可妄聽，宜依法窮竟。」
entries.en: Xie Jie answered, 'You cannot trust every rumor; investigate to the letter of the law.'
entries.literal: Jie said, "The words of the multitude must not be rashly trusted; one should according to law exhaust the case to the end."

entries.zh: 又問僚佐曰：「河北白壤膏粱，何故少人士，每以三品為中正？」
entries.en: He went on, 'Hebei is fat white farmland—why are there so few eminent families that every third-rank house rates as zhongzheng?'
entries.literal: He further asked his staff, "Hebei has white soil and rich fields—why are there few gentlemen, always using third rank as central assessor?"

entries.zh: 答曰：「《詩》稱'維嶽降神，生甫及申'。
entries.en: Someone replied, 'The 《Book of Odes》 says Heaven sends its finest spirits down from the sacred peaks.
entries.literal: They answered, "The 《Book of Odes》 states, 'From the great peak Heaven sent its spirits; it bore Fu and Shen.

entries.zh: 夫英偉大賢多出於山澤，河北土平氣均，蓬蒿裁高三尺，不足成林故也。」
entries.en: Heroes sprout from rough country; Hebei is flat and tame, its scrub barely shoulder high—no forest, no giants.'
entries.literal: Great heroes and grand worthies mostly come from mountains and marshes; Hebei's earth is level and its qi even, mugwort grows only three feet high—not enough to form a forest—that is the reason."

entries.zh: 結曰：「張彥真以為汝潁巧辯，恐不及青徐儒雅也。」
entries.en: Xie Jie quoted Zhang Yanzhen: 'The clever talkers of Run and Ying cannot rival the classical scholars of Qing and Xu.'
entries.literal: Jie said, "Zhang Yanzhen thought the Run-Ying sophists could not match the ru elegance of Qing and Xu."

entries.zh: 頵曰：「彥真與元禮不協，故設過言。
entries.en: Chen Yun said, 'Yanzhen feuded with Yuanli—that slander was personal, not geography.
entries.literal: Yun said, "Yanzhen was not on good terms with Yuanli, therefore he set forth excessive words.

entries.zh: 老子、莊周生陳梁，伏羲、傅說、師曠、大項出陽夏，漢魏二祖起於沛譙，准之眾州，莫之與比。」
entries.en: Laozi and Zhuang Zhou were Chen and Liang men; Fuxi, Fu Yue, Shi Kuang, and Xiang Yu hailed from Yangxia; the Han and Wei founders rose in Pei and Qiao—name a province that can match that roll call.'
entries.literal: Laozi and Zhuang Zhou were born in Chen and Liang; Fuxi, Fu Yue, Shi Kuang, and great Xiang came from Yangxia; the two founders of Han and Wei rose from Pei and Qiao—measured against the host of provinces, none can compare."

entries.zh: 結甚異之，曰：「豫州人士常半天下，此言非虛。」
entries.en: Xie Jie stared, then said, 'They say half the realm's talent comes from Yuzhou—now I believe it.'
entries.literal: Jie greatly marveled at him and said, "The gentlemen of Yu Province are always half the realm—this saying is not empty."

entries.zh: 會結遷尚書，結恨不得盡其才用。
entries.en: Soon Xie Jie went to the ministry in the capital and regretted he had not used Chen Yun to the full.
entries.literal: Before long Jie was transferred to minister; Jie regretted that he could not exhaust his employment of Chen's talent.

entries.zh: 初，趙王倫篡位，三王起義，制《己亥格》，其後論功雖小，亦皆依用。
entries.en: When Sima Lun seized the throne, the three princes issued the 《Yihai Precedent》 to rank wartime merit, and afterward even small merit awards all continued to use that code.
entries.literal: At first, when Prince of Zhao Lun usurped the throne, the three princes raised the righteous army and established the 《Yihai Precedent》; afterward, in discussing merit, even small cases all relied on it.

entries.zh: 頵意謂不宜以為常式，駁之曰：「聖王懸爵賞功，制罰糾違，斯道苟明，人赴水火。
entries.en: Chen Yun argued it must not become permanent law: 'Sage kings reward merit and punish crime—make that clear and men will walk through fire for you.
entries.literal: Yun held that it should not be taken as a constant model and refuted it, saying, "The sage kings suspend ranks to reward merit and institute punishments to correct transgressions—if this way is clear, men will throw themselves into water and fire.

entries.zh: 且名器之實，不可妄假，非才謂之致寇，寵厚戒在斯亡。
entries.en: Titles are not party favors; calling fools worthy invites rebellion; showering empty rank is how dynasties die.
entries.literal: Moreover the substance of names and vessels must not be rashly lent; calling the unworthy talented is what brings bandits; the warning that thick favor lies in this perishing.

entries.zh: 昔孫秀口唱篡逆，手弄天機，惠皇失禦，九服無戴。
entries.en: Sun Xiu preached treason and toyed with the edict; Emperor Hui lost control, and no one in the nine circuits wore the cap straight.
entries.literal: Formerly Sun Xiu mouthed usurpation and treason and with his hands played with Heaven's mechanism; Emperor Hui lost the reins, and within the nine domains there was none who wore the cap of loyalty.

entries.zh: 三王建議，席捲四海，合起義之眾，結天下之心，故設《己亥義格》以權濟難。
entries.en: The three princes swept the realm, welded the loyal armies, and issued the 《Yihai Righteousness Precedent》 as a temporary wartime ladder.
entries.literal: The three princes set up the plan; they rolled up the four seas; they combined the hosts of the righteous uprising and bound the mind of all under Heaven; therefore they established the 《Yihai Righteousness Precedent》 to weigh and relieve the hardship.

entries.zh: 此自一切之法，非常倫之格也。
entries.en: That was an emergency rulebook, not a peacetime statute.
entries.literal: This was itself an expedient one-time law, not a standard for ordinary categories.

entries.zh: 其起義以來，依格雜猥，遭人為侯，或加兵伍，或出皁僕，金紫佩士卒之身，符策委庸隸之門，使天官降辱，王爵黷賤，非所以正皇綱重名器之謂也。
entries.en: Since then the code has handed marquisates to pull, put silks on privates, and stuffed tally books into lackeys' sleeves—that is not how you mend the net of state or honor a title.
entries.literal: From the uprising onward, according to the precedent it has been mixed and base: persons have been made marquis by pull, some added to the ranks of soldiers, some issued from black servants; gold and purple hang on troopers' persons; tallies and registers lie in menial slaves' gates—this is not what is called rectifying the imperial net and valuing names and vessels.

entries.zh: 請自今以後宜停之。」
entries.en: Abolish it from this day forward.'
entries.literal: I ask that from now on it be stopped."

entries.zh: 頵以孤寒，數有奏議，朝士多惡之，出除譙郡太守。
entries.en: Chen Yun had no faction and a cold pedigree; his blunt papers earned him enemies, and the court parked him as grand administrator of Qiao.
entries.literal: Because Yun was isolated and of cold background, he repeatedly had memorials and proposals; court gentlemen mostly hated him, and he was sent out as grand administrator of Qiao commandery.

entries.zh: 史臣曰：昔張良拙說項氏，巧謀於沛公；
entries.en: The historians write: Zhang Liang could not move Xiang Yu with words, yet he read Liu Bang's mind to perfection;
entries.literal: The historiographer says: In olden times Zhang Liang was clumsy persuading the Xiang house but clever in plotting for the Duke of Pei;

entries.zh: 孫惠沮計齊王，耀奇於東海，終而誓甘之旅炎運載昌，稱狩之師金行不競。
entries.en: Sun Hui checked Sima Jiong yet dazzled Sima Yue; still, the loyalist oaths that fired Western Jin could not repeat Han's blazing rise, and the great hosts that marched under the hunt banner never secured the metal mandate of Sima Jin.
entries.literal: Sun Hui thwarted the Prince of Qi's plan and displayed strange stratagem to the Prince of the Eastern Sea, yet in the end the hosts that swore the sweet pledge saw the fiery fortune ride to glory, while the armies that styled themselves on the imperial hunt could not make the metal line prevail.

entries.zh: 豈遭時之會斯蹇，將謀國之道未通？
entries.en: Was the hour itself unkind, or did their statecraft never quite measure up?
entries.literal: Was it that meeting the times' conjunction was this hard, or the way of plotting for the state was not thorough?

entries.zh: 迷於委質之貞，暗于所修之慮，本既顛矣，何以能終！
entries.en: They mistook personal loyalty for policy and misread what truly needed tending—uproot a tree and it cannot stand long.
entries.literal: Lost in the fidelity of surrendering allegiance, blind in the considerations of what they cultivated—once the root is overturned, how can they reach the end!

entries.zh: 熊遠、王鑒有毗濟之道，比之大廈，其榱桷之佐乎！
entries.en: Xiong Yuan and Wang Jian were the men who steadied the timbers—never the central pillar, yet without their braces the hall would have fallen.
entries.literal: Xiong Yuan and Wang Jian had the way of aiding and sustaining; compared to a great hall, were they perhaps the rafter-end assistants!

entries.zh: 崧之詆溫，頵之距結，挫其勞役之策，申其汝潁之論，采郭嘉之風旨，挹硃育之餘波，故桓溫輟許攸之謀，解結欽王朗之跡。
entries.en: Gao Song's letter to Huan Wen and Chen Yun's stand against Xie Jie broke reckless mobilization, revived the Run-Ying argument, echoed Guo Jia's bluntness and Zhu Yu's wit—so Huan Wen dropped a rash Xu You scheme and Xie Jie learned to admire Wang Lang's example.
entries.literal: Song's rebuke of Wen, Yun's resistance to Jie—frustrated their schemes of forced labor, set forth the Run-Ying thesis, sampled Guo Jia's intent, scooped Zhu Yu's after-ripples—therefore Huan Wen set aside a Xun You-style plot, and Xie Jie looked up to Wang Lang's traces.

entries.zh: 緝之時典，用此道歟！
entries.en: Even Xiong Jin's later service seems to have walked the same path.
entries.literal: As for Xiong Jin's timely norms in office—did he employ this same way!

entries.zh: 孫惠
entries.en: Sun Hui.
entries.literal: Section heading: Sun Hui.

entries.zh: 或以潘岳《金穀詩序》方其文，羲之比于石崇，聞而甚喜。
entries.en: Some likened his piece to Pan Yue's preface to the Golden Valley poems and compared Wang Xizhi himself to Shi Chong; he was delighted to hear it.
entries.literal: Some with Pan Yue's "Jingu Poems Preface" compared his text; Xizhi compared to Shi Chong, hearing was greatly pleased.

entries.zh: 王羲之
entries.en: Wang Xizhi
entries.literal: Wang Xizhi.

entries.zh: 羊鑒，字景期，太山人也。
entries.en: Yang Jian, styled Jingqi, came from Taishan commandery.
entries.literal: Yang Jian, courtesy name Jingqi, was a native of Taishan.

entries.zh: 父濟，匈奴中郎將。
entries.en: His father Ji had been Central Commandant of the Xiongnu.
entries.literal: His father Ji was Central Commandant of the Xiongnu.

entries.zh: 兄煒，曆太僕、兗徐二州刺史。
entries.en: His elder brother Wei had held the imperial stud ministry and the inspectorates of Yan and Xu.
entries.literal: His elder brother Wei successively served as Minister of the Imperial Stud and Inspector of Yan and Xu provinces.

entries.zh: 鑒為東陽太守，累遷太子左衛率。
entries.en: Yang Jian governed Dongyang and rose to left commander of the crown prince's guard.
entries.literal: Jian served as Administrator of Dongyang and was promoted to Left Commander of the Crown Prince's Guard.

entries.zh: 時徐龕反叛，司徒王導以鑒是龕州裏冠族，必能制之，請遣北討。
entries.en: When Xu Kan rebelled, Wang Dao argued that Yang Jian, foremost clan of Kan's home province, could master him and asked that he be sent north.
entries.literal: When Xu Kan rebelled, Minister of Education Wang Dao held that Jian, as the leading clan of Kan's province, would surely be able to control him, and requested that he be sent north to campaign.

entries.zh: 鑒深辭才非將帥。
entries.en: Yang Jian refused firmly, protesting that he was no general.
entries.literal: Jian firmly declined, saying he lacked the talent of a commander.

entries.zh: 太尉郗鑒亦表謂鑒非才，不宜妄使。
entries.en: Grand Commandant Xi Jian likewise warned that Yang Jian was unfit for the post.
entries.literal: Grand Commandant Xi Jian also memorialized that Jian lacked ability and should not be rashly employed.

entries.zh: 導不納，強啟授以征討都督，果敗績。
entries.en: Wang Dao overruled them, pushed the appointment as superintendent of punitive campaigns, and defeat followed.
entries.literal: Dao would not accept this; he forcefully memorialized and had him appointed Superintendent of Punitive Campaigns, with defeat the result.

entries.zh: 導以舉鑒非才，請自貶，帝不從。
entries.en: Wang Dao asked to demote himself for misjudging Yang Jian; the emperor refused.
entries.literal: Dao, for having recommended Jian though he lacked talent, asked to demote himself; the Emperor did not agree.

entries.zh: 有司正鑒斬刑，元帝詔以鑒太妃外屬，特免死，除名。
entries.en: Officials sought Yang Jian's head, but Emperor Yuan spared him as a maternal kinsman of the grand consort and struck his name from office.
entries.literal: The authorities judged Jian deserving of execution by decapitation; Emperor Yuan issued an edict that because Jian was a maternal relative of the Grand Consort, he was specially spared death and struck from the rolls.

entries.zh: 久之，為少府。
entries.en: Years later he was named minister of the palace economy.
entries.literal: After a long while he became Minister of the Palace Economy.

entries.zh: 及王敦反，明帝以鑒敦舅，又素相親黨，微被嫌責。
entries.en: When Wang Dun rebelled, Emperor Ming eyed Yang Jian as Dun's uncle and old ally and lightly censured him.
entries.literal: When Wang Dun rebelled, Emperor Ming, because Jian was Dun's maternal uncle and had long been intimate with his faction, was slightly suspected and reproached.

entries.zh: 及成帝即位，豫討蘇峻，以功封豐城縣侯，徙光祿勳，卒。
entries.en: Under Emperor Cheng he helped crush Su Jun, won Fengcheng marquisate, became superintendent of the imperial household, and died.
entries.literal: When Emperor Cheng ascended the throne, Jian took part in punishing Su Jun; for merit he was enfeoffed Marquis of Fengcheng county, transferred to Superintendent of the Imperial Household, and died.

entries.zh: 王遜 蔡豹 羊鑒 劉胤 桓宣
entries.en: Biographies grouped here open with Wang Xun, Cai Bao, Yang Jian, Liu Yin, and Huan Xuan.
entries.literal: Wang Xun; Cai Bao; Yang Jian; Liu Yin; Huan Xuan.

entries.zh: 〈（族子伊）〉
entries.en: (Their kinsman Huan Yi)〉
entries.literal: (Clansman Huan Yi)〉

entries.zh: 朱伺 毛寶
entries.en: Zhu Si and Mao Bao.
entries.literal: Zhu Si; Mao Bao.

entries.zh: 〈（子穆之）〉
entries.en: (His son Mao Muzhi)〉
entries.literal: (Son Mao Muzhi)〉

entries.zh: 劉遐 鄧嶽
entries.en: Liu Xia and Deng Yue.
entries.literal: Liu Xia; Deng Yue.

entries.en: (His son Liu Xia)〉
entries.literal: (Son Liu Xia)〉

entries.zh: 朱序
entries.en: Zhu Xu.
entries.literal: Zhu Xu.

entries.zh: 劉毅，字希樂，彭城沛人也。
entries.en: Liu Yi, whose courtesy name was Xile, came from Pei in the Pengcheng region.
entries.literal: Liu Yi, courtesy name Xile, was a native of Pei in Pengcheng commandery.

entries.zh: 曾祖距，廣陵相。
entries.en: His great-grandfather Liu Ju had served as chancellor of Guangling.
entries.literal: His great-grandfather Ju had been Chancellor of Guangling.

entries.zh: 叔父鎮，左光祿大夫。
entries.en: His uncle Liu Zhen had held the post of left household grandee with the golden seal and purple ribbon.
entries.literal: His uncle Zhen had been Left Household Grandee of Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.

entries.zh: 毅少有大志，不修家人產業，仕為州從事，桓弘以為中兵參軍屬。
entries.en: From his youth Liu Yi aimed high and kept no careful household estate. He entered service as a provincial clerk, and Huan Hong made him an aide in the central army staff.
entries.literal: In youth Yi cherished great ambitions, did not attend to household property, and took office as a provincial clerk; Huan Hong appointed him subordinate to the central army adjutant.

entries.zh: 桓玄篡位，毅與劉裕、何無忌、魏詠之等起義兵，密謀討玄，毅討徐州刺史桓修于京口、青州刺史桓弘于廣陵。
entries.en: After Huan Xuan seized the throne, Liu Yi joined Liu Yu, He Wuji, Wei Yongzhi, and others in raising a loyal army and secretly planning to bring Huan Xuan down. Liu Yi himself struck at Inspector of Xuzhou Huan Xiu at Jingkou and Inspector of Qingzhou Huan Hong at Guangling.
entries.literal: When Huan Xuan usurped the throne, Yi together with Liu Yu, He Wuji, Wei Yongzhi, and others raised loyal troops, secretly plotting to punish Xuan; Yi attacked Xuzhou Inspector Huan Xiu at Jingkou and Qingzhou Inspector Huan Hong at Guangling.

entries.zh: 裕率毅等至竹裏，玄使其將皇甫敷、吳甫之北距義軍，遇之于江乘，臨陣斬甫之，進至羅落橋，又斬敷首。
entries.en: Liu Yu brought Liu Yi and the rest as far as Zhuli. Huan Xuan dispatched his generals Huangfu Fu and Wu Fuzhi to block the loyal forces from the north. They met at Jiangsheng, where Wu Fuzhi was beheaded in the fighting. The army pushed on to Luoluo Bridge and there took Huangfu Fu’s head as well.
entries.literal: Yu led Yi and the others to Zhuli; Xuan sent his generals Huangfu Fu and Wu Fuzhi north to block the loyal army, met them at Jiangsheng, beheaded Fuzhi on the field, advanced to Luoluo Bridge, and also cut off Fu’s head.

entries.zh: 玄大懼，使桓謙、何澹之屯覆舟山。
entries.en: Huan Xuan panicked and ordered Huan Qian and He Danzhi to camp at Mount Fuzhou.
entries.literal: Xuan was greatly frightened and had Huan Qian and He Danzhi encamp at Mount Fuzhou.

entries.zh: 毅等軍至蔣山，裕使羸弱登山，多張旗幟，玄不之測，益以危懼。
entries.en: When Liu Yi’s men reached Mount Jiang, Liu Yu sent feebler troops up the slopes with a forest of banners. Huan Xuan could not read their strength and only grew more alarmed.
entries.literal: When Yi and the others reached Mount Jiang, Yu had the weak climb the hill and raise many banners; Xuan could not fathom it and grew still more fearful.

entries.zh: 謙等士卒多北府人，素懾伏裕，莫敢出鬥。
entries.en: Most of Huan Qian’s troops were Northern Headquarters veterans who had always feared Liu Yu, and none would step forward to offer battle.
entries.literal: Many of Qian’s soldiers were men of the Northern Headquarters and had long stood in awe of Yu; none dared come out to fight.

entries.zh: 裕與毅等分為數隊，進突謙陣，皆殊死戰，無不一當百。
entries.en: Liu Yu and Liu Yi split into several columns and hurled themselves at Huan Qian’s formation. Every man fought as if his life depended on it, each worth a hundred ordinary soldiers.
entries.literal: Yu together with Yi and the others divided into several columns, charged Qian’s line, and all fought to the death, each man worth a hundred.

entries.zh: 時東北風急，義軍放火，煙塵張天，鼓噪之音震駭京邑，謙等諸軍一時奔散。
entries.en: A stiff northeasterly wind was blowing. The loyal army kindled fires; smoke and dust blotted out the sky, and the roar of drums and war cries shook the capital. Huan Qian’s army scattered in a single rush.
entries.literal: At that time a fierce wind blew from the northeast; the loyal army set fires, smoke and dust filled the sky, and the din of drums and shouts shook the capital; Qian’s host broke and fled all at once.

entries.zh: 玄既西走，裕以毅為冠軍將軍、青州刺史，與何無忌、劉道規躡玄。
entries.en: Once Huan Xuan had fled westward, Liu Yu named Liu Yi champion general and inspector of Qingzhou and, with He Wuji and Liu Daogui, set off in pursuit.
entries.literal: After Xuan fled west, Yu appointed Yi Champion General and Inspector of Qingzhou, and together with He Wuji and Liu Daogui they pressed Xuan.

entries.zh: 玄逼帝及琅邪王西上，毅與道規及下邳太守孟懷玉等追及玄，戰于崢嶸洲。
entries.en: Huan Xuan drove the emperor and the prince of Langye upriver. Liu Yi, Liu Daogui, and Xiapi prefect Meng Huaiyu caught him and gave battle at Zhengrong Islet.
entries.literal: Xuan forced the emperor and the Prince of Langye westward; Yi together with Daogui and Xiapi Prefect Meng Huaiyu overtook Xuan and fought at Zhengrong Islet.

entries.zh: 毅乘風縱火。
entries.en: Liu Yi used the wind to his advantage and set the enemy fleet ablaze.
entries.literal: Yi exploited the wind to spread fire.

entries.zh: 盡銳爭先，玄眾大潰，燒輜重夜走。
entries.en: His picked troops vied to lead the charge. Huan Xuan’s army collapsed completely, torched its baggage, and slipped away under cover of darkness.
entries.literal: With every elite vying to be first, Xuan’s host was utterly routed; they burned the baggage train and fled by night.

entries.zh: 玄將郭銓、劉雅等襲陷尋陽，毅遣武威將軍劉懷肅討平之。
entries.en: Huan Xuan’s generals Guo Quan and Liu Ya seized Xunyang by surprise. Liu Yi sent General Who Displays Might Liu Huaisu, who crushed them and restored order.
entries.literal: Xuan’s generals Guo Quan and Liu Ya raided and took Xunyang; Yi sent General Who Displays Might Liu Huaisu and pacified them.

entries.zh: 劉毅
entries.en: Liu Yi.
entries.literal: Liu Yi.

entries.zh: 張軌，字士彥，安定烏氏人，漢常山景王耳十七代孫也。
entries.en: Zhang Gui, whose courtesy name was Shiyan, came from Wushi in Anding; he traced his line to Zhang Er, the Han Prince Jing of Changshan, seventeen generations back.
entries.literal: Zhang Gui, courtesy name Shiyan, was a native of Wushi in Anding commandery, the seventeenth-generation descendant of Liu Er, the Prince Jing of Changshan of the Han.

entries.zh: 家世孝廉，以儒學顯。
entries.en: His clan had long supplied xiaolian candidates and was known for Confucian learning.
entries.literal: For generations his family had produced men recommended as xiaolian, and they were eminent in Confucian scholarship.

entries.zh: 父溫，為太官令。
entries.en: His father Zhang Wen held the post of Director of the Imperial Kitchen.
entries.literal: His father, Zhang Wen, served as Director of the Imperial Kitchen.

entries.zh: 軌少明敏好學，有器望，姿儀典則，與同郡皇甫謐善，隱于宜陽女幾山。
entries.en: As a young man he was bright, eager to learn, and carried an air of capacity; his deportment was exemplary. He befriended Huangfu Mi of Anding and withdrew to Mount Nüji in Yiyang.
entries.literal: In youth Gui was quick, perceptive, and fond of learning; he had presence and high repute, and his bearing was dignified and correct. He was on good terms with Huangfu Mi of the same commandery and lived in seclusion on Mount Nüji in Yiyang.

entries.zh: 泰始初，受叔父錫官五品。
entries.en: Early in the Taishi reign he was given fifth-rank office through his uncle Zhang Xi.
entries.literal: At the beginning of the Taishi era he received from his uncle Xi an office of the fifth rank.

entries.zh: 中書監張華與軌論經義及政事損益，甚器之，謂安定中正為蔽善抑才，乃美為之談，以為二品之精。
entries.en: Zhang Hua, the Palace Library director, debated classical doctrine and policy with him and came to esteem him deeply, blaming Anding’s impartial judge for hiding talent and praising Zhang Gui as the outstanding man of the second-grade roster.
entries.literal: Director of the Palace Library Zhang Hua discussed with him the meaning of the Classics and the gains and losses of government affairs, thought very highly of him, and said that the commandery impartial judge of Anding was concealing the worthy and suppressing talent; he therefore spoke well of him, deeming him the finest among those rated in the second grade.

entries.zh: 衛將軍楊珧辟為掾，除太子舍人，累遷散騎常侍、征西軍司。
entries.en: Yang Yao, General of the Guards, took him on as a clerk; he was made a gentleman attendant at the heir’s household and eventually promoted through posts to cavalier attendant-in-ordinary and western-expedition army supervisor.
entries.literal: General of the Guards Yang Yao summoned him as a clerk; he was appointed Gentleman Attendant at the Heir Apparent’s Household, then rose in stages to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Army Supervisor on the Western Expedition.

entries.zh: 晉昌張越，涼州大族，讖言張氏霸涼，自以才力應之。
entries.en: Zhang Yue of Jinchang, a powerful Liangzhou lineage, read a prophecy that the Zhangs would dominate the west and believed he was the man.
entries.literal: Zhang Yue of Jinchang, a great clan of Liangzhou, believed a prophecy that the Zhang house would rule Liangzhou and thought his own talents matched it.

entries.zh: 從隴西內史遷梁州刺史。
entries.en: He transferred from Longxi interior administrator to Liangzhou inspector.
entries.literal: He moved from interior administrator of Longxi to inspector of Liangzhou.

entries.zh: 越志在涼州，遂託病歸河西，陰圖代軌，乃遣兄鎮及曹祛、麹佩移檄廢軌，以軍司杜耽攝州事，使耽表越為刺史。
entries.en: His sights were fixed on Liangzhou, so he pretended illness, slipped back to Hexi, and conspired to oust Zhang Gui, circulating a manifesto through his brother Zhang Zhen, Cao Qu, and Qu Pei, installing army supervisor Du Dan and urging the court to name himself inspector.
entries.literal: Yue’s ambition lay in Liangzhou; he therefore feigned illness and returned to the west of the river, secretly plotting to supplant Gui. He sent his elder brother Zhen together with Cao Qu and Qu Pei to circulate a proclamation deposing Gui, had Army Supervisor Du Dan act in provincial affairs, and had Dan memorialize recommending Yue as inspector.

entries.zh: 軌令曰：「吾在州八年，不能綏靖區域，又值中州兵亂，秦隴倒懸，加以寢患委篤，實思斂跡避賢。
entries.en: Zhang Gui issued a notice: “Eight years in office and I have still not quieted the frontier; the heartland is at war and Longyou reels, while my sickness worsens—I would gladly step aside for someone abler.
entries.literal: Gui issued an order saying, ‘I have been in this province eight years yet have been unable to pacify the region; moreover the central plain is torn by soldiers, Qin and Long hang upside down, and my illness grows grave—I truly wish to retire and yield the worthy.

entries.zh: 但負荷任重，未便輒遂。
entries.en: Yet the charge is too heavy to cast off on a whim.
entries.literal: But the burden on my shoulders is heavy, and I cannot lightly walk away.

entries.zh: 不圖諸人橫興此變，是不明吾心也。
entries.en: I never thought you would stir such a revolt; you misread my intentions.
entries.literal: I did not expect you gentlemen suddenly to raise this trouble—you do not understand my heart.

entries.zh: 吾視去貴州如脫屣耳！」
entries.en: To me, leaving your fine province would be as easy as kicking off a slipper!”
entries.literal: I regard leaving your noble province as lightly as kicking off a sandal!’

entries.zh: 欲遣主簿尉髦奉表詣闕，便速脂轄，將歸老宜陽。
entries.en: He meant to send chief clerk Wei Mao to the capital with a memorial, then pack his carriage and retire to Yiyang.
entries.literal: He wished to send his chief clerk Wei Mao to present a memorial at the palace gates, then quickly grease the axle hubs and retire to old age in Yiyang.

entries.zh: 長史王融、參軍孟暢蹋折鎮檄，排闔諫曰：「晉室多故，人神塗炭，實賴明公撫寧西夏。
entries.en: Chief clerk Wang Rong and adjutant Meng Chang shredded Zhang Zhen’s edict, forced their way in, and pleaded: “The Jin court is in crisis; only you can steady the western regions.
entries.literal: The chief clerk Wang Rong and adjutant Meng Chang tore up Zhen’s proclamation, burst through the doors, and remonstrated, saying, ‘The house of Jin faces many crises; gods and men are smeared with ashes; we truly depend on you, sir, to soothe the western Xia.

entries.zh: 張鎮兄弟敢肆凶逆，宜聲其罪而戮之，不可成其志也。」
entries.en: Zhang Zhen’s faction must be denounced and cut down; you cannot let their plot stand.”
entries.literal: The brothers Zhang Zhen dare to commit such violence; you should proclaim their crimes and execute them—you must not let them succeed.’

entries.zh: 軌嘿然。
entries.en: Zhang Gui said nothing.
entries.literal: Gui was silent.

entries.zh: 融等出而戒嚴。
entries.en: When they withdrew, they put the army on full alert.
entries.literal: After Rong and the others left, they ordered the troops on alert.

entries.zh: 武威太守張琠遣子坦馳詣京，表曰：「魏尚安邊而獲戾，充國盡忠而被譴，皆前史之所譏，今曰之明鑒也。
entries.en: Wuwei’s grand administrator Zhang Tian rushed his son Tan to court with a memorial saying, "Wei Shang secured the border yet incurred blame; Zhao Chongguo gave his utmost loyalty yet suffered impeachment—both were mocked by earlier histories and are clear mirrors for today.
entries.literal: The grand administrator of Wuwei, Zhang Tian, sent his son Tan posthaste to the capital with a memorial saying, "Wei Shang secured the border yet incurred blame; Zhao Chongguo gave his utmost loyalty yet suffered impeachment—both were mocked by earlier histories and are clear mirrors for today.

entries.zh: 順陽之思劉陶，守闕者千人。
entries.en: At Shunyang a thousand people besieged the gates for Liu Tao’s sake.
entries.literal: In Shunyang a thousand men thronged the palace gates thinking of Liu Tao.

entries.zh: 刺史之蒞臣州，若慈母之于赤子，百姓之愛臣軌，若旱苗之得膏雨。
entries.en: Your inspector has been a mother to us; the people cherish Zhang Gui as parched shoots welcome rain.
entries.literal: When the inspector came to my province it was like a loving mother toward an infant; the people’s love for your servant Gui is like drought-stricken seedlings meeting timely rain.

entries.zh: 伏聞信惑流言，當有遷代，民情嗷嗷，如失父母。
entries.en: Rumors of his replacement have left the populace wailing like orphans.
entries.literal: We have heard that credulous rumors speak of a change of office; the folk wail as if they had lost father and mother.

entries.zh: 今戎夷猾夏，不宜騷動一方。」
entries.en: With barbarians ravaging the heartland, the west must not be thrown into turmoil.”
entries.literal: Now the barbarians are raiding the Xia lands; you ought not to stir up trouble in this region.’

entries.zh: 尋以子寔為中督護，率兵討鎮。
entries.en: He then named his son Zhang Shi central army supervisor and marched against Zhang Zhen.
entries.literal: Shortly thereafter he appointed his son Shi as central army supervisor and led troops against Zhen.

entries.zh: 遣鎮外甥太府主簿令狐亞前喻鎮曰：「舅何不審安危，明成敗？
entries.en: He sent Zhang Zhen’s nephew Linghu Ya ahead to ask: “Have you weighed the odds, uncle?
entries.literal: He sent Zhen’s nephew, chief clerk of the grand treasury Linghu Ya, ahead to lecture Zhen, saying, ‘Uncle, have you not weighed safety against danger and understood success and failure?

entries.zh: 主公西河著德，兵馬如雲，此猶烈火已焚，待江漢之水，溺於洪流，望越人之助，其何及哉！
entries.en: His lordship’s fame fills the west and his host is like a cloud—waiting for the Yangzi when the blaze has started is futile.
entries.literal: Our lord’s virtue is renowned west of the Yellow River, and his soldiers are like clouds—this is like a fire already blazing while you wait for the waters of the Yangzi and Han, or drowning in a flood while you look for help from the Yue—how could that arrive in time!

entries.zh: 今數萬之軍已臨近境，今唯全老親，存門戶，輸誠歸官，必保萬全之福。」
entries.en: Tens of thousands stand at your gates; save your family by submitting in good faith and you will keep fortune whole."
entries.literal: Now several tens of thousands of troops are already at your border; your only course is to preserve your aged kin, save your household, and surrender in good faith to the authorities, and you are sure to win the blessing of perfect safety."

entries.zh: 鎮流涕曰：「人誤我也！」
entries.en: Zhang Zhen wept, “I was led astray!”
entries.literal: Zhen wept and said, ‘Men have misled me!’

entries.zh: 乃委罪功曹魯連而斬之，詣寔歸罪。
entries.en: He blamed merit clerk Lu Lian, executed him, and went to Zhang Shi to surrender.
entries.literal: Thereupon he shifted blame to his merit clerk Lu Lian, beheaded him, and went to Shi to confess guilt.

entries.zh: 南討曹祛，走之。
entries.en: Zhang Shi took the army south, struck Cao Qu, and sent him fleeing.
entries.literal: Zhang Shi marched south against Cao Qu and drove him off.

entries.zh: 張坦至自京師，帝優詔勞軌，依模所表，命誅曹祛。
entries.en: Zhang Tan’s arrival from Luoyang brought an imperial rescript praising Zhang Gui and, on Sima Mo’s recommendation, commanding Cao Qu’s death.
entries.literal: When Tan arrived from the capital, the emperor issued a gracious edict comforting Gui, following Mo’s memorial, and ordered Cao Qu executed.

entries.zh: 軌大悅，赦州內殊死已下。
entries.en: Zhang Gui rejoiced and declared an amnesty short of capital crimes.
entries.literal: Gui was greatly pleased and granted amnesty within the province for all crimes short of capital ones.

entries.zh: 命寔率尹員、宋配步騎三萬討祛，別遣從事田迥、王豐率騎八百自姑臧西南出石驢，據長寧。
entries.en: He told Zhang Shi to take Yin Yuan, Song Pei, and thirty thousand men against Cao Qu while aides Tian Jiong and Wang Feng led eight hundred horse southwest from Guzang via Stone Mule to seize Changning.
entries.literal: He ordered Shi to lead Yin Yuan, Song Pei, and thirty thousand foot and horse against Qu, and separately sent aides Tian Jiong and Wang Feng with eight hundred cavalry southwest from Guzang out through Stone Mule to hold Changning.

entries.zh: 怯遣麹晁距戰于黃阪。
entries.en: Cao Qu dispatched Qu Chao to hold them at Yellow Slope.
entries.literal: Cao Qu sent Qu Chao to oppose them at Yellow Slope.

entries.zh: 寔詭道出浩亹，戰於破羌。
entries.en: Zhang Shi slipped through Haomen and fought at Poqiang.
entries.literal: Shi took a concealed route through Haomen and fought at Poyang.

entries.zh: 軌斬祛及牙門田囂。
entries.en: Zhang Gui executed Cao Qu and gate captain Tian Xiao.
entries.literal: Zhang Gui put Cao Qu and gate guard Tian Ao to death.

entries.zh: 遣治中張閬送義兵五千及郡國秀孝貢計、器甲方物歸於京師。
entries.en: He dispatched headquarters aide Zhang Lang with five thousand volunteer troops, provincial examination graduates, tribute tallies, arms, and native goods to Luoyang.
entries.literal: He sent headquarters aide Zhang Lang to escort five thousand righteous troops together with commandery and kingdom “filial and incorrupt” candidates, tribute accounts, armor, weapons, and local products to the capital.

entries.zh: 令有司可推詳立州已來清貞德素，嘉遁遺榮：「高才碩學，著述經史；
entries.en: He told officials to compile, from the founding of the province, lists of the incorrupt, the reclusive, and "men of high talent and broad learning who have authored Classics and histories;
entries.literal: He ordered the relevant offices to investigate thoroughly, since the province was founded, for chaste integrity and plain virtue, for reclusion with honor renounced, for "men of high talent and broad learning who have authored Classics and histories;

entries.zh: 臨危殉義，殺身為君；
entries.en: those who died for loyalty in crisis;
entries.literal: for those who faced peril and died for righteousness, giving their lives for the ruler;

entries.zh: 忠諫而嬰禍，專對而釋患；
entries.en: those who remonstrated at the cost of their lives and diplomats who talked their way out of danger;
entries.literal: for loyal remonstrators who met disaster, and envoys who by eloquence dispelled peril;

entries.zh: 權智雄勇，為時除難；
entries.en: strategists and champions who removed threats to the state;
entries.literal: for men of bold stratagem and heroic courage who removed difficulties for the age;

entries.zh: 謅佞誤主，傷陷忠賢；
entries.en: and flatterers who led rulers astray and ruined good men;
entries.literal: for sycophants who misled their lords and injured the loyal and worthy;

entries.zh: 具狀以聞。」
entries.en: each case to be reported in detail."
entries.literal: submit full particulars in memorials."

entries.zh: 州中父老莫不相慶。
entries.en: The province’s elders rejoiced together.
entries.literal: Not one of the elders of the province failed to rejoice.

entries.zh: 光祿傅祗、太常摯虞遺軌書，告京師饑匱，軌即遣參軍杜勳獻馬五百匹、毯布三萬匹。
entries.en: Fu Zhi and Zhi Yu wrote that Luoyang was starving; Zhang Gui at once sent adjutant Du Xun with five hundred horses and thirty thousand bolts of felt and cloth.
entries.literal: Superintendent of the Household Fu Zhi and Chamberlain for Ceremonies Zhi Yu sent Gui letters telling him that the capital was starving; Gui immediately sent adjutant Du Xun to present five hundred horses and thirty thousand bolts of felt and cloth.

entries.zh: 帝遣使者進拜鎮西將軍、都督隴右諸軍事，封霸城侯，進車騎將軍、開府辟如、儀同三司。
entries.en: Imperial envoys promoted him to General Who Garrisons the West, commander of all Longyou armies, marquis of Bacheng, then chariot-and-horse general with independent staff and honors matching the three dukes.
entries.literal: The emperor dispatched envoys promoting him to General Who Garrisons the West and Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs on the right of Long, enfeoffing him as Marquis of Baling, then advancing him to chariot-and-horse general with a separate establishment equal to the Three Excellencies and ceremonies matching the Three Councillors.

entries.zh: 策未至，而王彌遂逼洛陽，軌遣將軍張斐、北宮純、郭敷等率精騎五千來衛京都。
entries.en: Before the patent reached him, Wang Mi threatened Luoyang, so he sent Zhang Fei, Beigong Chun, and Guo Fu with five thousand elite horse to the capital’s relief.
entries.literal: Before the patent arrived, Wang Mi pressed Luoyang; Gui sent generals Zhang Fei, Bei Gong Chun, and Guo Fu with five thousand picked cavalry to defend the capital.

entries.zh: 及京都陷，斐等皆沒於賊。
entries.en: When Luoyang fell, those generals died in the enemy ranks.
entries.literal: When the capital fell, Fei and the others all perished among the bandits.

entries.zh: 中州避難來者日月相繼，分武威置武興郡以居之。
entries.en: Fugitives from the east streamed in daily, so he carved Wuxing commandery out of Wuwei to house them.
entries.literal: Refugees from the central provinces arrived day after day; he divided off part of Wuwei to form Wuxing commandery to settle them.

entries.zh: 太府主簿馬魴言於軌曰：「四海傾覆，乘輿未反，明公以全州之力徑造平陽，必當萬里風披，有征無戰。
entries.en: The chief clerk of the grand treasury Ma Fang said to Gui, ‘The four seas are overturned and the imperial carriage has not returned; if you, sir, with the strength of a whole province marched straight on Pingyang, you would scatter the enemy for ten thousand li without a battle.
entries.literal: The chief clerk of the grand treasury Ma Fang said to Gui, ‘The four seas are overturned and the imperial carriage has not returned; if you, sir, with the strength of a whole province marched straight on Pingyang, you would scatter the enemy for ten thousand li without a battle.

entries.zh: 未審何憚不為此舉？」
entries.en: I do not understand what you fear that keeps you from doing this.’
entries.literal: I do not understand what you fear that keeps you from doing this.’

entries.zh: 軌曰：「是孤心也。」
entries.en: Zhang Gui answered, “That has been my own mind as well.”
entries.literal: Gui said, ‘That is this solitary one’s own heart.’

entries.zh: 又聞秦王入關，乃馳檄關中曰：「主上遘危，遷幸非所，普天分崩，率土喪氣。
entries.en: Learning that the Prince of Qin had entered the passes, he fired a manifesto into Guanzhong: “The Son of Heaven is in jeopardy, driven to an unworthy refuge; the realm is shattered and morale is broken.
entries.literal: When he also heard that the Prince of Qin had entered the passes, he hurriedly sent a proclamation into Guanzhong saying, ‘The sovereign has met peril and been moved to a place that is not fitting; all under heaven is split apart, and every inch of soil has lost its breath.

entries.zh: 秦王天挺聖德，神武應期。
entries.en: The Prince of Qin bears heaven’s sagely virtue, a warlike spirit born for the moment.
entries.literal: The Prince of Qin is heaven-endowed with sagely virtue, divine in arms and fitted to the hour.’

entries.zh: 世祖之孫，王今為長。
entries.en: You are of Shizu’s line, and among the princes you now stand first.
entries.literal: He is a grandson of Emperor Shizu; you, Prince, are now the senior among us.

entries.zh: 凡我晉人，食土之類，龜筮克從，幽明同款。
entries.en: Every Jin subject dwelling on this earth finds tortoise and milfoil in accord, and both realms of the unseen give their assent.
entries.literal: All of us people of Jin who live on this soil—tortoise-shell and milfoil approve, and the spirits of light and dark are of one mind.

entries.zh: 宜簡令奪奉登皇位。
entries.en: The time has come to choose a worthy man and set him on the throne.
entries.literal: It is fitting to select the worthy and raise him to the imperial throne.

entries.zh: 今遣前鋒督護宋配步騎二萬，徑至長安，翼衛乘輿，折沖左右。
entries.en: He dispatches Song Pei, forward supervisor, with twenty thousand troops to Chang’an to guard the emperor and clear the flanks.
entries.literal: Now I send Forward Army Supervisor Song Pei with twenty thousand foot and horse straight to Chang’an to shield the imperial carriage and strike down foes on either side.

entries.zh: 西中郎寔中軍三萬，武威太守張琠胡騎二萬，駱驛繼發，仲秋中旬會于臨晉。」
entries.en: Zhang Shi, as western household general, leads thirty thousand from the central army; Zhang Tian of Wuwei brings twenty thousand Hu horse—all marching in relays to rendezvous at Linjin by mid-autumn."
entries.literal: Western Household General Zhang Shi with thirty thousand central-army troops; Grand Administrator Zhang Tian of Wuwei with twenty thousand Hu cavalry—these are to follow in continuous columns and assemble at Linjin in the middle ten days of mid-autumn."

entries.zh: 張軌
entries.en: The subject of this biography is Zhang Gui.
entries.literal: Zhang Gui.

entries.zh: 晉自元康之後，政亂朝昏，禍難薦興，艱虞孔熾，遂使奸凶放命，戎狄交侵，函夏沸騰，蒼生塗炭，干戈日用，戰爭方興。
entries.en: After the Yuankang years, Jin fell into turmoil: the administration unraveled and the court grew dim; calamities piled up and distress burned hot. Villains defied authority, northern tribes took turns raiding the heartland, the realm convulsed, and common folk were ground to dust under ceaseless arms and spreading war.
entries.literal: From after the Yuankang era of Jin, government was chaotic and the court dark; disasters arose in succession and hardship blazed fiercely, so that villains threw off restraint and Rong and Di invaded in turn; the heartland seethed, the black-haired people were smeared with charcoal; arms were wielded daily and war had just begun to rise.

entries.zh: 雖背恩忘義之徒不可勝載，而蹈節輕生之士無乏于時。
entries.en: Traitors who threw away obligation were beyond counting, yet men who chose principle over life were never absent in those same years.
entries.literal: Though men who betrayed grace and forgot duty could not be fully recorded, yet men who embraced integrity and held life lightly were not lacking in that age.

entries.zh: 至若嵇紹之衛難乘輿，卞壼之亡軀鋒鏑，桓雄之義高田叔，周崎之節邁解揚，羅丁致命於舊君，辛吉恥臣於戎虜，張禕引鴆以全節，王諒斷臂以厲忠，莫不志烈秋霜，精貫白日，足以激清風于萬古，厲薄俗于當年者歟！
entries.en: Think of Ji Shao guarding the emperor's carriage in peril, Bian Kun falling to blades and shafts, Huan Xiong matching Tian Shu in devotion, Zhou Qi outdoing Jie Yang in steadfastness, Luo Ding dying for a former sovereign, Xin Ji refusing to bow to alien rulers, Zhang Yi drinking poison to keep his honor, Wang Liang cutting off an arm to prove his loyalty—each will like autumn frost, each spirit bright as noon, enough to quicken moral clarity for ages and shame a degenerate age.
entries.literal: As for Ji Shao shielding the imperial carriage in crisis, Bian Kun losing his body to spearheads and arrows, Huan Xiong, whose righteousness rivaled Tian Shu, Zhou Qi, whose integrity surpassed Jie Yang, Luo Ding laying down his life for his former lord, Xin Ji ashamed to serve barbarians as minister, Zhang Yi draining poison to preserve his integrity, Wang Liang severing an arm to steel his loyalty—all alike bore wills fierce as autumn frost and spirits piercing as the noon sun, enough to stir pure wind through ten thousand ages and shame shallow ways in their own day!

entries.zh: 所謂亂世識忠臣，斯之謂也。
entries.en: This is what men mean when they say troubled times reveal who the loyal ministers are.
entries.literal: What is called "in troubled times one recognizes loyal ministers" refers to this.

entries.zh: 卞壼、劉超、鐘雅、周虓等已入列傳，其餘即敘其行事以為《忠義傳》，用旌晉氏之有人焉。
entries.en: Bian Kun, Liu Chao, Zhong Ya, Zhou Xiao, and the like already have full biographies elsewhere; those who remain are collected here under Loyalty and Righteousness to show that the Jin court could still claim men of honor.
entries.literal: Bian Kun, Liu Chao, Zhong Ya, Zhou Xiao, and others have already entered the standard biographies; the rest are here narrated in conduct gathered as the "Biographies of Loyalty and Righteousness," to signal that the House of Jin still had such men.

entries.zh: 紹始入洛，或謂王戎曰：「昨于稠人中始見嵇紹，昂昂然如野鶴之在雞群。」
entries.en: When Shao first arrived in Luoyang, someone remarked to Wang Rong: "Yesterday, in the press of people, I saw Ji Shao for the first time—stately as a crane among barnyard fowl."
entries.literal: When Shao first entered Luoyang, someone said to Wang Rong: "Yesterday amid the crowd I first saw Ji Shao—towering, like a wild crane among chickens."

entries.zh: 戎曰：「君復未見其父耳。」
entries.en: Wang Rong answered: "Then you have not met his father."
entries.literal: Rong said: "You have still not seen his father."

entries.zh: 累遷汝陰太守。
entries.en: He rose through successive posts to Administrator of Ruyin.
entries.literal: He was promoted in stages to Administrator of Ruyin.

entries.zh: 尚書左僕射裴頠亦深器之，每曰：「使延祖為吏部尚書，可使天下無復遺才矣。」
entries.en: Pei Yi, Vice Director of the Left of the Secretariat, thought the world of him and used to say: "Put Yanzu in charge of personnel and no able man in the empire would go unused."
entries.literal: Vice Director of the Left of the Secretariat Pei Yi also deeply esteemed him, often saying: "Were Yanzu made Minister of Personnel, he could make it so the realm had no overlooked talent again."

entries.zh: 沛國戴晞少有才智，與紹從子含相友善，時人許以遠致，紹以為必不成器。
entries.en: Dai Xi of Pei was clever as a youth and close to Shao's nephew Ji Han; contemporaries predicted a brilliant career, yet Shao insisted he would never amount to anything.
entries.literal: Dai Xi of Pei was clever from youth and friendly with Shao's nephew Ji Han; people of the time promised him far-reaching success, but Shao believed he would surely fail to become a useful vessel.

entries.zh: 晞後為司州主簿，以無行被斥，州黨稱紹有知人之明。
entries.en: Xi later served as Si Province registrar until dismissed for scandalous behavior; locals then credited Shao with sound judgment of character.
entries.literal: Xi later became Registrar of Si Province and was dismissed for misconduct; his provincial circle praised Shao's discernment of men.

entries.zh: 轉豫章內史，以母憂，不之官。
entries.en: He was named Interior Governor of Yuzhang but stayed home to mourn his mother and never took up the post.
entries.literal: He was transferred to Interior Governor of Yuzhang but, owing to mourning for his mother, did not take up the post.

entries.zh: 服闋，拜徐州刺史。
entries.en: When mourning ended, he received appointment as Governor of Xuzhou.
entries.literal: When the mourning period ended, he was appointed Governor of Xuzhou.

entries.zh: 時石崇為都督，性雖驕暴，而紹將之以道，崇甚親敬之。
entries.en: Shi Chong was regional commander then—arrogant and harsh by nature—but Shao guided him with moral authority, and Chong came to trust and respect him deeply.
entries.literal: At the time Shi Chong was area commander; though by nature arrogant and violent, Shao led him by principle, and Chong greatly favored and respected him.

entries.zh: 後以長子喪去職。
entries.en: He later resigned when his eldest son died.
entries.literal: Later he left office upon the death of his eldest son.

entries.zh: 元康初，為給事黃門侍郎。
entries.en: Early in the Yuankang era he was appointed Palace Attendant and Gentleman at the Yellow Gate.
entries.literal: At the beginning of the Yuankang era he became Palace Attendant and Gentleman at the Yellow Gate.

entries.zh: 時侍中賈謐以外戚之寵，年少居位，潘岳、杜斌等皆附托焉。
entries.en: Palace Attendant Jia Mi then rode high as an imperial in-law; though barely grown, he wielded real power, and men such as Pan Yue and Du Bin clustered around him.
entries.literal: At the time Palace Attendant Jia Mi enjoyed favor as an imperial in-law; though young he held high rank, and Pan Yue, Du Bin, and others all attached themselves to him.

entries.zh: 謐求交於紹，紹距而不答。
entries.en: Jia Mi courted Shao's friendship; Shao kept him at arm's length and gave no answer.
entries.literal: Mi sought friendship with Shao, but Shao kept his distance and did not respond.

entries.zh: 及謐誅，紹時在省，以不阿比凶族，封弋陽子，遷散騎常侍，領國子博士。
entries.en: After Mi's execution, Shao—still at his post—was rewarded for refusing to truck with that villainous clan: he received the Yiyang barony, promotion to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, and concurrent charge of the Imperial Academy doctorate.
entries.literal: When Mi was executed, Shao was at the bureau; because he had not curried favor with the wicked clan, he was enfeoffed as Baron of Yiyang, promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, and placed in charge of the doctorate of the Imperial Academy.

entries.zh: 太尉、廣陵公陳准薨，太常奏諡，紹駁曰：「諡號所以垂之不朽，大行受大名，細行受細名，文武顯于功德，靈厲表於暗蔽。
entries.en: When Grand Commandant Chen Zhun, Duke of Guangling, died, the Chamberlain for Ceremonial proposed a posthumous honorific; Shao protested: titles are meant to endure—major deeds earn weighty names, slight deeds modest ones; civil and martial labels reflect true achievement, while epithets such as 'spirit' or 'severe' signal moral darkness.
entries.literal: When Grand Commandant and Duke of Guangling Chen Zhun died, the Chamberlain for Ceremonial proposed a posthumous title; Shao objected: "Posthumous titles exist to last forever—great conduct receives a great name, minor conduct a minor name; civil and martial virtue shines forth in merit, while 'spirit' and 'severe' mark hidden darkness.

entries.zh: 自頃禮官協情，諡不依本。
entries.en: Lately the ritualists have let sentiment bend the rules, and posthumous names no longer match the facts.
entries.literal: Recently ritual officials have bent to feeling so that posthumous titles no longer follow the truth.

entries.zh: 准諡為過，宜諡曰繆。」
entries.en: The proposed title for Zhun is too generous; he ought to be posthumously styled Miu—'Errant.'
entries.literal: Zhun's title is excessive; he should be styled 'Errant' (Miu)."

entries.zh: 事下太常。
entries.en: The case went to the Chamberlain for Ceremonial.
entries.literal: The matter was referred to the Chamberlain.

entries.zh: 時雖不從，朝廷憚焉。
entries.en: The court did not adopt his view, yet officials took his stance seriously.
entries.literal: Though the court did not follow him at the time, the officials stood in awe.

entries.zh: 趙王倫篡位，署為侍中。
entries.en: When Prince of Zhao Sima Lun seized the throne, Shao was named Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: When Prince Zhao Lun usurped the throne, Shao was appointed Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 惠帝復阼，遂居其職。
entries.en: After Emperor Hui was restored, Shao kept the same office.
entries.literal: When Emperor Hui resumed the throne, Shao remained in that role.

entries.zh: 司空張華為倫所誅，議者追理其事，欲復其爵，紹又駁曰：「臣之事君，當除煩去惑。
entries.en: When Minister of Works Zhang Hua was put to death by Lun, some argued for restoring his titles; Shao objected again: "A minister's duty is to clear away trouble and delusion for his sovereign.
entries.literal: Minister of Works Zhang Hua was executed by Lun; debaters revisited the matter and wished to restore his noble rank, but Shao again objected: "A minister serves his lord by removing confusion and distraction.

entries.zh: 華歷位內外，雖粗有善事，然闔棺之責，著於遠近，兆禍始亂，華實為之。
entries.en: Zhang Hua moved between palace and camp and did some good in small ways, yet his final reckoning was visible everywhere: the seeds of disaster were largely of his planting.
entries.literal: Hua held posts inside and outside the court; though he had some decent deeds, the blame that closes the coffin was plain far and near—the omens that began the calamity were really his doing.

entries.zh: 故鄭討幽公之亂，斫子家之棺；
entries.en: So Zheng, punishing Duke You of Lu's rebellion, split minister Zijia's coffin open with an axe.
entries.literal: Hence when Zheng punished the turmoil of Duke You, they hacked open Zijia's coffin;

entries.zh: 魯戮隱罪，終篇貶翬。
entries.en: Lu executed Guan Yin for his crime, and the Spring and Autumn closes by censuring Hui.
entries.literal: Lu executed Yin for his guilt, and the classic ends by censuring Hui.

entries.zh: 未忍重戮，事已弘矣，謂不宜復其爵位，理其無罪。」
entries.en: I will not press for harsher punishment than death; the case is already settled. Restoring his titles or declaring him blameless would be wrong."
entries.literal: I cannot bear to urge heavier punishment; the matter is already broad enough—I say his rank should not be restored nor his innocence proclaimed."

entries.zh: 時帝初反正，紹又上疏曰：「臣聞改前轍者則車不傾，革往弊者則政不爽。
entries.en: With the emperor newly restored, Shao submitted another memorial: "They say that straightening the wheel tracks keeps the carriage upright, and curing old abuses keeps government true.
entries.literal: At the time the emperor had just been restored; Shao further submitted a memorial: "I have heard that those who correct the rut keep the cart from tipping; those who mend past abuses keep government sound.

entries.zh: 太一統于元首，百司役於多士，故周文興于上，成康穆於下也。
entries.en: The supreme pivot sits with the ruler; every ministry depends on capable men—thus King Wen flourished on high while kings Cheng and Kang enjoyed peace below.
entries.literal: The Grand Unity rests in the sovereign's head; myriad offices labor through many officers—thus King Wen rose above and Cheng and Kang were tranquil below.

entries.zh: 存不忘亡，《易》之善義；
entries.en: The Changes teaches us to remember peril even in safety—
entries.literal: To remember survival amid peril is the fine meaning of the Changes;

entries.zh: 願陛下無忘金墉，大司馬無忘潁上，大將軍無忘黃橋，則禍亂之萌無由而兆矣。」
entries.en: May Your Majesty remember the fortress at Jinyong; may the Grand Marshal remember Yingshang; may the Grand General remember Huang Bridge—then the seeds of calamity will never sprout."
entries.literal: I pray Your Majesty will not forget Jinyong; the Grand Marshal will not forget Yingshang; the Grand General will not forget Huang Bridge—then the sprouts of disaster will have nowhere to arise."

entries.zh: 尋徵為御史中丞，未拜，復為侍中。
entries.en: He was soon summoned as assistant chief of the Censorate but, before taking up the post, was again named Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: Soon he was summoned as Palace Assistant Clerk of the Censorate; before he took office he again became Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 河間王顒、成都王穎舉兵向京都，以討長沙王乂，大駕次於城東。
entries.en: Prince of Hejian Sima Yong and Prince of Chengdu Sima Ying marched on the capital against Prince of Changsha Sima Yi; the imperial train halted east of the walls.
entries.literal: Prince of Hejian Sima Yong and Prince of Chengdu Sima Ying raised troops toward the capital to strike Prince of Changsha Sima Yi; the imperial carriage halted east of the city.

entries.zh: 乂言於眾曰：「今日西討，欲誰為都督乎？」
entries.en: Yi asked the gathered officers: "For this western campaign, whom do you want as overall commander?"
entries.literal: Yi said to the assembly: "Today we march west—whom do you wish as commander?"

entries.zh: 六軍之士皆曰：「願嵇侍中戮力前驅，死猶生也。」
entries.en: The men of the six armies shouted: "We want Palace Attendant Ji in the van—we would rather die beside him than live elsewhere!"
entries.literal: The troops of the six armies said: "We wish Palace Attendant Ji to strain every nerve in the vanguard—to die would be as living."

entries.zh: 遂拜紹使持節、平西將軍。
entries.en: So Shao received the credential-bearing commission and the title General Who Pacifies the West.
entries.literal: Shao was therefore appointed commissioner bearing credentials and General Who Pacifies the West.

entries.zh: 屬乂被執，紹復為侍中。
entries.en: After Yi was captured, Shao returned to the post of Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: When Yi was seized, Shao again became Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 公王以下皆詣鄴謝罪於穎，紹等咸見廢黜，免為庶人。
entries.en: Every prince and noble went to Ye to submit to Sima Ying; Shao and his peers were stripped of office and reduced to common status.
entries.literal: All ranks from dukes and princes downward went to Ye to apologize to Ying; Shao and others were all cashiered and reduced to commoners.

entries.zh: 尋而朝廷復有北征之役，征紹，復其爵位。
entries.en: Soon the court launched another northern campaign, recalled Shao, and restored his titles.
entries.literal: Soon the court mounted another northern expedition and summoned Shao, restoring his noble rank.

entries.zh: 紹以天子蒙塵，承詔馳詣行在所。
entries.en: With the emperor on the run, Shao took the edict and rode hard for the imperial headquarters.
entries.literal: Because the Son of Heaven was in exile, Shao received the edict and galloped to the temporary residence.

entries.zh: 值王師敗績于蕩陰，百官及侍衛莫不散潰，唯紹儼然端冕，以身捍衛，兵交御輦，飛箭雨集，紹遂被害於帝側，血濺御服，天子深哀歎之。
entries.en: At Dangyin the imperial army collapsed; ministers and guards fled—only Shao, erect in full court dress, threw himself between the emperor and the blades. Weapons clashed around the carriage, arrows fell like rain, and Shao died at the sovereign's side, his blood staining the imperial robe while the emperor wept over him.
entries.literal: When the royal army was routed at Dangyin, officials and guards scattered in panic—only Shao, unmoved in full court garb, shielded the ruler with his body; weapons clashed about the imperial carriage and arrows fell like rain; Shao was thus slain beside the emperor, his blood splashing the imperial robe, and the Son of Heaven mourned him deeply.

entries.zh: 及事定，左右欲浣衣，帝曰：「此嵇侍中血，勿去。」
entries.en: Afterward, servants wanted to launder the robe; the emperor said: "That is Palace Attendant Ji's blood—leave it."
entries.literal: When things settled, attendants wished to wash the robe; the emperor said: "This is Palace Attendant Ji's blood—do not remove it."

entries.zh: 齊王冏辟為征西參軍，襲爵武昌鄉侯。
entries.en: Prince of Qi Sima Jiong appointed him adjutant on the western campaign, and he inherited the village marquisate at Wuchang.
entries.literal: Prince of Qi Sima Jiong summoned him as adjutant on the western expedition and he inherited the village marquisate of Wuchang.

entries.zh: 長沙王乂召為驃騎記室督、尚書郎。
entries.en: Prince of Changsha Sima Yi appointed him recorder-in-chief to the chief commander and Gentleman of the Secretariat.
entries.literal: Prince of Changsha Sima Yi summoned him as recorder-in-chief to the chief commander and Gentleman of the Secretariat.

entries.zh: 乂與成都王穎交戰，穎軍轉盛，尚書郎旦出督戰，夜還理事。
entries.en: When Yi clashed with Prince of Chengdu Sima Ying, Ying's forces gained ground; the Secretariat gentlemen rode out at dawn to supervise the fighting and returned after dark to manage paperwork.
entries.literal: Yi fought Prince of Chengdu Sima Ying; Ying's army grew stronger; the Secretariat gentlemen went out at dawn to oversee battle and returned at night to handle affairs.

entries.zh: 含言於乂曰：「昔魏武每有軍事，增置掾屬。
entries.en: Han urged Yi: "Whenever Emperor Wu of Wei faced war, he expanded aide posts.
entries.literal: Han said to Yi: "In old days whenever Wu of Wei had military affairs, he added aides and staff.

entries.zh: 青龍二年，尚書令陳矯以有軍務，亦奏增郎。
entries.en: In Qinglong 2, Director of the Secretariat Chen Jiao, citing military business, likewise petitioned for added Secretariat gentlemen.
entries.literal: In the second year of Qinglong, Director of the Secretariat Chen Jiao, because there were military matters, also memorialized to add gentlemen.

entries.zh: 今奸逆四逼，王路擁塞，倒懸之急，不復過此。
entries.en: Today rebels ring us on every side; the imperial highways clog; we hang by our heels—nothing could be more urgent.
entries.literal: Now treason presses from four sides; the royal road is blocked; the urgency of hanging upside down could not be greater.

entries.zh: 但居曹理事，尚須增郎，況今都官中騎三曹晝出督戰，夜還理事，一人兩役，內外廢乏。
entries.en: Stationery offices still need extra hands in quiet times—how much more when the Capital, Palace, and Cavalry sections march out by day to direct combat and draft orders by night; one officer pulling double duty exhausts both camp and capital.
entries.literal: Yet merely sitting in headquarters handling business still requires added gentlemen—how much more now when the Capital Bureau, Palace Bureau, and Cavalry Bureau go out by day to oversee battle and return by night to handle affairs—one man bearing two duties, inner and outer alike exhausted.

entries.zh: 含謂今有十萬人，都督各有主帥，推轂授綏，委付大將，不宜復令台僚雜與其間。」
entries.en: Han argues that with a hundred thousand troops under distinct commanders—each lieutenant invested with drum and reins—a chief general should hold the line; secretariat aides ought not clutter the chain of command."
entries.literal: Han holds that with one hundred thousand men, each command has its commander; push the carriage and hand the reins—entrust it to a great general; you should not again let terrace aides mix among them."

entries.zh: 乂從之，乃增郎及令史。
entries.en: Yi agreed and expanded the Secretariat rolls with added gentlemen and clerks.
entries.literal: Yi followed him and added gentlemen and clerks.

entries.zh: 冏令曰：「得前後白事，具意，輒別思量也。」
entries.en: Jiong replied: "I have your successive memorials in full; I will weigh them separately."
entries.literal: Jiong ordered: "I have received your successive reports in full; I will consider them separately."

entries.zh: 會長沙王乂至，於冏案上見豹箋，謂冏曰：「小子離間骨肉，何不銅駝下打殺！」
entries.en: When Prince of Changsha Sima Yi arrived, he spotted Bao's paper on Jiong's desk and snarled: "This whelp sows strife in the royal family—beat him to death under the bronze camels!"
entries.literal: When Prince of Changsha Sima Yi arrived, he saw Bao's memorandum on Jiong's desk and said to Jiong: "This boy sows discord among flesh and blood—why not beat him to death under the bronze camels!"

entries.zh: 冏既不能嘉豹之策，遂納乂言，乃奏豹曰：「臣忿奸凶肆逆，皇祚顛墜，與成都、長沙、新野共興義兵，安復社稷，唯欲戮力皇家，與親親宗室腹心從事，此臣夙夜自誓，無負神明。
entries.en: Jiong spurned Bao's advice and took Yi's bait, memorializing: "Your servant burns as traitors overturn heaven; with Chengdu, Changsha, and Xinyue I raised righteous armies to heal the altars—my vow night and day is to exhaust myself for the throne alongside true kinsmen—may the spirits witness me.
entries.literal: Jiong could not embrace Bao's plan; he accepted Yi's words and therefore memorialized concerning Bao: "Your subject resents how villains ran riot and the imperial fortune toppled; with Chengdu, Changsha, and Xinyue he jointly raised loyal troops to restore the altars—my sole wish is to strain every nerve for the royal house and work heart to heart with close imperial kin—this is what your subject swears day and night, not betraying the spirits.

entries.zh: 而主簿王豹比有白事，敢造異端，謂臣忝備宰相，必遘危害，慮在一旦，不祥之聲可蹻足而待，欲臣與成都分陝為伯，盡出籓王。
entries.en: Yet chief clerk Wang Bao keeps forwarding heterodox schemes—claiming this minister, unworthy though I am of the chancellorship, faces doom within days and ill omens before we lift a foot—demanding that I split the realm with Chengdu like the ancient elders and banish every prince to his fief.
entries.literal: Yet chief clerk Wang Bao has repeatedly submitted reports daring to craft strange heterodoxy, claiming your subject, shamefully filling the role of chief minister, is sure to meet harm and that peril waits within the day—inauspicious cries may arrive as soon as one lifts a heel—wishing your subject with Chengdu to divide Shan as elders and send out all the feudal princes.

entries.zh: 上誣聖朝鑒御之威，下長妖惑，疑阻眾心，噂背憎，巧賣兩端，訕上謗下，讒內間外，遘惡導奸，坐生猜嫌。
entries.en: He traduces imperial majesty above while sowing panic below; he sets minds doubting and breeds whispered hatred; he plays both ends, mocks superiors and baits inferiors, slanders court and alienates the regions—drawing villains together until suspicion festers.
entries.literal: Above he slanders the sagely court's awesome governance; below he fosters weird delusion, doubts and blocks the host of hearts—backbiting and hatred; he craftily sells to both sides, mocks above and slanders below, slanders within and estranges without—encountering evil and guiding villainy, sitting and breeding suspicion.

entries.zh: 昔孔丘匡魯，乃誅少正；
entries.en: Confucius restored Lu by executing Shaozheng Mao—
entries.literal: In old days Confucius restored Lu and thus executed Shaozheng Mao;

entries.zh: 子產相鄭，先戮鄧析，誠以交亂名實，若趙高詭怪之類也。
entries.en: Zichan governed Zheng and executed Deng Xi first—both struck down men who twisted name and fact like Zhao Gao's breed.
entries.literal: Zichan served Zheng as minister and first executed Deng Xi—truly because they confused name with reality, like Zhao Gao's deceitful sort.

entries.zh: 豹為臣不忠不順不義，輒敕都街考竟，以明邪正。」
entries.en: Wang Bao is disloyal, unfilial, unjust—I order him beaten to death in the capital street to mark the line between treason and right."
entries.literal: Bao as a subject was disloyal, unfilial, and unjust—your subject orders him interrogated to death in the capital avenue to clarify evil and upright."

entries.zh: 豹將死，曰：「懸吾頭大司馬門，見兵之攻齊也。」
entries.en: Facing death Bao said: "Hang my head on the Grand Marshal's gate—you will see armies march against Qi."
entries.literal: As Bao was about to die he said: "Hang my head at the Grand Marshal's gate—watch the armies attack Qi."

entries.zh: 眾庶冤之。
entries.en: The crowd counted him wronged.
entries.literal: The common people thought him wronged.

entries.zh: 俄而冏敗。
entries.en: Soon Sima Jiong fell.
entries.literal: Soon Jiong was defeated.

entries.zh: 劉沈，字道真，燕國薊人也。
entries.en: Liu Shen, courtesy name Daozhen, came from Ji in Yan.
entries.literal: Liu Shen, courtesy name Daozhen, was a man of Ji in the state of Yan.

entries.zh: 世為北州名族。
entries.en: His clan ranked among the north's great families for generations.
entries.literal: For generations his clan was a distinguished house of the northern provinces.

entries.zh: 少仕州郡，博學好古。
entries.en: Youth brought minor provincial posts; he read widely and revered antiquity.
entries.literal: In youth he served in provincial posts; he was broadly learned and loved antiquity.

entries.zh: 太保衛瓘辟為掾，領本邑大中正。
entries.en: Grand Mentor Wei Guan took him on as an aide and put him in charge of local personnel appraisal as senior rectifier.
entries.literal: Grand Mentor Wei Guan summoned him as aide and assigned him concurrent duty as senior rectifier for his native district.

entries.zh: 敦儒道，愛賢能，進霍原為二品，及申理張華，皆辭旨明峻，為當時所稱。
entries.en: He championed scholarship, prized talent, promoted Huo Yuan to the second grade, and defended Zhang Hua—each memorial lucid and uncompromising, earning wide acclaim.
entries.literal: He honored Confucian teaching and loved worthy talent; advancing Huo Yuan to the second rank and arguing Zhang Hua's case—all were marked by bright, stern wording and praised by contemporaries.

entries.zh: 齊王冏輔政，引為左長史，遷侍中。
entries.en: Prince of Qi Sima Jiong, while directing government, brought Liu Shen in as Left Senior Clerk and soon promoted him to Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: When Prince of Qi Sima Jiong directed affairs, he summoned Shen as Left Senior Clerk and promoted him to Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 于時李流亂蜀，詔沈以侍中、假節，統益州刺史羅尚、梁州刺史許雄等以討流。
entries.en: While Li Liu ravaged Shu, the throne named Liu Shen Palace Attendant with credential staff to coordinate Luo Shang of Yi Province, Xu Xiong of Liang Province, and others against him.
entries.literal: At that time Li Liu rebelled in Shu; an edict appointed Shen as Palace Attendant with credential staff to oversee Inspector of Yi Province Luo Shang, Inspector of Liang Province Xu Xiong, and others to strike Liu.

entries.zh: 行次長安，河間王顒請留沉為軍司，遣席薳代之。
entries.en: His march paused at Chang'an; Prince of Hejian Sima Yong asked to keep Liu Shen as army marshal and dispatched Xi Yuan to replace him on campaign.
entries.literal: Marching, he halted at Chang'an; Prince of Hejian Yong requested to retain Shen as army marshal and sent Xi Yuan to replace him.

entries.zh: 後領雍州刺史。
entries.en: He later added concurrent duty as Inspector of Yong Province.
entries.literal: Later he concurrently served as Inspector of Yong Province.

entries.zh: 及張昌作亂，詔顒遣沉將州兵萬人並征西府五千人，自藍田關以討之，顒不奉詔。
entries.en: When Zhang Chang rose, an edict told Yong to send Liu Shen with ten thousand Yong troops and five thousand western expedition troops through Lantian Pass—Yong ignored it.
entries.literal: When Zhang Chang rebelled, an edict ordered Yong to send Shen leading ten thousand provincial troops plus five thousand from the western expedition headquarters through Lantian Pass to attack him; Yong did not obey the edict.

entries.zh: 沉自領州兵至藍田，顒又逼奪其眾。
entries.en: Liu Shen drove the provincial army to Lantian anyway; Yong seized those troops from him.
entries.literal: Shen himself led provincial troops to Lantian; Yong again pressed and seized his forces.

entries.zh: 長沙王乂命沉將武吏四百人還州。
entries.en: Prince of Changsha Sima Yi ordered Liu Shen to march four hundred armed clerks back to Yong Province.
entries.literal: Prince of Changsha Yi ordered Shen to lead four hundred martial clerks back to the province.

entries.zh: 張方既逼京都，王師屢敗，王瑚、祖逖言於乂曰：「劉沈忠義果毅，雍州兵力足制河間，宜啟上詔與沈，使發兵襲顒，顒窘急，必召張方以自救，此計之良也。」
entries.en: With Zhang Fang threatening Luoyang and imperial armies failing, Wang Hu and Zu Ti urged Sima Yi: "Liu Shen is loyal and bold; Yong Province can pin Prince of Hejian—petition the emperor to order Shen to strike Yong; Yong, desperate, will recall Zhang Fang—that breaks the siege."
entries.literal: Once Zhang Fang threatened the capital and the royal army repeatedly lost, Wang Hu and Zu Ti said to Yi: "Liu Shen is loyal, righteous, resolute, and daring; Yong Province's military strength is enough to control Hejian—you should memorialize the throne to issue an edict to Shen ordering him to raise troops and strike Yong; Yong, embarrassed and pressed, is sure to summon Zhang Fang to rescue himself—this is an excellent plan."

entries.zh: 乂從之。
entries.en: Yi agreed.
entries.literal: Yi followed them.

entries.zh: 沈奉詔馳檄四境，合七郡之眾及守防諸軍、塢壁甲士萬餘人，以安定太守衛博、新平太守張光、安定功曹皇甫澹為先登，襲長安。
entries.en: Liu Shen rode the edict to rally seven counties, garrisons, and fortress troops—more than ten thousand—then struck Chang'an with Wei Bo of Anding, Zhang Guang of Xinping, and Huangfu Dan leading the van.
entries.literal: Shen received the edict and galloped proclamations through the four borders, assembling the hosts of seven counties together with garrison defenders and fort warriors—over ten thousand—and with Administrator of Anding Wei Bo, Administrator of Xinping Zhang Guang, and merit evaluator Huangfu Dan of Anding as van bearers, attacked Chang'an.

entries.zh: 顒時頓于鄭縣之高平亭，為東軍聲援，聞沈兵起，還鎮渭城，遣督護虞夔率步騎萬餘人逆沈於好畤。
entries.en: Sima Yong had camped at Gaoping Pavilion to screen eastern reinforcements; hearing Liu Shen move, he pulled back to Weicheng and sent Yu Kui with ten thousand horse and foot to intercept Shen at Haozhi.
entries.literal: Yong at that time was halted at Gaoping Pavilion in Zheng County as eastern-army support; hearing Shen's troops had risen, he returned to guard Weicheng and sent Protector Yu Kui with over ten thousand infantry and cavalry to oppose Shen at Haozhi.

entries.zh: 接戰，夔眾敗，顒大懼，退入長安，果急呼張方。
entries.en: Kui lost the engagement; Yong fled into Chang'an in panic and screamed for Zhang Fang.
entries.literal: They engaged in battle; Kui's host was defeated; Yong was greatly afraid and withdrew into Chang'an, urgently summoning Zhang Fang.

entries.zh: 沈渡渭而壘，顒每遣兵出鬥，輒不利，沈乘勝攻之，使澹、博以精甲五千，從長安門而入，力戰至顒帳下。
entries.en: Liu Shen crossed the Wei and walled up; Yong's sallies failed again and again—Shen pressed the advantage, sending Huangfu Dan and Wei Bo with five thousand elite armored men through Chang'an Gate to fight through to Yong's headquarters.
entries.literal: Shen crossed the Wei and built ramparts; Yong repeatedly sent troops out to fight but consistently failed; Shen exploited victory to attack him, ordering Dan and Bo with five thousand picked armored troops to enter through Chang'an Gate and fight fiercely to Yong's command tent.

entries.zh: 沈軍來遲，顒軍見澹等無繼，氣益倍。
entries.en: Shen's main body arrived late; Yong's men saw Dan had no backup and doubled their fighting spirit.
entries.literal: Shen's army arrived late; Yong's troops saw Dan and others had no reinforcements and their morale doubled.

entries.zh: 馮翊太守張輔率眾救顒，橫擊之，大戰於府門，博父子皆死之，澹又被擒。
entries.en: Zhang Fu of Fengyi slammed into Shen's flank before Yong's yamen—Wei Bo and his son died there; Huangfu Dan was taken.
entries.literal: Administrator of Fengyi Zhang Fu led a host to rescue Yong and struck them sideways; they fought a great battle at the headquarters gate—Bo and his son both died in it, and Dan was also captured.

entries.zh: 顒奇澹壯勇，將活之。
entries.en: Yong admired Dan's courage and meant to spare him.
entries.literal: Yong marveled at Dan's bravery and wished to spare him.

entries.zh: 澹不為之屈，於是見殺。
entries.en: Dan refused to bend, so Yong executed him.
entries.literal: Dan would not yield and was therefore executed.

entries.zh: 沈軍遂敗，率余卒屯于故營。
entries.en: Shen's line collapsed; he gathered survivors at the old camp.
entries.literal: Shen's army was thus defeated; he led surviving troops to camp at the old stockade.

entries.zh: 張方遣其將敦偉夜至，沈軍大驚而潰，與麾下百餘人南遁，為陳倉令所執。
entries.en: Zhang Fang's officer Dun Wei struck by night; Shen's men broke and fled—he escaped south with a hundred riders until the Chencang magistrate seized him.
entries.literal: Zhang Fang sent his general Dun Wei by night; Shen's army panicked and scattered; with over a hundred followers he fled south and was seized by the magistrate of Chencang.

entries.zh: 沈謂顒曰：「夫知己之顧輕，在三之節重，不可違君父之詔，量強弱以苟全。
entries.en: Liu Shen told Yong: "Private kindness weighs little beside the three great bonds—I cannot defy sovereign and father to save myself by calculating odds.
entries.literal: Shen said to Yong: "Though favor from a confidant may be light, the obligation of the three bonds weighs heavily—I may not disobey father and lord's edicts nor gauge strength and weakness to preserve myself cheaply.

entries.zh: 投袂之日，期之必死，菹醢之戮，甘之如薺。」
entries.en: The day I raised arms I accepted death—mincing and saucing would taste to me like spring greens."
entries.literal: The day I cast aside my sleeve I fixed my heart on death—pickling and mincing punishment I would relish like shepherd's purse."

entries.zh: 辭義慷慨，見者哀之。
entries.en: He spoke with blazing conviction; onlookers wept for him.
entries.literal: His words were righteous and stirring; those who saw pitied him.

entries.zh: 顒怒，鞭之而後腰斬。
entries.en: Yong had him flogged, then cut in half at the waist.
entries.literal: Yong angrily flogged him and then cut him in two at the waist.

entries.zh: 有識者以顒干上犯順，虐害忠義，知其滅亡不久也。
entries.en: Thoughtful observers saw Yong defying heaven and torturing loyal men—they knew he would not last.
entries.literal: Knowing men considered that Yong had offended superiors and violated propriety and cruelly harmed loyalty and righteousness—they knew his destruction would come soon.

entries.zh: 王育，字伯春，京兆人也。
entries.en: Wang Yu, courtesy name Bochun, hailed from Jingzhao.
entries.literal: Wang Yu, courtesy name Bochun, was a man of Jingzhao.

entries.zh: 少孤貧，為人傭牧羊，每過小學，必歔欷流涕。
entries.en: Poor and orphaned early, he hired out as a shepherd—passing village schools he always wept.
entries.literal: Orphaned young and poor, he hired out shepherding sheep for others; whenever he passed a village school he always sobbed and shed tears.

entries.zh: 時有暇，即折蒲學書，忘而失羊，為羊主所責，育將鬻己以償之。
entries.en: He stole moments to scratch letters on rushes—lost sheep and faced his master's wrath—ready to sell himself to pay.
entries.literal: When he had spare time he broke rushes to practice writing—forgetting and losing sheep—blamed by the sheep owner; Yu was about to sell himself to compensate.

entries.zh: 同郡許子章，敏達之士也，聞而嘉之，代育償羊，給其衣食，使與子同學，遂博通經史。
entries.en: Xu Zizhang of the same commandery, a generous scholar, paid his debt, clothed and fed him, and enrolled him beside his sons until Yu mastered the canon.
entries.literal: Xu Zizhang of the same commandery, a keen and accomplished man, heard and praised him; he compensated Yu's sheep for him and supplied clothes and food, had him study with his sons—thereupon Yu broadly mastered classics and histories.

entries.zh: 身長八尺餘，須長三尺，容貌絕異，音聲動人。
entries.en: He stood over eight chi tall with a three-chi beard—features unforgettable, voice compelling.
entries.literal: His height exceeded eight chi; his beard was three chi; his appearance was strikingly unusual; his voice moved others.

entries.zh: 子章以兄之子妻之，為立別宅，分之資業，育受之無愧色。
entries.en: Zizhang married a niece to him, built him a house, and split property—Yu accepted without false modesty.
entries.literal: Zizhang married his elder brother's daughter to him, built him a separate residence, and divided property with him—Yu accepted without shame.

entries.zh: 然行己任性，頗不偶俗。
entries.en: Yet he followed his own bent and ignored fashionable manners.
entries.literal: Yet in conduct he indulged his nature and largely did not conform to common ways.

entries.zh: 妻喪，吊之者不過四五人，然皆鄉閭名士。
entries.en: Only four or five mourners attended his wife's funeral—all were local worthies.
entries.literal: At his wife's funeral only four or five mourners came—yet all were eminent men of village and lane.

entries.zh: 太守杜宣命為主簿。
entries.en: Prefect Du Xuan named him chief clerk.
entries.literal: Administrator Du Xuan appointed him chief clerk.

entries.zh: 俄而宣左遷萬年令，杜令王攸詣宣，宣不迎之，攸怒曰：「卿往為二千石，吾所敬也。
entries.en: Soon Du Xuan became magistrate of Wannian; Wang You of Duling visited—Xuan refused a reception—You snapped: "You once ranked two thousand shi—I honored you.
entries.literal: Shortly Xuan was transferred down to magistrate of Wannian; Magistrate Wang You called on Xuan—Xuan did not go out to welcome him; You angrily said: "You formerly held two thousand shi—we respected you.

entries.zh: 今吾儕耳，何故不見迎？
entries.en: We are equals now—why no welcome?
entries.literal: Now we are peers—why do you not come welcome me?

entries.zh: 欲以小雀遇我，使我畏死鷂乎？」
entries.en: Do you treat me like a sparrow and expect terror before your goshawk?"
entries.literal: Do you mean to treat me like a little sparrow and make me fear a death hawk?"

entries.zh: 育執刀叱攸曰：「君辱臣死，自昔而然。
entries.en: Wang Yu drew a blade and roared at Magistrate You: "When the master is shamed, his man must die—the rule is ancient.
entries.literal: Wang Yu seized a knife and shouted at You: "When the lord is insulted the minister dies—it has been so since antiquity.

entries.zh: 我府君以非罪黜降，如日月之蝕耳，小縣令敢輕辱吾君！
entries.en: Our prefect fell without guilt—like a passing eclipse—how dare a county clerk insult him!
entries.literal: Our prefect was dismissed without crime—like an eclipse of sun or moon—how dare a petty county magistrate lightly insult our lord!

entries.zh: 汝謂吾刀鈍邪，敢如是乎！」
entries.en: You think this blade dull—how dare you!"
entries.literal: Do you say my blade is dull—how dare you behave thus!"

entries.zh: 前將殺之。
entries.en: He pressed forward to strike.
entries.literal: He stepped forward to kill him.

entries.zh: 宣懼，跣下抱育，乃止。
entries.en: Xuan sprang barefoot to hug him still.
entries.literal: Xuan feared, slipped barefoot down and embraced Yu—only then stopped.

entries.zh: 自此知名。
entries.en: His name spread from that day.
entries.literal: From this he became known.

entries.zh: 司徒王渾辟為掾，除南武陽令。
entries.en: Minister of Works Wang Hun took him as aide, then named him magistrate of Nanwuyang.
entries.literal: Minister of Works Wang Hun summoned him as aide; he was appointed magistrate of Nanwuyang.

entries.zh: 為政清約，宿盜逃奔他郡。
entries.en: His rule was spare and clean—veteran bandits fled to other counties.
entries.literal: His governance was clear and restrained—long-standing bandits fled to other commanderies.

entries.zh: 遷并州督護。
entries.en: He rose to Bing Province supervisor.
entries.literal: He was promoted to supervisor of Bing Province.

entries.zh: 成都王穎在鄴，又以育為振武將軍。
entries.en: Prince of Chengdu Sima Ying, camped at Ye, added the title General Who Rouses Might.
entries.literal: Prince of Chengdu Sima Ying was at Ye and again made Yu General Who Rouses Might.

entries.zh: 劉元海之為北單于，育說穎曰：「元海今去，育請為殿下促之，不然，懼不至也。」
entries.en: When Liu Yuan became Northern Chanyu, Yu urged Ying: "Let me ride after him now or he may never come."
entries.literal: When Liu Yuan became Northern Chanyu, Yu urged Ying: "Yuan is departing now—I beg to hurry him for Your Highness—otherwise I fear he will not come."

entries.zh: 穎然之，以育為破虜將軍。
entries.en: Ying agreed and named him General Who Breaks the Caitiffs.
entries.literal: Ying agreed and made Yu General Who Breaks the Caitiffs.

entries.zh: 元海遂拘之，其後以為太傅。
entries.en: Liu Yuan seized him—later raised him to Grand Tutor.
entries.literal: Yuan then detained him; afterward appointed him Grand Tutor.
