entries.zh: 韋忠字子節，平陽人也。
entries.en: Wei Zhong, courtesy name Zijie, came from Pingyang.
entries.literal: Wei Zhong, courtesy name Zijie, was a man of Pingyang.

entries.zh: 少慷慨，有不可奪之志。
entries.en: From youth he burned with principle nothing could break.
entries.literal: From youth he was impassioned and had an unshakeable will.

entries.zh: 好學博通，性不虛諾。
entries.en: He read widely and kept every pledge.
entries.literal: He loved learning and was broadly conversant; by nature he did not make empty promises.

entries.zh: 閉門修己，不交當世，每至吉凶，親表贈遺，一無所受。
entries.en: He shut his gate, shunned fashion, and refused every gift from kin at weddings or funerals.
entries.literal: He closed his gate and cultivated himself, did not mingle with contemporaries; whenever kin came with gifts for auspicious or inauspicious occasions he accepted nothing.

entries.zh: 年十二，喪父，哀慕毀悴，杖而後起。
entries.en: At twelve he buried his father—grief wasted him until he needed a cane to rise.
entries.literal: At twelve he lost his father; he mourned in grief emaciation and needed a staff to rise.

entries.zh: 司空裴秀吊之，匍匐號訴，哀慟感人。
entries.en: Minister Pei Xiu condoled—Zhong crawled forward wailing until listeners wept.
entries.literal: Minister of Works Pei Xiu condoled with him; he crawled and wailed his grievance—his grief moved others.

entries.zh: 秀出而告人曰：「此子長大必為佳器。」
entries.en: Pei Xiu left saying: "This boy will be worthy timber grown."
entries.literal: Xiu went out and told people: "This boy when grown will surely become fine timber."

entries.zh: 歸而命子頠造焉。
entries.en: He sent his son Pei Yi to call.
entries.literal: On returning he ordered his son Yi to visit him.

entries.zh: 服闋，遂廬於墓所。
entries.en: When mourning ended he built a hut at his father's tomb.
entries.literal: When mourning ended he therefore built a hut at the tomb site.

entries.zh: 頠慕而造之，皆托行不見。
entries.en: Pei Yi admired him and visited twice—Zhong pleaded errands and refused audience.
entries.literal: Yi admired him and went to visit—both times Zhong pleaded absence and did not see him.

entries.zh: 家貧，藜藿不充，人不堪其憂，而忠不改其樂。
entries.en: His house knew hunger—wild greens barely filled the bowl—others would despair; Zhong stayed content.
entries.literal: His household was poor—wild greens scarcely enough—others could not endure such sorrow yet Zhong did not alter his joy.

entries.zh: 頠為僕射，數言之于司空張華，華辟之，辭疾不起。
entries.en: When Pei Yi rose to Vice Director he praised Zhong to Zhang Hua—Zhang summoned him but Zhong pleaded illness.
entries.literal: When Yi became Vice Director, he repeatedly spoke of Zhong to Minister of Works Zhang Hua; Hua summoned him—Zhong declined illness and did not rise.

entries.zh: 人問其故，忠曰：「吾茨簷賤士，本無宦情。
entries.en: Asked why, he said: "I am a nobody under a thatched eaves—no taste for office.
entries.literal: People asked his reason; Zhong said: "I am a mean scholar under a thatched roof—originally without appetite for office.

entries.zh: 且茂先華而不實，裴頠欲而無厭，棄典禮而附賊後，若此，豈大丈夫之所宜行邪！
entries.en: Moreover Zhang Hua blooms without fruit; Pei Yi covets without limit—they betray ritual and cling to usurpers—what worthy man would walk that road!
entries.literal: Moreover Maoxian is flowery without substance; Pei Yi desires without satiety—they abandon canonical rites and attach themselves to villain successors—with conduct like this, how could it be fitting for a great man!

entries.zh: 裴常有心托我，常恐洪濤蕩岳，餘波見漂，況可臨尾閭而窺沃焦哉！」
entries.en: Pei Yi keeps pressing his patronage—I dread tidal waves that bury mountains and folk tossed on the backwash; why would I cling to the cosmic drain or stare into the burning shoal?"
entries.literal: Pei Yi has always wished to patronize me; I always feared great billows would scour the peaks and survivors drift on the wake—how much more dare I cling to Weilu's torrent and peek at Wojiao's shoals!"

entries.zh: 太守陳楚迫為功曹。
entries.en: Prefect Chen Chu forced him into the merit-evaluator post.
entries.literal: Administrator Chen Chu compelled him to serve as merit evaluator.

entries.zh: 會山羌破郡，楚攜子出走，賊射之，中三創。
entries.en: Mountain Qiang raiders shattered the district; Chu fled with his son until bandits shot them three times.
entries.literal: When Shanqiang tribes smashed the commandery, Chu fled carrying his son—the bandits shot them and struck three wounds.

entries.zh: 忠冒刃伏楚。
entries.en: Zhong threw himself onto Chu beneath the blades.
entries.literal: Zhong braved blades to shield Chu.

entries.zh: 以身捍之，泣曰：「韋忠願以身代君，乞諸君哀之。」
entries.en: Covering Chu with his body he wept: "Take me instead—spare him."
entries.literal: Using his body to defend him, weeping he said: "Wei Zhong wishes to substitute body for lord—I beg you gentlemen pity him."

entries.zh: 亦遭五矢。
entries.en: Five shafts struck him as well.
entries.literal: He also suffered five arrows.

entries.zh: 賊相謂曰：「義士也！」
entries.en: The bandits murmured: "A true righteous man!"
entries.literal: The bandits said to each other: "A man of principle!"

entries.zh: 舍之。
entries.en: They let them go.
entries.literal: They released him.

entries.zh: 忠於是負楚以歸。
entries.en: Zhong bore Chu home across his shoulders.
entries.literal: Zhong therefore carried Chu on his back home.

entries.zh: 後仕劉聰，為鎮西大將軍，平羌校尉，討叛羌，矢盡，不屈節而死。
entries.en: Under Liu Cong he became Grand General Who Guards the West and Colonel Who Pacifies the Qiang—fighting rebel Qiang until his arrows failed, he died unbroken.
entries.literal: Later he served Liu Cong as Grand General Who Guards the West and Colonel Who Pacifies the Qiang; campaigning against rebel Qiang he exhausted his arrows and died without yielding his integrity.

entries.zh: 張禕
entries.en: Zhang Yi
entries.literal: Zhang Yi

entries.zh: 張禕，吳郡人也。
entries.en: Zhang Yi came from Wu commandery.
entries.literal: Zhang Yi was a man of Wu commandery.

entries.zh: 少有操行。
entries.en: Even young he lived upright.
entries.literal: In youth he had conduct and integrity.

entries.zh: 恭帝為琅邪王，以禕為郎中令。
entries.en: As Prince of Langye, Emperor Gong named him palace captain.
entries.literal: When Emperor Gong was Prince of Langye—appointed Yi Palace Captain.

entries.zh: 及帝踐阼，劉裕以禕帝之故吏，素所親信，封藥酒一罌付禕密令鴆帝。
entries.en: After Gong took the throne, Liu Yu—trusting Yi as an old aide—handed him sealed wine to poison the retired emperor.
entries.literal: When the emperor ascended the throne—Liu Yu because Yi was the emperor's former clerk—long intimate—sealed a jug of poisoned wine—delivered it to Yi with secret order to poison the sovereign.

entries.zh: 禕既受命而歎曰：「鴆君而求生，何面目視息世間哉，不如死也！」
entries.en: Yi cried: "Murder my lord and yet seek to live—what face would I show breathing in this world—better to die!"
entries.literal: Yi having received the charge sighed: "Poisoning the ruler yet seeking life—what face to breathe in this world—better to die!

entries.zh: 因自飲之而死。
entries.en: He swallowed the draught and died.
entries.literal: Thereupon drank it himself and died.

entries.zh: 序
entries.en: Preface
entries.literal: Preface

entries.zh: 魯芝，字世英，扶風郿人也。
entries.en: Lu Zhi (courtesy Shiying) came from Mei county in Fufeng.
entries.literal: Lu Zhi, courtesy name Shiying, was a native of Mei in Fufeng.

entries.zh: 世有名德，為西州豪族。
entries.en: His clan had long been celebrated for integrity and ranked among the great houses of the northwest.
entries.literal: For generations his family had enjoyed renowned virtue and was a powerful clan of the western provinces.

entries.zh: 父為郭氾所害，芝繈褓流離，年十七，乃移居雍，耽思墳籍。
entries.en: Guo Si murdered his father; Zhi was still an infant when the family was scattered. At seventeen he settled in Yong and buried himself in the canon.
entries.literal: His father was killed by Guo Si; Zhi, still in swaddling clothes, wandered destitute, and at seventeen he moved to Yong, immersing himself in study of the classics.

entries.zh: 郡舉上計吏，州辟別駕。
entries.en: The commandery nominated him accounts clerk; the province called him up as provincial aide.
entries.literal: The commandery recommended him as clerk for the annual accounting; the province summoned him as provincial aide.

entries.zh: 魏車騎將軍郭淮為雍州刺史，深敬重之。
entries.en: Wei general Guo Huai, as inspector of Yong, treated him with exceptional respect.
entries.literal: Guo Huai, General of Chariots and Cavalry of Wei, was Inspector of Yong Province and held him in deep respect.

entries.zh: 舉孝廉，除郎中。
entries.en: Recommended as filial and incorrupt, he received a gentleman-of-the-interior appointment.
entries.literal: He was recommended as filial and incorrupt and appointed gentleman of the interior.

entries.zh: 會蜀相諸葛亮侵隴右，淮復請芝為別駕。
entries.en: When Zhuge Liang of Shu struck Longyou, Guo Huai again kept him on as provincial aide.
entries.literal: When the Shu chancellor Zhuge Liang invaded Longyou, Huai again asked Zhi to serve as provincial aide.

entries.zh: 事平，薦於公府，辟大司馬曹真掾，轉臨淄侯文學。
entries.en: After hostilities ended he went to the central ministries, served as staff to Grand Marshal Cao Zhen, then moved to tutor of literature for the marquis of Linzi.
entries.literal: When the affair was settled, [Zhi] was recommended to the ministerial offices and summoned as aide to the Grand Marshal Cao Zhen; he was transferred to literary instructor to the Marquis of Linzi.

entries.zh: 鄭袤薦于司空王朗，朗即加禮命。
entries.en: Zheng Mao introduced him to Wang Lang, minister of works, who honored him with an immediate posting.
entries.literal: Zheng Mao recommended him to Minister of Works Wang Lang, and Lang at once treated him with courtesy and appointed him.

entries.zh: 後拜騎都尉、參軍事、行安南太守，遷尚書郎。
entries.en: He rose through Commandant of Cavalry, military adviser, acting administrator of An'nan, and gentleman at the Masters of Writing.
entries.literal: Later he was appointed Commandant of Cavalry, joined military affairs, acted as Administrator of An'nan, was promoted to Gentleman of the Masters of Writing.

entries.zh: 曹真出督關右，又參大司馬軍事。
entries.en: When Cao Zhen supervised the region west of the passes, Zhi again served on the grand marshal's staff.
entries.literal: When Cao Zhen went out to supervise the west of the Pass, [Zhi] again joined the Grand Marshal's military staff.

entries.zh: 真薨，宣帝代焉，乃引芝參驃騎軍事，轉天水太守。
entries.en: After Cao Zhen died Sima Yi took his place and attached Zhi to the agile-cavalry command; Zhi then became administrator of Tianshui.
entries.literal: When Zhen died, the Emperor Xuan [Sima Yi] replaced him and then brought Zhi in to join the military staff of the General of Agile Cavalry; [Zhi] was transferred to Administrator of Tianshui.

entries.zh: 郡鄰於蜀，數被侵掠，戶口減削，寇盜充斥，芝傾心鎮衛，更造城市，數年間舊境悉復。
entries.en: Tianshui lay against Shu and suffered repeated raids: population fell and bandits multiplied. Zhi threw himself into defense, rebuilt the city, and within a few years the district recovered its old bounds.
entries.literal: The commandery bordered Shu and repeatedly suffered invasion and plunder; households dwindled and bandits swarmed. Zhi devoted himself to guarding and defending, rebuilt the walls and town, and within a few years the former territory was fully restored.

entries.zh: 遷廣平太守。
entries.en: He was transferred to Guangping.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Administrator of Guangping.

entries.zh: 天水夷夏慕德，老幼赴闕獻書，乞留芝。
entries.en: Yi tribesmen and Han alike cherished him; young and old traveled to the capital with petitions begging the court to keep him.
entries.literal: Both Yi and Han Chinese in Tianshui admired his virtue; old and young went to the capital to submit petitions asking that Zhi be kept [in office].

entries.zh: 魏明帝許焉，仍策書嘉歎，勉以黃霸之美，加討寇將軍。
entries.en: Emperor Ming agreed, issued a warm commendation comparing him to Huang Ba, and added the title General Who Suppresses Brigands.
entries.literal: Emperor Ming of Wei granted this; an edict was still issued praising him, encouraging him with the fine example of Huang Ba, and he was additionally granted the title General Who Suppresses Brigands.

entries.zh: 曹爽輔政，引為司馬。
entries.en: When Cao Shuang controlled the regency he took Zhi on as marshal.
entries.literal: When Cao Shuang dominated the government, [Shuang] brought [Zhi] in as marshal.

entries.zh: 芝屢有讜言嘉謀，爽弗能納。
entries.en: Zhi gave blunt, sound advice again and again; Shuang refused to listen.
entries.literal: Zhi repeatedly offered forthright counsel and fine plans, which Shuang could not accept.

entries.zh: 及宣帝起兵誅爽，芝率餘眾犯門斬關，馳出赴爽，勸爽曰：「公居伊周之位，一旦以罪見黜，雖欲牽黃犬，復可得乎！
entries.en: When the Emperor Xuan [Sima Yi] raised troops to execute Shuang, Zhi led the remaining troops to force the gates and break through the barriers, galloping out to join Shuang, and urged Shuang: 'You occupy the position of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou—once you are dismissed for crime, even if you wished to lead a yellow dog [on a hunt], could you have it again?
entries.literal: When the Emperor Xuan [Sima Yi] raised troops to execute Shuang, Zhi led the remaining troops to force the gates and break through the barriers, galloping out to join Shuang, and urged Shuang: 'You occupy the position of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou—once you are dismissed for crime, even if you wished to lead a yellow dog [on a hunt], could you have it again?

entries.zh: 若挾天子保許昌，杖大威以羽檄征四方兵，孰敢不從！
entries.en: If you seize the Son of Heaven and hold Xuchang, wielding great awe and dispatching feathered summons to levy troops from the four quarters, who would dare not follow?
entries.literal: If you seize the Son of Heaven and hold Xuchang, wielding great awe and dispatching feathered summons to levy troops from the four quarters, who would dare not follow?

entries.zh: 舍此而去，欲就東市，豈不痛哉！」
entries.en: To abandon this and depart, only to go to the eastern market [for execution]—how could it not be bitter?'
entries.literal: To abandon this and depart, only to go to the eastern market [for execution]—how could it not be bitter?'

entries.zh: 爽懦惑不能用，遂委身受戮。
entries.en: Shuang was timid and bewildered and ignored him; he surrendered and died under the blade.
entries.literal: Shuang was cowardly and confused and could not use [the advice]; he thereupon submitted his person and was executed.

entries.zh: 芝坐爽下獄，當死，而口不訟直，志不苟免。
entries.en: Zhi, tied to Shuang's faction, went to prison facing death, yet he neither whined for mercy nor grasped at an unworthy reprieve.
entries.literal: Zhi, implicated under Shuang, was imprisoned and sentenced to death, yet he did not argue his innocence aloud and was resolved not to seek escape unworthily.

entries.zh: 宣帝嘉之，赦而不誅。
entries.en: Sima Yi admired him and spared his life.
entries.literal: The Emperor Xuan admired him and pardoned him without execution.

entries.zh: 俄而起為使持節、領護匈奴中郎將、振威將軍、并州刺史。
entries.en: Soon he held credentials as commissioner, concurrent colonel of the central Xiongnu corps, General Who Rouses Might, and inspector of Bing.
entries.literal: Shortly afterward he was appointed commissioner with credentials, concurrent Colonel for the Xiongnu of the Center, General Who Rouses Might, and Inspector of Bing Province.

entries.zh: 以綏緝有方，遷大鴻臚。
entries.en: His skill at pacifying and administering won him promotion to grand herald.
entries.literal: For skilled pacification and administration he was promoted to Grand Herald.

entries.zh: 毗字長基。
entries.en: Du Pi, courtesy Changji.
entries.literal: Pi, courtesy name Changji.

entries.zh: 州舉秀才，成都王穎辟大將軍掾，遷尚書郎，參太傅軍事。
entries.en: Recommended as a cultivated talent, he entered Prince Chengdu Sima Ying's staff as grand-general aide, then became gentleman of the Masters of Writing and adviser on the grand tutor's army council.
entries.literal: The province raised him as cultivated talent; Prince Chengdu Sima Ying summoned him as aide to the grand general; he was promoted Gentleman of the Masters of Writing and joined the Grand Tutor's military staff.

entries.zh: 及洛陽覆沒，毗南渡江，王敦表為益州刺史，將與宜都太守柳純共固白帝。
entries.en: After the Luoyang catastrophe he fled south; Wang Dun nominated him for Yi Province so he could join Yidu prefect Liu Chun in holding Baidi.
entries.literal: When Luoyang fell he crossed south of the Yangzi; Wang Dun recommended him as Inspector of Yi Province; he was to cooperate with Administrator of Yidu Liu Chun in holding Ba Di.

entries.zh: 杜弢遣軍要毗，遂遇害。
entries.en: The rebel Du Tao ambushed him and cut him down.
entries.literal: Du Tao sent troops to intercept Pi; Pi was killed.

entries.zh: 軫弟烈，明政事，察孝廉，曆平康、安陽令，所居有異績，遷衡陽太守。
entries.en: Du Lie, another brother of Du Zhen, excelled at governance; as filial-and-incorrupt nominee he magistrated Pingkang and Anyang with distinction, then became prefect of Hengyang.
entries.literal: Zhen's younger brother Lie understood practical administration; recommended as filial and incorrupt, he served as magistrate of Pingkang and Anyang with outstanding records at each post; promoted Administrator of Hengyang.

entries.zh: 聞軫亡，因自表兄子幼弱，求去官，詔轉犍為太守，蜀土榮之。
entries.en: Learning of Du Zhen's death, he asked leave on the ground that his nephews were infants; the court moved him to Qianwei instead, a gesture Shu folk deeply respected.
entries.literal: When he heard of Zhen's death he memorialized that his elder brother's sons were still young and weak and begged to resign; an edict transferred him to Administrator of Qianwei; the people of Shu honored him for it.

entries.zh: 後遷湘東太守，為成都王穎郎中令，病卒。
entries.en: He later governed Xiangdong and served as Chamberlain of the Palace Gentlemen to Prince Chengdu, then died of illness.
entries.literal: Later promoted Administrator of Xiangdong, he served as Chamberlain of the Palace Attendants (langzhongling) to Prince Chengdu Sima Ying; died of illness.

entries.zh: 曹攄，字顏遠，譙國譙人也。
entries.en: Cao Shu (courtesy Yanyuan) came from Qiao in the Qiao princedom.
entries.literal: Cao Shu, courtesy name Yanyuan, was a native of Qiao in the Principality of Qiao.

entries.zh: 祖肇，魏衛將軍。
entries.en: His grandfather Cao Zhao had been Wei General of the Guards.
entries.literal: His grandfather Zhao was Wei General of the Guards.

entries.zh: 攄少有孝行，好學善屬文，太尉王衍見而器之，調補臨淄令。
entries.en: Filial from boyhood, bookish and eloquent, he impressed grand commandant Wang Yan, who moved him to magistrate of Linzi.
entries.literal: Shu from youth showed filial conduct, loved learning and was skilled at composition; Grand Commandant Wang Yan saw him and esteemed him; he was transferred and appointed magistrate of Linzi.

entries.zh: 縣有寡婦，養姑甚謹。
entries.en: The county had a widow who nursed her mother-in-law devotedly.
entries.literal: In the county was a widow who tended her mother-in-law very carefully.

entries.zh: 姑以其年少，勸令改適，婦守節不移。
entries.en: The elder, pitying her youth, urged her to remarry; the widow refused to abandon her vow.
entries.literal: The mother-in-law, because she was young, urged her to remarry; the woman kept her chastity and would not move.

entries.zh: 姑湣之，密自殺。
entries.en: The mother-in-law, heartsick for her, committed suicide in secret.
entries.literal: The mother-in-law pitied her and secretly killed herself.

entries.zh: 親党告婦殺姑，官為考鞫，寡婦不勝苦楚，乃自誣。
entries.en: Kin accused the widow of murder; torture broke her and she confessed to a crime she did not commit.
entries.literal: Relatives reported the woman had killed her mother-in-law; officials interrogated her under torture; the widow could not endure the pain and falsely confessed.

entries.zh: 獄當決，適值攄到。
entries.en: Sentence was about to fall when Cao Shu took office.
entries.literal: When the case was to be decided, it happened that Shu arrived.

entries.zh: 攄知其有冤，更加辯究，具得情實，時稱其明。
entries.en: He sensed a miscarriage, reopened the file, and extracted the truth; contemporaries praised his insight.
entries.literal: Shu knew there was injustice and investigated further; he obtained the full truth of the situation; he was at the time praised for his clarity.

entries.zh: 獄有死囚，歲夕，攄行獄，湣之，曰：「卿等不幸致此非所，如何？
entries.en: In the jail were condemned prisoners; at year's end Shu inspected the prison and pitied them, saying: 'You have unfortunately come to this place—what can be done?
entries.literal: In the jail were condemned prisoners; at year's end Shu inspected the prison and pitied them, saying: 'You have unfortunately come to this place—what can be done?

entries.zh: 新歲人情所重，豈不欲暫見家邪？」
entries.en: New Year's is what human feelings most treasure—do you not wish briefly to see your families?'
entries.literal: New Year's is what human feelings most treasure—do you not wish briefly to see your families?'

entries.zh: 眾囚皆涕泣曰：「若得暫歸，死無恨也。」
entries.en: All the prisoners wept and said: 'If we could return for a little while, we would die without regret.'
entries.literal: All the prisoners wept and said: 'If we could return for a little while, we would die without regret.'

entries.zh: 攄悉開獄出之，克日令還。
entries.en: He threw open the gates, freed them all, and named the day they must return.
entries.literal: Shu opened all the prisons and released them, setting a deadline for their return.

entries.zh: 掾吏固爭，咸謂不可。
entries.en: His aides protested that the risk was insane.
entries.literal: The clerks firmly objected, all saying it could not be done.

entries.zh: 攄曰：「此雖小人，義不見負，自為諸君任之。」
entries.en: Shu said: 'Though these are petty men, in honor they will not betray me; I myself answer for them to you gentlemen.'
entries.literal: Shu said: 'Though these are petty men, in honor they will not betray me; I myself answer for them to you gentlemen.'

entries.zh: 至日，相率而還，並無違者，一縣嘆服，號曰聖君。
entries.en: Every man returned on time; the county hailed him as a sage official.
entries.literal: When the day came they came back together; none broke the promise—the whole county marveled and submitted, calling him the sage lord.

entries.zh: 入為尚書郎，轉洛陽令，仁惠明斷，百姓懷之。
entries.en: He reached the Masters of Writing and then Luoyang county—kind, sharp, and beloved.
entries.literal: He entered [court] as Gentleman of the Masters of Writing, transferred to magistrate of Luoyang; benevolent, kind, and clear in judgment—the common people cherished him.

entries.zh: 時天大雨雪，宮門夜失行馬，群官檢察，莫知所在。
entries.en: One night of blizzard the palace gate's traveling barriers vanished; no search turned them up.
entries.literal: At that time heaven sent great rain and snow; at night the traveling barriers at the palace gate were lost; the various officials searched and none knew where they were.

entries.zh: 攄使收門士，眾官咸謂不然。
entries.en: Cao Shu arrested the gate guards; colleagues called it nonsense.
entries.literal: Shu ordered the gate guards seized; all the officials said it was wrong.

entries.zh: 攄曰：「宮掖禁嚴，非外人所敢盜，必是門士以燎寒耳。」
entries.en: Shu said: 'The palace is strictly forbidden—outsiders would not dare steal them; it must be the gate guards taking them to warm themselves by fire.'
entries.literal: Shu said: 'The palace is strictly forbidden—outsiders would not dare steal them; it must be the gate guards taking them to warm themselves by fire.'

entries.zh: 詰之，果服。
entries.en: Questioning proved him right.
entries.literal: When questioned, they indeed confessed.

entries.zh: 以病去官。
entries.en: Illness forced him out.
entries.literal: He left office due to illness.

entries.zh: 復為洛陽令。
entries.en: Luoyang eventually recalled him.
entries.literal: Again became magistrate of Luoyang.

entries.zh: 及齊王冏輔政，攄與左思俱為記室督。
entries.en: When Prince Qi Sima Jiong directed the regime, Cao Shu and Zuo Si jointly supervised the secretariat.
entries.literal: When Prince of Qi Sima Jiong assisted the government, Shu together with Zuo Si both served as supervisors of the secretariat.

entries.zh: 冏嘗從容問攄曰：「天子為賊臣所逼，莫有能奮。
entries.en: Jiong once calmly asked Shu: 'The Son of Heaven was coerced by traitorous ministers; none could rouse himself.
entries.literal: Jiong once calmly asked Shu: 'The Son of Heaven was coerced by traitorous ministers; none could rouse himself.

entries.zh: 吾率四海義兵興復王室，今入輔朝廷，匡振時艱，或有勸吾還國，於卿意如何？」
entries.en: I led righteous troops from within the four seas to restore the royal house; now I enter and assist the court, aiding the hardship of the times—some urge me to return to my princedom; what is your thought?'
entries.literal: I led righteous troops from within the four seas to restore the royal house; now I enter and assist the court, aiding the hardship of the times—some urge me to return to my princedom; what is your thought?'

entries.zh: 攄曰：「蕩平國賊，匡復帝祚，古今人臣之功未有如大王之盛也。
entries.en: Shu said: 'Sweeping away state rebels and restoring the imperial throne—among ministers through history none has achieved merit as great as the great king's.
entries.literal: Shu said: 'Sweeping away state rebels and restoring the imperial throne—among ministers through history none has achieved merit as great as the great king's.

entries.zh: 然道罔隆而不殺，物無盛而不衰，非唯人事，抑亦天理。
entries.en: Yet the Way never rises without decline; nothing flourishes without fading—not only in human affairs but also in the pattern of Heaven.
entries.literal: Yet the Way never rises without decline; nothing flourishes without fading—not only in human affairs but also in the pattern of Heaven.

entries.zh: 竊預下問，敢不盡情。
entries.en: Having received your humble inquiry below, how dare I not speak my whole mind.
entries.literal: Having received your humble inquiry below, how dare I not speak my whole mind.

entries.zh: 願大王居高慮危，在盈思沖，精選百官，存公屏欲，舉賢進善，務得其才，然後脂車秣馬，高揖歸籓，則上下同慶，攄等幸甚。」
entries.en: I wish the great king, dwelling high, to think of peril; in fullness to think of emptiness; carefully select the hundred officials; preserve impartiality and restrain desire; promote the worthy and advance the good, striving to obtain true talent—then grease the carriage and feed the horses, bow deeply and return to your fief; then high and low alike will rejoice, and Shu and the rest will be greatly fortunate.'
entries.literal: I wish the great king, dwelling high, to think of peril; in fullness to think of emptiness; carefully select the hundred officials; preserve impartiality and restrain desire; promote the worthy and advance the good, striving to obtain true talent—then grease the carriage and feed the horses, bow deeply and return to your fief; then high and low alike will rejoice, and Shu and the rest will be greatly fortunate.'

entries.zh: 冏不納。
entries.en: Sima Jiong brushed the counsel aside.
entries.literal: Jiong did not accept the advice.

entries.zh: 尋轉中書侍郎。
entries.en: He soon moved to vice director of the Secretariat.
entries.literal: Shortly he was transferred to vice director of the Secretariat.

entries.zh: 長沙王乂以為驃騎司馬。
entries.en: Prince Changsha Sima Yi named him staff marshal on the agile-cavalry command.
entries.literal: Prince Changsha Sima Yi appointed him marshal for the General of Agile Cavalry.

entries.zh: 乂敗，免官。
entries.en: After Prince Changsha fell, Cao Shu lost his post.
entries.literal: When Yi was defeated, [Shu] was dismissed from office.

entries.zh: 因丁母憂。
entries.en: He then withdrew to mourn his mother.
entries.literal: Thereupon he observed mourning for his mother.

entries.zh: 惠帝末，起為襄城太守，
entries.en: Late in Emperor Hui's reign he returned as Xiangcheng prefect.
entries.literal: At the end of Emperor Hui's reign he was raised up as Administrator of Xiangcheng.

entries.zh: 范晷，字彥長，南陽順陽人也。
entries.en: Fan Gui (courtesy Yanchang) came from Shunyang in Nanyang.
entries.literal: Fan Gui, courtesy name Yanchang, was a native of Shunyang in Nanyang.

entries.zh: 少遊學清河，遂徙家僑居。
entries.en: He studied in Qinghe as a youth and moved his family there.
entries.literal: In youth he studied in Qinghe and then relocated his household there as a sojourner.

entries.zh: 郡命為五官掾，曆河內郡丞。
entries.en: The commandery gave him the five-bureaus clerkship; he became assistant administrator of Henei.
entries.literal: The commandery appointed him clerk of the five offices; he served as assistant administrator of Henei.

entries.zh: 太守裴楷雅知之，薦為侍御史。
entries.en: Prefect Pei Kai admired him and nominated him attendant censor.
entries.literal: Administrator Pei Kai esteemed him and recommended him as attendant censor.

entries.zh: 調補上谷太守，遭喪，不之官。
entries.en: Ordered to Shanggu, he stayed home mourning instead.
entries.literal: Transferred to Administrator of Shanggu; he met bereavement and did not take up the post.

entries.zh: 後為司徒左長史，轉馮翊太守，甚有政能，善於綏撫，百姓愛悅之。
entries.en: He advanced to senior clerk under the minister of education, then governed Pingyi with strong relief efforts and popular affection.
entries.literal: Later he became senior clerk of the left to the Minister of Education, transferred to Administrator of Pingyi—very capable in administration, skilled at pacification; the people loved him.

entries.zh: 徵拜少府，出為涼州刺史，轉雍州。
entries.en: The court called him privy treasurer, then sent him west as Liang inspector and Yong inspector.
entries.literal: Summoned as Privy Treasurer; went out as Inspector of Liang Province, transferred to Yong Province.

entries.zh: 于時西土荒毀，氏羌蹈藉，田桑失收，百姓困弊，晷傾心化導，勸以農桑，所部甚賴之。
entries.en: The northwest was shattered by Di and Qiang raids and crop failure; Fan Gui preached farming and care until the region stabilized.
entries.literal: At that time the western regions lay in ruins; Di and Qiang rampaged; harvests failed; the people were desperate; Gui devoted himself to moral suasion, urging farming and silk; his jurisdictions depended on him.

entries.zh: 元康中，加左將軍，卒于官。
entries.en: Under Yuankang he added General of the Left and died in harness.
entries.literal: In the Yuankang era he was additionally appointed General of the Left and died in office.

entries.zh: 二子：廣、稚。
entries.en: He left two sons, Guang and Zhi.
entries.literal: Two sons: Guang and Zhi.

entries.zh: 喬智明，字元達，鮮卑前部人也。
entries.en: Qiao Zhiming (courtesy Yuanda) belonged to the forward wing of the Xianbei confederation.
entries.literal: Qiao Zhiming, courtesy name Yuanda, was a man of the forward division of the Xianbei.

entries.zh: 少喪二親，哀毀過禮，長而以德行著稱。
entries.en: Orphaned young, he mourned beyond ritual and matured renowned for character.
entries.literal: In youth he lost both parents; his grief exceeded ritual propriety; grown, he was famed for virtuous conduct.

entries.zh: 成都王穎辟為輔國將軍。
entries.en: Prince Chengdu Sima Ying appointed him General Who Supports the State.
entries.literal: Prince Chengdu Sima Ying summoned him as General Who Supports the State.

entries.zh: 穎之敗趙王倫也，表智明為殄寇將軍、隆慮、共二縣令。
entries.en: After defeating Prince Zhao Sima Lun, Sima Ying named him General Who Exterminates Brigands and magistrate of Longlu and Gong.
entries.literal: When Ying defeated Prince Zhao Sima Lun, he memorialized Zhiming as General Who Exterminates Brigands and magistrate of Longlu and Gong counties.

entries.zh: 二縣愛之，號為「神君」。
entries.en: Both counties loved him; they called him the "divine magistrate."
entries.literal: Both counties loved him; they called him the "divine magistrate."

entries.zh: 部人張兌為父報仇，母老單身，有妻無子，智明湣之，停其獄。
entries.en: Commoner Zhang Dui killed for vengeance; his mother lived alone and he lacked an heir; Qiao Zhiming stayed judgment out of mercy.
entries.literal: A local man Zhang Dui avenged his father; his mother was old and lived alone; he had a wife but no son; Zhiming pitied him and stayed the case.

entries.zh: 歲餘，令兌將妻入獄，兼陰縱之。
entries.en: After a year he let Zhang bring his wife into custody and quietly allowed intimacy.
entries.literal: After more than a year he ordered Dui to bring his wife into jail and secretly allowed conjugal visits.

entries.zh: 人有勸兌逃者，兌曰：「有君如此，吾何忍累之！
entries.en: Someone urged Dui to flee; Dui said: "With a magistrate like this, how could I bear to drag him down!
entries.literal: Someone urged Dui to flee; Dui said: "With a magistrate like this, how could I bear to drag him down!

entries.zh: 縱吾得免，作何面目視息世間！」
entries.en: Even if I could escape, what face would I have to face the world and breathe!"
entries.literal: Even if I could escape, what face would I have to face the world and breathe!"

entries.zh: 於獄產一男。
entries.en: His wife delivered a son in prison.
entries.literal: In the jail his wife bore a boy.

entries.zh: 會赦，得免。
entries.en: An amnesty freed him.
entries.literal: An amnesty arrived and he obtained release.

entries.zh: 其仁感如是。
entries.en: Such was the power of his humane rule.
entries.literal: His humane kindness moved people thus.

entries.zh: 惠帝之伐鄴也，穎以智明為折沖將軍、參丞相前鋒軍事。
entries.en: During Emperor Hui's expedition against Ye, Sima Ying made him General Who Charges the Enemy on the vanguard staff.
entries.literal: When Emperor Hui campaigned against Ye, Ying appointed Zhiming General Who Charges the Enemy and adjutant on the prime minister's vanguard staff.

entries.zh: 智明勸穎奉迎乘輿，穎大怒曰：「卿名曉事，投身事孤。
entries.en: Zhiming urged Ying to welcome the emperor's carriage; Ying raged: "Your reputation says you understand affairs—yet you entered my service.
entries.literal: Zhiming urged Ying to welcome the emperor's carriage; Ying raged: "Your reputation says you understand affairs—yet you entered my service.

entries.zh: 主上為群小所逼，將加非罪於孤，卿奈何欲使孤束手就刑邪！
entries.en: The sovereign was forced by petty men and will heap false crimes on me—why would you have me bind my hands for execution!
entries.literal: The sovereign was forced by petty men and will heap false crimes on me—why would you have me bind my hands for execution!

entries.zh: 共事之義，正若此乎？」
entries.en: Is comradeship supposed to mean this?"
entries.literal: Is comradeship supposed to mean this?"

entries.zh: 智明乃止。
entries.en: Qiao Zhiming fell silent.
entries.literal: Zhiming thereupon desisted.

entries.zh: 尋屬永嘉之亂，仕于劉曜。
entries.en: When Yongjia chaos erupted he entered Liu Yao's Han-Zhao regime.
entries.literal: Soon the Yongjia turmoil came; he served Liu Yao.

entries.zh: 序
entries.en: Preface
entries.literal: Preface

entries.zh: 詳觀往誥，逖聽前聞，階緣外戚以致顯榮者，其所由來尚矣。
entries.en: A close reading of past injunctions and the lessons of earlier ages shows that riding kinship with the imperial consorts to wealth and rank is an old story.
entries.literal: Carefully examining the admonitions of old and heeding what was heard in former times, those who climbed by ties to imperial affines to reach high honor—their origins go back a long way.

entries.zh: 而多至禍敗，鮮克令終者，何哉？
entries.en: Yet so many of them end in ruin, and precious few die in peace. Why is that?
entries.literal: Yet many come to disaster and ruin, and few achieve a good end—why?

entries.zh: 豈不由祿以恩升，位非德舉；
entries.en: Surely it is because their salaries come from imperial favor rather than merit, and their posts are not won by moral weight.
entries.literal: Is it not because emolument rises through favor, and office is not raised up by virtue?

entries.zh: 識慚明悊。
entries.en: Their judgment cannot bear comparison with true sagacity.
entries.literal: In insight they are ashamed before clear wisdom.

entries.zh: 材謝經通；
entries.en: Their abilities fall short of real command of the canon.
entries.literal: In talent they decline short of mastery of the classics.

entries.zh: 假椒房之寵靈，總軍國之樞要。
entries.en: They lean on the consort’s favor to seize the levers of military and civil power.
entries.literal: Borrowing the favor and numinous power of the harem, they grasp the pivot of both army and state.

entries.zh: 或威權震主，或勢力傾朝；
entries.en: Some overshadow the throne; others bend the entire bureaucracy to their will.
entries.literal: Some awe the ruler with their might and authority; some tilt the whole court with their power and influence.

entries.zh: 居安而不慮危，務進而不知退；
entries.en: They bask in ease and ignore danger; they press always forward and never learn when to step back.
entries.literal: Dwelling in safety they do not think of peril; striving to advance they do not know to withdraw.

entries.zh: 驕奢既至，釁隙隨之者乎！
entries.en: Arrogance and excess invite their own undoing—is that not how the cracks appear?
entries.literal: Once arrogance and extravagance have arrived, do breach and rift not follow!

entries.zh: 是以呂霍之家，誅夷于西漢，梁鄧之族，剿絕於東都，其餘干紀亂常、害時蠹政者，不可勝載。
entries.en: Hence the Lü and Huo lines were slaughtered in Western Han, and the Liang and Deng families extirpated at Luoyang; the roll of affines who broke the law, subverted custom, and poisoned the state would fill volumes.
entries.literal: Therefore the houses of Lü and Huo were exterminated in Western Han; the clans of Liang and Deng were cut off in the Eastern capital; as for the rest who violated the norm, threw order into chaos, harmed the age, and worm-eaten governance—they cannot all be recorded.

entries.zh: 至若樊靡卿之父子，竇廣國之弟兄，陰興之守約戒奢，史丹之掩惡揚善，斯並后族之所美者也。
entries.en: Then there are the shining exceptions: Fan Miqing and his father, Dou Guangguo and his brothers, Yin Xing with his frugality and discipline, Shi Dan who muted scandal and lifted virtue—all models among imperial in-laws.
entries.literal: As for Fan Miqing’s father and son, Dou Guangguo’s brothers, Yin Xing’s keeping restraint and warning against extravagance, and Shi Dan’s covering evil and proclaiming good—these are what the empress’s kin have to praise.

entries.zh: 由此觀之，干時縱溢者必以凶終，守道謙沖者永保貞吉，古人所謂禍福無門，惟人所召，此非其效歟！
entries.en: From this it is plain: those who ride the moment to excess come to a bad end, while the modest who hold to the Way keep their good name. The old saying that we make our own fortune or ruin—here is the evidence.
entries.literal: Viewed from this, those who flaunt excess against the times surely end in ill fortune; those who keep the Way and are modest and yielding forever preserve steadfast good fortune. What the ancients called ‘fortune and disaster have no gate—only men summon them’—is this not its proof!

entries.zh: 逮于晉難，始自宮掖。
entries.en: The Jin dynasty’s catastrophe began in the inner palace.
entries.literal: When it came to the Jin calamity, it began in the palace apartments.

entries.zh: 楊駿藉武帝之寵私，叨竊非據，賈謐乘惠皇之蒙昧，成此厲階，遂使悼后遇雲林之災，湣懷濫湖城之酷。
entries.en: Yang Jun parlayed Emperor Wu’s favor into a post he never deserved; Jia Mi exploited Emperor Hui’s weakness and laid the steps to ruin—so Empress Dao met disaster at Yunlin, and Min Huai suffered cruel abuse at Hucheng.
entries.literal: Yang Jun relied on Emperor Wu’s private favor and grasped what he should not have held; Jia Mi rode Emperor Hui’s dullness and made this stair of evil, so that Empress Dao met disaster at Yunlin, and Min Huai suffered cruel abuse at Hucheng.

entries.zh: 天人道盡，喪亂弘多，宗廟以之顛覆，黎庶於焉殄瘁。
entries.en: Heaven and earth seemed to abandon the house of Jin; chaos spread without end, the altars fell, and the people were ground down.
entries.literal: The way of Heaven and men was exhausted; bereavement and chaos were vast; the ancestral temple thereby was overturned; the common people thereby were worn to the bone.

entries.zh: 《詩》云：「赫赫宗周，褒姒滅之。」
entries.en: The Book of Songs says: ‘Grand stood the house of Zhou—and Baosi brought it down.’
entries.literal: The Classic of Poetry says: ‘Splendid was the Zhou of the ancestors—Baosi destroyed it.’

entries.zh: 其此之謂也。
entries.en: That is exactly what happened here.
entries.literal: ’—this is what is meant by that.

entries.zh: 爰及江左，未改覆車。
entries.en: South of the river they repeated the same fatal mistake.
entries.literal: Extending to the left bank of the Yangzi, they did not change the overturned cart.

entries.zh: 庾亮世族羽儀，王恭高門領袖，既而職兼出納，任切股肱。
entries.en: Yu Liang stood at the head of the great families; Wang Gong led the high-born elite; both held posts that controlled access to the throne and served as the emperor’s right arm.
entries.literal: Yu Liang was the plume and standard of great clans; Wang Gong was leader of eminent houses; thereafter their offices combined intake and outgo, and their charge was as close as thigh and arm.

entries.zh: 孝伯竟以亡身，元規幾于敗國，豈不哀哉！
entries.en: Wang Gong died for it; Yu Liang nearly destroyed the realm—is that not a tragedy?
entries.literal: Xiaobo in the end thereby lost his life; Yuankui nearly thereby ruined the state—is it not lamentable!

entries.zh: 若褚季野之畏避朝權，王叔仁之固求出鎮，用能全身遠害，有可稱焉。
entries.en: Chu Pou shrank from wielding power at court, and Wang Shu begged to be sent to the frontier; both kept their skins and their honor, and deserve mention.
entries.literal: As for Chu Yeye’s fearing and avoiding court power, and Wang Shuren’s firmly seeking to go out and hold a command, by this they were able to preserve the body and keep far from harm—there is something to praise in that.

entries.zh: 賈充、楊駿、庾亮、王獻之、王恭等已入列傳，其餘既敘其成敗，以為《外戚篇》云。
entries.en: Jia Chong, Yang Jun, Yu Liang, Wang Xianzhi, and Wang Gong already have their own chapters; what follows records the rest, gathered here under ‘Imperial Affines.’
entries.literal: Jia Chong, Yang Jun, Yu Liang, Wang Xianzhi, Wang Gong, and others have already entered the arrayed biographies; as for the rest, having narrated their success and failure, it is made into this ‘Imperial Affines’ chapter.

entries.zh: 初，杜預拜鎮南將軍，朝士畢賀，皆連榻而坐。
entries.en: When Du Yu was named South-Pacifying General, the whole court came to congratulate him, seating themselves on contiguous daybeds.
entries.literal: At first, when Du Yu was appointed South-Pacifying General, court gentlemen all congratulated him and all sat with joined couches.

entries.zh: 琇與裴楷後至，曰：「杜元凱乃復以連榻而坐客邪？」
entries.en: Yang Xiu and Pei Kai arrived late and said, ‘Is Du Yu really receiving guests sprawled on shared couches like this?’
entries.literal: Xiu and Pei Kai arrived late and said: ‘Du Yuankai would again use joined couches to seat guests?’

entries.zh: 遂不坐而去。
entries.en: He refused to sit down and walked out.
entries.literal: ’ Then he did not sit and left.

entries.zh: 愷字君夫。
entries.en: Wang Kai’s courtesy name was Junfu.
entries.literal: Kai styled Junfu.

entries.zh: 少有才力，歷位清顯，雖無細行，有在公之稱。
entries.en: Capable from youth, he rose to high office; though his private morals were loose, he was thought diligent in public duty.
entries.literal: In youth he had talent and strength; he passed through posts pure and eminent; though he had no fine conduct in small things, he had a reputation for public-mindedness.

entries.zh: 以討楊駿勳，封山都縣公，邑千八百戶。
entries.en: For his part in bringing down Yang Jun he was made Duke of Shandu with eighteen hundred households.
entries.literal: On account of merit in punishing Yang Jun, he was enfeoffed as Duke of Shandu County, fief of one thousand eight hundred households.

entries.zh: 遷龍驤將軍，領驍騎將軍，加散騎常侍，尋坐事免官。
entries.en: He advanced to Dragon-Prancing General and Valiant Cavalry commander with the additional title of Regular Cavalier Attendant, then lost his posts after an incident.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Dragon-Prancing General, concurrent Valiant Cavalry General, added as Regular Cavalier Attendant; soon he sat on a matter and was dismissed from office.

entries.zh: 起為射聲校尉，久之，轉後將軍。
entries.en: He was brought back as Colonel of the Sound-of-the-Bowstring Archers and later became Rear General.
entries.literal: He was raised as Colonel of the Sound-of-the-Bowstring Archers; after a long time, he was transferred to Rear General.

entries.zh: 愷既世族國戚，性復豪侈，用赤石脂泥壁。
entries.en: As both a great-clan magnate and imperial in-law, Wang Kai lived in ostentatious luxury, plastering his walls with costly red bole.
entries.literal: Kai was both a great-clan man and state kin; his nature was again grand and extravagant; he used red halloysite to mud walls.

entries.zh: 石崇與愷將為鴆毒之事，司隸校尉傅祗劾之，有司皆論正重罪，詔特原之。
entries.en: When he and Shi Chong were implicated in a plot to poison each other, Metropolitan Commandant Fu Zhi impeached them; the courts recommended harsh sentences, but an imperial edict let them off.
entries.literal: Shi Chong and Kai were about to do a matter of zhen poison; Metropolitan Commandant Fu Zhi impeached them; the authorities all judged proper heavy crimes; an edict specially pardoned them.

entries.zh: 由是眾人僉畏愷，故敢肆其意，所欲之事無所顧憚焉。
entries.en: Thereafter everyone feared him, and he indulged every whim without scruple.
entries.literal: By this all men equally feared Kai; therefore he dared unleash his intent; in matters he desired there was nothing he looked to or feared.

entries.zh: 及卒，諡曰醜。
entries.en: At his death he received the harsh posthumous name Chou, ‘the Repulsive.’
entries.literal: When he died, his posthumous name was Chou (‘Ugly’).

entries.zh: 羊玄之，惠皇后父，尚書右僕射瑾之子也。
entries.en: Yang Xuanzhi, father of Empress Hui, was the son of Yang Jin, Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
entries.literal: Yang Xuanzhi was the father of Empress Hui and the son of Right Vice Director Jin.

entries.zh: 玄之初為尚書郎，以后父，拜光祿大夫、特進、散騎常侍，更封興晉侯。
entries.en: He began as a junior secretary in the Department of State Affairs; as the empress’s father he rose to Grand Master of Splendid Carriage, Exalted Marcher, and Regular Cavalier Attendant, and was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Rising Jin.
entries.literal: Xuanzhi at first was a Gentleman of the Department of State Affairs; on account of being the empress’s father, he was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Carriage, Exalted Marcher, Regular Cavalier Attendant, and re-enfeoffed as Marquis Who Rouses Jin.

entries.zh: 遷尚書右僕射，加侍中，進爵為公。
entries.en: He became Right Vice Director, was given the additional post of Palace Attendant, and was raised to ducal rank.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, added as Palace Attendant, and advanced in nobility to duke.

entries.zh: 成都王穎之攻長沙王乂也，以討玄之為名，遂憂懼而卒。
entries.en: When Sima Ying marched against Sima Yi under the pretext of punishing Yang Xuanzhi, Xuanzhi died of fear and anxiety.
entries.literal: When Prince of Chengdu Ying attacked Prince of Changsha Yi, taking punishing Xuanzhi as the name, then in worry and fear he died.

entries.zh: 追贈車騎將軍、開府儀同三司。
entries.en: He was posthumously honored as General of Chariots and Cavalry with full Three Dukes’ establishment.
entries.literal: He was posthumously awarded General of Chariots and Cavalry, opener of office, peer with the Three Dukes.

entries.zh: 杜乂，字弘理，成恭皇后父，鎮南將軍預孫，尚書左丞錫之子也。
entries.en: Du Yi, courtesy name Hongli, father of Empress Chenggong, was a grandson of Du Yu, South-Pacifying General, and son of Du Xi, Left Assistant Director in the Department of State Affairs.
entries.literal: Du Yi, styled Hongli, was the father of Empress Chenggong, grandson of South-Pacifying General Yu, and son of Left Assistant Director Xi.

entries.zh: 性純和，美姿容，有盛名于江左。
entries.en: Gentle in temper and strikingly handsome, he was famous throughout the south.
entries.literal: By nature pure and mild, handsome in bearing, he had a great reputation south of the Yangzi.

entries.zh: 王羲之見而目之曰：「膚若凝脂，眼如點漆，此神仙人也。」
entries.en: Wang Xizhi said of him, ‘His skin is like curdled cream, his eyes like drops of ink—he might be an immortal walking among us.’
entries.literal: Wang Xizhi saw him and marked him, saying: ‘Skin like congealed fat, eyes like dabs of lacquer—this is an immortal among men.’

entries.zh: 桓彝亦曰：「衛玠神清，杜乂形清。」
entries.en: Huan Yi added, ‘Wei Jie shines in spirit; Du Yi shines in the flesh.’
entries.literal: ’ Huan Yi also said: ‘Wei Jie is clear in spirit; Du Yi is clear in form.’

entries.zh: 襲封當陽侯，辟公府掾，為丹陽丞。
entries.en: He inherited the marquisate of Dangyang, was summoned as a clerk in a ducal office, and became Assistant to the Administrator of Danyang.
entries.literal: ’ He inherited enfeoffment as Marquis of Dangyang, was summoned as a clerk in the duke’s office, and became Assistant to the Administrator of Danyang.

entries.zh: 早卒，無男，生后而乂終，妻裴氏嫠居養后，以禮自防，甚有德音。
entries.en: He died young and sonless soon after his daughter was born. Lady Pei raised the girl alone, kept strict propriety as a widow, and was widely praised.
entries.literal: He died early, without sons; the empress was born and then Yi ended; his wife Lady Pei as widow dwelt rearing the empress, by ritual guarding herself, and had very virtuous repute.

entries.zh: 咸康初，追贈金紫光祿大夫，諡曰穆。
entries.en: Early in Xiankang he was posthumously named Grand Master of the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon with the posthumous title Mu.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Xiankang, he was posthumously awarded Grand Master of the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon; his posthumous name was Mu (‘Solemn’).

entries.zh: 封裴氏為高安鄉君，邑五百戶。
entries.en: Lady Pei was made Village Mistress of Gao’an with a fief of five hundred households.
entries.literal: Lady Pei was enfeoffed as Village Mistress of Gao’an, fief of five hundred households.

entries.zh: 至孝武帝時，崇進為廣德縣君。
entries.en: Under Emperor Xiaowu her title was raised to County Mistress of Guangde.
entries.literal: By the time of Emperor Xiaowu, she was advanced in honor to County Mistress of Guangde.

entries.zh: 裴氏壽考，百姓號曰杜姥。
entries.en: Lady Pei lived to a ripe old age, and folk called her ‘Granny Du.’
entries.literal: Lady Pei lived to great age; the common people called her Granny Du.

entries.zh: 初，司徒蔡謨甚器重乂，嘗言於朝曰：「恨諸君不見杜乂也。」
entries.en: Minister Cai Mo thought the world of Du Yi and once told the court, ‘It is your loss never to have laid eyes on Du Yi.’
entries.literal: At first, Minister of Education Cai Mo greatly esteemed Yi and once said at court: ‘I regret that you gentlemen have not seen Du Yi.’

entries.zh: 其為名流所重如此。
entries.en: Such was the regard the leading men of the age had for him.
entries.literal: ’ Thus was he esteemed by the famous and eminent.

entries.zh: 簡文帝之為會稽王也，嘗與孫綽商略諸風流人，綽言曰：「劉惔清蔚簡令，王濛溫潤恬和，桓溫高爽邁出。
entries.en: While still Prince of Kuaiji, Emperor Jianwen once asked Sun Chuo to rank the leading gentlemen. Sun Chuo said, ‘Liu Tan is spare and luminous; Wang Meng is gentle and serene; Huan Wen is bold and towering.’
entries.literal: When Emperor Jianwen was Prince of Kuaiji, he once with Sun Chuo discussed and surveyed the various men of elegant bearing; Chuo spoke, saying: ‘Liu Tan is clear, lush, terse, and fine; Wang Meng is warm, moist, quiet, and mild; Huan Wen is lofty, bright, and strides beyond.’

entries.zh: 謝尚清易令達，而濛性和暢，能言理，辭簡而有會。」
entries.en: Xie Shang is lucid and open; Wang Meng’s temper is even, he reasons well, and his words are brief but hit the mark.’
entries.literal: Xie Shang is clear, easy, fine, and penetrating; but Meng’s nature is harmonious and smooth, able to speak principle, phrasing terse yet having convergence.’

entries.zh: 及簡文帝輔政，益貴幸之，與劉惔號為入室之賓。
entries.en: When the prince became regent, Wang Meng grew ever closer to him; he and Liu Tan were called intimates who might enter the inner rooms.
entries.literal: ’ When Emperor Jianwen assisted governance, he increasingly honored and favored him; with Liu Tan he was styled guests who entered the inner chamber.

entries.zh: 轉司徒左長史。
entries.en: He was transferred to senior clerk on the left of the Minister of Education.
entries.literal: He was transferred to senior clerk on the left of the Minister of Education.

entries.zh: 晚求為東陽，不許。
entries.en: Late in life he asked to be sent to Dongyang; the court refused.
entries.literal: In late years he sought to be Dongyang; it was not permitted.

entries.zh: 及濛病，乃恨不用之。
entries.en: Only when Wang Meng fell ill did the prince regret not granting his request.
entries.literal: When Meng fell ill, then he regretted not having used him.

entries.zh: 濛聞之曰：「人言會稽王癡，竟癡也！」
entries.en: Wang Meng heard and said, ‘They call the Prince of Kuaiji slow-witted—they are right!’
entries.literal: Meng heard it and said: ‘People say the Prince of Kuaiji is dull—he really is dull!’

entries.zh: 疾漸篤，於燈下轉麈尾視之，歎曰：「如此人曾不得四十也！」
entries.en: As his illness worsened, he turned his fly-whisk in the lamplight and sighed, ‘A man like me will not see forty.’
entries.literal: ’ His illness gradually grew grave; under the lamp he turned a yak-tail chowry and looked at it, sighing: ‘Such a man could not even reach forty!’

entries.zh: 年三十九卒。
entries.en: He died at thirty-nine.
entries.literal: ’ At age thirty-nine he died.

entries.zh: 臨殯，劉惔以犀杷麈尾置棺中，因慟絕久之。
entries.en: At the funeral Liu Tan laid a rhinoceros-handled fly-whisk in the coffin and sobbed until he collapsed.
entries.literal: At the laying-in for burial, Liu Tan with a rhinoceros-ivory handle placed a yak-tail chowry in the coffin; thereupon he wailed and fainted for a long time.

entries.zh: 謝安亦常稱濛云：「王長史語甚不多，可謂有令音。」
entries.en: Xie An used to say of him, ‘Chief Clerk Wang spoke little, but every word rang true.’
entries.literal: Xie An also often praised Meng, saying: ‘Chief Clerk Wang’s words are very few; one may say he has a fine tone.’

entries.zh: 有二子：修、蘊。
entries.en: He had two sons, Wang Xiu and Wang Yun.
entries.literal: ’ He had two sons: Xiu and Yun.

entries.zh: 修字敬仁，小字苟子。
entries.en: Wang Xiu, courtesy name Jingren, was called Gouzi in childhood.
entries.literal: Xiu styled Jingren, childhood name Gouzi.

entries.zh: 明秀有美稱，善隸書，號曰流奕清舉。
entries.en: Brilliant and admired, he excelled at clerical script in a style praised as fluid, lucid, and lifted.
entries.literal: Bright and elegant, he had a fine reputation; he was good at clerical script, titled Flowing Brightness, Clear Uplift.

entries.zh: 年十二，作《賢全論》。
entries.en: At twelve he wrote the Treatise on Worthy Wholeness.
entries.literal: At age twelve, he composed ‘Treatise on Worthy Wholeness.’

entries.zh: 濛以示劉惔曰：「敬仁此論，便足以參微言。」
entries.en: Wang Meng showed it to Liu Tan and said, ‘Jingren’s essay already touches the subtlest teachings.’
entries.literal: Meng showed it to Liu Tan, saying: ‘Jingren’s treatise is enough to join subtle words.’

entries.zh: 起家著作郎、琅邪王文學，轉中軍司馬，未拜而卒，年二十四。
entries.en: He began as editorial director and tutor to the Prince of Langye, then was named major on the central army staff but died before assuming duty, at twenty-four.
entries.literal: ’ From family rise he was editorial director and literary instructor to the Prince of Langye, transferred to army major under the Central Army; before taking office he died, age twenty-four.

entries.zh: 臨終，歎曰：「無愧古人，年與之齊矣。」
entries.en: On his deathbed he said, ‘I need not blush before the ancients—I have lived as long as many of them.’
entries.literal: Facing the end, he sighed, saying: ‘I have no shame before the ancients; my years match theirs.’

entries.zh: 范粲，字承明，陳留外黃人，漢萊蕪長丹之孫也。
entries.en: Fan Can, courtesy name Chengming, was from Waihuang in Chenliu—a grandson of Fan Dan, who had been magistrate of Laiwu under the Han.
entries.literal: Fan Can, styled Chengming, was a man of Waihuang in Chenliu, a grandson of Fan Dan, magistrate of Laiwu in Han.

entries.zh: 粲高亮貞正，有丹風，而博涉強記，學皆可師，遠近請益者甚眾，性不矜莊，而見之皆肅如也。
entries.en: He was as stern and honest as his grandfather Fan Dan, with a memory that drank in books. Students flocked to him from every quarter. He wore no air of pomp, yet everyone who met him stood straighter.
entries.literal: Can was lofty, bright, chaste, and upright; he had Dan's bearing, yet was broadly read with a strong memory, and all his learning could serve as a model; those near and far who sought instruction were very many; by nature he was not stiffly solemn, yet all who saw him were awed.

entries.zh: 魏時州府交辟，皆無所就。
entries.en: During the Wei, provincial and commandery posts came again and again; he refused them all.
entries.literal: In Wei times the province and prefecture repeatedly summoned him; he took none of the posts.

entries.zh: 久之，乃應命為治中，轉別駕，辟太尉掾、尚書郎，出為征西司馬，所曆職皆有聲稱。
entries.en: At length he accepted a place as administrative adviser, rose to chief clerk, served as aide to the grand commandant and gentleman of the palace, then marched west as army marshal—winning praise in each office.
entries.literal: After a long while he then answered appointment as administrative adviser, transferred to chief clerk, was summoned as aide to the grand commandant and as gentleman of the palace, then went out as marshal on the western campaign; in every post he held he had a fine reputation.

entries.zh: 及宣帝輔政，遷武威太守。
entries.en: When Emperor Xuan took charge of the regency, Can was named governor of Wuwei.
entries.literal: When Emperor Xuan assisted the government, he was moved to governor of Wuwei.

entries.zh: 到郡，選良吏，立學校，勸農桑。
entries.en: There he picked able officers, opened schools, and pushed farming and silk work.
entries.literal: Arriving in the commandery, he selected good clerks, established schools, and urged farming and sericulture.

entries.zh: 是時戎夷頗侵疆場，粲明設防備，敵不敢犯，西域流通，無烽燧之警。
entries.en: Barbarians harried the frontier, but his clear dispositions kept them out; the Silk Road stayed open and the signal fires stayed cold.
entries.literal: At that time the Rong and Yi often raided the borders; Can clearly set defenses so the enemy did not dare attack; the Western Regions flowed through trade and there was no alarm from beacon fires.

entries.zh: 又郡壤富實，珍玩充積，粲檢制之，息其華侈。
entries.en: The prefecture was rich and temptation everywhere; he tightened discipline and cut back extravagance.
entries.literal: Moreover the commandery soil was rich and treasures filled the storehouses; Can checked and regulated this and stilled its luxury.

entries.zh: 以母老罷官。
entries.en: He left office when his mother grew frail.
entries.literal: Because his mother was old he resigned office.

entries.zh: 郡既接近寇戎，粲又重鎮輒去職，朝廷尤之，左遷樂涫令。
entries.en: The court faulted him for walking away from a sensitive post on the barbarian edge and demoted him to magistrate of Leku.
entries.literal: The commandery being close to raiding enemies, and Can again a key stronghold who abruptly left his post, the court blamed him and demoted him to magistrate of Leku.

entries.zh: 武帝踐阼，泰始中，粲同郡孫和時為太子中庶子，表薦粲，稱其操行高潔，久嬰疾病，可使郡縣輿致京師，加以聖恩，賜其醫藥，若遂瘳除，必有益於政。
entries.en: After Jin Wudi took the throne, Sun He—then junior tutor to the heir apparent and a townsman of Can—memorialized that Can's life was ascetic and his body long ill, that the counties should bring him to Luoyang in a litter, and that imperial physicians might restore him to the state's service.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu ascended the throne, in the Taishi years Sun He of Can's commandery, then junior tutor to the heir apparent, submitted a memorial recommending Can, praising his conduct as lofty and pure, long afflicted by illness, and saying the commandery and county could carry him in a litter to the capital; if the sagely favor granted him medicine and he then recovered, he would surely benefit governance.

entries.zh: 乃詔郡縣給醫藥，又以二千石祿養病，歲以為常，加賜帛百匹。
entries.en: The throne ordered local officials to furnish physic and pay him a two-thousand-bushel stipend year after year to nurse his health, plus a hundred rolls of silk.
entries.literal: An edict then ordered the commandery and county to supply medicine, and also to support his illness with the salary of a two-thousand-bushel rank, yearly as a rule, adding a gift of one hundred bolts of silk.

entries.zh: 子喬以父疾篤，辭不敢受，詔不許。
entries.en: His son Fan Qiao, thinking the sickness grave, tried to decline the bounty; the edict refused the refusal.
entries.literal: His son Qiao, because his father's illness was grave, declined and dared not accept; the edict did not permit refusal.

entries.zh: 乙太康六年卒，時年八十四，不言三十六載，終於所寢之車。
entries.en: He died in Taikang 6 at eighty-four, having kept silence thirty-six years, and breathed his last in the cart that was his bed.
entries.literal: He died in the sixth year of Taikang at age eighty-four; for thirty-six years he did not speak, and ended in the carriage in which he slept.

entries.zh: 長子喬。
entries.en: His eldest son was Fan Qiao.
entries.literal: The eldest son was Qiao.

entries.zh: 喬好學不倦。
entries.en: Qiao never wearied of books.
entries.literal: Qiao loved learning and did not tire.

entries.zh: 父粲陽狂不言，喬與二弟並棄學業，絕人事，侍疾家庭，至粲沒，足不出邑里。
entries.en: When his father feigned madness and silence, Qiao and his two brothers quit school, shut out the world, and nursed him until he died—never leaving their hamlet in all those years.
entries.literal: When his father Can feigned madness and would not speak, Qiao with his two younger brothers abandoned their studies, cut off human affairs, and nursed the illness in the household until Can died, not stepping beyond the village.

entries.zh: 司隸校尉劉毅嘗抗論於朝廷曰：「使范武威疾若不篤，是為伯夷、叔齊復存於今。
entries.en: Liu Yi once told the court, "If Governor Fan's sickness is feigned, then Bo Yi and Shu Qi walk among us again.
entries.literal: Metropolitan Governor Liu Yi once spoke bluntly at court, saying, "If Fan Wuwei's illness is not grave, then Bo Yi and Shu Qi live again today.

entries.zh: 如其信篤，益是聖主所宜哀矜。
entries.en: If it is genuine, a sage king should pity him all the more.
entries.literal: If it is truly grave, all the more is it what a sage ruler ought to pity.

entries.zh: 其子久侍父疾，名德著茂，不加敘用，深為朝廷惜遺賢之譏也。」
entries.en: The sons have served a sick father for years with shining virtue; to leave them unranked is to invite the charge that the throne wastes good men."
entries.literal: His sons have long attended a father's sickness; their fame and virtue shine bright—failure to employ them is a reproach the court will bear for wasting worthies."

entries.zh: 元康中，詔求廉讓沖退覆道寒素者，不計資，以參選敘。
entries.en: Under Yuankang the throne sought modest scholars of cold pedigree, rank no object.
entries.literal: In the Yuankang period an edict sought men who were honest, yielding, retiring, and covered the Way in humble plainness, without regard to seniority, to be entered in selection.

entries.zh: 尚書郎王琨乃薦喬曰：「喬稟德真粹，立操高潔，儒學精深，含章內奧，安貧樂道，棲志窮巷，簞瓢詠業，長而彌堅，誠當今之寒素，著厲俗之清彥。」
entries.en: Palace gentleman Wang Kun recommended him: pure in endowment, high in principle, steeped in the canon yet inward-turned, happy in poverty and fixed in purpose—"the very cold-clad scholar the age needs."
entries.literal: Gentleman of the palace Wang Kun then recommended Qiao, saying, "Qiao is endowed with virtue true and pure, established in conduct lofty and clean, deep in Confucian learning, holding pattern within, content with poverty and joyful in the Way, lodging his intent in a poor lane, with basket and gourd chanting his occupation—longer yet more firm—truly the cold plainness of today, a clear paragon to brace vulgar ways."

entries.zh: 時張華領司徒，天下所舉凡十七人，于喬特發優論。
entries.en: Zhang Hua presided over the ministry; seventeen names came up from the realm, but only Qiao drew a special encomium.
entries.literal: At the time Zhang Hua headed the ministry of education; of all the empire's nominees seventeen were listed, and for Qiao alone a superior appraisal was issued.

entries.zh: 又吏部郎郗隆亦思求海內幽遁之士，喬供養衡門，至於白首，於是除樂安令。
entries.en: Personnel director Xi Long also combed for hidden talent; learning that Qiao had kept his parents in a lane of wattles until their hair turned white, the court named him magistrate of Le'an.
entries.literal: Also personnel director Xi Long wished to seek recluses within the seas; Qiao supported his parents at a brushwood gate until hoary age—thereupon he was appointed magistrate of Le'an.

entries.zh: 辭疾不拜。
entries.en: He pleaded illness and never went.
entries.literal: He pleaded illness and did not take up the post.

entries.zh: 喬凡一舉孝廉，八薦公府，再舉清白異行，又舉寒素，一無所就。
entries.en: He was nominated once as filial-incorrupt, eight times to the Three Ducal Offices, twice for outstanding purity, once again for cold pedigree—and never accepted.
entries.literal: Qiao in all was once recommended filial and incorrupt, eight times recommended to the ducal offices, twice recommended for unsullied conduct out of the ordinary, and again recommended for cold plainness—he took none of them.

entries.zh: 魯勝，字叔時，代郡人也。
entries.en: Lu Sheng, courtesy name Shushi, came from Dai commandery.
entries.literal: Lu Sheng, styled Shushi, was a man of Dai commandery.

entries.zh: 少有才操，為佐著作郎。
entries.en: Young, able, and principled, he became assistant editorialist.
entries.literal: In youth he had talent and integrity, and served as assistant editorialist.

entries.zh: 元康初，遷建康令。
entries.en: Early in Yuankang he was named magistrate of Jiankang.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Yuankang he was moved to magistrate of Jiankang.

entries.zh: 到官，著《正天論》云：「以冬至之後立晷測影，准度日月星。
entries.en: On taking office he wrote a treatise called "Setting Heaven Right," arguing that from the winter solstice one should set a gnomon and read shadows to calibrate sun, moon, and stars.
entries.literal: Arriving at office, he composed the "Correcting Heaven Treatise," saying, "After the winter solstice set a gnomon and measure shadow to gauge sun, moon, and stars.

entries.zh: 臣案日月裁徑百里，無千里；
entries.en: He maintained that sun and moon span only a hundred leagues, not a thousand;
entries.literal: Your subject investigates: sun and moon are only a hundred li across, not a thousand li;

entries.zh: 星十里，不百里。」
entries.en: and stars ten leagues, not a hundred."
entries.literal: stars ten li, not a hundred li."

entries.zh: 遂表上求下群公卿士考論。
entries.en: He tabled the essay and begged the high ministers to debate it.
entries.literal: Thereupon he submitted a memorial asking that it be sent down for the assembled dukes, ministers, and gentlemen to examine and debate.

entries.zh: 「若臣言合理，當得改先代之失，而正天地之紀。
entries.en: "If I speak with reason," he wrote, "let the court mend the mistakes of earlier calendars and set heaven's pattern straight.
entries.literal: "If your subject's words accord with reason, then let him amend the errors of former ages and set right the pattern of heaven and earth.

entries.zh: 如無據驗，甘即刑戮，以彰虛妄之罪。」
entries.en: If I cannot prove my case, I will gladly die to show the world I was a fraud."
entries.literal: If there is no supporting verification, I willingly accept execution at once to expose the crime of empty falsehood."

entries.zh: 事遂不報。
entries.en: The throne never answered.
entries.literal: The matter in the end received no reply.

entries.zh: 嘗歲日望氣，知將來多故，便稱疾去官。
entries.en: Watching the year's omens at New Year he foresaw chaos and resigned on grounds of illness.
entries.literal: On New Year's Day he once observed vapors and knew that coming years would bring much turmoil; then he pleaded illness and left office.

entries.zh: 中書令張華遣子勸其更仕，再徵博士，舉中書郎，皆不就。
entries.en: Zhang Hua sent his son to coax him back; twice the court called him as erudite and nominated him palace secretary—he refused each time.
entries.literal: Director Zhang Hua sent his son to urge him to take office again; twice he was summoned as erudite and recommended as palace secretary—he took none of them.

entries.zh: 霍原，字休明，燕國廣陽人也。
entries.en: Huo Yuan, courtesy name Xiuming, was from Guangyang in Yan.
entries.literal: Huo Yuan, styled Xiuming, was a man of Guangyang in the state of Yan.

entries.zh: 少有志力，叔父坐法當死，原入獄訟之，楚毒備加，終免叔父。
entries.en: While still young he took tortures in prison to save an uncle condemned to die.
entries.literal: In youth he had determination and strength; his uncle by law of a crime deserved death, Yuan entered prison to plead the case, full torture was applied, and in the end he spared his uncle.

entries.zh: 年十八，觀太學行禮，因留習之。
entries.en: At eighteen he watched the academy rites and stayed to master them.
entries.literal: At eighteen he watched the Grand Academy perform rites and therefore stayed to practice them.

entries.zh: 貴游子弟聞而重之，欲與相見，以其名微，不欲晝往，乃夜共造焉。
entries.en: Great lords' sons respected him but thought his name too slight for a daylight call, so they came by torchlight.
entries.literal: Sons of the nobility heard and esteemed him, wishing to meet him; because his name was lowly they did not wish to go by day, so together they visited him by night.

entries.zh: 父友同郡劉岱將舉之，未果而病篤，臨終，敕其子沈曰：「霍原慕道清虛，方成奇器，汝後必薦之。」
entries.en: Liu Dai, his father's friend, meant to sponsor him but died first, telling his son Shen, 'Huo Yuan is a vessel in the making—remember to lift him up.'
entries.literal: His father's friend Liu Dai of the same commandery was about to recommend him, but without result fell gravely ill; at the point of death he charged his son Shen, saying, "Huo Yuan loves the Way, clear and empty; he will become a rare vessel—you must recommend him later."

entries.zh: 後歸鄉里。
entries.en: Later Yuan went home to the hills.
entries.literal: Later he returned to his home village.

entries.zh: 高陽許猛素服其名，會為幽州刺史，將詣之，主簿當車諫不可出界，猛歎恨而止。
entries.en: Governor Xu Meng of Gaoyang meant to call on him until his clerk barred a governor from crossing the line—Meng gave up with a sigh.
entries.literal: Xu Meng of Gaoyang had long admired his name; when he became governor of Youzhou he meant to visit him, but his chief clerk remonstrated from the cart that he could not go beyond the border, and Meng sighed with regret and desisted.

entries.zh: 原山居積年，門徒百數，燕王月致羊酒。
entries.en: He taught a hundred disciples in the hills while the prince of Yan sent monthly sheep and wine.
entries.literal: Yuan dwelt in the mountains many years; disciples numbered in the hundreds; the prince of Yan monthly sent sheep and wine.

entries.zh: 及劉沈為國大中正，元康中，進原為二品，司徒不過，沈乃上表理之。
entries.en: Liu Shen ranked him second class; the ministry of education balked until Shen memorialized again.
entries.literal: When Liu Shen became grand impartial and just for the state, in Yuankang he advanced Yuan to second rank; the minister of education would not pass it, so Shen submitted a memorial to argue the case.

entries.zh: 詔下司徒參論，中書監張華令陳准奏為上品，詔可。
entries.en: Zhang Hua had Chen Zhun move him to the top grade, and the throne agreed.
entries.literal: An edict ordered the minister of education to deliberate jointly; director Zhang Hua ordered Chen Zhun to memorialize him as highest grade, and the edict approved.

entries.zh: 元康末，原與王褒等俱以賢良徵，累下州郡，以禮發遣，皆不到。
entries.en: Late in Yuankang he was summoned with Wang Bao as a worthy; the counties escorted him with full rites and he still would not go.
entries.literal: At the end of Yuankang, Yuan with Wang Bao and others was summoned as worthy and good; repeatedly the commandery was ordered to dispatch him with ritual, and each time he did not arrive.

entries.zh: 後王浚稱制謀僭，使人問之，原不答，浚心銜之。
entries.en: When Wang Jun seized the government and sounded him out, Yuan stayed silent, and Jun nursed a grudge.
entries.literal: Later Wang Jun seized power and plotted usurpation; he sent men to ask him, and Yuan did not answer; Jun harbored resentment.

entries.zh: 又有遼東囚徒三百餘人，依山為賊，意欲劫原為主事，亦未行。
entries.en: Three hundred Liaodong fugitives in the hills wanted him for chieftain but never acted.
entries.literal: Moreover more than three hundred convicts of Liaodong, relying on the mountains as bandits, wished to seize Yuan to be their leader, but also did not carry it out.

entries.zh: 時有謠曰：「天子在何許？
entries.en: A children's rhyme asked, 'Where sits the Son of Heaven?
entries.literal: At the time a rhyme said, "Where is the Son of Heaven?

entries.zh: 近在豆田中。」
entries.en: In the bean patch just ahead.'
entries.literal: Near at hand in the bean field."

entries.zh: 浚以豆為霍，收原斬之，懸其首。
entries.en: Wang Jun read bean as Huo, seized Yuan, beheaded him, and spiked his head.
entries.literal: Jun took bean as Huo and seized Yuan and executed him, hanging up his head.

entries.zh: 諸生悲哭，夜竊屍共埋殯之。
entries.en: His students stole the body by night and gave him burial.
entries.literal: The students wept in grief; by night they stole the corpse and together buried it.

entries.zh: 遠近駭愕，莫不冤痛之。
entries.en: The realm cried injustice.
entries.literal: Far and near were shocked; none did not feel him wronged.

entries.zh: 郭琦，字公偉，太原晉陽人也。
entries.en: Guo Qi, courtesy name Gongwei, came from Jinyang in Taiyuan.
entries.literal: Guo Qi, styled Gongwei, was a man of Jinyang in Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 少方直，有雅量，博學，善五行，作《天文志》、《五行傳》，注《穀梁》、《京氏易》百卷。
entries.en: Young, upright, and learned in astrology, he wrote treatises on heaven, the five phases, and a hundred fascicles on the Guliang and Jing Changes.
entries.literal: In youth he was square and straight, had a refined capacity, was broadly learned, skilled in the five phases, and composed the Monograph on Heaven, the Traditions of the Five Phases, and a hundred rolls of commentary on the Guliang Annals and the Jing family Changes.

entries.zh: 鄉人王遊等皆就琦學。
entries.en: Townsmen such as Wang You studied at his feet.
entries.literal: His townsman Wang You and others all came to Qi to study.

entries.zh: 武帝欲以琦為佐著作郎，問琦族人尚書郭彰。
entries.en: Emperor Wu meant to name him assistant editor and asked his kinsman Guo Zhang.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu wished to make Qi assistant editorialist and asked Qi's clansman Minister Guo Zhang.

entries.zh: 彰素疾琦，答云：「不識」。
entries.en: Zhang hated him and said flatly, 'I never heard of him.'
entries.literal: Zhang by nature detested Qi and answered, "I do not know him."

entries.zh: 帝曰：「若如卿言，烏丸家兒能事卿，即堪為郎矣。」
entries.en: The emperor retorted, 'If a Wuhuan stable-boy is good enough for you, he is good enough for my editorial office.'
entries.literal: The emperor said, "If it is as you say, then a Wuhuan household lad who can serve you would be fit to be a gentleman!"

entries.zh: 遂決意用之。
entries.en: So the emperor appointed Qi anyway.
entries.literal: Thereupon he resolved to employ him.

entries.zh: 及趙王倫篡位，又欲用琦，琦曰：「我已為武帝吏，不容復為今世吏。」
entries.en: When Sima Lun seized the throne and offered a post, Qi answered, "I served Emperor Wu; I will not serve your court."
entries.literal: When Prince Zhao of Lun usurped the throne, he again wished to use Qi; Qi said, "I have already been an official to Emperor Wu; I cannot again be an official to today's world."

entries.zh: 終身處於家。
entries.en: He stayed home for life.
entries.literal: To the end of his life he remained at home.

entries.zh: 孟陋，字少孤，武昌人也。
entries.en: Meng Lou, courtesy name Shaogu, came from Wuchang.
entries.literal: Meng Lou, styled Shaogu, was a man of Wuchang.

entries.zh: 吳司空宗之曾孫也。
entries.en: He was great-grandson of Wu minister Meng Zong.
entries.literal: He was great-grandson of Wu's minister of works Meng Zong.

entries.zh: 兄嘉，桓溫征西長史。
entries.en: His brother Meng Jia had been chief clerk under Huan Wen.
entries.literal: His elder brother Meng Jia was chief clerk on Huan Wen's western campaign.

entries.zh: 陋少而貞立，清操絕倫，布衣蔬食，以文籍自娛。
entries.en: Young, he was chaste, austere, in sackcloth and gruel, happy only in books.
entries.literal: Lou in youth was chaste and established, his pure conduct unmatched, in plain cloth and coarse food, taking pleasure in books.

entries.zh: 口不及世事，未曾交遊，時或弋釣，孤興獨往，雖家人亦不知其所之也。
entries.en: He never gossiped, rarely visited anyone, fished or hunted alone—his family never knew his path.
entries.literal: His mouth did not touch the affairs of the age; he never socialized; sometimes he shot or fished, alone with his whim—even his household did not know where he went.

entries.zh: 喪母，毀瘠殆於滅性，不飲酒食肉十有餘年。
entries.en: His mother's death left him skeletal; he ate no meat over ten years.
entries.literal: When his mother died, he wasted his flesh almost to extinguishing nature; for more than ten years he drank no wine and ate no meat.

entries.zh: 親族迭謂之曰：「少孤！
entries.en: Kinsmen pleaded, "Shaogu!
entries.literal: Lineage kin in turn said to him, "Shaogu!

entries.zh: 誰無父母？
entries.en: Who has no parents?
entries.literal: Who lacks parents?

entries.zh: 誰有父母！
entries.en: Who keeps parents forever?
entries.literal: Who has parents!

entries.zh: 聖人制禮，令賢者俯就，不肖企及。
entries.en: The sages set rites so the wise may ease grief and fools may aim higher.
entries.literal: The sages fixed ritual to let the worthy bend down and the unworthy strive up.

entries.zh: 若使毀性無嗣，更為不孝也。」
entries.en: To die childless is the greater unfilial act."
entries.literal: If you destroy your nature and leave no heir, that is again unfilial.

entries.zh: 陋感此言，然後從吉。
entries.en: He heard them, relented, and ended mourning properly.
entries.literal: Lou was moved by these words; then afterward he followed auspicious rites.

entries.zh: 由是名著海內。
entries.en: His name then filled the empire.
entries.literal: From this his name was famed within the seas.

entries.zh: 簡文帝輔政，命為參軍，稱疾不起。
entries.en: Emperor Jianwen summoned him as adviser; he pleaded illness.
entries.literal: When Emperor Jianwen assisted the government, he ordered him as adviser; he claimed illness and did not rise.

entries.zh: 桓溫躬往造焉。
entries.en: Huan Wen himself knocked on his door.
entries.literal: Huan Wen in person went to visit him.

entries.zh: 或謂溫曰：「孟陋高行，學為儒宗，宜引在府，以和鼎味。」
entries.en: A friend told Huan Wen, 'Meng Lou's virtue tops the scholars; bring him to your staff to leaven the court.'
entries.literal: Someone said to Wen, "Meng Lou's conduct is lofty; his learning is patriarch of Confucians—it is fitting to draw him into the office to harmonize the cauldron's flavor."

entries.zh: 溫歎曰：「會稽王尚不能屈，非敢擬議也。」
entries.en: Wen sighed, 'Even the prince of Kuaiji could not move him—I hardly dare speak of hiring him.'
entries.literal: Wen sighed, saying, "The prince of Kuaiji still could not bend him—how dare I presume to discuss it."

entries.zh: 陋聞之曰：「桓公正當以我不往故耳。
entries.en: Lou heard and said, 'Huan Wen only thinks I snubbed him on purpose.
entries.literal: Lou heard it and said, "Lord Huan only thinks it is because I did not go.

entries.zh: 億兆之人，無官者十居其九，豈皆高士哉！
entries.en: Nine men in ten lack office—are they all recluses?
entries.literal: Of the myriad million men, nine in ten have no office—are they all lofty gentlemen!

entries.zh: 我疾病不堪恭相王之命，非敢為高也。」
entries.en: I am too sick to obey the prince's summons—that is no pose of pride.'
entries.literal: I am ill and cannot bear the respectful commands of the minister king—it is not that I dare be lofty."

entries.zh: 由是名稱益重。
entries.en: His name only grew weightier after that.
entries.literal: From this his reputation and title grew heavier.

entries.zh: 博學多通，長於《三禮》。
entries.en: He mastered the Three Rites.
entries.literal: He was broadly learned and penetrating, excelling in the Three Rites.

entries.zh: 注《論語》，行於世。
entries.en: His Analects commentary circulates still.
entries.literal: He annotated the Analects, which circulated in the world.

entries.zh: 卒以壽終。
entries.en: He died in ripe old age.
entries.literal: He ended his life at a full old age.

entries.zh: 刺史王弘以元熙中臨州，甚欽遲之，後自造焉。
entries.en: Wang Hong came to govern and longed to meet him.
entries.literal: Inspector Wang Hong in the Yuanxi years came to the province, greatly admired and waited for him, afterward personally visited him.

entries.zh: 潛稱疾不見，既而語人云：「我性不狎世，因疾守閑，幸非潔志慕聲，豈敢以王公紆軫為榮邪！
entries.en: Qian claimed illness and would not see; afterward said to people, "My nature does not cozy with the world; because of illness I guard quiet—luckily it is not a clean intent admiring fame—how dare I take a prince's bending axle as glory!
entries.literal: Qian claimed illness and would not see; afterward said to people, "My nature does not cozy with the world; because of illness I guard quiet—luckily it is not a clean intent admiring fame—how dare I take a prince's bending axle as glory!

entries.zh: 夫謬以不賢，此劉公幹所以招謗君子，其罪不細也。」
entries.en: To be wrongly deemed unworthy—that is why Liu Gonggan drew slander from gentlemen; the fault is not small."
entries.literal: To be wrongly deemed unworthy—that is why Liu Gonggan drew slander from gentlemen; the fault is not small."

entries.zh: 弘每令人候之，密知當往廬山，乃遣其故人龐通之等齎酒，先於半道要之。
entries.en: Wang Hong sent a friend with wine mid-road to Lu.
entries.literal: Hong always ordered men to watch him; secretly knowing he would go to Mount Lu, then sent his old friend Pang Tongzhi and others carrying wine beforehand to waylay him halfway.

entries.zh: 潛既遇酒，便引酌野亭，欣然忘進。
entries.en: Tao stopped for wine and forgot the journey.
entries.literal: When Qian met the wine, he then drew drink in a wild pavilion, gladly forgot to advance.

entries.zh: 弘乃出與相見，遂歡宴窮日。
entries.en: Wang Hong joined the feast.
entries.literal: Hong then came out and met him; then they feasted merrily all day.

entries.zh: 潛無履，弘顧左右為之造履。
entries.en: Tao had no shoes; Wang ordered sandals made.
entries.literal: Qian had no sandals; Hong looked to left and right to have sandals made for him.

entries.zh: 左右請履度，潛便於坐申腳令度焉。
entries.en: Tao stretched his bare feet to be measured.
entries.literal: Attendants asked for foot measure; Qian at the seat stretched out his feet and let them measure.

entries.zh: 弘要之還州，問其所乘，答云：「素有腳疾，向乘藍輿，亦足自反。」
entries.en: He answered, "Plainly I have foot ailment; lately I ride a blue litter—still enough to return myself."
