entries.en: Scholars everywhere treated the edict as a public joke.
entries.literal: At the time scholars all took it as a jest.

entries.zh: 玄宗崩，肅宗詔晉卿攝冢宰。
entries.en: When Emperor Xuanzong died, Emperor Suzong ordered Jingqing to serve as regent during the mourning period.
entries.literal: When Xuanzong died, Suzong ordered Jingqing to act as regent.

entries.zh: 上表固辭曰：「臣聞古者殷高宗在諒闇之中，百官聽於冢宰，更無事跡，但存文字。
entries.en: He submitted a firm refusal, writing: 'I have read that in antiquity, when King Gaozong of the Yin was in mourning seclusion, the hundred officials took their orders from the regent—but beyond that tradition we have only written records, not living precedent.
entries.literal: He submitted a memorial firmly declining, saying: 'Your servant has heard that in antiquity, when King Gaozong of Yin was in the dark of mourning, the hundred officials listened to the regent—there are no further traces of events, only written records remain.

entries.zh: 且一時之事，禮不相沿。
entries.en: Moreover, rites suited to one age are not simply carried forward into another.
entries.literal: Moreover, affairs of one time are not carried on by ritual from another.

entries.zh: 今殘寇猶虞，日殷萬務，皆緣兵馬屯守討襲，善算良謀，立勝擒敵。
entries.en: Today remnant rebels still threaten the realm, and ten thousand urgent matters press upon us daily—all depending on armies in the field, on sound planning and bold strategy to win swift victories and capture the enemy.
entries.literal: Now remnant bandits still give concern; daily the myriad affairs press urgently—all depend on armies garrisoned, stationed, attacking, and raiding, on good calculation and fine strategy to achieve swift victory and capture the enemy.

entries.zh: 陛下若行古之道，居喪不言，蒼生何依，百事皆廢。
entries.en: If Your Majesty were to follow the ancient way, remain in mourning, and hold your tongue, what would become of the people? Every affair of state would come to a halt.
entries.literal: If Your Majesty follows the ancient way, dwells in mourning and does not speak, on what will the common people rely? A hundred affairs will all be abandoned.

entries.zh: 伏讀國家起居註，亦於禮部檢見舊敕，恭惟太宗、高宗、、大行皇帝在位之日，皆有國哀，視事不輟，以為君臨天下，難徇常情。
entries.en: I have carefully read the court diaries and found old edicts in the Ministry of Rites showing that Emperors Taizong, Gaozong, Zhongzong, and the late emperor, even during periods of national mourning, never ceased to conduct state business—for one who rules the realm, ordinary private feeling cannot be indulged.
entries.literal: Your servant has respectfully read the court diaries of the state and also in the Ministry of Rites examined old edicts; respectfully considering that during the days when Taizong, Gaozong, Zhongzong, and the late emperor held the throne, there were all national mourning periods yet they did not cease conducting affairs, taking it that to rule all under Heaven one cannot indulge ordinary feeling.

entries.zh: 今遺詔有處分，皇帝宜三日而聽政。
entries.en: The late emperor's testamentary edict expressly provides that the new emperor should assume governance after three days.
entries.literal: Now the testamentary edict has provisions: the emperor ought on the third day to hear government.

entries.zh: 陛下遵太宗故事，則無冢宰；
entries.en: If Your Majesty follows Emperor Taizong's precedent, no regent is needed;
entries.literal: If Your Majesty follows Taizong's precedent, then there is no regent;

entries.zh: 遵大行皇帝遺詔，便合聽朝。
entries.en: if Your Majesty follows the late emperor's testamentary edict, you should take the throne at once.
entries.literal: if Your Majesty follows the late emperor's testamentary edict, then it is fitting to hear court.

entries.zh: 萬姓颙颙，不勝大願。
entries.en: The people look to you with eager hope—they can scarcely contain their longing.
entries.literal: The myriad people look up in eager longing—they cannot bear their great wish [unfulfilled].

entries.zh: 伏惟陛下知理國之重，順人心之切，以義斷恩，從宜無改。
entries.en: I beg Your Majesty to recognize how heavy is the burden of governing the realm, how urgent the people's need, and to let duty override private grief—to do what the occasion requires and not waver.
entries.literal: Your servant respectfully considers that Your Majesty knows the weight of ordering the state, follows the urgency of people's hearts, breaks affection by righteousness, and should follow what is fitting without change.

entries.zh: 今朝臣一命已上，皆言臣心昏貌朽，加以疾病，事有急速，斷在須臾，凡聖不同，豈合受詔。
entries.en: Today every minister of the highest rank declares that my mind is clouded, my body worn out, and my illnesses many; urgent affairs must be decided in a moment—how can an ordinary man be equal to a sage? I am not fit to receive such an appointment.
entries.literal: Today court ministers of the first rank and above all say your servant's mind is dim and his appearance decayed; added to this are illness; affairs of urgency must be decided in an instant; ordinary and sage are not the same—how is it fitting to receive the edict?

entries.zh: 陛下發哀已五日矣，願準遺詔聽政，則四夷萬國，無任悲幸。」
entries.en: Your Majesty has already mourned for five days. I pray that you will follow the testamentary edict and take up governance—then the four quarters and all nations will know both grief and boundless relief.'
entries.literal: Your Majesty has begun mourning for five days already; I wish you would follow the testamentary edict and hear government—then the four barbarians and ten thousand states will be without limit in grief and joy.'

entries.zh: 肅宗時疾彌留，覽表殞絕，乃許。
entries.en: Suzong was then gravely ill. When he read the memorial he was overcome with emotion, but he granted the request.
entries.literal: Suzong's illness at the time was lingering near death; reading the memorial he collapsed as if dead, then granted it.

entries.zh: 數日，肅宗晏駕，代宗踐祚，又詔晉卿攝冢宰。
entries.en: Within days Emperor Suzong died. When Emperor Daizong took the throne he again ordered Jingqing to serve as regent.
entries.literal: Several days later Suzong died; Daizong ascended the throne and again ordered Jingqing to act as regent.

entries.zh: 晉卿上表懇辭曰：「臣以昔者天子居喪之時，百官聽於冢宰者，蓋君幼小，禦極事殷，情理當然。
entries.en: Jingqing submitted another earnest refusal, writing: 'In former ages, when the Son of Heaven was in mourning, the hundred officials took orders from a regent only because the ruler was a child and the burdens of rule were too heavy for him—circumstance made it necessary.
entries.literal: Jingqing submitted a memorial earnestly declining, saying: 'Your servant considers that in former times when the Son of Heaven dwelt in mourning, the hundred officials listened to the regent—this was because the ruler was young and small, and assuming the apex while affairs were pressing was in reason and feeling naturally so.

entries.zh: 沿革不一，今古異同，而周武、漢文，合於通變，垂範作則，可舉而行。
entries.en: Customs have changed from age to age, yet King Wu of Zhou and Emperor Wen of Han adapted rites to circumstance and left models we may follow today.
entries.literal: Continuity and change are not uniform; present and past differ and agree; yet King Wu of Zhou and Emperor Wen of Han conformed to adapting through change, handed down models and made standards that can be raised up and carried out.

entries.zh: 又士或墨缞，時遇金革，豈非銜恤，謂義在斷恩。
entries.en: Moreover, a gentleman in deep mourning may still take up arms when the state is at war—he does not cease to grieve, but duty requires him to set private feeling aside.
entries.literal: Moreover, a gentleman may wear ink mourning garb yet encounter weapons and armor—this is not contrary to holding grief; it means righteousness lies in breaking affection.

entries.zh: 且百善之至，無加於孝也，其有容瘁心絕，指景悼生，此匹夫守節之常情，殊王者嗣續之大計。
entries.en: Filial piety is the highest of virtues, yet the common man who wastes away in grief, who can scarcely bear to live—such feeling belongs to private life, not to the great business of a king who must continue the dynastic line.
entries.literal: Moreover, of the hundred virtues none surpasses filial piety; yet there are those whose appearance is haggard and whose heart is severed, who point to the sun and mourn life—this is the ordinary feeling of a common man keeping integrity, quite different from the great plan of a king continuing the succession.

entries.zh: 昨二十日，陛下於大行皇帝柩前即位，是承先帝遺顧之言，亦前代不易之典。
entries.en: Only twenty days ago Your Majesty took the throne before the late emperor's coffin—fulfilling his final charge and following an immemorial precedent.
entries.literal: Yesterday, the twentieth day, Your Majesty at the bier of the late emperor assumed the throne—this carries out the late emperor's parting charge and is also an unchanging institution of former ages.

entries.zh: 則知所略不為害，所存是適權，防威滅端，所利者大。
entries.en: What is set aside does no harm; what is preserved serves the greater good. To guard against danger at its root brings the greatest benefit.
entries.literal: Thus one knows that what is set aside is not harmful, what is preserved is fitting expedience, guarding against peril and extinguishing beginnings—the benefit is great.

entries.zh: 陛下因心純至，天地明察。
entries.en: Your Majesty's filial heart is utterly sincere—Heaven and Earth themselves bear witness.
entries.literal: Your Majesty's heart arising in purity reaches utmost sincerity; Heaven and Earth clearly perceive.

entries.zh: 伏以報劬勞之恩，申罔極之思，終身之痛，豈計朝夕！
entries.en: To repay a parent's labor, to express boundless grief—such sorrow lasts a lifetime and cannot be measured by days alone.
entries.literal: Your servant considers that repaying the grace of toil and hardship, expressing boundless longing, a lifetime's pain—how could it be reckoned by days and nights!

entries.zh: 但以一日之內，萬務在中，須達宸聰，始成國政。
entries.en: Yet within a single day ten thousand affairs demand the throne's attention; only when Your Majesty's ear is open to them can the state be governed.
entries.literal: Yet within a single day the myriad affairs lie at the center; the imperial ear must be reached before state government can be accomplished.

entries.zh: 百僚萬姓及僧道耆壽等，相顧聚言，以臣老且無能，愚豈測聖，況久無居攝，臣不敢奉詔。
entries.en: Officials, common people, monks, Daoist priests, and elders alike declare that I am old and incompetent, far too dull to measure up to a sage ruler—and besides, regency has long been out of use. I dare not accept this appointment.
entries.literal: The hundred officials, myriad people, monks and Daoists, elders of long years, and others look at one another and gather in speech, saying your servant is old and without ability—how could stupidity fathom sageliness? Moreover, for long there has been no regency; your servant dares not accept the edict.

entries.zh: 特乞陛下遵遺命，三日而政。
entries.en: I earnestly beg Your Majesty to follow the testamentary command and assume governance after three days.
entries.literal: I especially beg Your Majesty to follow the testamentary command and govern after three days.

entries.zh: 臣博聽眾情，不勝懇願，伏望割痛抑哀，則天下悲幸。」
entries.en: Having heard the people's voice throughout the realm, I cannot contain my earnest plea: I beg Your Majesty to master your grief for the sake of the empire—then the world will know both sorrow and deliverance.'
entries.literal: Your servant broadly hears the multitude's feelings and cannot bear the earnest wish; I respectfully hope you will cut pain and restrain grief—then all under Heaven will grieve and rejoice.'

entries.zh: 上號泣從之。
entries.en: The emperor wept and assented.
entries.literal: The emperor wailed and followed it.

entries.zh: 時晉卿年已衰暮，又患兩足，上特許肩輿至中書，入閣不趨，累日一視事。
entries.en: By then Jingqing was elderly and afflicted in both legs. The emperor specially allowed him to be carried in a sedan chair to the Secretariat, to enter the hall without hurrying, and to conduct business only every few days.
entries.literal: At the time Jingqing's years were already declining into old age and he also suffered in both feet; the emperor specially permitted him to be carried in a shoulder litter to the Secretariat, to enter the gate without hastening, and to review affairs once every several days.

entries.zh: 歷三朝，皆以謹密見稱。
entries.en: Through three reigns he was esteemed for his caution and discretion.
entries.literal: Through three reigns he was all praised for cautious discretion.

entries.zh: 初，樞自歙州罷郡歸朝，路經大梁，時硃全忠兵威已振，樞以兄事之，全忠由是重之。
entries.en: Earlier, when Shu left his post at She and returned to court, his route took him through Daliang. Zhu Quanzhong's military power was already formidable, and Shu treated him with the deference due an elder brother—whereupon Quanzhong came to esteem him.
entries.literal: Earlier, when Shu from She prefecture left his command and returned to court, his route passed through Daliang; at the time Zhu Quanzhong's military prestige was already rising; Shu treated him as an elder brother, and Quanzhong therefore valued him.

entries.zh: 及樞傳詔，全忠皆稟朝旨，獻奉相繼，昭宗甚悅，遷兵部侍郎。
entries.en: When Shu delivered the imperial edict, Quanzhong obeyed the court's every instruction and sent tribute in unbroken succession. Emperor Zhaozong was greatly pleased and promoted Shu to vice minister of war.
entries.literal: When Shu transmitted the edict, Quanzhong all followed court intent; tribute and offerings followed in succession; Zhaozong was very pleased and transferred him to Vice Minister of War.

entries.zh: 時崔胤專政，亦倚全忠，二人因是相結，改樞吏部侍郎。
entries.en: Cui Yin was then dominant at court and also relied on Quanzhong. The two formed an alliance, and Shu was made vice minister of personnel.
entries.literal: At the time Cui Yin monopolized government and also relied on Quanzhong; the two therefore joined together and changed Shu to Vice Minister of Personnel.

entries.zh: 未幾，換戶部侍郎、同平章事。
entries.en: Before long he was transferred to vice minister of revenue and appointed a chief minister.
entries.literal: Before long he was transferred to Vice Minister of Revenue and made a chief minister (tong pingzhangshi).

entries.zh: 其年冬，昭宗幸華州，崔胤貶官，樞亦為工部尚書。
entries.en: That winter Emperor Zhaozong went to Hua. When Cui Yin was demoted, Shu was made minister of works.
entries.literal: That winter Zhaozong went to Hua prefecture; Cui Yin was demoted, and Shu also became Minister of Works.

entries.zh: 天子自岐下還宮，以樞檢校右僕射、同平章事，出為廣南節度使。
entries.en: When the emperor returned to the capital from Qi, Shu was made investigating right vice director and chief minister, then sent out as military commissioner of Guangnan.
entries.literal: When the Son of Heaven returned to the palace from below Qi, Shu was made Investigating Right Vice Director and Concurrent Regular Attendant, and sent out as Military Commissioner of Guangnan.

entries.zh: 制出，硃全忠保薦之，言樞有經世才，不可棄之嶺表，尋復拜門下侍郎，監修國史，累兼吏部尚書，判度支。
entries.en: When the appointment was issued, Zhu Quanzhong intervened on his behalf, declaring that Shu possessed talent to govern the realm and should not be banished to the far south. Shu was soon made vice director of the Chancellery, put in charge of compiling the national history, and eventually also minister of personnel with charge of revenue.
entries.literal: When the appointment was issued, Zhu Quanzhong recommended and protected him, saying Shu had talent to order the age and could not be abandoned to the southern ranges; soon he was again appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery, supervised compilation of the national history, repeatedly held concurrently Minister of Personnel, and decided revenue affairs.

entries.zh: 崔胤誅，以全忠素厚，相位如故。
entries.en: After Cui Yin was executed, Shu retained his chief ministry unchanged, thanks to his long-standing ties with Quanzhong.
entries.literal: When Cui Yin was executed, because Quanzhong had long been close his chief-minister position remained as before.

entries.zh: 從昭宗遷洛陽，駐蹕陜州，進右僕射、弘文館大學士、太清宮使，充諸道鹽鐵轉運使。
entries.en: He accompanied Emperor Zhaozong to Luoyang and, when the court halted at Shan, was promoted to right vice director, grand academician of the Hongwen Hall, commissioner of the Great Pure Palace, and transport commissioner for salt and iron across all circuits.
entries.literal: He followed Zhaozong in moving to Luoyang, halted at Shan prefecture, was advanced to Right Vice Director, Grand Academician of the Hongwen Hall, Commissioner of the Great Pure Palace, and served as Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner of all circuits.

entries.zh: 哀帝初嗣位，柳璨用事，全忠嘗奏用牙將張廷範為太常卿，諸相議，樞曰：「廷範勛臣，幸有方鎮節鉞之命，何藉樂卿？
entries.en: When Emperor Aidi first took the throne, Liu Can was in power. Quanzhong once recommended his military officer Zhang Tingfan as director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices. The chief ministers deliberated, and Shu said, 'Tingfan is a meritorious officer who may yet receive a regional command—why does he need the directorship of the Court of Sacrifices?
entries.literal: When Aidi first succeeded to the throne, Liu Can held power; Quanzhong once memorialized to employ his military officer Zhang Tingfan as Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices; the chief ministers discussed it, and Shu said: 'Tingfan is a meritorious minister—fortunately he may receive a regional command with military commission; what need has he of the Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices?

entries.zh: 恐非元帥梁王之旨。」
entries.en: I fear this is not what the Prince of Liang, our commander-in-chief, intends.'
entries.literal: I fear this is not the intent of the Marshal, King of Liang.'

entries.zh: 乃持之不下。
entries.en: He therefore withheld the appointment and would not issue it.
entries.literal: He therefore held it and did not issue it.

entries.zh: 俄而全忠聞樞言，謂賓佐曰：「吾常以裴十四器識真純，不入浮薄之伍，觀此議論，本態露矣。」
entries.en: When Quanzhong heard of Shu's words he told his staff, 'I always thought Pei the Fourteenth was genuinely upright and would never join the frivolous crowd—but this opinion shows his true colors.'
entries.literal: Soon Quanzhong heard Shu's words and said to his guests and aides: 'I always considered Pei the Fourteenth's capacity and insight truly pure, not entering the ranks of the frivolous and shallow—viewing this discussion, his true nature is revealed.'

entries.zh: 切齒含怒。
entries.en: He ground his teeth in fury.
entries.literal: He gnashed his teeth and harbored anger.

entries.zh: 柳璨聞全忠言，尋希旨罷樞相位，和陵祔享，拜尚書左僕射。
entries.en: Liu Can, hearing Quanzhong's anger, soon had Shu removed from the chief ministry in accord with his wishes. At the joint offering at He Mausoleum Shu was made left vice director of the Secretariat.
entries.literal: Liu Can heard Quanzhong's words and soon, to suit the intent, removed Shu from the chief-minister position; at the joint offering at He Mausoleum he was appointed Left Vice Director of the Secretariat.

entries.zh: 五月，責授朝散大夫、登州刺史，尋再貶瀧州司戶。
entries.en: In the fifth month he was demoted to grand master of palace leisure and prefect of Deng, then soon further demoted to registrar of Long prefecture.
entries.literal: In the fifth month he was punished and appointed Grand Master of Palace Leisure and Prefect of Deng, soon again demoted to Registrar of Long prefecture.

entries.zh: 六月十一日，行及滑州，全忠遣人殺之於白馬驛，投屍於河，時年六十五。
entries.en: On the eleventh day of the sixth month, when he reached Hua prefecture on the Yellow River on his way into exile, Quanzhong sent men to kill him at Baima Post and throw his body into the river. He was sixty-five years old.
entries.literal: On the eleventh day of the sixth month, when his journey reached Hua prefecture, Quanzhong sent men to kill him at Baima Post, threw the corpse into the river—he was sixty-five years of age.

entries.zh: 子樞，字紀聖，咸通十二年登進士第。
entries.en: His son Shu, courtesy name Jisheng, passed the jinshi examination in Xiantong 12 (871).
entries.literal: His son Shu, courtesy name Jisheng, in the twelfth year of Xiantong passed the jinshi examination.

entries.zh: 宰相杜審權出鎮河中，辟為從事，得秘書省校書郎，再遷藍田尉。
entries.en: When Chief Minister Du Shenquan went out to command Hezhong, he recruited Shu as administrative aide. Shu was appointed collator in the Secretariat and later promoted twice to magistrate of Lantian.
entries.literal: Chief Minister Du Shenquan went out to garrison Hezhong and recruited him as administrative aide; he obtained Collator in the Secretariat and was twice transferred to Magistrate of Lantian.

entries.zh: 直弘文館。
entries.en: He served on duty at the Hongwen Hall.
entries.literal: He served on duty at the Hongwen Hall.

entries.zh: 大學士王鐸深知之，鐸罷相失職，樞亦久之不調。
entries.en: Grand Academician Wang Duo thought highly of him. When Duo lost the chief ministry and fell from power, Shu too went long without a new appointment.
entries.literal: Grand Academician Wang Duo deeply knew him; when Duo was removed from the chief ministry and lost his post, Shu also for a long time received no transfer.

entries.zh: 從僖宗幸蜀，中丞李煥奏為殿中侍御史，遷起居郎。
entries.en: He accompanied Emperor Xizong to Shu. Vice censor-in-chief Li Huan recommended him as attending censor in the palace, and he was promoted to diarist.
entries.literal: He followed Xizong to Shu; Vice Censor-in-Chief Li Huan memorialized him as Attending Censor in the Palace, and he was transferred to Diarist.

entries.zh: 中和初，王鐸復見用，以舊恩徙為鄭滑掌書記、檢校司封郎中，賜金紫，入朝歷兵、吏二員外郎。
entries.en: Early in the Zhonghe era Wang Duo returned to power. Out of old friendship Shu was made secretary to the Zheng-Hua command and investigating director in the Bureau of Enfeoffments, granted the gold-and-purple insignia, and after returning to court served as vice director in the ministries of War and Personnel.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Zhonghe Wang Duo was again employed; because of old grace he was transferred to Secretary of Zheng and Hua, Investigating Director of the Bureau of Enfeoffments, granted gold and purple, entered court and passed through Vice Director in the Ministries of War and Personnel.

entries.zh: 龍紀初，擢拜給事中，改京兆尹。
entries.en: At the beginning of the Longji era he was promoted to drafting attendant and then made metropolitan prefect.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Longji he was promoted and appointed Drafting Attendant, then changed to Metropolitan Prefect.

entries.zh: 宰相孔緯尤深獎遇。
entries.en: Chief Minister Kong Wei especially favored and promoted him.
entries.literal: Chief Minister Kong Wei especially deeply rewarded and favored him.

entries.zh: 大順中，緯以用兵無功貶官，樞坐累為右庶子，尋出為歙州刺史。
entries.en: In the Dashun era Kong Wei was demoted for military failure. Shu was implicated and made right guardian of the heir apparent, then sent out as prefect of She.
entries.literal: In Dazhun Wei was demoted for using troops without merit; Shu was implicated and made Right Guardian of the Heir Apparent, soon sent out as Prefect of She.

entries.zh: 乾寧初，入為右散騎常侍，從昭宗幸華州，為汴州宣諭使。
entries.en: Early in the Qianning era he was recalled as right regular attendant of the cavalry, accompanied Emperor Zhaozong to Hua, and was appointed commissioner to proclaim the court's will at Bian.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Qianning he entered as Right Regular Attendant of the Cavalry, followed Zhaozong to Hua prefecture, and served as Proclamation and Consolation Commissioner to Bian.

entries.zh: 史臣曰：晉卿謹身蒞事，足為純臣，避寇全忠，固彰大節。
entries.en: The historiographer comments: Jingqing conducted himself with scrupulous care in office and may truly be called a loyal minister; in fleeing the rebels he preserved his integrity and displayed great moral courage.
entries.literal: The historiographer says: Jingqing kept himself cautious in attending to affairs—sufficient to be a pure minister; avoiding bandits he preserved complete loyalty, truly displaying great integrity.

entries.zh: 然博達精審，豈不知寬猛之道哉！
entries.en: Yet he was learned, penetrating, and exact in judgment—how could he not have known the balance of leniency and severity!
entries.literal: Yet broad, penetrating, and precise in examination—how could he not know the way of leniency and severity!

entries.zh: 奉林甫之旨，順胥吏之意，悅附張倚，欺罔時君。
entries.en: He carried out Li Linfu's wishes, indulged the clerks, curried favor with Zhang Yi, and deceived his sovereign.
entries.literal: He followed Linfu's intent, complied with the clerks' wishes, delighted in attaching to Zhang Yi, and deceived and misled the ruler of the age.

entries.zh: 生為重臣，諂林甫之勢也；
entries.en: In life he rose to the highest office by flattering Li Linfu's power;
entries.literal: While alive he was a great minister—this was fawning on Linfu's power;

entries.zh: 歿改美謚，引元載之恩焉。
entries.en: after death he received a flattering posthumous title through Yuan Zai's favor.
entries.literal: after death he received a fine posthumous title—this drew on Yuan Zai's grace.

entries.zh: 或言晉卿不為巧宦者，誠不信也。
entries.en: Those who claim Jingqing was no crafty courtier simply cannot be believed.
entries.literal: If some say Jingqing was not a crafty official, truly one cannot believe it.

entries.zh: 冕力贊中興，名居大位，奉公抱義，可以致身；
entries.en: Mian vigorously supported the restoration and rose to the highest rank. In serving the state with integrity he might have won lasting honor;
entries.literal: Mian vigorously praised the restoration, his name occupied the great position, he served the public and embraced righteousness—by this one could establish oneself;

entries.zh: 賣官度僧，是何為政？
entries.en: yet what sort of governance is it to sell offices and sell ordinations?
entries.literal: selling offices and licensing monks—what kind of government is this?

entries.zh: 及其老也，貪冒尤深。
entries.en: In his old age his greed knew no bounds.
entries.literal: When he reached old age, his greed and presumption were especially deep.

entries.zh: 遵慶學術貞明，為國忠所出；
entries.en: Zunqing's learning was upright and his conduct clear, yet Yang Guozhong had him posted to the provinces;
entries.literal: Zunqing's learning was upright and clear, yet he was sent out by Guozhong;

entries.zh: 恭儉謹密，遇蕭華素知。
entries.en: he was respectful, frugal, and discreet, and won recognition from Xiao Hua, who had long known his worth.
entries.literal: respectful, frugal, cautious and discreet—he met Xiao Hua, who had long known him.

entries.zh: 位重行純，老而彌篤，彼二公固有慚德。
entries.en: He held high office with pure conduct and grew only more steadfast in old age—beside him, the other two men had reason to feel ashamed.
entries.literal: His position was weighty and his conduct pure; in old age he became all the more earnest—those two lords naturally had conduct to be ashamed of.

entries.zh: 向克荷堂構，不墜門風。
entries.en: Xiang upheld the family estate and did not let its reputation fall.
entries.literal: Xiang was able to bear the hall's beams and did not let the family's style fall.

entries.zh: 樞因盜而振，盜憎而亡，宜哉！
entries.en: Shu rose through the rebel's favor, and when the rebel turned against him he perished—as was only fitting!
entries.literal: Shu rose through the bandit, the bandit hated him and he perished—fitting indeed!

entries.zh: 君子守道遠刑，蓋慮此也。
entries.en: The gentleman holds to the Way and keeps clear of punishment—surely he takes warning from such examples.
entries.literal: The gentleman keeps the Way and stays far from punishment—probably he considers this.

entries.zh: 苗晉卿裴冕裴遵慶子向向子寅寅子樞
entries.en: Miao Jingqing; Pei Mian; Pei Zunqing; his son Xiang; Xiang's son Yin; Yin's son Shu.
entries.literal: Miao Jingqing, Pei Mian, Pei Zunqing, son Xiang, Xiang's son Yin, Yin's son Shu.

entries.zh: 前後在蜀累年，肆誌逞欲，恣行猛政。
entries.en: During his long years in Shu he gave free rein to his appetites and ruled with arbitrary severity.
entries.literal: Over many years before and after in Shu he indulged his will and desires and arbitrarily carried out harsh government.

entries.zh: 梓州刺史章彜初為武判官，及是小不副意，赴成都杖殺之，由是威震一方。
entries.en: Zhang Yi of Zizhou had once served as his aide; when Yi displeased him even slightly, Wu summoned him to Chengdu and had him clubbed to death, and thereafter his terror held the whole region.
entries.literal: Zhang Yi, Prefect of Zizhou, had first been Wu's aide; when he fell slightly short of Wu's wishes, Wu had him brought to Chengdu and beaten to death with the staff, and from this his awe filled the region.

entries.zh: 蜀土頗饒珍產，武窮極奢靡，賞賜無度，或由一言賞至百萬。
entries.en: Shu was rich in rare goods, and Wu spent without limit; a single pleasing word from him could bring a reward of a million cash.
entries.literal: The land of Shu was quite rich in rare products; Wu pursued luxury to the extreme, his rewards without limit, and sometimes for a single remark he would grant up to a million.

entries.zh: 蜀方閭裏以征斂殆至匱竭，然蕃虜亦不敢犯境。
entries.en: Taxes and levies nearly beggared the countryside, yet frontier tribes likewise dared not cross his borders.
entries.literal: In the villages of Shu, levies brought them nearly to exhaustion, yet the barbarians of the frontier also did not dare to violate the borders.

entries.zh: 而性本狂蕩，視事多率胸臆，雖慈母言不之顧。
entries.en: By nature he was headstrong and impulsive, governing mostly on whim; he would not even listen to his own mother.
entries.literal: Yet his nature was fundamentally reckless; in conducting affairs he mostly followed his breast and belly, and even his loving mother's words he did not heed.

entries.zh: 初為劍南節度使，舊相房琯出為管內刺史，琯於武有薦導之恩，武驕倨，見琯略無朝禮，甚為時議所貶。
entries.en: When he first took command in Jiannan, his former patron Fang Guan was serving as a circuit prefect; though Guan had launched his career, Wu treated him with arrogant disrespect and scarcely a trace of formal courtesy, drawing widespread condemnation.
entries.literal: When he first became Military Commissioner of Jiannan, the former Chief Minister Fang Guan went out as a prefect within the circuit; Guan had the grace of recommending and guiding Wu, but Wu was arrogant and haughty and on seeing Guan showed hardly any court etiquette, and this was much decried in contemporary opinion.

entries.zh: 永泰元年四月，以疾終，時年四十。
entries.en: He died of illness in the fourth month of 765, at the age of forty.
entries.literal: In the fourth month of the first year of Yongtai he died of illness; he was then forty.

entries.zh: 嚴武，中書侍郎挺之子也。
entries.en: Yan Wu was the son of Ting, who had served as Vice Director of the Secretariat.
entries.literal: Yan Wu was the son of Ting, Vice Director of the Secretariat.

entries.zh: 神氣雋爽，敏於聞見。
entries.en: He had a keen, commanding presence and was unusually quick to grasp what he heard and saw.
entries.literal: His spirit and bearing were sharp and lofty, and he was quick in what he heard and observed.

entries.zh: 幼有成人之風，讀書不究精義，涉獵而已。
entries.en: Even as a boy he carried himself like an adult; he read widely but never troubled to master texts in depth.
entries.literal: In youth he had the manner of a grown man; in reading he did not pursue the deepest meanings but merely ranged broadly.

entries.zh: 弱冠以門廕策名，隴右節度使哥舒翰奏充判官，遷侍御史。
entries.en: At his coming of age he qualified through family privilege; Geshu Han, military commissioner of Longyou, had him appointed as aide on memorial and then promoted him to Attending Censor.
entries.literal: Upon reaching the capping age he entered the rolls through hereditary privilege; the Longyou Military Commissioner Geshu Han memorialized to appoint him as aide, and he was promoted to Attending Censor.

entries.zh: 至德初，肅宗興師靖難，大收才傑，武杖節赴行在。
entries.en: Early in the Zhide reign, as Emperor Suzong mobilized to put down the rebellion and recruited talent far and wide, Wu took up his commission and hurried to the emperor's camp.
entries.literal: At the beginning of the Zhide era, when Emperor Suzong raised armies to quell the rebellion and gathered outstanding men on a large scale, Wu took the staff of office and went to the mobile court.

entries.zh: 宰相房琯以武名臣之子，素重之，及是，首薦才略可稱，累遷給事中。
entries.en: Chief Minister Fang Guan had always held Wu in esteem as the son of a distinguished official; now he was first to recommend him for his ability and was instrumental in promoting him repeatedly until he reached Supervising Secretary.
entries.literal: The Chief Minister Fang Guan, because Wu was the son of a famous minister, had long valued him; on this occasion he was the first to recommend that his talent and strategy were commendable, and Wu was repeatedly promoted to Supervising Secretary.

entries.zh: 既收長安，以武為京兆少尹、兼御史中丞，時年三十二。
entries.en: Once Chang'an had been retaken, he was appointed Vice Governor of the capital district and concurrent Vice Censor-in-Chief at the age of thirty-two.
entries.literal: After Chang'an was recovered, Wu was made Vice Governor of Jingzhao and concurrently Vice Censor-in-Chief; he was then thirty-two.

entries.zh: 以史思明阻兵不之官，優遊京師，頗自矜大。
entries.en: With Shi Siming's armies blocking the routes, he never took up his post and instead lingered in the capital, growing rather full of himself.
entries.literal: Because Shi Siming obstructed the roads with his troops, he did not take up the post but idled in the capital, quite self-important.

entries.zh: 出為綿州刺史，遷劍南東川節度使；
entries.en: He was sent out to serve as prefect of Mianzhou and later promoted to military commissioner of eastern Jiannan.
entries.literal: He went out as Prefect of Mianzhou and was transferred to Military Commissioner of Jiannan East Circuit;

entries.zh: 入為太子賓客、兼御史中丞。
entries.en: He was recalled to the capital as a guest of the heir apparent and concurrent Vice Censor-in-Chief.
entries.literal: He entered the capital as Guest of the Heir Apparent and concurrently Vice Censor-in-Chief.

entries.zh: 曜，子儀長子。
entries.en: Yao was Ziyi's eldest son.
entries.literal: Yao was Ziyi's eldest son.

entries.zh: 性孝友廉謹。
entries.en: He was filial, friendly, honest, and careful.
entries.literal: By nature filial, friendly, honest, and careful.

entries.zh: 子儀薨，出征於外，留曜治家，少長千人，皆得其所。
entries.en: When Ziyi died on campaign, Yao ran the household of a thousand kin fairly.
entries.literal: When Ziyi died, campaigning abroad, he left Yao to manage the house; old and young a thousand—all obtained their place.

entries.zh: 諸弟爭飾池館，盛其車服，曜以儉樸自處。
entries.en: Brothers flaunted wealth; Yao lived plainly.
entries.literal: Younger brothers competed to adorn pools and halls and magnify carriage and dress; Yao kept himself frugal and plain.

entries.zh: 累遷至太子賓客。
entries.en: He rose to crown prince's guest.
entries.literal: He successively rose to Crown Prince's Guest.

entries.zh: 建中初，子儀罷兵柄，乃遍加諸子官，以曜為太子少保。
entries.en: When Ziyi lost command, Yao became crown prince's junior mentor.
entries.literal: At the start of Jianzhong, when Ziyi lost military power, he broadly added offices to the sons, making Yao Crown Prince's Junior Mentor.

entries.zh: 子儀曜遵遺命，四朝所賜名馬珍玩，悉皆上獻，德宗復賜之，曜乃散諸昆弟。
entries.en: They surrendered imperial gifts per Ziyi's will; Dezong returned them and Yao shared them among kin.
entries.literal: Ziyi and Yao followed the testament: famous horses and precious playthings granted by the four reigns were all presented above; Dezong returned them, and Yao then distributed them among the brothers.

entries.zh: 子儀薨後，楊炎、盧杞相次秉政，奸諂用事，尤忌勛族。
entries.en: After Ziyi's death Yang Yan and Lu Qi persecuted great clans.
entries.literal: After Ziyi's death, Yang Yan and Lu Qi successively held power; wicked flatterers handled affairs, especially jealous of meritorious clans.

entries.zh: 子儀之婿太仆卿趙縱、少府少監李洞清、光祿卿王宰，皆以有人告訐細過，相次貶黜。
entries.en: Sons-in-law Zhao Zong, Li Dongqing, and Wang Zai were demoted on petty denunciations.
entries.literal: Ziyi's sons-in-law Grand Master of the Imperial Stud Zhao Zong, Vice Director of the Palace Workshops Li Dongqing, and Minister of Imperial Sacrifices Wang Zai—all because someone informed on minor faults were in succession demoted and dismissed.

entries.zh: 曜家大恐，賴宰相張鎰力為庇護。
entries.en: Yao's family feared ruin until Zhang Yi protected them.
entries.literal: Yao's household was greatly afraid, relying on chief councilor Zhang Yi to exert strength in shelter.

entries.zh: 奸人幸其危懼，多論奪田宅奴婢，曜不敢訴。
entries.en: Predators seized their property while Yao dared not protest.
entries.literal: Wicked men, rejoicing in their peril and fear, mostly argued to seize fields, houses, and slaves; Yao did not dare complain.

entries.zh: 德宗微知之，詔曰：「尚父子儀，有大勛力，保乂皇家，嘗誓以山河，琢之金石，十世之宥，其可忘也！
entries.en: Dezong decreed: "Imperial Father Ziyi's ten-generation pardon must not be forgotten!
entries.literal: Dezong slightly knew this and issued an edict: "Imperial Father Guo Ziyi had great merit and strength, preserving and comforting the royal house; he once swore on mountains and rivers, carved on metal and stone—a pardon for ten generations—how can it be forgotten!

entries.zh: 其家前時與人為市，以子儀身歿，名被誣構，欲論奪之，有司無得為理。」
entries.en: If in former times his family made purchases from others, and now, because Ziyi himself has died and his name is falsely entangled, someone wishes to contest and seize them, the responsible offices must not process the claim."
entries.literal: If in former times his family made purchases from others, and now, because Ziyi himself has died and his name is falsely entangled, someone wishes to contest and seize them, the responsible offices must not process the claim."

entries.zh: 詔下方已。
entries.en: When the edict was promulgated, the seizures stopped.
entries.literal: When the edict was issued below, it stopped.

entries.zh: 曜居喪得禮，若儒家子，服未闋寢疾，或勸其茹蔥薤，曜竟不屬口。
entries.en: Yao mourned by Confucian rites; ill before mourning ended, he refused even scallions and leeks.
entries.literal: Yao observed mourning with proper rites like a Confucian son; before mourning ended he took to bed with illness; some urged him to eat scallions and leeks; Yao ultimately did not put them to mouth.

entries.zh: 建中四年三月卒，贈太子太傅。
entries.en: In Jianzhong 4, third month, he died and was posthumously made grand mentor of the crown prince.
entries.literal: In the third month of the fourth year of Jianzhong he died; posthumously granted Grand Mentor of the Crown Prince.

entries.zh: 郭子儀子曜晞曖曙晤映晞子鋼曖子釗鏦釗子仲文族弟幼明子昕
entries.en: Guo Ziyi's line included his sons Yao, Xi, Ai, Shu, Wu, and Ying, another son Xi, his son Gang, Ai's son Zhao (whose sons were Cong and Zhongwen), and his clansman Youming's son Xin.
entries.literal: Guo Ziyi's sons: Yao, Xi, Ai, Shu, Wu, Ying, and Xi; Ziyi's son Gang; Ai's son Zhao; Zhao's sons Cong and Zhongwen; clan younger brother Youming's son Xin.

entries.zh: 盧鸑，幽州范陽人也，貞觀中工部侍郎義恭玄孫也。
entries.en: Lu Bie was a native of Fanyang in Youzhou and the great-great-grandson of Yigong, who had served as Vice Minister of Public Works in the Zhenguan era.
entries.literal: Lu Bie was a native of Fanyang in Youzhou and the great-great-grandson of Yigong, Vice Minister of Public Works in the Zhenguan era.

entries.zh: 父子騫，潁王府諮議參軍，以鸑贈秘書少監。
entries.en: His father Ziqian had been advisory staff officer of the Prince of Ying's household; because of Bie he was posthumously made Vice Director of the Secretariat.
entries.literal: His father Ziqian was advisory staff officer of the Prince of Ying's household; because of Bie he was posthumously made Vice Director of the Secretariat.

entries.zh: 鸑少以門廕入仕，在職以幹局稱。
entries.en: Bie entered office early through yin privilege and was known in service for practical ability.
entries.literal: Bie early entered office through yin privilege and in service was known for practical ability.

entries.zh: 累授閬州錄事參軍、監察殿中御史、侍御史、金州刺史。
entries.en: He rose through appointments as records officer of Langzhou, investigating palace censor, attendant censor, and prefect of Jinzhou.
entries.literal: He was repeatedly appointed records officer of Langzhou, investigating palace censor, attendant censor, and prefect of Jinzhou.

entries.zh: 宰相楊炎遇之頗厚，召入左司郎中、京兆少尹，遷大尹。
entries.en: Chief Minister Yang Yan treated him generously, brought him to court as bureau director in the Left Secretariat and junior magistrate of the capital district, and then promoted him to chief magistrate.
entries.literal: Chief Minister Yang Yan treated him very generously, summoned him in as bureau director in the Left Secretariat and junior magistrate of the capital district, and promoted him to chief magistrate.

entries.zh: 鸑無術學，善事權要，為政苛躁。
entries.en: Bie had no scholarly training, was skilled at cultivating the powerful and favored, and governed harshly and rashly.
entries.literal: Bie had no learning in the arts, was skilled at serving the powerful and favored, and in governing was harsh and rash.

entries.zh: 盧杞甚惡之，諷有司彈奏，坐貶撫州司馬同正，改饒州刺史，遷福州刺史、福建觀察使。
entries.en: Lu Qi hated him and prompted the relevant offices to impeach him. He was demoted to vice prefect of Fu Prefecture, then reassigned as prefect of Raozhou, and later transferred to prefect of Fuzhou and observation commissioner of Fujian.
entries.literal: Lu Qi greatly hated him, hinted that the relevant offices impeach him, and he was demoted to vice prefect of Fu Prefecture with concurrent regular status, then changed to prefect of Raozhou and transferred to prefect of Fuzhou and observation commissioner of Fujian.

entries.zh: 貞元二年七月，以疾終。
entries.en: In the seventh month of the second year of Zhenyuan he died of illness.
entries.literal: In the seventh month of the second year of Zhenyuan he died of illness.

entries.zh: 史臣曰：李揆發言沃心，幸遇明主；
entries.en: The historian comments: Li Kui's words enriched the sovereign's heart, and he was fortunate to meet an enlightened ruler;
entries.literal: The historian says: Li Kui's words enriched the heart and he was fortunate to meet an enlightened lord;

entries.zh: 蔽賢固位，終非令人。
entries.en: yet in screening out the worthy and clinging to his post he was not, in the end, a man to be admired.
entries.literal: yet in screening out the worthy and holding fast to his post he was in the end not a man to be admired.

entries.zh: 少遊逐勢利隨時，盧惎事權要巧宦，察言觀行，皆無可稱。
entries.en: Shaoyou chased profit and power as the times shifted; Lu Ji cultivated the powerful and favored as a crafty office-seeker—in examining their words and conduct, none is praiseworthy.
entries.literal: Shaoyou chased profit and power as times shifted; Lu Ji served the powerful and favored as a crafty office-seeker—in examining words and observing conduct, none is praiseworthy.

entries.zh: 涵節行著聞，谞和易為理，庶幾近仁也。
entries.en: Han's conduct was renowned, and Xu governed with easy mildness—they come close to true benevolence.
entries.literal: Han's conduct was renowned, and Xu governed with easy mildness—they come close to benevolence.

entries.zh: 贊曰李、陳、盧鸑，言行非真。
entries.en: The eulogy says: Li, Chen, and Lu Yue—their words and conduct were not genuine.
entries.literal: The eulogy says: Li, Chen, and Lu Yue—their words and conduct were not genuine.

entries.zh: 涵、谞和易，庶乎近仁。
entries.en: Han and Xu, easy and mild in manner—they come close to benevolence.
entries.literal: Han and Xu, easy and mild—they come close to benevolence.

entries.zh: 李揆字端卿，隴西成紀人，而家於鄭州，代為冠族。
entries.en: Li Kui, whose courtesy name was Duanqing, came from Longxi Chengji but his family had long lived in Zhengzhou, where for generations they ranked among the foremost great houses.
entries.literal: Li Kui, styled Duanqing, was a native of Longxi Chengji but his family resided in Zhengzhou; for generations they were a leading clan.

entries.zh: 秦府學士、給事中玄道玄孫，秘書監、贈吏部尚書成裕之子。
entries.en: He was the great-great-grandson of Xuandao, who had served as a scholar in the Prince of Qin's household and as a supervising remonstrator, and was the son of Chengyu, Director of the Secretariat, who was posthumously made Minister of Personnel.
entries.literal: He was the great-great-grandson of Xuandao, a scholar of the Prince of Qin's household and a supervising remonstrator; and the son of Chengyu, Director of the Secretariat and posthumously Minister of Personnel.

entries.zh: 少聰敏好學，善屬文。
entries.en: As a youth he was quick-witted and devoted to study, and he excelled at literary composition.
entries.literal: In youth he was clever and fond of learning, and skilled at literary composition.

entries.zh: 開元末，舉進士，補陳留尉，獻書闕下，詔中書試文章，擢拜右拾遺。
entries.en: Near the end of the Kaiyuan reign he passed the jinshi examination and was appointed defender of Chenliu. After he submitted a book to the court, the emperor ordered the Secretariat to examine his writings and promoted him to Right Remonstrance-reminder.
entries.literal: At the end of the Kaiyuan era he passed the jinshi examination, was appointed Chenliu district defender, presented a memorial at the palace gates; on imperial order the Secretariat tested his literary compositions and he was promoted to Right Remonstrance-reminder.

entries.zh: 改右補闕、起居郎，知宗子表疏。
entries.en: He was then made Right Supplementation-reminder and Imperial Diarist, with responsibility for memorials from members of the imperial clan.
entries.literal: He was transferred to Right Supplementation-reminder and Imperial Diarist, and was charged with imperial-clan memorials.

entries.zh: 遷司勛員外郎、考功郎中，並知制誥。
entries.en: He rose to outer office director of the Bureau of Merits and bureau director of Evaluations in the Ministry of Personnel, serving in both offices as a drafter of imperial rescripts.
entries.literal: He was promoted to outer office director of the Bureau of Merits and bureau director of Evaluations in the Ministry of Personnel, and in both posts drafted imperial rescripts.

entries.zh: 扈從劍南，拜中書舍人。
entries.en: When the court went to Jiannan he accompanied it and was appointed a drafter of the Secretariat.
entries.literal: He followed the emperor to Jiannan and was appointed Secretariat drafter.

entries.zh: 劉晏，字士安，曹州南華人。
entries.en: Liu Yan, styled Shi'an, came from Nanhua in Caozhou.
entries.literal: Liu Yan, courtesy name Shi'an, was a native of Nanhua in Caozhou.

entries.zh: 年七歲，舉神童，授秘書省正字。
entries.en: At seven he was nominated as a precocious youth and made Regular Scribe in the Secretariat.
entries.literal: At age seven he was recommended as a child prodigy and appointed Regular Scribe of the Secretariat.

entries.zh: 累授夏縣令，有能名。
entries.en: Through successive appointments he became magistrate of Xia County and became known for administrative ability.
entries.literal: He was repeatedly appointed magistrate of Xia County and gained a reputation for competence.

entries.zh: 歷殿中侍御史，遷度支郎中、杭隴華三州刺史，尋遷河南尹。
entries.en: He held the post of palace attendant censor, then rose to vice director of the revenue bureau and prefect of Hang, Long, and Hua, and shortly afterward became Intendant of the Henan circuit.
entries.literal: He served as Attendant Censor in the Palace, was promoted to Vice Director in the Bureau of Revenue, and became prefect of Hang, Long, and Hua; soon after he was transferred to Intendant of Henan.

entries.zh: 時史朝義盜據東都，寄理長水。
entries.en: With Shi Chaoyi holding the Eastern Capital, Yan governed from Changshui as his provisional seat.
entries.literal: At that time Shi Chaoyi was occupying the Eastern Capital by force, so he administered affairs from Changshui.

entries.zh: 入為京兆尹，頃之，加戶部侍郎、兼御史中丞，判度支，委府事於司錄張群、杜亞，綜大體，議論號為稱職。
entries.en: Recalled to serve as metropolitan governor of Chang'an, he soon added the titles of vice minister of revenue and concurrent vice censor-in-chief, with charge of the revenue bureau. He left routine office work to Zhang Qun and Du Ya as recorders while he kept the broad direction in hand, and contemporaries judged his policy judgments sound.
entries.literal: He entered the capital as Metropolitan Governor; shortly thereafter he was additionally appointed Vice Minister of Revenue and Concurrent Vice Censor-in-Chief, with charge of revenue; he entrusted administrative affairs to Clerks Zhang Qun and Du Ya, while he handled overall policy, and his deliberations were said to be competent.

entries.zh: 無何，為酷吏敬羽所構，貶通州刺史。
entries.en: Not long after, the notorious official Jing Yu engineered charges against him, and he was demoted to prefect of Tongzhou.
entries.literal: Before long he was framed by the harsh official Jing Yu and demoted to prefect of Tongzhou.

entries.zh: 復入為京兆尹、戶部侍郎，判度支。
entries.en: He returned to Chang'an as metropolitan governor and vice minister of revenue, again supervising the revenue bureau.
entries.literal: He was recalled to serve again as Metropolitan Governor and Vice Minister of Revenue, with charge of revenue.

entries.zh: 時顏真卿以文學正直出為利州刺史，晏舉真卿自代為戶部，乃加國子祭酒。
entries.en: When Yan Zhenqing, admired for scholarship and integrity, had been posted to Lizhou, Liu Yan proposed that Zhenqing succeed him at the Ministry of Revenue and was himself made chancellor of the national university in addition.
entries.literal: At that time Yan Zhenqing, known for literary learning and uprightness, had been sent out as prefect of Lizhou; Yan recommended Zhenqing to succeed him in the Revenue Ministry, and Yan was additionally made Chancellor of the Directorate of Education.

entries.zh: 寶應二年，遷吏部尚書、平章事，領度支鹽鐵轉運租庸使。
entries.en: In 763 he became minister of civil appointments and chief minister, continuing to head the combined revenue, salt, iron, transport, and corvée administration.
entries.literal: In the second year of Baoying he was transferred to Minister of Personnel and made Grand Councilor, while retaining his posts as Commissioner for Revenue, Salt, Iron, Transport, and the Corvée Tax.

entries.zh: 坐與中官程元振交通，元振得罪，晏罷相，為太子賓客。
entries.en: Charged with ties to the eunuch Cheng Yuanzhen, he lost the premiership when Yuanzhen was disgraced and was appointed mentor to the crown prince.
entries.literal: He was punished for associating with the eunuch Cheng Yuanzhen; when Yuanzhen fell from power, Yan was removed from the chancellorship and made Mentor to the Heir Apparent.

entries.zh: 尋授御史大夫，領東都、河南、江淮、山南等道轉運租庸鹽鐵使如故。
entries.en: He was soon made Censor-in-Chief while retaining his former commissions for transport, zu-yong taxes, salt, and iron over the Eastern Capital, Henan, Jianghuai, Shannan, and related circuits.
entries.literal: Soon after he was appointed Censor-in-Chief and continued to hold his former posts as Transport Commissioner for the Eastern Capital, Henan, Jianghuai, Shan'nan, and other circuits, as well as Commissioner for the Corvée Tax, Salt, and Iron.

entries.zh: 時新承兵戈之後，中外艱食，京師米價鬥至一千，官廚無兼時之積，禁軍乏食，畿縣百姓乃挼穗以供之。
entries.en: The realm was still recovering from war. Food was desperately short everywhere; in Chang'an a dou of rice cost a thousand cash. The imperial kitchens held barely one meal's reserve, the palace guards went hungry, and peasants in the suburbs threshed ears of grain by hand to feed them.
entries.literal: The dynasty had newly emerged from warfare; inside and outside the capital food was scarce; rice in the capital reached a thousand cash per dou; the government kitchens had no stores beyond a single meal; the palace guards lacked food; and the people of the capital districts pounded grain spikes by hand to supply them.

entries.zh: 晏受命後，以轉運為己任，凡所經歷，必究利病之由。
entries.en: Once charged with the task, Yan treated grain transport as his own mission and wherever he went traced every cause of waste or efficiency.
entries.literal: After Yan received his mandate, he made transport his personal responsibility, and wherever he traveled he thoroughly investigated the causes of profit and harm.

entries.zh: 至江淮，以書遺元載曰：
entries.en: Reaching Jianghuai, he wrote Yuan Zai:
entries.literal: When he reached the Jianghuai region, he sent a letter to Yuan Zai saying:

entries.zh: 浮於淮、泗，達於汴，入於河，西循底柱、硤石、少華，楚帆越客，直抵建章、長樂，此安社稷之奇策也。
entries.en: Grain could float up the Huai and Si, reach Bian, enter the Yellow River, and run west past Dizhu, Xiaoshi, and Shaohua so that Chu and Yue shipping would berth straight at the imperial palaces—this was the bold plan to stabilize the dynasty.
entries.literal: Floating on the Huai and Si, reaching Bian, entering the Yellow River, and proceeding west along Dizhu, Xiaoshi, and Shaohua—Chu sails and Yue merchants arriving straight at Jianzhang and Changle: this is the extraordinary stratagem to secure the state.

entries.zh: 晏賓於東朝，猶有官謗，相公終始故舊，不信流言，賈誼復召宣室，弘羊重興功利，敢不悉力以答所知。
entries.en: Though as a guest at the Eastern Court I still face official slander, you have remained my old friend from first to last and will not heed idle talk. Just as Jia Yi was called back to the privy chamber and Sang Hongyang was trusted again to manage state revenue, I dare not spare myself in repaying your confidence.
entries.literal: Yan, though favored at the Eastern Court, still bore official slander; the Chancellor had been my friend from first to last—do not believe wandering rumors; Jia Yi was summoned again to the Xuan Chamber, and Sang Hongyang revived profit and utility—how dare I not exert every effort to repay one who knows me?

entries.zh: 驅馬陜郊，見三門渠津遺跡。
entries.en: Traveling through the lands west of Shan, I found the remains of the Sanmen canal works.
entries.literal: Riding through the Shaan suburbs, I saw the vestiges of the canals and crossings at Sanmen.

entries.zh: 到河陰、鞏、洛，見宇文愷置梁公堰，分黃河水入通濟渠；
entries.en: At Heyin, Gong, and Luoyang I inspected Yuwen Kai's weir diverting Yellow River water into the Tongji Canal;
entries.literal: At Heyin, Gong, and Luo I saw how Yuwen Kai had built the Duke of Liang's weir to divide the Yellow River into the Tongji Canal;

entries.zh: 大夫李傑新堤故事，飾像河廟，凜然如生。
entries.en: and Li Jie's later embankment, with life-like images set up at the River God shrine.
entries.literal: and the story of Censor-in-Chief Li Jie's new embankment, with statues adorned at the River Temple, stern as though living.

entries.zh: 涉滎郊、浚澤，遙瞻淮甸，步步探討，知昔人用心，則潭、衡、桂陽必多積谷，關輔汲汲，只緣兵糧。
entries.en: Passing through the Song riverland and dredging the marshes, scanning the Huai plain at every turn, I saw why the ancients labored as they did: the lake districts around Tan, Heng, and Guiyang must hold huge reserves, while Guanzhong starves chiefly for want of army rations.
entries.literal: Crossing the Song suburbs and dredging marshes, gazing from afar at the Huai district, investigating step by step—I knew how our predecessors applied their minds: Tan, Heng, and Guiyang surely store abundant grain; the Guanzhong region strains only because of military grain.

entries.zh: 漕引瀟、湘、洞庭，萬里幾日，淪波卦席，西指長安。
entries.en: Once grain is floated down the Xiao, the Xiang, and Dongting Lake, ten thousand li can be covered in days, with sails quartering the waves all the way west to Chang'an.
entries.literal: Transport by water from the Xiao and Xiang and Dongting—in a few days over ten thousand li—the waves rolling like mat patterns on deck, pointing west to Chang'an.

entries.zh: 三秦之人，待此而飽；
entries.en: The people of the Three Qin regions would at last eat their fill;
entries.literal: The people of the Three Qins will rely on this to be fed;

entries.zh: 六軍之眾，待此而強。
entries.en: the imperial armies would grow strong on it.
entries.literal: the masses of the Six Armies will rely on this to be strengthened.

entries.zh: 天子無側席之憂，都人見泛舟之役；
entries.en: The emperor would no longer fret from hunger, and the capital would see grain boats plying the canals again;
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven will have no worry of sitting sideways on his mat; the capital populace will see boats passing to and fro;

entries.zh: 四方旅拒者可以破膽，三河流離者於茲請命。
entries.en: rebels in the provinces would lose heart, and refugees along the Yellow, Huai, and other rivers could beg for relief.
entries.literal: those who resist from the four quarters can have their courage broken; those displaced along the Three Rivers can here plead for their lives.

entries.zh: 相公匡戴明主，為富人侯，此今之切務，不可失也。
entries.en: By supporting our enlightened sovereign you would become a great lord of wealth—this is the urgent task of the moment and must not be let slip.
entries.literal: The Chancellor aids and supports the enlightened sovereign and becomes a marquis among wealthy men—this is today's urgent task and must not be missed.

entries.zh: 使仆湔洗瑕穢，率罄愚懦，當憑經義，請護河堤，冥勤在官，不辭水死。
entries.en: Give me leave to clear my name and give all my poor wits to the cause. On principle I ask to defend the river works myself, to labor at my post in silence, and not to shirk death by drowning.
entries.literal: Enable this servant to wash away stains, lead with all my foolish timidity, rely on canonical principles, request to guard the river dikes, labor in office in obscurity, and not refuse death by water.

entries.zh: 然運之利病，各有四五焉。
entries.en: Yet transport has its own four or five advantages and as many drawbacks.
entries.literal: Yet the profit and harm of transport each have four or five aspects.

entries.zh: 晏自尹京入為計相，共五年矣。
entries.en: I have been metropolitan governor and then chief fiscal officer for five years altogether.
entries.literal: Yan, from governing the capital to becoming chief of finance, has served five years in all.

entries.zh: 京師三輔百姓，唯苦稅畝傷多，若使江、湖米來每年三二十萬，即頓減徭賦，歌舞皇澤，其利一也。
entries.en: The people around Chang'an groan under heavy land taxes; if two or three hundred thousand piculs of Jianghu grain arrived yearly, levies could drop at once and they would praise the throne's bounty—that is the first gain.
entries.literal: The people of the capital and the Three Adjuncts suffer only from excessive land tax; if two or three hundred thousand piculs of grain from the rivers and lakes came each year, corvée and levies would be sharply reduced and they would sing of the sovereign's grace—this is the first benefit.

entries.zh: 東都殘毀，百無一存。
entries.en: The Eastern Capital is in ruins; scarcely one building in a hundred still stands.
entries.literal: The Eastern Capital lies in ruins; not one part in a hundred remains.

entries.zh: 若米運流通，則饑人皆附，村落邑厘，從此滋多。
entries.en: If grain shipping revives, starving refugees will settle there and hamlets will spring up again.
entries.literal: If grain transport flows freely, the hungry will all gather, and villages and hamlets will multiply from this.

entries.zh: 受命之日引海陵之倉以食鞏、洛，是計之得者，其利二也。
entries.en: From the day I took office I have drawn Hailing's stores to feed Gong and Luoyang—a sound plan and the second gain.
entries.literal: From the day of my mandate I have drawn on the granaries of Hailing to feed Gong and Luo—this is a sound plan; that is the second benefit.

entries.zh: 諸將有在邊者，諸戎有侵敗王略者，或聞三江、五湖，貢輸紅粒，雲帆桂楫，輸納帝鄉，軍誌曰：「先聲後實，可以震耀夷夏。」
entries.en: Frontier generals and tribes that raid the borders, hearing that red grain from the Yangzi lakes is shipped on cloud-white sails and cassia-prowed boats to the capital, will recall the maxim that reputation should precede force—thus aweing both barbarian and Chinese.'
entries.literal: Generals stationed on the frontier and barbarians who encroach on the imperial domain—when they hear that from the Three Rivers and Five Lakes red grain is presented in tribute, with cloudlike sails and cassia oars shipping it to the imperial capital, military doctrine says: 'Sound precedes substance; this can awe barbarians and Chinese alike.'

entries.zh: 其利三也。
entries.en: That is the third gain.
entries.literal: That is the third benefit.

entries.zh: 自古帝王之盛，皆云書同文，車同軌，日月所照，莫不率俾。
entries.en: Since antiquity the height of imperial power has been described as one script, one track, and universal submission to the throne.
entries.literal: From antiquity the glory of emperors has been described as identical script and identical wheel-gauge, and all beneath the sun and moon submitting in obedience.

entries.zh: 今舟車既通，商賈往來，百貨雜集，航海梯山，聖神輝光，漸近貞觀、永徽之盛，其利四也。
entries.en: With waterways and roads open again, merchants travel freely, goods pile up, and trade spans sea and mountain—the court's glory would approach the prosperity of the Zhenguan and Yonghui eras; that is the fourth gain.
entries.literal: Now that boats and carts are connected, merchants come and go, goods of every kind gather, and trade crosses seas and mountains—the sage sovereign's radiance approaches the splendor of Zhenguan and Yonghui; that is the fourth benefit.

entries.zh: 所可疑者，函、陜雕殘，東周尤甚。
entries.en: What gives pause is the devastation of Hangu Pass and Shaan, worst of all in the old Eastern Zhou heartland.
entries.literal: What gives pause is that Hangu and Shaan are carved to ruin, and the Eastern Zhou region is worst of all.

entries.zh: 過宜陽、熊耳，至武牢、成臯，五百里中，編戶千余而已。
entries.en: From Yiyang and Xiong'er to Wulao and Chenggao, five hundred li hold barely a thousand registered households.
entries.literal: From Yiyang and Xiong'er to Wulao and Chenggao, within five hundred li there are only a little over a thousand registered households.

entries.zh: 居無尺椽，人無煙爨，蕭條淒慘，獸遊鬼哭。
entries.en: Not a rafter stands, no hearth smoke rises; the land is desolate, beasts roam, and it seems ghosts wail.
entries.literal: Homes lack a single rafter; people lack cooking smoke; desolation is bleak and beasts roam while ghosts seem to wail.

entries.zh: 牛必羸角，輿必說輹，棧車輓漕，亦不易求。
entries.en: Oxen are emaciated, cart wheels fall off, and even simple haulage carts are hard to find.
entries.literal: Oxen are sure to be scrawny-horned, carts sure to have wheels come loose; even plank carts for haulage are not easily found.

entries.zh: 今於無人之境，興此勞人之運，固難就矣，其病一也。
entries.en: To launch this laborious transport through uninhabited country is bound to fail—that is the first drawback.
entries.literal: To launch this labor-consuming transport in a land without people is inherently hard to accomplish—that is the first drawback.

entries.zh: 河、汴有初，不修則毀澱，故每年正月發近縣丁男，塞長茭，決沮淤，清明桃花已後，遠水自然安流，陽侯、宓妃，不復太息。
entries.en: The Yellow River and Bian Canal must be dredged yearly or they silt shut; each New Year laborers from nearby counties clear reeds and sediment, and after Qingming the distant reaches run clear again without the river gods' lament.
entries.literal: The Yellow River and Bian Canal had their beginnings; if not maintained they silt up, so every first month conscript labor from nearby counties blocks long reeds and clears sediment; after Qingming and the peach blossoms, distant waters flow smoothly of themselves, and the River Lord and Lady Mi need sigh no more.

entries.zh: 頃因寇難，總不掏拓，澤滅水，岸石崩，役夫需於沙，津吏旋於濘，千里洄上，罔水舟行，其病二也。
entries.en: Since the rebellions dredging has stopped entirely; marshes have swallowed the channel, banks have collapsed, laborers wait on sandbars, clerks flounder in mud, and for a thousand li upstream boats cannot sail—that is the second drawback.
entries.literal: Recently because of rebellion dredging has altogether ceased; marshes have swallowed the water, bank stones have collapsed, laborers wait on sandbars, ferry clerks turn in the mud, and for a thousand li upstream there is no water for boats—that is the second drawback.

entries.zh: 東垣、底柱，澠池、二陵，北河運處五六百里，戍卒久絕，縣吏空拳。
entries.en: From Dongyuan and Dizhu to Mianchi and the Two Mounds, five or six hundred li of the northern transport route have no garrisons left and county officials are powerless.
entries.literal: From Dongyuan and Dizhu to Mianchi and the Two Mounds, five or six hundred li along the northern river transport route—garrison troops have long been cut off and county clerks are empty-handed.

entries.zh: 奪攘奸宄，窟穴囊橐。
entries.en: Bandits and outlaws raid and hide in caves with their plunder.
entries.literal: Robbers and villains plunder and nest in caves with their loot.

entries.zh: 夾河為藪，豺狼狺狺，舟行所經，寇亦能往，其病三也。
entries.en: Marshes line the river, wolves howl, and wherever boats can go bandits can follow—that is the third drawback.
entries.literal: Along the river are marshes; wolves and jackals snarl; wherever boats pass, bandits can also go—that is the third drawback.

entries.zh: 東自淮陰，西臨蒲阪，亙三千里，屯戍相望。
entries.en: From Huaiyin in the east to Pufan in the west, three thousand li of garrisons stand face to face.
entries.literal: From Huaiyin in the east to Pufan in the west, spanning three thousand li, garrisons face one another.

entries.zh: 中軍皆鼎司元侯，賤卒儀同青紫，每雲食半菽，又雲無挾纊，輓漕所至，船到便留，即非單車使折簡書所能制矣，其病四也。
entries.en: Central Army posts are held by chief ministers and great lords; common soldiers dress like officers; they claim to eat half rations and lack winter coats; wherever grain convoys arrive the boats are seized on the spot—not something a lone commissioner with a letter can restrain—that is the fourth drawback.
entries.literal: Central Army posts are held by chief ministers and great marquises; lowly soldiers dress like the purple-clad elite; they always say they eat half beans and have no padded coats; wherever transport grain arrives, boats are detained on arrival—this is not something a lone envoy with a letter can control; that is the fourth drawback.

entries.zh: 惟小子畢其慮奔走之，惟中書詳其利病裁成之。
entries.en: I alone will give all my thought and effort to the task; only the Secretariat can weigh the pros and cons and bring the plan to completion.
entries.literal: Only this humble servant will exhaust his thought and run about it; only the Secretariat will weigh profit and harm and complete the plan.

entries.zh: 晏累年已來，事缺名毀，聖慈含育，特賜生全。
entries.en: For years my duties were curtailed and my name slandered; the emperor's mercy spared my life.
entries.literal: Yan for many years has had his duties cut short and his name slandered; the sage's compassion nurtured him and specially granted him life.

entries.zh: 月余家居，遽即臨遣，恩榮感切，思殞百身。
entries.en: After barely a month at home I was suddenly dispatched on imperial business; overwhelmed by grace, I would gladly die a hundred deaths in return.
entries.literal: After a month at home he was suddenly sent on imperial mission; moved by grace and honor, he wished to die a hundred deaths in return.

entries.zh: 見一水不通，願荷鍤而先往；
entries.en: Wherever a channel was blocked I wished to take a spade and go first;
entries.literal: seeing one waterway blocked, he wished to shoulder a spade and go first;

entries.zh: 見一粒不運，願負米而先趨。
entries.en: wherever a grain was not moved I wished to carry rice and hurry ahead.
entries.literal: seeing one grain not transported, he wished to carry rice and hurry ahead.

entries.zh: 焦心苦形，期報明主，丹誠未克，漕引多虞，屏營中流，掩泣獻狀。
entries.en: I wore myself out in body and mind to repay my sovereign; my loyal effort had not yet succeeded and transport still faced many perils; pacing midstream in anxiety, I wept as I submitted this memorial.
entries.literal: He tormented heart and body, hoping to repay the enlightened sovereign; his red sincerity had not yet succeeded, and grain transport had many worries; pacing anxiously midstream, he wept as he presented his memorial.

entries.zh: 自此每歲運米數十萬石以濟關中。
entries.en: From then on several hundred thousand piculs of grain were shipped yearly to supply Guanzhong.
entries.literal: From this time each year several hundred thousand piculs of grain were transported to relieve Guanzhong.

entries.zh: 德宗嗣位，言事者稱轉運可罷多矣。
entries.en: When Emperor Dezong succeeded, many memorialists urged abolishing the transport commission.
entries.literal: When Dezong succeeded to the throne, memorialists often said grain transport could be abolished.

entries.zh: 初，楊炎為吏部侍郎，晏為尚書，各恃權使氣，兩不相得。
entries.en: Earlier Yang Yan was vice minister of personnel while Yan was minister; each abused his power and the two could not abide each other.
entries.literal: At first Yang Yan was Vice Minister of Personnel and Yan was Minister; each relied on power and threw his weight about; the two did not get along.

entries.zh: 炎坐元載貶，晏快之，昌言於朝。
entries.en: When Yang was demoted over Yuan Zai's case, Yan rejoiced and spoke openly at court.
entries.literal: When Yang was demoted because of Yuan Zai, Yan rejoiced and spoke openly at court.

entries.zh: 及炎入相，追怒前事，且以晏與元載隙憾，時人言載之得罪，晏有力焉。
entries.en: When Yang became chancellor he pursued old grievances, and because Yan had feuded with Yuan Zai, contemporaries said Yan had helped bring Zai down.
entries.literal: When Yang entered the chancellorship he pursued old grievances, and because Yan had enmity with Yuan Zai, people of the time said Yan had had a hand in Zai's downfall.

entries.zh: 炎將為載復仇，又時人風言代宗寵獨孤妃而又愛其子韓王迥，晏密啟請立獨孤為皇后。
entries.en: Yang meant to avenge Zai, and rumor held that Daizong favored Consort Dugu and loved her son Jiong, Prince of Han; Yan had secretly urged making Dugu empress.
entries.literal: Yang was about to avenge Zai, and moreover rumor said Emperor Daizong favored Consort Dugu and also loved her son, Prince Han Huai; Yan had secretly memorialized asking that Dugu be made empress.

entries.zh: 炎因對敭流涕奏言：「賴祖宗福祐，先皇與陛下不為賊臣所間。
entries.en: Yang seized an audience to declare tearfully: "Thanks to our ancestors' blessing, the late emperor and Your Majesty were not estranged by treacherous ministers.
entries.literal: Yang, taking advantage of an audience, tearfully memorialized: "Thanks to the ancestors' blessing, the late emperor and Your Majesty were not estranged by treacherous ministers.

entries.zh: 不然，劉晏、黎幹之輩，搖動社稷，兇謀果矣。
entries.en: Otherwise men like Liu Yan and Li Gan would have shaken the throne and their wicked plot would have succeeded.
entries.literal: Otherwise men like Liu Yan and Li Gan would have shaken the altars of state and their wicked plot would have succeeded.

entries.zh: 今幹以伏罪，晏猶領權，臣為宰相，不能正持此事，罪當萬死。」
entries.en: Now Gan has been punished, yet Yan still holds power; as chancellor I cannot rectify this—I deserve death ten thousand times."
entries.literal: Now Gan has confessed his crime, yet Yan still holds power; I as chancellor cannot rectify this matter—I deserve death ten thousand times."

entries.zh: 崔祐甫奏言：「此事曖昧，陛下以廓然大赦，不當究尋虛語。」
entries.en: Cui Youfu replied: "This matter is vague; Your Majesty has proclaimed a broad amnesty and should not pursue idle rumor."
entries.literal: Cui Youfu memorialized: "This matter is vague; Your Majesty has proclaimed a broad amnesty and should not pursue empty talk."

entries.zh: 硃泚、崔寧又從傍與祐甫救解之，寧言頗切，炎大怒，故斥寧令出鎮鄜坊以摧挫之。
entries.en: Zhu Ci and Cui Ning also sided with Youfu; Ning spoke sharply; Yang was furious and banished Ning to command the Fu-Fang region to break his spirit.
entries.literal: Zhu Ci and Cui Ning also joined Youfu from the side in mediation; Ning's words were rather sharp; Yang was greatly angered and therefore expelled Ning to command Fu and Fang circuits to break his spirit.

entries.zh: 遂罷晏轉運等使，尋貶為忠州刺史。
entries.en: Liu Yan was stripped of his transport commissioner posts and, before long, demoted to prefect of Zhongzhou.
entries.literal: Thereupon Yan's posts as transport commissioner and the like were abolished; soon after he was demoted to prefect of Zhongzhou.

entries.zh: 炎欲誣構其罪，知庾準與晏素有隙，舉為荊南節度，以伺晏動靜。
entries.en: Yang Yan wanted to frame him on false charges, so he appointed Yu Zhun—who had long been at odds with Liu Yan—as military commissioner of Jingnan to watch Yan's every move.
entries.literal: Yang Yan wished to fabricate crimes against him; knowing Yu Zhun and Liu Yan had long borne a grudge, he recommended Yu as military commissioner of Jingnan to spy on Liu Yan's movements.

entries.zh: 準乃奏晏與硃泚書祈救解，言多怨望，炎又證成其事，上以為然。
entries.en: Yu Zhun reported that Yan had written to the rebel Zhu Ci pleading for rescue, his language seething with grievance; Yang Yan bolstered the accusation, and the emperor believed it.
entries.literal: Yu Zhun then memorialized that Yan had written to Zhu Ci begging rescue and release, his words full of resentment; Yang Yan further corroborated the matter, and the emperor considered it so.

entries.zh: 是月庚午，晏已受誅，使回奏報，誣晏以忠州謀叛，下詔暴言其罪，時年六十六，天下冤之。
entries.en: On the gengwu day of that month Yan had already been put to death. When the envoy returned, he falsely claimed Yan had plotted rebellion from his exile in Zhongzhou; the court issued an edict publicly listing his alleged crimes. Yan was sixty-six years old, and people everywhere regarded his execution as a gross injustice.
entries.literal: That month on the gengwu day, Yan had already been executed; the envoy returned to report, slandering Yan as plotting rebellion at Zhongzhou; an edict was issued proclaiming his crimes. He was then sixty-six; all under heaven deemed it an injustice.

entries.zh: 家屬徙嶺表，連累者數十人。
entries.en: His family was banished to the far south beyond the mountain passes, and dozens of others were dragged down with them.
entries.literal: His household was relocated beyond the Ling passes; several tens were implicated.

entries.zh: 貞元五年，上悟，方錄晏子執經，授太常博士；
entries.en: In 789, once the emperor realized his error, he took Yan's son Zhijing into service and appointed him erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices;
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Zhenyuan, when the emperor came to understand, he only then recorded Yan's son Zhijing and appointed him erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices;

entries.zh: 少子宗經，秘書郎。
entries.en: His youngest son, Zongjing, was appointed secretary in the Palace Library.
entries.literal: His younger son Zongjing became a secretary in the Palace Library.

entries.zh: 執經上請削官贈父，特追贈鄭州刺史。
entries.en: Zhijing petitioned to surrender his own office so his father might be honored posthumously; the throne made a special grant and posthumously enfeoffed Liu Yan as prefect of Zhengzhou.
entries.literal: Zhijing memorialized asking to relinquish his rank to posthumously honor his father; a special posthumous appointment as prefect of Zhengzhou was granted.

entries.zh: 又至德初，為國用不足，令第五琦於諸道榷鹽以助軍用，及晏代其任，法益精密，官無遺利。
entries.en: Early in the Zhide era, with state funds short, Di Wuqi was ordered to monopolize salt in the circuits for military expenses; when Yan took over, the system grew more precise and the treasury left no revenue uncollected.
entries.literal: Moreover, at the beginning of Zhide, because state revenue was insufficient, Di Wuqi was ordered to monopolize salt in the various circuits to aid military expenses; when Yan succeeded to his post, the law grew more precise and the government left no profit uncollected.

entries.zh: 初，歲入錢六十萬貫，季年所入逾十倍，而人無厭苦。
entries.en: At first annual revenue was six hundred thousand strings of cash; in later years it exceeded ten times that, yet the people bore no bitterness.
entries.literal: At first annual intake was six hundred thousand strings of cash; in later years intake exceeded ten times that, yet the people felt no resentment.

entries.zh: 大歷末，通計一歲征賦所入總一千二百萬貫，而鹽利且過半。
entries.en: By the end of the Dali era, total annual tax revenue reached twelve million strings of cash, with salt profits alone exceeding half.
entries.literal: By the end of Dali, total annual tax and levy intake amounted to twelve million strings of cash, and salt profits alone exceeded half.

entries.zh: 累遷吏部尚書。
entries.en: He rose step by step to minister of civil appointments.
entries.literal: He was repeatedly promoted to Minister of Personnel.

entries.zh: 大歷四年六月，與右僕射裴遵慶同赴本曹視事，敕尚食增置儲供，許內侍魚朝恩及宰臣已下常朝官鹹詣省送上。
entries.en: In the sixth month of Dali 4 (AD 769) he and Right Vice Director Pei Zunqing took up office at the Ministry of Personnel; the emperor ordered extra provisions from the imperial kitchen and allowed Eunuch Yu Chaoen and all regular court officials down to the chancellors to visit the ministry with congratulations.
entries.literal: In the sixth month of the fourth year of Dali, together with Right Vice Director Pei Zunqing he went to his ministry to assume duties; an edict ordered the Imperial Kitchen to increase provisions, and allowed Eunuch Yu Chaoen and all regular court officials down to the chancellors to come to the ministry to present congratulations.

entries.zh: 八年，知三銓選事。
entries.en: In 773 he took charge of appointments in all three selection boards.
entries.literal: In the eighth year he took charge of selection affairs in all three boards.

entries.zh: 十二年三月，誅宰臣元載，晏奉詔訊鞫。
entries.en: In the third month of Dali 12 (AD 777) Chancellor Yuan Zai was executed; Yan was ordered to conduct the interrogation.
entries.literal: In the third month of the twelfth year the chancellor Yuan Zai was executed; Yan received an edict to interrogate and try the case.

entries.zh: 晏以載居任樹黨，布於天下，不敢專斷，請他官共事。
entries.en: Because Zai had built a faction network across the empire during his tenure, Yan did not dare decide alone and asked other officials to join the investigation.
entries.literal: Yan, because Zai during his tenure had built factions spread throughout the realm, did not dare decide alone and requested other officials to join the case.

entries.zh: 敕御史大夫李涵、右散騎常侍蕭昕、兵部侍郎袁傪、禮部侍郎常袞、諫議大夫杜亞同推，載皆款伏。
entries.en: The emperor ordered Chief Censor Li Han, Regular Attendant Xiao Xin, Vice Minister of War Yuan Kan, Vice Minister of Rites Chang Gun, and Remonstrance Officer Du Ya to join the inquiry; Zai confessed to all charges.
entries.literal: An edict ordered Censor-in-Chief Li Han, Right Regular Attendant Xiao Xin, Vice Minister of War Yuan Kan, Vice Minister of Rites Chang Gun, and Remonstrance Officer Du Ya to join the inquiry; Zai confessed to all charges.

entries.zh: 初，晏承旨，門下侍郎、同平章事王縉亦處極法，晏謂涵等曰：重刑再覆，國之常典，況誅大臣，得不覆奏？
entries.en: When Yan first received the order, Vice Director Wang Jin was also slated for execution; Yan told Han and the others: 'Heavy sentences require double review—that is state law; in executing a great minister, must we not report back for confirmation?'
entries.literal: At first, when Yan received the imperial directive, Vice Director of the Secretariat and Concurrent Grand Councilor Wang Jin was also to receive the extreme penalty; Yan said to Han and the others: 'Heavy punishments require double review—this is the state's constant rule; moreover, in executing a great minister, must we not report back for confirmation?'

entries.zh: 又法有首從，二人同刑，亦宜重取進止。」
entries.en: 'The law also distinguishes principal and accomplice; when two men face the same sentence, we should seek the throne's decision again.'
entries.literal: 'Moreover the law distinguishes principal and accomplice; when two men share the same sentence, we should also seek renewed imperial decision.'

entries.zh: 涵等從命。
entries.en: Han and the others agreed.
entries.literal: Han and the others obeyed.

entries.zh: 及晏等覆奏，代宗乃減縉罪從輕。
entries.en: When Yan and the others reported back, Emperor Daizong lightened Jin's sentence.
entries.literal: When Yan and the others reported back, Emperor Daizong reduced Jin's crime to a lighter punishment.

entries.zh: 縉之生，晏平反之力也。
entries.en: Jin owed his life to Yan's intervention.
entries.literal: That Jin lived was due to Yan's effort to reverse the verdict.

entries.zh: 十三年十二月，為尚書左僕射。
entries.en: In the twelfth month of Dali 13 (AD 778) he was appointed Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
entries.literal: In the twelfth month of the thirteenth year he was made Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.

entries.zh: 時宰臣常袞專政，以晏久掌銓衡，時議平允，兼司儲蓄，職舉功深，慮公望日崇，上心有屬。
entries.en: Chancellor Chang Gun then dominated the court. Yan had long controlled appointments with a reputation for fairness and also managed state granaries with deep achievement; Gun feared Yan's rising prestige and that the emperor might favor him for higher office.
entries.literal: At that time Chancellor Chang Gun monopolized government; because Yan had long controlled personnel selection, public opinion deemed him fair, and he also managed storage—his duties were fulfilled and his achievements deep; Gun feared Yan's public standing rising daily and that the sovereign's heart might turn to him.

entries.zh: 竊忌之，乃奏晏朝廷舊德，宜為百吏師長，外示崇重，內實去其權。
entries.en: Secretly jealous, he memorialized that Yan, a veteran of the court, should be mentor to all officials—honoring him in name while stripping his real authority.
entries.literal: Secretly jealous, he memorialized that Yan was an old merit of the court and should be moral teacher to all officials—outwardly showing honor while inwardly stripping his power.

entries.zh: 及奏上，以晏使務方理，代其任者難其人，使務、知三銓並如故。
entries.en: When the memorial was submitted, because Yan's fiscal duties were still in order and no replacement could be found, his transport commission and control of the three selection boards remained unchanged.
entries.literal: When the memorial was submitted, because Yan's commission affairs were still being managed and no replacement could be found, his commission duties and charge of the three selection boards remained as before.

entries.zh: 李靈曜之亂也，河南節帥所據，多不奉法令，征賦亦隨之；
entries.en: During Li Lingyao's rebellion the Henan military governors mostly ignored imperial law, and tax collection suffered likewise;
